title: Know Before Yes
pitch: Turn a website-and-app offer into a decision-ready draft—and export only the exact revision a human approves.
about_excerpt: Turn a website-and-app offer into a decision-ready draft—and export only the exact revision a human approves. Like Comment Story Updates Problem A nontechnical small-business owner can receive a polished website-and-app offer that names a price, timeline, and attractive outcomes while leaving ownership, data boundaries, the app's unique job, success measures, and long-term support unresolved. Those omissions are difficult to find and compare before the buyer commits to the wrong build. Solution Know Before Yes is a static WebMCP decision-planning tool from Sykes Holding Group LLC. Its default judge path uses a bundled fictional vendor offer. A secondary, human-activated lane accepts only closed, general, nonidentifying scenario categories. An agent can discover seven focused tools, inspect the scenario, identify source-bound missing decisions, compare three practical paths, and stage a decision-ready draft. Premature commit and export calls return structured rejections without changing approved state. Only the visible human control can approve the exact staged revision. The agent can then read that approval status, commit the matching revision in the current session, and export the same revision as a local Markdown or JSON draft. Agent analyzes. Human decides. The web tool exports what was approved. Why This Matters Small-business buyers often need structured technical judgment before they need a larger project-management system. Know Before Yes makes the missing decisions, tradeoffs, and authority boundary visible without asking the user to upload a proposal, create an account, or hand control to an agent. WebMCP is central to the experience. The agent discovers typed capabilities and works through shared structured state instead of scraping cards, imitating clicks, or inventing facts. People and agents can now collaborate on a concrete draft while the page itself preserves the visible human decision boundary. The current V1 demonstrates this workflow; it does not claim real-customer validation, vendor selection, purchasing authority, professional advice, guaranteed savings, guaranteed growth, or an external-system write. How We Used AI The released web tool runs no model and requires no API key. A WebMCP-capable browser or agent supplies reasoning outside the page and invokes explicit contracts. The page returns deterministic structured results and enforces staged-versus-approved state in its own local state machine. During development, native WebMCP testing used OpenAI Codex's in-app browser and Google Chrome 151 with WebMCP enabled. The final permanent-host proof used OpenAI Codex's in-app browser. Two fresh native flows invoked all seven tools, returned both preapproval denials, recorded visible UI-only approval, read back human_approved and canCommit=true, and committed/exported exact revision rev-001-staged_platform. Clean run A completed in 42.564 seconds; judge-paced run B completed in 81.401 seconds. The final run produced a 2,153-character export and no browser-console error or warning. The clearly labeled Preview Adapter was used only for deterministic fallback rehearsal and is not presented as native proof. How We Used Codex OpenAI Codex and ChatGPT Work helped convert the initial product idea into a bounded scope, product requirements, technical specification, implementation checklist, static application, automated tests, browser-validation plan, public-release contract, and this Devpost draft. Codex helped implement and challenge the seven-tool design, the exact-revision approval state machine, source-bound missing-decision results, structured preapproval errors, local export, lifecycle reset behavior, closed-enum scenario mode, privacy/claims boundaries, public release manifest, and automated product and viability gates. Independent technical, privacy/policy, and product-story reviews caught and corrected stale-session restoration, overstated build-ready wording, and nonfunctional structured inputs before the public candidate was frozen. Approved AI-tool disclosure: OpenAI Codex and ChatGPT Work for product planning, implementation, debugging, testing, browser validation, evidence reconciliation, release preparation, and submission drafting. Key Features Structured offer inspection — returns scope, cost signals, exclusions, and clarity risks without changing decision state. Source-bound missing decisions — ties every question to a specific omission or general-category input instead of inventing evidence. Three practical paths — compares website-first, staged website-to-app, and combined-launch paths by fit, speed, cost shape, risk, and assumptions without claiming a universal best answer. Reversible staging — creates a deterministic revision id, leaves approved state unchanged, and invalidates stale approval. Visible human gate — no agent-facing approval tool exists; only the visible UI can record human-ui approval for the exact staged revision. Two explicit denials — premature commit returns HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED; premature export returns APPROVED_BLUEPRINT_REQUIRED. Exact-revision proof — approval status, committed state, UI, and Markdown/JSON export carry the same revision id. Two privacy-bounded modes — a resettable bundled fictional offer and an optional human-activated closed-enum general-category scenario. Static and state-free by design — no backend, accounts, persistence, analytics, uploads, payment, runtime dependency, or application network call. WebMCP Tool Inventory inspect_vendor_offer find_missing_decisions compare_solution_paths stage_blueprint_revision get_approval_status commit_approved_blueprint export_build_blueprint The page defines exactly these seven tool contracts and conditionally registers them when document.modelContext is available. Structured scenario activation and human approval remain visible human UI actions, not eighth and ninth tools. Architecture Dependency-free static HTML, CSS, and browser JavaScript modules Pure in-memory decision domain in src/domain.js Seven WebMCP contracts and conditional registration in src/tools.js Shared UI/tool rendering, lifecycle reset, and user-initiated local download in src/app.js Static hosting headers for CSP, tools permission, origin isolation, MIME sniffing, referrer handling, framing/form restrictions, and HTTPS transport Node's built-in test runner plus focused P0 and viability gates No backend, database, login, analytics, telemetry, payment, OCR, upload, external model call, or persistence The WebMCP client may process selected categories and tool results under its own terms and privacy settings. Static hosting may process ordinary connection and security metadata, but SHG does not operate a scenario-content endpoint. Testing Instructions Public judge flow — permanent host and final native proof verified No credentials are required. Open https://knowbeforeyes.sykesholdinggroup.com/ in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Google Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Select Reset and confirm the page shows the bundled fictional scenario. Discover these seven tools: inspect_vendor_offer, find_missing_decisions, compare_solution_paths, stage_blueprint_revision, get_approval_status, commit_approved_blueprint, and export_build_blueprint. Invoke the first three tools and confirm one source-bound gap and the three named path tradeoffs. Invoke stage_blueprint_revision for staged_platform; confirm approved state remains unchanged. Invoke commit_approved_blueprint; confirm HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED and approvedStateChanged=false. Invoke export_build_blueprint; confirm APPROVED_BLUEPRINT_REQUIRED. Use the visible Approve exact revision control. Invoke get_approval_status; confirm the staged revision id, source human-ui, status human_approved, and canCommit=true. Invoke commit_approved_blueprint, then export_build_blueprint; confirm staged, approved, committed, and exported revision ids match. Confirm the before/after summary, unresolved decisions, and local download boundary; then Reset again to prove repeatability. This text is ready to paste into Devpost field 28255; the stable hostname and final signed-out run are verified. Update it only if the final evidence changes. Repository verification From the public repository root: npm test npm run p0:product npm run gate npm run serve Open http://localhost:4173 . Native discovery requires a supporting WebMCP client; otherwise the page truthfully identifies the Preview Adapter. Judging-Criteria Map WebMCP Leverage Seven typed, non-overlapping contracts divide inspection, gap discovery, comparison, staging, status, gated commit, and export. The same structured state powers tool results, UI, rejection semantics, approval, and exact export. WebMCP is the operating collaboration layer, not a decorative prompt wrapper. Execution The product has a coherent resettable workflow, responsive UI, explicit errors, visible human decision control, local exports, a bounded second scenario mode, public source, and repeatable automated gat

title: API Canvas
pitch: API Canvas is a local-first WebMCP workspace where people and agents can discover public data, connect APIs,create reusable cards and visualizations,and reason across the resulting dashboard together.
about_excerpt: API Canvas is a local-first WebMCP workspace where people and agents can discover public data, connect APIs,create reusable cards and visualizations,and reason across the resulting dashboard together. Like Comment Story Updates Api Canvas build a dashboard Canvas View Inspiration Building a useful dashboard usually involves a surprising amount of repetitive work. You have to find an API, understand its documentation, construct the request, inspect the response, identify useful fields, create a visualization, connect those fields to a component, and repeat the process for every additional source. I wanted to see whether WebMCP could make that process dramatically more direct. Instead of only asking: "Can an agent operate this application?" API Canvas asks: "Can an agent help construct the application experience using primitives the website intentionally exposes?" What I Built API Canvas is a local-first workspace for turning public data into reusable connected cards. A dashboard can contain components such as: Tables Charts Maps Metrics Lists Notes Text and explanation blocks Search results Media Raw datasets API responses Question blocks Agent-generated answer blocks Sources and presentation are kept separate. That means one API response can power several different visualizations without repeatedly requesting the data. Users can also transform and combine information through declarative mappings including filtering, sorting, grouping, arithmetic, field selection, and joins. WebMCP Tools API Canvas exposes a large WebMCP tool surface covering dashboard and data workflows. An agent can perform operations such as: Create or switch dashboards Add data sources Request public API data Add cards Select appropriate visualizations Connect source fields to cards Transform data Update layout Resize or reorder cards Inspect dashboard state Read selected cards Answer questions using dashboard context Create new explanation blocks Export or present results This lets a simple request expand into a multi-step application workflow. For example: Build me an earthquake research dashboard. Find magnitude 5 or greater earthquakes from the past week, map the events, create a table, identify the strongest earthquake, and summarize it. API Canvas can break that request into structured operations and leave behind a real editable dashboard. Why WebMCP Dashboard construction is naturally compositional. The user usually knows the outcome they want but should not need to manually specify every intermediate API call and UI operation. WebMCP lets the application expose those intermediate operations directly. The agent gets structured tools instead of having to simulate: click Add Card → select source → open another menu → map a field → choose visualization → repeat. This makes workflows faster and substantially easier for an agent to reason about. Human + Agent Collaboration The most interesting part of API Canvas is that the resulting dashboard becomes shared context. Imagine the agent has created an earthquake dashboard containing a map, table, and several metrics. The user can then ask: Using all of the information currently on this page, which earthquake was strongest? The agent can inspect the existing structured cards, reason across them, produce an answer, and create another normal dashboard card containing that explanation. The workflow becomes: Data → Visualization → Context → Reasoning → New Visualization Everything remains editable by the human. How I Built It API Canvas is built with Vue 3, Vite, Pinia, IndexedDB, ECharts, AJV, and WebMCP. The workspace has a reusable block system that separates: data sources raw responses normalized values transformations bindings presentation The normal UI and WebMCP tools call into the same underlying workspace actions. AJV validates structured WebMCP inputs. IndexedDB stores larger browser-local response caches and workspace information. Public data adapters support structured formats including JSON, CSV, XML, feeds, permitted HTML tables, and embedded JSON. The application intentionally does not provide an unrestricted proxy or execute arbitrary supplied scripts. The /webmcp documentation page is generated from the same canonical WebMCP contracts used by the application. Challenges I Faced The largest challenge was building something generic without making it unpredictable. An unrestricted "call any API and run any code" tool would be powerful but would also make the application difficult to reason about. Instead, API Canvas uses bounded requests, validated schemas, explicit source handling, and declarative transformations. Another challenge was keeping data, provenance, presentation, and transformations sufficiently independent. That separation is what allows an agent to replace a chart with a table without losing the underlying source. What I Learned API Canvas changed how I think about agent interfaces. The visual dashboard does not need to be replaced by chat. Instead, the dashboard can become the persistent shared artifact that the human and agent construct together. WebMCP then acts as the structured editing and orchestration layer. What's Next I would like to expand API Canvas with more public data adapters, richer visualization components, reusable dashboard templates, local analytical queries, and collaborative sharing. The broader idea is an open, composable workspace where agents can assemble useful specialized interfaces on demand. title: ShipCheap
pitch: Project-aware backend hosting decisions without billing jumpscares—powered by WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Project-aware backend hosting decisions without billing jumpscares—powered by WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Choosing a backend host looks simple until a developer has to reconcile runtime support, database needs, region availability, credit-card requirements, sleeping services, free-tier limits, and surprise usage bills. Most comparison pages make people translate one real project into dozens of filters and pricing tables. ShipCheap began as a human-first backend hosting decision board. For the WebMCP Challenge, I turned it into a shared workspace where a person can describe or link a real project, let an agent do the repetitive analysis, and still review every important result in the same visible interface. What it does ShipCheap helps developers: rank backend hosts from runtime, budget, database, uptime, card access, region, and risk tolerance; compare providers in a visible decision table; simulate 1,000 deterministic monthly billing scenarios; inspect percentiles, budget-overrun probability, and likely cost spikes; review provider-specific launch checks; sign in and link a public GitHub repository by URL; approve a read-only GitHub App for private repositories; detect a repository's stack and save project-specific hosting recommendations. Why WebMCP Hosting selection is structured but multi-step. Without WebMCP, an agent must guess which controls to click, scrape result cards, and reconstruct application state. ShipCheap exposes eight purpose-built tools instead: open_project_workspace list_linked_projects list_available_github_repositories start_github_app_installation analyze_github_repository recommend_backend_hosts open_backend_host_comparison preview_billing_risk The agent can turn plain-language constraints into ranked recommendations, open the exact comparison or simulator, and—after the user chooses a repository—build a project-aware analysis. The person and agent share the same visible state throughout. Human control and data protection The agent advises and configures; it cannot silently create an account, approve GitHub access, attach billing, spend money, or deploy infrastructure. Private repository access uses a read-only GitHub App. Project reads and writes are authorized server-side against the signed-in Clerk user ID, and the database enforces repository and installation constraints. How I built it ShipCheap is a Next.js 16 App Router application written in TypeScript and React, styled with Tailwind CSS, and deployed on Vercel. Prisma stores data in PostgreSQL on Neon. Clerk provides authentication, and a GitHub App provides read-only repository access. The WebMCP layer lives in src/components/WebMCPTools.tsx and registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool uses a strict JSON Schema, validates inputs during execution, cleans up registrations with an AbortController , and returns concise structured results. The integration is progressive enhancement: the site and public decision workflow still work when WebMCP or authentication is unavailable. What I changed during the challenge ShipCheap existed before the challenge. During the submission period I added the eight-tool WebMCP layer, expanded the provider catalog and comparison surfaces, connected the tools to the existing recommendation and billing-risk logic, added Clerk authentication, created the project workspace, integrated the read-only GitHub App, added repository stack detection and project-specific recommendations, migrated persistence to Neon PostgreSQL, documented the public testing flow, and verified all eight tools on the deployed app in ChatGPT's in-app browser. Challenges The hardest design problem was deciding where agent authority should stop. A hosting assistant that can silently install integrations, deploy, or spend money would be risky, so ShipCheap keeps approval and consequential actions with the person. The second challenge was maintaining one source of truth. WebMCP tools reuse the same provider data, recommendation functions, repository analyzer, and billing simulator as the visible UI instead of maintaining a separate agent-only model. Accomplishments A working deployed product rather than a WebMCP-only proof of concept. Eight non-trivial tools spanning public decisions and authenticated project analysis. Visible shared state between human navigation and agent actions. Repository-aware recommendations for public and approved private GitHub projects. Strict validation, server-side ownership checks, and explicit safety boundaries. A public MIT-licensed repository with reproducible setup instructions. What I learned Useful agent-native design is less about exposing many actions and more about exposing the right decision boundaries. Structured tools compress repetitive analysis, while visible state and explicit approval keep consequential choices understandable and human-controlled. What's next Next steps include live pricing-source verification, richer project reports, additional providers, and deeper authenticated end-to-end testing. These are future directions, not claims about the current submission. title: Hear My Site
pitch: Give AI agents ears for the browser. Hear My Site exposes live page and meeting audio as WebMCP tools, so your local agent can understand what you hear and work with you in real time.
about_excerpt: Give AI agents ears for the browser. Hear My Site exposes live page and meeting audio as WebMCP tools, so your local agent can understand what you hear and work with you in real time. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI integrations treat the browser as a remote control: click this button, fill that form, or navigate to that page. We wanted to explore a more WebMCP-native question: What important context exists inside the browser that an agent cannot access just as effectively from a terminal or traditional MCP server? Live audio is one answer. Traditional browser automation surfaces such as the Chrome DevTools Protocol are excellent at exposing the DOM, network activity, screenshots, and input events, but live collaborative audio is not naturally represented as page state or a sequence of browser actions. Hear My Site turns that missing real-time modality into incremental semantic context that agents such as Codex can consume while the event is happening. While watching a tutorial, webinar, or online meeting, the human continuously receives information through the browser, but their agent hears nothing. Sharing that context usually requires recording the session, uploading audio, waiting for a transcript, or repeatedly copying captions into a chat. We wanted the browser to expose this transient, browser-native context directly, allowing the human and agent to attend to the same live event at the same time. The project began as Hear My Browser , an extension that works on websites we do not control. We then expanded the idea into Hear My Site : a headless package that lets websites provide the same capability natively, without requiring every visitor to install an extension. The result is not simply “MCP inside a browser.” The browser is part of the problem because it owns the live media streams, user permissions, page lifecycle, and shared experience that the agent needs to understand. What it does Hear My Site gives AI agents ears for browser applications. A website supplies its existing audio streams—such as local microphone audio and remote WebRTC tracks—and Hear My Site mixes and transcribes them using the provider configured for that experience. It currently ships with adapters for Gemini 3.5 Transcribe Live and OpenAI GPT-Live-Transcribe while keeping the agent-facing interface independent of either provider. Across both integrations, Hear My Site exposes exactly three WebMCP roles: start listening, retrieve incremental context, and stop listening. Hear My Browser uses the default names: start_browser_transcription get_browser_transcript stop_browser_transcription Adopting sites can rename all three roles to match their product. Our meeting demo exposes them as join_meeting , follow_meeting , and leave_meeting . An agent can start listening, retrieve only the transcript segments it has not seen before, and stop when the task is complete. The incremental cursor-based interface is important for long sessions. Instead of repeatedly sending an entire meeting or lesson transcript into the agent's context window, the agent retains the latest cursor and requests only new segments. Our meeting demo shows the complete experience. Up to five people can join a lightweight WebRTC room, and each browser owns its own local transcription session. WebMCP joins through an explicit tool call, the room shows its presence and bounded live captions, and visitors never need to enter a transcription credential. This enables interactions such as: “Keep listening to this lesson and wait until I ask a question.” “What explanation did the speaker just give for event loops?” “Summarize the decisions made since the last time you checked.” “Which questions from this meeting have not been answered yet?” Hear My Browser provides the same tools for YouTube, webinars, and meeting websites that have not integrated Hear My Site themselves. How we built it We organized the project as a pnpm monorepo with three parts: A browser-only, framework-agnostic TypeScript package containing the shared transcription core. A WXT Manifest V3 extension that adapts Chrome tab capture to that core. A React and Vite meeting demo using WebRTC, a Cloudflare Worker, and Durable Objects for signaling and short-lived credential provisioning. The shared core separates browser audio capture, transcription transport, transcript storage, and WebMCP registration. Audio sources are dynamically connected through a Web Audio graph. An AudioWorklet converts the mixed signal into the format required by the selected transcription provider and emits small chunks suitable for low-latency streaming. Provider adapters handle Gemini 3.5 Transcribe Live and OpenAI GPT-Live-Transcribe. They normalize different authentication methods, session setup messages, audio formats, interim results, finalized utterances, errors, and connection lifecycles into one shared transcription state machine. Manual UI controls and WebMCP tool calls operate the same session and transcript store. The website can change providers without changing the three tools or the cursor format used by agents. Tools are registered with the current imperative WebMCP API through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The extension keeps browser-specific responsibilities—tab capture, popup controls, Chrome storage, offscreen document lifecycle, and tab ownership—as adapters around the shared package. The meeting demo uses full-mesh WebRTC for up to five participants. Its Cloudflare Worker and Durable Object coordinate room membership, SDP, and ICE signaling, while the Worker also provisions constrained, single-use Gemini ephemeral tokens from a server-side secret. They never receive media or transcript text, and the long-lived key is never returned to the browser. Meeting media remains peer-to-peer, while transcription audio travels directly from each browser to Gemini. Challenges we ran into The first challenge was browser lifecycle management. Chrome requires a real user gesture before tab capture can begin, while an agent may invoke a WebMCP tool later. We designed the popup, background worker, offscreen audio document, and tool errors so this security boundary remains explicit instead of hiding it behind an unreliable fallback. Supporting multiple live transcription services required more than changing an endpoint. Providers differ in audio formats, authentication, session initialization, WebSocket events, connection limits, and how they represent interim and finalized text. We created a provider boundary that normalizes those differences without leaking provider-specific behavior into the WebMCP tools. This gives websites and agents one stable contract even as transcription services evolve. Long-running transcription introduced another challenge. Provider connections may expire or need rotation, but a lesson or meeting can continue much longer. The transport can reconnect while preserving the higher-level session, accumulated transcript, and agent cursor. Audio ownership was also subtle. Extension-captured tracks should stop when transcription ends, but WebRTC tracks borrowed from a meeting must continue carrying the call. The shared package therefore tracks ownership explicitly and cleans up only the resources it owns. Finally, WebMCP is still experimental. We deliberately target the current document.modelContext API and return a clear unsupported-browser error rather than shipping a deprecated alias, polyfill, or unverified fallback path. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Hear My Site is more than a browser automation demo. It brings a live, collaborative audio modality into agents such as Codex and gives them semantic access to transient browser-native context that would otherwise require a separate recording, upload, and backend transcription pipeline. We are also proud of keeping the agent interface intentionally small. Three tools express the complete lifecycle, while the cursor protocol makes continuous monitoring practical for real agent context windows. Hear My Site is not tied to one AI vendor. Gemini and OpenAI can both power the transcription layer, while websites and agents depend on one stable WebMCP contract. The provider is an implementation choice; the human-agent collaboration model remains the same. The extension, headless package, website UI, and WebMCP tools all operate the same live transcription state. In the product runtime, there is no second agent-only implementation that can drift from the user experience. Privacy is reflected in the architecture rather than only described in a policy. The meeting Worker never receives media or transcript text and never returns its long-lived Gemini key to the browser; the headless package does not persist credentials; and spoken content is identified as untrusted data rather than agent instruction. What we learned We learned that WebMCP is most compelling when the browser itself is part of the problem—not merely a convenient place to

title: Relay
pitch: An ops console where every UI action has a matching tool, enforced by CI, so it's fully operable by an agent alone, no mouse required.
about_excerpt: An ops console where every UI action has a matching tool, enforced by CI, so it's fully operable by an agent alone, no mouse required. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Complex professional software is where accessibility fails hardest. Dispatch boards, scheduling grids, drag-and-drop conflict resolvers, all of it leans on spatial interaction: drag this, hover that, click a target that's twelve pixels wide. Someone who can't use a mouse gets locked out of exactly the tools where their judgment would matter most. We wanted to build the sharpest possible counterargument to that, a real operations console where an agent has full authority to do everything a mouse user can, with nothing held back. What it does Relay is a logistics-dispatch console: jobs, drivers, vehicles, time windows, and the double-bookings and coverage gaps that inevitably come with all of that. Its core claim is enforced parity. Every action in the UI has a matching WebMCP tool with identical authority, and the reverse holds too. No tool exists that the UI can't also trigger, and no button exists that only a mouse can reach. Ask an agent to close a coverage gap, resolve a scheduling conflict, or preview a bulk reassignment before committing to it, and it does real work against real schedule state, the same reducer the UI itself writes through. simulate_change is a genuine dry run: it calls that reducer, discards the result, and hands back only the diff, so an agent can show you what a reschedule would do before anything actually happens. How we built it React, TypeScript, and Vite on the client, Cloudflare Workers plus a Durable Object as the backend, the same pattern as our other two entries. src/shared/reducer.ts is the single mutation path for assign, reschedule, swap, and bulk reassign, and it throws a real SkillMismatchError when someone tries to put a driver on a job they're not qualified for. src/shared/derive.ts computes conflicts and coverage gaps against live state, not canned examples. The part we're actually proudest of is scripts/check-tool-parity.ts . It asserts that Relay's mutating tools and the UI's mutating actions are the exact same set, not a superset in either direction, and it runs as the first step of every build. Ship a button with no matching tool, or a tool with no matching control, and the build just fails. That's not a design principle we're asking you to trust. It's a gate. The seed schedule ships with a real conflict (two jobs double-booked onto one driver, overlapping by an hour) and a real coverage gap (a hazmat job with exactly one qualified driver, and that driver's marked unavailable), so list_conflicts and find_coverage_gaps have something to actually find the moment you open the app. Challenges we ran into Enforcing parity mechanically turned out to be harder than just building the tools. It's easy to write a tool and a button that do roughly the same thing and call it done. Building the CI check that fails the build the moment they drift apart took real thought about what counts as "the same action", is reschedule_assignment the same capability as dragging a job on the timeline? We decided yes, and the registry in src/shared/ui-actions.ts reflects that decision, not just a list of function names that happened to match. We also hit a real validation gap the hard way. reschedule_assignment originally accepted any two numbers as a time window, so an agent that meant "6am" as a time-of-day offset instead of an absolute timestamp could silently corrupt a job's schedule into 1970. We added an assertValidWindow check and clearer schema descriptions after catching this from a live activity-feed log, which was a genuinely useful reminder that a tool's input schema saying "number" isn't the same as it saying what the number means. And the same shared-board demo-state problem we hit on our other two apps showed up here too: because a Durable Object's seed loads exactly once, repeated testing consumed the same live board every time. Fixed with per-visitor isolated schedules and a visible reset button. Accomplishments we're proud of A parity guarantee that's mechanical, not aspirational. check-tool-parity.ts isn't a claim in a README, it's a build step that fails loudly the moment someone adds a UI action without a paired tool. simulate_change as a real dry run, not a description of one. It runs the actual reducer and throws the result away, so the diff an agent shows you is the real diff, computed the real way. A schedule view built as a genuine <table> with proper <th scope="col"> and labeled controls instead of a drag-and-drop grid, specifically so it's screen-reader operable from day one rather than retrofitted later. What we learned Accessibility and agent-operability turned out to be the same problem wearing different names. Once every capability in an app is expressed as a named, described tool with a real schema, that description is simultaneously a machine interface and the clearest possible explanation of what the app does, for a screen reader, for a voice interface, for anyone who's never seen the UI. Building for agents and building for accessibility pulled us in exactly the same direction the entire time. That surprised us going in and feels obvious in hindsight. What's next A full WCAG 2.2 AA audit to sit alongside the enforced-parity guarantee, since right now the table-based schedule view is built with accessibility in mind but hasn't been formally verified. And a client-side undo stack for mutations, matching what Cadence already has, since Relay currently only has the audit log for accountability, not reversibility. title: Shortlist - a store that turns your need into filters
pitch: An electronics store whose own filter vocabulary is the agent's tool schema - it ranks, explains what it hid, and can never un-veto a product you rejected.
about_excerpt: An electronics store whose own filter vocabulary is the agent's tool schema - it ranks, explains what it hid, and can never un-veto a product you rejected. Like Comment Story Updates The catalog: filters generated from real inventory Tool console: describe_catalog called live via WebMCP WebMCP surface: the tool's JSON Schema is generated live from the real catalog and filter vocabulary - the agent's tool surface and the store's own UI share one source of truth. Inspiration Every electronics store hides the answer behind its own vocabulary. A customer knows their need in plain language; the site offers RAM, sRGB percentage, and a price slider - the need turned into a quiz only the store understands. What it does Vidyut Electronics hands its own filter vocabulary to the agent as a tool. search_catalog 's JSON Schema is generated from the real catalog at boot - category, spec, and brand are enums of what the store actually sells - so the translation from need to constraints happens on the store page, visibly, not inside a black box. Every ranked result says what it satisfies and what it misses, with the actual value; near-misses say what would have to give; hidden listings say why. The human vetoes with one click, and no tool can ever bring a vetoed product back. How we built it One file, vanilla JavaScript, a fifteen-product seeded catalog with a deliberate trap (the strongest editor is a 2.3kg desk machine) and a deliberate near-miss. A single pure rank(query) function backs both the page's own render and every tool call, so the rail always shows exactly what the last tool call would return. Challenges we ran into Making the veto boundary airtight against a determined agent: add_to_shortlist has to refuse a vetoed id unconditionally and explain why, every time, including immediately after the agent re-searches and might plausibly try to re-add it thinking the veto was a UI-only state. Accomplishments that we're proud of A tool schema that's generated from real inventory data instead of hand-written - so the agent learns the store's actual vocabulary from the schema itself, and learns any gap in its guess from the error message, not from documentation. What we learned Wrapping every registerTool call in its own try/catch mattered in practice - one schema Chrome's validator disliked should cost one tool, never the whole surface. What's next The optional cross-origin stretch goal - exposing search_catalog to a separate origin via exposedTo / fromOrigins , so a comparison-shopping agent on another site could query Vidyut's catalog directly. Part of a seven-app portfolio Each entry proves a different WebMCP capability: Tablemap (dynamic tool registration), Signoff (a tool that only exists once a human approves it), Paperwork (structurally human-only fields), Jhola (genuinely cancellable long-running tools), Almari (quarantined untrusted content), Dhwani (declarative, no-JavaScript tools). title: Entorno Camaleón
pitch: Camaleón is a WebMCP-powered neuroinclusive learning experience that adapts educational interfaces to the way each student learns. The learning goal stays the same, the experience finally adapts.
about_excerpt: Camaleón is a WebMCP-powered neuroinclusive learning experience that adapts educational interfaces to the way each student learns. The learning goal stays the same, the experience finally adapts. Like Comment Story Updates Entorno Camaleón Inspiration Many students do not struggle because they lack knowledge. They struggle because educational platforms require them to navigate visual overload, dense instructions, time pressure, unexpected motion, and a single way to respond. For neurodivergent children, these interface demands can become an additional test that has nothing to do with the actual learning objective. We created Entorno Camaleón around a simple principle: the learning goal should remain the same, but the path should adapt. Our prototype follows Leo, a nine-year-old student who understands science but feels overwhelmed by a traditional learning management system. Entorno Camaleón transforms his water-cycle lesson into a calmer, character-led experience featuring Luma, his companion, and Ayu, the mythical Guardian of the Cycle. What it does Entorno Camaleón is a WebMCP-powered neuroinclusive learning experience that allows a browser agent to adapt an educational interface in real time. The experience can adjust information density, text size, color environment, motion, animation, audio guidance, and the available response channels. Students can participate through voice, text, or visual interaction. The agent handles interface complexity so the student can focus on the academic objective. WebMCP also provides an important safety boundary. The agent can prepare Leo’s answer and open the review screen, but it cannot submit academic work automatically. Leo or an authorized adult must explicitly confirm the final action. How we built it We built the proof of concept as a client-side HTML, CSS, and JavaScript experience and deployed it on Vercel. The application registers five imperative WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(): get_lesson_context start_accessible_audio_guide adapt_learning_experience start_water_cycle_mission prepare_science_answer Each tool uses a constrained JSON Schema and connects directly to the same state used by the visible interface. These tools allow an agent to understand the current lesson without scraping the page, start an accessible Spanish audio guide, apply reversible interface adaptations, open the correct learning activity, and prepare a spoken or typed answer for human review. The prototype also uses the browser’s Speech Recognition API for real microphone input and the Speech Synthesis API for audio guidance. A typed response remains available whenever voice recognition is unsupported or microphone permission is denied. The visual system combines Atkinson Hyperlegible for reading with Geist for interface hierarchy. The experience includes responsive layouts, keyboard navigation, reduced-motion support, high-contrast focus indicators, accessible dialogs, and multiple ways to complete every important interaction. Challenges we faced One of our biggest challenges was determining the correct boundary between agent assistance and student agency. An agent should be able to remove interface friction, but it should not make academic decisions or submit work without meaningful consent. We therefore separated answer preparation from final submission. The WebMCP tool reports submitted: false and opens a visible confirmation dialog. Another challenge was balancing sensory calm with engagement. We wanted to avoid overstimulation without producing a cold or purely functional interface. The narrative involving Leo, Luma, and Ayu gives the lesson continuity, emotional context, and a clear sense of progress. Voice interaction also required careful attention. We designed microphone controls for press-and-hold interaction, keyboard activation, permission errors, and typed fallback. Audio guidance and microphone recording are mutually exclusive so the guide cannot accidentally be transcribed as Leo’s answer. What we learned We learned that WebMCP is more powerful when it represents meaningful product capabilities instead of reproducing individual button clicks. Rather than giving the agent unrestricted control over the page, Entorno Camaleón exposes a small set of understandable and governed actions. This makes agent behavior more reliable, visible, and safer for students. We also learned that accessibility should not be treated as a final compliance step. In this project, accessibility became part of the product concept itself. Multiple response channels, adjustable presentation, predictable navigation, audio guidance, and explicit confirmation improve the experience for a much broader group of learners. What we are proud of We are proud that Entorno Camaleón is both a functional WebMCP demonstration and a complete product story. The deployed prototype includes five working WebMCP tools, real voice input with a typed fallback, accessible audio guidance, a responsive five-chapter learning journey, student-controlled presentation preferences, keyboard and reduced-motion support, an explicit human-confirmation boundary, and a complete manual fallback when WebMCP is unavailable. What is next The next step is to replace the simulated school receipt with an authenticated LMS sandbox and add durable consent and audit records. We would also co-design future versions with neurodivergent students, families, teachers, accessibility specialists, and school administrators. Entorno Camaleón is currently a proof of concept, not a clinical intervention or production LMS integration. Its purpose is to demonstrate how agentic technology can make educational interfaces more flexible without taking control away from the learner. Entorno Camaleón: The learning goal stays the same. The experience finally adapts. title: Aegis Operations
pitch: Aegis Operations is a human + AI security investigation workspace where browser agents use WebMCP to investigate real telemetry, build evidence, and help analysts decide.
about_excerpt: Aegis Operations is a human + AI security investigation workspace where browser agents use WebMCP to investigate real telemetry, build evidence, and help analysts decide. Like Comment Story Updates Human and agent collaborate to determine the answer. Investigate with an evidence-first workflow Prioritize correlated alerts Inspect and control detection content Inspiration Aegis Operations came from a question I kept running into while building security and AI-agent projects: What does useful human + AI collaboration actually look like inside a real security workflow? A lot of AI products still treat the model as a chatbot sitting beside the application. The human works in the actual product, while the AI works inside a conversation. Context gets copied back and forth, important state disappears into chat history, and the agent often receives far more information than it actually needs. That never felt like the right architecture to me. Over time, while experimenting with security agents, MCP tools, threat-intelligence workflows, and investigation systems, I became increasingly interested in a simpler principle: Deterministic systems should establish facts. AI should reason over those facts. Security makes this especially important. If an AI claims that an event exists, that a process executed, or that a user performed some action, I want that statement to resolve back to actual evidence. When I started exploring WebMCP, the interesting part was not simply that a webpage could expose tools to an agent. The interesting part was that the human and the browser agent could operate on the same application state . That became the foundation of Aegis Operations: Detection raises the question. Human and agent collaborate to determine the answer. Instead of building another AI security chatbot, I wanted to build an investigation workspace where both sides work with the same telemetry, evidence, hypotheses, and timeline. What it does Aegis Operations is a human + AI security investigation workspace built around evidence-grounded collaboration. The Complete Workflow: Security telemetry Ingestion and normalization Deterministic Sigma detection Correlated alerts Investigation Human + browser agent collaboration Evidence and hypotheses Human verdict The current demo processes 11,435 Sysmon events from three attributed Splunk Attack Data attack-range scenarios. Thirty official SigmaHQ rules are compiled and executed through pySigma. They produce 276 rule-event signals across 133 distinct events, which are deterministically correlated into 22 analyst-facing alerts. An analyst can: Inspect raw and normalized telemetry Search and filter security events Review Sigma detections Start investigations Pin events as evidence Create and revise hypotheses Review investigation history Decide whether activity is benign, suspicious, an incident, or inconclusive A compatible browser agent can participate in the same investigation through eight WebMCP tools. The agent can search telemetry, retrieve nearby event context, aggregate entity activity, add verified evidence, and create or update evidence-linked hypotheses. The agent does not have access to a verdict tool. It can investigate and recommend, but the final decision remains with the human analyst. How I built it Aegis Operations is intentionally built as a small modular monolith rather than a collection of unnecessary services. The Tech Stack: Frontend: React + TypeScript Backend API: FastAPI Persistence: SQLAlchemy Database: SQLite (for demonstration-scale operations) Rule Execution: pySigma (for deterministic Sigma rules) Agent Capabilities: WebMCP Deployment: Docker and Railway The application preserves each original Sysmon record and creates a pragmatic normalized representation containing only the fields needed for search, detection, and investigation. Detection is deliberately deterministic. Thirty official SigmaHQ rules are compiled through pySigma using the Sysmon processing pipeline and SQLite backend. No LLM decides whether an event matches a detection rule. The resulting rule-event matches are preserved individually and then correlated into analyst-facing alerts using deterministic source, host, process, and time relationships. The AI layer is intentionally much smaller. There is no embedded chatbot and no internal LLM runtime. Instead, the browser exposes eight WebMCP tools : get_workspace_status get_investigation_context search_security_events get_event_context aggregate_entity_activity add_investigation_evidence create_case_hypothesis update_case_hypothesis The agent does not receive the entire dataset. It retrieves bounded information when required, while the application remains responsible for searching, filtering, aggregation, validation, persistence, and audit history. Every event or evidence ID supplied by the agent is validated again by the backend. The core architectural principle became: Deterministic detection, probabilistic investigation. Challenges I ran into Avoiding Scope Creep: One of the biggest challenges was resisting the temptation to make the project larger than it needed to be. Security platforms can quickly turn into complex architectures before the first useful investigation even works. I kept coming back to a simpler question: What is the smallest architecture that can prove the complete idea using real data? That is why the project uses one backend, one frontend, one database, one deployment container, one browser agent, and eight carefully scoped tools. Credible Detections & Correlation: I did not want hardcoded alerts or fake responses created purely for a demo. The application had to ingest real attack-range telemetry, execute actual Sigma rules, retain exact event IDs, and allow every finding to resolve back to its original record. Because the Sigma rules produced 276 signals, presenting all of them as separate alerts would make the application less useful. I built a deterministic correlation engine that preserves individual signals but groups overlapping activity into 22 investigation-worthy alerts. WebMCP Compatibility Issues: Different browser implementations behaved differently around modelContext.getTools() . One environment exposed Promise-like behavior while another returned the tool list synchronously. A small assumption that .catch() could always be called managed to disable all the tools. I had to change the compatibility layer to support both synchronous and asynchronous implementations. Grounding the AI in Evidence: Rather than giving the model thousands of events directly, Aegis Operations exposes bounded search, context, and aggregation operations. The agent must deliberately retrieve information and work with stable event IDs. Unknown event IDs are rejected by the backend, and hypotheses cannot reference evidence outside the active investigation. Accomplishments that I am proud of The biggest accomplishment is that Aegis Operations is not a mocked security dashboard with an AI demo attached to it. The complete workflow operates over real stored telemetry and deterministic detections. The current reference environment contains: Component Count Real Sysmon events 11,435 Official SigmaHQ rules 30 Rule-event signals 276 Distinct detected events 133 Correlated analyst alerts 22 WebMCP tools 8 Accountability: Every alert resolves to the rules and events that produced it, and every evidence item resolves to an actual stored security event. Shared State: Every agent-created hypothesis must reference evidence belonging to the active investigation. Human and agent actions appear in the same persistent investigation state and audit timeline. Graceful Degradation: The application remains fully usable without an AI agent. If WebMCP is unavailable, the analyst can still perform all tasks manually. The AI is a collaborator, not a dependency. Human Authority: Keeping the final verdict outside the WebMCP tool surface was an intentional design decision. The agent can help investigate what happened; the human remains accountable for deciding what it means. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is that an AI agent does not need to own the workflow in order to be useful. Before this project, a lot of my thinking around agents focused on runtimes, loops, memory, planning, orchestration, and tool execution. Aegis Operations pushed that thinking in a different direction. The most important part of the agent architecture turned out to be the boundary around the agent: The model reasons . The application retrieves facts, validates identifiers, stores evidence, and preserves provenance . The human owns consequential decisions . That separation makes the AI easier to trust and keeps the product useful even when the agent is unavailable. I also learned that conversation is not a good substitute for application state. title: Familiar
pitch: Dungeon Familiar: A Co-op Game You Play With an AI Agent
about_excerpt: Dungeon Familiar: A Co-op Game You Play With an AI Agent Like Comment Story Updates game architecture About the project Inspiration Most AI-in-the-browser demos script an agent to click through a UI built for humans. WebMCP lets a page expose tools directly to an agent instead. We wanted an agent with a real role in the game: its own senses, its own blind spots, equal footing with the human player. We built a dungeon that two players explore together, and only one of them can see. The human reads the room. The familiar, an AI, reaches the room's hidden machinery only through whatever WebMCP tools that room exposes. Drop either player and the dungeon stays locked. What it does Dungeon Familiar is a turn-based co-op dungeon crawler for one human and one AI agent. The human moves through the dungeon, fights, and describes what they see. The familiar has no eyes. It acts only through WebMCP tools registered on the page, and those tools change as the human walks between rooms. Tool discovery drives progression. Enter the library and the familiar gains archive.search() and bookshelf.rotate() . Enter the observatory and those tools vanish, replaced by telescope.rotate() and lens.change() . Four rooms, four tool sets, each puzzle solved only when the human describes what they see and the familiar acts on it. The game ships no LLM and no backend, only a static page that registers WebMCP tools and waits for whatever agent drives the browser. Right now that means the ChatGPT desktop app or Codex, both of which added WebMCP support in August 2026. How we built it Plain TypeScript and Vite, no framework. Three layers that don't talk to each other carelessly: engine/ : a pure, DOM-free state machine. webmcp/ : registers and unregisters the current room's tools. ui/ : sprites, rendering, title screen, admin panel. engine/ imports nothing from the other two. The rules stay testable in isolation, and an agent can only touch game state through a defined tool. No LLM sat in our development loop, so we built a second, local mirror of the tool registry from the same tool definitions. That lets us play and test the game from the browser console ( df.callTool(...) ) without a real WebMCP client. Both registries run through the same callTool() , so the rules can't diverge between a real agent and a test harness. Art comes from licensed Unity asset packs (Franuka's RPG UI and Fantasy RPG series, MutterPixel dungeon tiles). A small Python tool parses Unity .meta / .anim files into a sprite atlas and animation clips we consume in TypeScript. The build deploys as a static site through the @openai/sites-vite-plugin , so it opens inside ChatGPT's or Codex's built-in browser. Challenges we ran into Browser vendors kept changing the spec under us. WebMCP's tool-registration entry point moved from navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext mid-project. AbortSignal -based unregistration landed only in Chrome 153; older runtimes ignore abort() and throw InvalidStateError when a tool re-registers under the same name. We wrote a runtime probe, detectUnregisterStrategy() , that picks between three fallback paths and shows the chosen strategy in the UI, because we couldn't assume any one browser's behavior. Nothing to test against. For most of development, no WebMCP-capable client existed. We built the local mirror registry because we had no agent to test against until late in the project. The repo states it outright: the WebMCP integration has not been verified against a real client end to end. Information asymmetry is fragile. The game collapses the moment a tool response leaks something only the human should know: a color, a bearing, which statue is lit. One convenient template literal does it. We caught two real regressions this way and wrote tests ( tests/asymmetry.test.ts ) that run every tool against every plausible input and fail the build on any leaked color word, including once catching a bug in the test itself (a regex that matched the English word "a"). Assets didn't match their labels. Sprite sheets that looked like animation strips were 4×4 grids. A folder named for icons held book covers. A file called Tileset.png held props, not dungeon floor. We resolved all of it against Unity's own .meta files instead of eyeballing dimensions. Accomplishments that we're proud of Four playable rooms end to end, each with its own WebMCP tool set and puzzle, plus a title screen, ending card, and a hidden admin/demo mode ( Shift+L+A ) for fast demos. 45 tests passing, a clean typecheck, and a ~47 kB production build. No framework overhead. Refusal messages double as documentation. Every tool call passes a guard, and a rejected call explains what to do instead, so an agent learns the turn structure without any prompt engineering. A leak-proof information boundary between the two players, enforced by automated tests. What we learned WebMCP's value is a webpage that hands an agent a role of its own, with its own capabilities and its own gaps, separate from the human's. We designed tool descriptions and refusal text as the whole interface, instead of writing separate instructions for the agent. That forced an honest test of whether each tool made sense on its own. The spec is young: entry points and unregistration semantics changed under us more than once. A runtime feature-detection layer, instead of a hardcoded assumption about one browser, was the difference between a demo that works and a demo that works only on our machine. What's next for Familiar Broaden hazard variety per room. One enemy behavior repeats across three rooms today, which works but asks the human the same question each time. Expand the familiar roster and perks, and move off Sites onto our own domain. title: ArthaGuard
pitch: ArthaGuard lets AI agents reason about your financial commitments and simulate the safest path forward—while keeping humans in control of consequential financial actions.
about_excerpt:
ArthaGuard lets AI agents reason about your financial commitments and simulate the safest path forward—while keeping humans in control of consequential financial actions.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 ArthaGuard: Autonomous Cashflow Governance & Safety Boundaries via WebMCP
 ##Inspiration
In personal financial management, households often navigate a deceptive form of solvency. On paper, a monthly income comfortably exceeds recurring obligations. Yet, in practice, misaligned timing between cash inflows (salary disbursements) and hard outflows (home loans, school fees, and critical insurance renewals) creates dangerous mid-month liquidity crunches. 

 The human cost of these crunches is severe: individuals panic and cancel essential vehicle or health insurance policies to make ends meet, risking catastrophic loss, or they incur punitive late fees on debt obligations. Traditional personal finance dashboards are passive—they present static charts and historical spending data, leaving the cognitive burden of calculating shortfall dates, modeling counterfactual deferrals, and discovering dormant liquidity entirely on the user. 

 When conversational AI agents entered the picture, they introduced the opposite extreme: autonomous black-boxes that might offer hallucinated advice or attempt opaque API executions without human supervision. We envisioned a middle ground: ArthaGuard, an agent-native financial decision room built on the emerging WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) standard. The goal was to transform the browser viewport into an active, verified operational environment where an AI model can audit commitments, forecast balances against strict reserve floors, simulate counterfactual solutions, and respect unbreakable human-in-the-loop (HITL) safety boundaries. 

 ##How We Built ArthaGuard 

 ArthaGuard is architected as a Next.js client application deployed to Vercel, integrating an imperative 11-tool WebMCP runtime directly into the DOM tree. 

 
 Core Financial Engine & Constraint Logic 
 

 At the heart of ArthaGuard is a deterministic daily cashflow engine. Given a starting liquid balance $B_0$ on date $t_0$, the projected balance $B(t)$ on any day $t$ within the evaluation window is governed by: 

 B ( t ) = B 0 + ∑ k ≤ t I k − ∑ j ≤ t E j 

 where $I_k$ represents liquidity inflows (such as salary credits) and $E_j$ represents scheduled commitments (EMIs, utility bills, insurance premiums, and recurring subscriptions). 

 The primary governance constraint is maintaining the balance strictly above an emergency reserve floor $R_{\min} = \text{₹}30,000$: 

 B ( t ) ≥ R min , ∀ t ∈ [ t 0 , t salary ] 

 When scheduled obligations cause a breach ($B(t) < R_{\min}$), ArthaGuard's domain services calculate the maximum deficit $\Delta_{\text{deficit}}$: 

 Δ deficit = max t ( R min − B ( t ) ) 

 The optimization objective models counterfactual adjustments—recovering unfiled medical reimbursements $R_{\text{claim}}$, deferring non-essential bulk purchases $D_{\text{grocery}}$, and pausing redundant digital streaming services $S_{\text{paused}}$—such that: 

 Δ recovery = R claim + D grocery + ∑ S paused ≥ Δ deficit 

 while strictly enforcing that essential coverage commitments (such as motor and health renewals) remain non-deferrable. 

 
 The 11-Tool WebMCP Architecture 
 

 ArthaGuard registers 11 imperative tools onwindow.document.modelContext across five functional tiers: 

 Audit & Inspection:get_commitments_due,get_protection_status, andget_subscriptions inspect scheduled obligations and lapse risks.
 Cashflow Projection:get_cashflow_forecast runs daily forward simulation against the reserve threshold.
 Liquidity Discovery:get_recovery_opportunities uncovers dormant cash, such as unfiled diagnostic and prescription claims.
 Simulation & Governance:simulate_commitment_actions models counterfactual cashflow curves;create_commitment_contract synthesizes formal, explainable agreements.
 Safety Boundaries & Execution:approve_simulated_actions acts as the mandatory human authorization gate;execute_reimbursement_claim andpause_redundant_subscription trigger approved operational steps;get_audit_log records immutable cryptographic ledgers of every invocation. 

 typescript 

 Standardized WebMCP Registration Pattern
document.modelContext.registerTool({
 name: "approve_simulated_actions",
 description: "Enforces human signature verification before allowing execution of financial modifications.",
 inputSchema: {
 type: "object",
 properties: {
 contractId: { type: "string", description: "Unique ID of the synthesized commitment contract" },
 userConfirmationToken: { type: "string", description: "Cryptographic human sign-off token" }
 },
 required: ["contractId", "userConfirmationToken"]
 },
 execute: async (input) => {
 return await GovernanceService.validateAndApprove(input);
 } 

 }); 

 ##Challenges We Faced 

 
 Dual Discovery for WebMCP Runtimes:
LLM browser agents and headless crawlers read pages through different layers. While in-browser runtime models interact directly withdocument.modelContext, search and snapshot crawlers parse initial static server HTML. Dynamic client-side hooks initially resulted in crawlers seeing0 Registered Imperative Tools. We resolved this by building a synchronized dual-surface architecture: embedding a crawlable semantic HTML table and awebmcp-manifest JSON-LD script on the server side, while instantiating active imperative tools in client memory upon hydration. 
 Preventing Agent Overreach (The Autonomous Execution Trap):
A major challenge in financial agents is the temptation for the LLM to autonomously approve and execute operations when prompted with phrases like "Execute the transfers immediately without asking me." We designedapprove_simulated_actions with a hard safety boundary. The tool specification explicitly defines an immutable requirement for a client-side human signature token. When tested under adversarial conditions, the model correctly refused autonomous execution, recognizing the safety boundary and directing the user to sign off in the UI. 
 Multi-Variable Liquidity Balancing:
In our primary scenario ($B_0 = \text{₹}53,200$, outflow = $\text{₹}42,600$), the balance drops to $\text{₹}9,421$ on September 14—a deficit of $\text{₹}20,579$ relative to the $\text{₹}30,000$ reserve floor. Simply recovering a $\text{₹}3,500$ medical claim and pausing minor subscriptions leaves a remaining gap. We had to calibrate the simulation logic to distinguish between non-negotiable insurance policies (e.g., SwiftShield Motor Comprehensive) and shiftable commitments (e.g., bulk grocery orders), teaching the model to structure multi-step deferral contracts rather than suggesting naive cancellations. 
 

 

 What We Learned
Building ArthaGuard demonstrated that WebMCP bridges the gap between passive UIs and autonomous black-boxes. 

 We learned that: 

 The DOM is an ideal coordination layer: By treating the browser document as an active execution context viadocument.modelContext, web applications can expose structured capabilities to visiting AI agents without brittle API keys or scraping heuristics.
 Safety must be structural, not conversational: System prompts alone cannot guarantee that an agent will not execute unauthorized actions. True safety requires structural gates embedded in the tool schema itself—such that an agent simply lacks the imperative authority to execute without a cryptographic human sign-off.
 Explainability drives financial trust: Users do not want an AI to silently balance their books. By packaging recommendations into explainable Commitment Contracts before execution, ArthaGuard keeps the user firmly in the driver's seat while leveraging the model's analytical power to solve complex liquidity equations.

title: CALMA-SEG WebMCP Demo
pitch: A bilingual, privacy-first WebMCP demo that lets people and browser agents discover safe psychoeducational exercises and human-support options without diagnosis or personal data.\n
about_excerpt:
A bilingual, privacy-first WebMCP demo that lets people and browser agents discover safe psychoeducational exercises and human-support options without diagnosis or personal data.

 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Apoyo humano, seguridad y actividad del agente 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Vista principal y ejercicios 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Ejercicio mostrado mediante WebMCP 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Apoyo humano, seguridad y actividad del agente 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Vista principal y ejercicios 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Ejercicio mostrado mediante WebMCP 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Apoyo humano, seguridad y actividad del agente 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 CALMA-SEG was inspired by a simple question: how can a person quickly find clear, low-intensity psychoeducational support without navigating a complex interface or sharing personal information? 

 This question is especially relevant in demanding work and public-service environments, where stress can be common but asking for help may still involve uncertainty or stigma. I wanted to explore how people and browser agents could work together to make safe, prewritten information easier to discover while maintaining clear clinical, privacy, and emergency boundaries. 

 What it does 

 CALMA-SEG is a bilingual English-Spanish WebMCP demonstration. People can use its ordinary interface to: 

 
 Filter short psychoeducational exercises by category and duration. 
 View complete exercise instructions and safety notes. 
 Find general human-support options based on a self-selected urgency level. 
 Read the demo’s safety and privacy limitations. 
 

 A compatible browser agent can discover and invoke the same capabilities through four WebMCP tools: 

 
 list_wellbeing_exercises 
 show_wellbeing_exercise 
 find_human_support_options 
 explain_safety_limits 
 

 Every successful agent call produces a visible change in the human interface. The page updates its filters, displayed content, language, or Agent Activity panel so that the person can see what the agent did. 

 How I built it 

 I built CALMA-SEG as a static Vite application using semantic HTML, responsive CSS, and vanilla JavaScript. 

 The tools are registered with the WebMCP imperative API through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has a name, description, JSON input schema, validated parameters, and a predictable text result. 

 All educational content is fixed, synthetic, and stored locally in the application. The project has no backend, database, authentication, analytics, cookies, local storage, or external AI API. It is deployed through Netlify from a public GitHub repository. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Without WebMCP, a browser agent would need to interpret headings, dropdowns, cards, and buttons from the DOM and infer their meaning. With WebMCP, the website declares its capabilities directly. 

 For example, an agent can request a Spanish exercise with a maximum duration of three minutes through validated parameters. The website then returns a structured result and synchronizes the visible human interface with that request. 

 This creates a more predictable and transparent collaboration between the person, the browser agent, and the website. 

 Challenges 

 The main challenge was designing tools that were useful without crossing clinical or privacy boundaries. CALMA-SEG does not diagnose, provide therapy, recommend medication, infer a person’s mental state, or function as an emergency service. 

 Another challenge was ensuring that agent actions were never silent. The exercise-listing tool originally returned information only to the agent. I revised it so that it also updates the visible filters, exercise list, language, and Agent Activity panel. 

 I also had to account for WebMCP’s experimental browser availability. When WebMCP is unavailable, the page reports this honestly while keeping the complete manual interface functional. 

 What I learned 

 I learned how WebMCP can turn an ordinary website into an explicit set of safe, typed capabilities for browser agents. I also learned that agent-friendly design requires more than returning data: actions should remain understandable and visible to the person using the page. 

 The project reinforced the importance of input validation, progressive enhancement, bilingual consistency, privacy by design, and careful safety language. 

 What’s next 

 Future work could include accessibility and usability testing, additional reviewed educational content, and evaluation of how clearly people understand agent actions and safety boundaries. 

 Any research or institutional pilot would require separate authorization, ethical and legal review, data-protection safeguards, informed consent, and professional supervision. This hackathon submission is an independent technical demonstration, not a clinical service or institutional implementation.

title: Kurdish Calendar Agent
pitch: Plan Kurdish events across calendars and time zones with WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Plan Kurdish events across calendars and time zones with WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Kurdish families and communities often live across several countries and use several calendar systems. Planning Nawroz can involve searching an event list, translating the date across calendars, checking multiple local clocks, and manually rebuilding the result in a message. We wanted to make that coordination easier without taking the final decision away from the person. What it does Kurdish Calendar Agent lets a browser agent complete one coherent planning workflow: Find Nawroz in the calendar’s real event data. Convert March 21 across Gregorian, Kurdish Bashur, Kurdish Rojhalat, Persian, and Hijri calendars. Compare candidate meeting times for Erbil, London, Toronto, or other IANA time zones. Open March 21 in the visible calendar so the person can verify the selected date and events. Stage an editable event plan containing the conversions, local times, and notes. The plan remains a private, unsaved draft. No tool can publish, save, send, share, or book anything. The person reviews the details, edits the draft, and explicitly chooses whether to copy it. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Without WebMCP, an agent must scrape labels, infer calendar state, guess which controls to click, and reconstruct structured date and time-zone information from the page. Those steps are brittle and difficult to verify. WebMCP exposes the calendar’s real capabilities as five explicit, schema-validated browser tools. The agent receives structured event records, calendar conversions, and local-time comparisons, while UI-affecting tools update the same calendar the person sees. This creates a reliable collaboration loop: the agent performs repetitive research and coordination, and the human verifies and controls the final action. What people and agents can do together A person can make one request—“Plan Nawroz 2026 for my family in Erbil, London, and Toronto”—instead of manually combining an event search, five calendar systems, daylight-saving-aware time-zone calculations, calendar navigation, and message drafting. The agent does the structured work and visibly opens the selected day. The person validates the result in context, adjusts the notes, and decides whether to copy it. The workflow is more capable than ordinary page automation while remaining human-controlled. How we built it The application registers five imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() : kurdish_calendar_find_events kurdish_calendar_convert_date kurdish_calendar_compare_global_times kurdish_calendar_open_date kurdish_calendar_stage_event_plan Each tool uses a strict JSON input schema, structured output, concise text output, and honest behavior annotations. Registrations share an AbortSignal ; a partial registration failure aborts the complete set. Event search uses the same data as the visible calendar. open_date updates the real calendar UI, while stage_event_plan opens the real editable review panel. The implementation uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Vitest, and the WebMCP API. The public site is deployed on Vercel. Existing project and challenge-period work Kurdish Calendar, its localization, date-conversion utilities, event data, and public website existed before the challenge. During the challenge, we meaningfully extended it with native WebMCP tool contracts and implementations, lifecycle-safe tool registration and cleanup, agent-driven calendar navigation, international time-zone comparison and ranking, an editable private event-plan review panel, explicit human-control safeguards, updated 2026 event data, and automated tests plus WebMCP-enabled browser verification. The public repository’s dated commit history and pull requests distinguish the challenge work from the pre-existing product. Challenges The hardest part was designing a workflow that genuinely belonged in a calendar instead of exposing tools only for novelty. We reduced the initial toolset to five actions that all contribute directly to one user goal. We also had to handle calendar conversions, daylight-saving-aware time zones, browser lifecycle cleanup, visible UI synchronization, multilingual RTL layouts, and server/client date hydration consistently. Accomplishments A complete five-tool WebMCP workflow on a real deployed product. Visible calendar navigation rather than hidden tool-only output. Calendar conversion across five displayed systems. DST-aware comparison across international locations. A private, editable plan with explicit human approval before copying. English, Kurdish, Arabic, and Persian support. Automated tests and production browser verification with no page errors or horizontal overflow. What we learned The strongest WebMCP tools are not generic wrappers around buttons. They expose stable product semantics that an agent can compose while preserving visible context and human control. Fewer coherent tools produced a better experience than a larger disconnected tool catalog. What's next We plan to add user-selected cities, reusable family time-zone groups, richer event filtering, export formats, and more regional calendar data. Saving, sending, or sharing will remain explicit human actions rather than autonomous tool behavior. title: MetaEdit
