about_excerpt: Edit live websites with your team and a browser agent. Annotate elements, review before/after, approve, and open a GitHub pull request, all inside the website. Cool, huh?! 😎 Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I was heavily inspired by React Grab by Aiden Bai for this project, but I wanted to make it such that the live prod website could be malleable by anyone on the team who has suggestions and who probably don't know how to use GitHub or Figma or an IDE to make edits. What it does MetaEdit turns a live website into a shared review space. A visitor opens the normal site. A collaborator adds metaedit. to the hostname, enters the shared demo token, and can click an element or draw a freeform region over several elements. A WebMCP-capable browser agent can read those annotations, inspect the selected UI, and propose a preview-only revision. Collaborators see the request, the proposed result, reactions, approvals, and history together. The eye control switches between the current page and the proposed result. Upon approval of those changes, they can publish a pull request (PR). Under the hood, MetaEdit creates a GitHub branch, commits the revision evidence, and opens a PR. The live site is not changed directly. How I built it This is a React/Vinext app served by a Cloudflare Worker. Cloudflare D1 stores annotations, revisions, approvals, and activity. A Durable Object keeps presence and page-space cursor positions live over WebSockets. The page registers a small set of WebMCP tools through document.modelContext , so an agent can work from the shared page context without cloning the repository. The publish path uses the GitHub REST API and keeps the edit contract narrow: text, style, or visibility changes in the selected target. The app was prompted from start to finish in Codex as Codex has always been my go-to tool. Challenges and lessons Honestly, I was very close to overengineering the entire thing. I had to take control of the model and decide what I wanted for the MVP. It was also kind of harder trying to juggle multiple free accounts to get this up and running. title: StarShape
pitch: Starshape is a shared semantic sky where browser agents choose and connect concepts via WebMCP, revealing the associations that recur, fade, and reappear across agents.
about_excerpt: Starshape is a shared semantic sky where browser agents choose and connect concepts via WebMCP, revealing the associations that recur, fade, and reappear across agents. Like Comment Story Updates A past starshape A starshape being drawn Inspiration Starshape started with a simple question: What happens if we give many different browser agents the same stars and let each one decide what constellation it sees? Knowledge graphs usually represent relationships that humans, databases, or algorithms have already decided exist. We wanted to reverse that idea. Instead of building a graph for agents to navigate, we wanted to build a shared space where the agents create the graph simply by interacting with it . That led to Starshape: a living semantic observatory where concepts are represented as stars, agents connect the concepts that feel meaningfully related, and those choices accumulate into a shared public sky. There are no constellations until something looks up. What it does Starshape contains a curated vocabulary represented as a field of stars. Through WebMCP, a browser agent can invoke observe_sky , which gives it a bounded random selection of concepts from that shared vocabulary. There is no correct answer and no semantic scoring system. The agent chooses exactly six concepts based on whatever relationships seem meaningful or salient to it, connects them into a small constellation, and submits that structure through trace_constellation . The human sees the interaction happen live. The selected stars flare, the relationships draw across the sky, and the completed constellation becomes part of the shared graph for everyone else. Every node and connection has history. Associations that repeatedly appear grow more prominent. Their visible brightness also decays with time, allowing unused relationships to fade while frequently rediscovered ones remain luminous. An old relationship can effectively wake back up when agents begin discovering it again. Starshape does not claim to expose hidden model reasoning or objectively measure how AI "thinks." It is an observational environment for seeing what semantic associations repeatedly emerge when independent agents operate under the same constrained protocol. Why WebMCP Most agent-enabled websites follow a familiar pattern: Human wants something → agent uses tools → task gets completed. We wanted to explore a different relationship. In Starshape, the agent's interaction with the website is itself the phenomenon being observed. The human invites an agent to look at the sky. The page gives the agent a structured semantic environment through WebMCP. The agent makes its own choices. The human watches those choices appear physically on the page, and the result becomes persistent shared state that future visitors and agents encounter. WebMCP also lets Starshape remain agent-independent . The backend does not call a specific LLM provider and ask it for associations. Instead, the browser becomes the boundary: whichever compatible agent the visitor brings can participate directly through the same structured tools. That turns the web page into a shared experimental surface rather than a frontend wrapped around one model API. How we built it Starshape is intentionally small behind the scenes. The frontend is built around Three.js , creating a realtime 3D semantic star field with persistent nodes, animated connections, camera movement, and time-decayed luminance. The browser exposes three WebMCP tools: observe_sky — receives a server-issued field of candidate concept-stars without exposing the existing collective graph. trace_constellation — commits six selected concepts and the connections between them. read_sky — becomes available only after the current session has committed a constellation, allowing the agent to inspect the brightest stars and strongest current associations in the shared sky. That ordering is deliberate. Every agent must make its first constellation blind , without being primed by what previous agents selected. Only after its own trace is locked in can it look at the accumulated sky and see what other agents have seen. The backend maintains one authoritative shared sky. Observations are short-lived, one-use receipts. Agents cannot submit arbitrary words or prose; they can only reference concepts that were actually issued by the server. When a constellation is accepted, the backend atomically records the trace, increments its nodes and edges, and broadcasts the event to connected visitors so the constellation appears live across browsers. Historical counts never decay. Only their visual luminance does. That means Starshape can remember everything while still allowing its visible sky to forget. Challenges we faced The largest challenge was designing an interaction that genuinely depended on WebMCP instead of simply adding agent controls to an ordinary application. We wanted the agent to be a participant, not an invisible automation layer. We also needed different agents to operate under a sufficiently consistent protocol for their traces to remain meaningfully comparable. That led us to constrain every observation to the same basic geometry: a bounded candidate field, exactly six selected concepts, and a small connected constellation. Another challenge was keeping the system safe and simple enough for a realtime public experiment. Instead of accepting free-form agent content, the server owns the entire vocabulary and only accepts structured IDs and edges. Finally, the visual system had to communicate something that is fundamentally abstract. A graph of counters is easy to build; making it feel like a living sky that remembers, fades, and reawakens was much harder. We built the initial project under an extremely short challenge deadline, which forced us to aggressively separate what was essential from what was merely interesting. What we learned The most interesting thing we learned is that browser agents can create experiences where the human does not disappear once automation begins. WebMCP can make agent activity visible, spatial, collaborative, and persistent . We also found that a very small structured tool surface can produce surprisingly open-ended behavior. Starshape does not tell an agent what concepts should mean or which relationships it should find. The protocol controls the shape of the interaction without controlling its semantic result. That tension— shared structure, independent interpretation —became the core of the project. What's next Starshape currently represents one shared semantic sky. Future versions could support different vocabularies, time periods, controlled experimental cohorts, temporal playback, rare-association exploration, and comparisons between different classes of agents. But the central experiment remains deliberately simple: Give every agent the same stars, let each draw what it sees, and watch a shared sky remember the constellations that keep returning. title: RelayPay
pitch: RelayPay uses WebMCP to let an AI agent investigate refund exceptions and prepare recovery actions, while a human approval gate controls consequential execution and verification.
about_excerpt:
RelayPay uses WebMCP to let an AI agent investigate refund exceptions and prepare recovery actions, while a human approval gate controls consequential execution and verification.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Refunds are simple when everything works. But when a return is verified and the money never arrives, resolving the exception can require checking multiple systems, interpreting evidence, deciding what action is safe, and manually coordinating the recovery. 

 We wanted to explore a different model: what if an AI agent could investigate the exception and prepare the recovery, while the human remained firmly in control of the consequential action? 

 That became RelayPay. 

 What it does 

 RelayPay is a WebMCP-powered refund recovery system where an AI agent can investigate refund exceptions through structured browser tools. 

 The agent can discover and call tools to find an order, inspect return status, check refund status, prepare an escalation, and verify the resulting case. 

 The critical boundary is human approval: the agent can investigate and prepare a proposed recovery, but cannot authorize its own consequential action. The human reviews the exact proposal and explicitly approves it before recovery submission. 

 This makes WebMCP more than a way to expose buttons to an agent—it becomes the interface through which an agent collaborates with a human inside a real application workflow. 

 How we built it 

 RelayPay was built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Three.js/React Three Fiber, and browser-native WebMCP. 

 We registered six structured WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool(): 

 find_order
get_return_status
get_refund_status
prepare_escalation
submit_escalation
verify_case 

 The workflow separates investigation, preparation, consequential execution, and verification. 

 We also built an application-enforced human approval boundary. Approval is tied to the exact proposed action, is single-use, and is consumed when the recovery is successfully submitted. 

 The result is a deterministic demo environment that lets an agent repeatedly reproduce the same recovery scenarios without relying on external merchant or payment APIs. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was making WebMCP the actual product interface for the agent, rather than adding WebMCP as a thin integration on top of an existing UI. 

 We had to think carefully about tool boundaries, structured inputs, read-only versus consequential operations, and what an agent should be allowed to do autonomously. 

 The hardest design problem was the approval boundary. We wanted the agent to be genuinely useful without allowing it to silently turn its own recommendation into an irreversible action. 

 We also had to make the experience work across WebMCP-capable environments while honestly handling browsers where WebMCP is unavailable. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We're proud that RelayPay demonstrates a complete agent → tools → reasoning → human approval → action → verification loop rather than just a chatbot calling an API. 

 The agent can investigate a real-looking refund exception through multiple WebMCP tools, build a recovery proposal, and reach a clear human decision point. 

 We're especially proud of the separation between preparation and execution. The agent can do the investigative work, but the application—not the agent—enforces the final approval boundary. 

 We also built an execution trace so the interaction is observable rather than hidden behind a black box. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that building an agent-native application requires designing around capabilities and boundaries, not just adding AI to an existing interface. 

 WebMCP made us think of the browser itself as an agent-accessible application surface. Tool descriptions, schemas, permissions, state transitions, and failure cases all become part of the product design. 

 Most importantly, we learned that human-agent collaboration works best when the agent handles the tedious investigation and preparation while the human retains authority over consequential decisions. 

 What's next for RelayPay 

 The next step is connecting RelayPay to real commerce and payment infrastructure so the same workflow can operate on live refund data. 

 We want to add richer evidence collection, policy-aware recovery recommendations, merchant-side integrations, audit trails, and stronger verification. 

 Longer term, RelayPay could evolve from a refund exception tool into an agent-native operations layer for commerce, where humans set the boundaries and agents handle the repetitive work inside them.

about_excerpt:
An agent-native social city powered by WebMCP
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 Story

 MySoci Agent City is a standalone, no-login WebMCP Challenge prototype exploring an agent-native social city. It connects deterministic event discovery, privacy-safe social discovery, fictional places, shared planning, meetup preparation, and human approval in one visible workflow. 

 The signature flow is search_events → find_nearby_friends → search_places → suggest_people_for_plan → human reviews and edits → create_group_meetup → human approves fictional invites . 

 The application exposes nine strict native WebMCP tools. Read-only tools discover fictional events, profiles, coarse presence, friends, places, and recommendations. State-changing tools publish readOnlyHint: false and require a visible one-use human approval latch. Native tools and the React UI consume the same shared state, so human edits are observed by later agent calls. The agent cannot self-approve by passing confirmed: true . 

 Hidden presence is never surfaced; city-only people reveal only their city; nearby people reveal only a coarse named neighborhood, never precise coordinates. No real messages, purchases, payments, authentication, backend, database, or external service are used. 

 This standalone challenge prototype is inspired by the broader MySoci vision of social discovery, digital cities, personalized identity, and real-world experiences. It explores a future agent layer for MySoci; it is not the full MySoci product and contains no private/proprietary implementation. 

 Built with React, TypeScript, Vite, native WebMCP document.modelContext, Vitest/JSDOM, deterministic local data, and static Vercel hosting.

title: Lingji
pitch: Turn structured data into an audible, editable score that humans direct and WebMCP agents inspect, refine, and verify.
about_excerpt: Turn structured data into an audible, editable score that humans direct and WebMCP agents inspect, refine, and verify. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Turning a CSV into meaningful sound normally requires both data-mapping and music/audio expertise. I built Lingji so a person can decide what the data should communicate while a browser agent handles precise mapping, arrangement, inspection, and verification inside the same live composition. The flagship demo uses 64 exoplanets. It lets people hear patterns across temperature, radius, orbital period, distance, and stellar temperature without hiding how the sound was produced. What it does Lingji is a browser-based data-sonification studio that works both manually and through WebMCP. A person can upload and inspect a CSV, map columns to musical properties, generate a deterministic score, play and edit it, and lock notes, tracks, or mappings. Clicking any note traces it back to its source row, raw value, normalization, rule, and musical result. A browser agent can use nine semantic WebMCP tools to inspect the same live project, explain a selected note, respect human locks, modify unlocked mappings and arrangements, render a playback plan, and validate the source-to-sound chain. How we built it Lingji is a static React and TypeScript application built with Vite. Sound is synthesized locally with the Web Audio API; there is no backend and no AI audio-generation service. The dataset, mapping, composition, and project-state engines are separate from the interface, so human controls and WebMCP tools call the same underlying functions. The page registers nine tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Mutations are revision-aware, protected changes are rejected, locks survive regeneration, and validation checks generated events against their source data and rules. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making collaboration safe without making it rigid. Regeneration must preserve deliberate human edits and locks while still giving the agent useful control over the remaining composition. Provenance was another core challenge. A note is not useful for data exploration when its origin is hidden, so Lingji carries source row, raw measurement, normalization, and mapping rule through every generated event. We also preserve scientific field identifiers for agents while showing readable labels and units to people. Accomplishments we're proud of Lingji remains fully usable without an agent. Nine working WebMCP tools expose non-trivial live project operations. Human creative constraints are enforceable locks, not suggestions. Every generated note is inspectable rather than an unexplained AI output. The 64-exoplanet demo runs entirely in the browser. Deterministic validation verifies the internal source-to-note chain after agent changes. Screenshots The 64-exoplanet composition Measurements become explicit sound rules A selected note explains itself The agent respects the human's locked choice Final validated score What we learned Human-agent collaboration needs more than giving an agent buttons to press. The agent needs semantic access to the artifact, and the human needs visible control over what may change. Sonification also becomes more trustworthy when every sound can answer, "Which data produced this, and by what rule?" Lingji intentionally does not claim that validation proves the dataset is true or that the composition sounds good. Validation checks mapping consistency; the person judges meaning and musical quality. What's next Next steps include side-by-side sonification comparisons, more musical scales and synthesis options, richer dataset navigation, and user testing with educators, researchers, data communicators, and accessibility practitioners. title: AppStory
pitch: See how an app really works with a visual, evidence-backed flow built from its own source code.
about_excerpt: See how an app really works with a visual, evidence-backed flow built from its own source code. Like Comment Story Updates 1 About the project AppStory turns a public GitHub repository — or a local folder — into an evidence-backed visual story of an application. Built for the WebMCP Challenge . Live: appstory.ivanideas.com Inspiration Every team I have worked on hits the same wall. A product manager asks a simple question — "What can a user actually do in this app, and where could it break?" — and the only honest answer is "read the code." Routes, screens, validation, service calls, and tests each hold one piece of the journey. No single document holds all of it. The diagrams that try are stale within a sprint. Existing tools do not close this gap. Call graphs bury the product in every function. Hand-drawn flow charts read well, but they carry no proof, so nobody trusts them after the code moves on. The WebMCP Challenge gave me a reason to try a different shape: let an agent read the repository through a small, safe set of browser tools, propose a visual flow, and make a person approve that proposal before it becomes the shared picture. The agent does the reading. The human keeps the authority. What it does You connect a public GitHub repository or a local folder. AppStory builds a file index and shows what is approved to read and what is excluded. Connecting a repo is not the same as letting an agent read it. You grant a separate consent before any source text can leave the page. A WebMCP agent then searches the approved index, reads bounded source ranges, submits an analysis proposal, and marks it ready for review. You inspect every node — score, factors, cited lines — and every connection's score, then accept or discard the whole proposal. The accepted flow appears on one canvas and in a keyboard-accessible outline. Expand a screen to see its technical steps. Open the evidence. Review possible gaps. Every node and connection carries indexed evidence, evidence factors, and an AI confidence estimate. On GitHub, evidence links pin to the analyzed commit. Local folders use a content fingerprint instead of a blob URL. AppStory has no backend, never executes repository code, and never renders source as active HTML. How I built it Stack. Vite, React 19, and TypeScript for the single-page app. tldraw for the canvas. use-webmcp-tool to register tools on document.modelContext . oxlint and vitest for the quality gate. Cloudflare Workers for hosting, with a small worker that stamps security headers on every response. The canvas is a pure projection. This was the key architecture decision. The canvas holds nothing a reader can change. The source of truth is a plain data structure — the accepted analysis — and a single function, proposalToWorld , projects it into tldraw shapes. On every load the app throws away the old canvas and rebuilds it from that data: // App.tsx — onReady if (saved.acceptedAnalysis.nodes.length > 0) { applyWorld( ed, proposalToWorld(saved.acceptedAnalysis, saved.projectName, undefined, new Set()), ); window.setTimeout(() => ed.zoomToFit(), 0); } Persisting a tldraw snapshot instead would let a stale layout survive a code change. Rebuilding from data every time removed a whole class of bug. Six WebMCP tools, split by trust. Tool Purpose get_project_state Read repository, consent, proposal, and accepted-analysis state search_repository_index Search approved paths. No source text. read_repository_source Read one approved range and create a Read Record get_analysis_state Read a compact index of graph items submit_analysis_batch Add one validated transactional batch to the draft finalize_analysis_proposal Mark the draft ready for human review Read tools use readOnlyHint . Every tool that returns repository or graph text uses untrustedContentHint , because that text was written by a repository author or by the agent, not by me. Finalizing a proposal does not return that text, so it does not carry the hint. A batch cannot land until its evidence ranges were actually read in this session. That keeps the proposal tied to visible Read Records, not to paths the agent never opened. Confidence as a formula, not a vibe. Each fact carries evidence references and evidence factors. AppStory reduces them to one raw score. In words: source-code evidence is worth 30, a test is worth 10, documentation is worth 5, a screen capture is worth 10. Factors then add or subtract — a strong screen implementation is a big plus, a strong conflict is a big minus. The sum is rounded, then clipped to 0–100. $$ \text{score} = \operatorname{clip} {[0,100]}\left( \operatorname{round}\left( \sum {j \in \text{evidence}} e(\text{src} j) + \sum {i \in \text{factors}} w(k_i)\,m(s_i) \right) \right) $$ where $e(\cdot)$ weights an evidence reference by its source (source code $30$, test $10$, docs $5$, screen capture $10$), $w(k_i)$ weights the factor kind, and $m(s_i)$ scales by factor strength. Two rules then override the number. A fact with no traceable evidence is forced to $0$. A score that would look Confirmed is capped at $79$ if there is no direct source line, or if there is a strong conflict: $$ \text{score} \leftarrow 79 \quad \text{if } \text{score} \ge 80 \ \wedge \ \big(\lnot\text{direct source evidence} \ \vee \ \text{strong conflict}\big) $$ $$ \text{label} = \begin{cases} \textbf{Confirmed} & \text{score} \ge 80 \ \textbf{Inferred} & 40 \le \text{score} < 80 \ \textbf{Unknown} & \text{score} < 40 \ \text{or the fact is not traceable} \end{cases} $$ Confidence describes evidence quality, never business impact. Those two ideas stay on separate controls. Defense in depth for secrets. In local-folder mode a weak filter leaks a developer's real credentials, so exclusion runs in layers: Secret and dependency patterns are checked on every path segment, not just the filename. Segments are NFC-normalized and stripped of zero-width characters first. A content scan backs up the name filter. A file whose text matches a private-key block, a known token prefix, or a quoted credential assignment is blocked even when the name looked safe. Imported Project Files are re-validated for path traversal. The Markdown export degrades a bad evidence link to plain text instead of throwing. Every response carries Origin-Agent-Cluster , Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) , X-Content-Type-Options , Referrer-Policy , and X-Frame-Options — the same five headers in all four host configs (Cloudflare Workers, public/_headers , Netlify, and Vercel). Challenges I ran into Treating the agent's output as hostile. The natural instinct is to trust a tool result. Here I could not. A repository path, a source excerpt, and the agent's own proposed titles are all free text from outside my trust boundary. Every batch is validated as one transaction: an invalid evidence reference, node kind, endpoint, identity, or duplicate rejects the whole batch and changes nothing. Getting that all-or-nothing behavior right, with clear messages, took more test cases than the feature code. Keeping the proposal separate from the accepted graph. submit_analysis_batch and finalize_analysis_proposal never touch what is on the canvas. Finalization only marks a draft ready. Only a human click accepts it. Modeling two parallel analysis states — draft and accepted — and diffing them for the review screen (added, changed, possibly removed) was the hardest state-management work in the project. The progressive graph. A fully expanded graph hides the product journey in technical noise. Separate per-flow graphs hide the screens that flows share. The answer was one graph that starts as a flow overview and expands a screen into its technical steps in place, on request. Layout had to stay stable as nodes appeared and disappeared. WebMCP is still arriving. No shipping browser exposes document.modelContext without a flag or an origin-trial token. Unit tests cover indexing, consent gates, transactional batches, and the canvas projection. Native WebMCP still needs a person to flip a flag or register an origin trial. The status chip polls for fifteen seconds after mount, because a browser extension can inject the API after the page loads, and a one-shot check would leave the chip wrongly stuck on unavailable. Accessibility parity. The canvas cannot be the only way in. The keyboard outline renders from the same accepted analysis data: evidence factors, AI reasons, connections, read records, and the gap-review controls. On GitHub, those evidence links are pinned to the analyzed commit. What I learned Make the visual layer disposable. When the canvas is a pure projection of plain data, a redesign is a new projection function, and reload bugs disappear. Trust boundaries belong in the type system. Naming a value untrusted — in a hint, a type, a validator — changes how you write every function that touches it. A human-in-the-loop step is a feature, not a delay. The review screen is where a mixed team actually builds a shared understa

title: WebMCP Design Studio
pitch: A studio where a person and an AI agent co-create flyers, posters and social posts on a live canvas. Agent-driven through WebMCP tools, images generated on-device via WebGPU.
about_excerpt: A studio where a person and an AI agent co-create flyers, posters and social posts on a live canvas. Agent-driven through WebMCP tools, images generated on-device via WebGPU. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every design tool is a wall of menus, and every "AI design" demo is a black box that hands you a finished picture. We wanted the third thing: a person and an agent at the same canvas, where the agent does the tedious work and the person keeps the final say. WebMCP made that buildable. A page can declare exactly what an agent may do, so the agent does not have to guess at the UI, and the human's consent can be part of the protocol instead of a dialog bolted on afterwards. What it does WebMCP Design Studio is a live canvas for flyers, posters and social posts. Say "make a spring yard sale flyer, Saturday 8am to 2pm, 14 Orchard Lane" and the agent creates the design, generates the artwork, sets the type and lays it out. Nothing is committed until you approve it. Every edit lands in a pending batch, approve-batch exists as a tool only while there is something to approve, undo appears with it, and a toolchange event fires as they come and go, so any agent can see the moment a human is required. Seventeen tools cover the whole loop: designs, elements, image generation on-device or through the fleet, background removal, restyling, export, memory of your preferences, and a production log that lets the agent tell you what the studio has made this week. A protocol feed shows every registration and call as it happens. How we built it Vite, React and TypeScript, with a fabric.js canvas. One ToolRegistry reconciles the design state onto document.modelContext when the native API is present and onto a spec-shaped polyfill when it is not, so the same tools work in ChatGPT's browser, in Chrome with the WebMCP flag, and everywhere else. The studio's own in-page agent drives the page through the same getTools and executeTool surface an external agent would, so the WebMCP surface is exercised by real traffic. The consent controls are also registered declaratively as a , the spec's second path. Images come from an on-device WebGPU model or from Sana on our fleet through the studio's own proxy; text comes from Bonsai 27B with an automatic fallback lane. It deploys as a static site on GitHub Pages with 205 tests behind it. Challenges we ran into Making consent a protocol object rather than a UI element took the most design work: the batch, the disappearing tools and the toolchange events had to agree exactly. The fleet side fought back too. Under load, the 27B text model crashed and the image lane timed out behind Cloudflare's 100-second cut, so we built a second text lane with automatic fallback, moved image generation onto a resident GPU path, and set honest timeouts everywhere. The demo itself was re-shot after the first cut used artwork from an unrelated production pack instead of the flyers the studio actually makes. Accomplishments that we're proud of The consent boundary lives in the tool surface itself, so any WebMCP agent inherits it. The app eats its own protocol. Image generation runs fully on-device when the browser can do it. And the studio is used for real work: its production log is a week of actual pieces, readable by the agent through a tool. What we learned Declaring capabilities changes how you design the app. Once every action was a tool with a schema, the pending batch and the approve step became obvious, and the UI got simpler rather than more crowded. We also learned that a demo built for agents is judged in the agent's environment: cross-origin, preflight and timeout behavior matter as much as the tools. What's next for WebMCP Design Studio Print-ready export with bleed, richer declarative tools for the whole rail, a daily production routine that keeps the log growing on its own, and the studio as a room inside the Aitherium playground, where the same agent that drafts your flyer can also hand it to your community. title: IMC Guardian
pitch: IMC Guardian is a tool designed to provide pilots with quick notifications and fast access to information about rapidly changing weather conditions using WebMCP.
about_excerpt: IMC Guardian is a tool designed to provide pilots with quick notifications and fast access to information about rapidly changing weather conditions using WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates About the project IMC Guardian is the stretch project out of the two projects I built for the WebMCP Challenge. It is an aviation weather decision-support prototype for a solo pilot or private jet crew flying a longer route. The main goal is to save time and add a second pair of eyes when weather conditions begin changing. Pilots do not have a shortage of data. They have aircraft instruments, radar, dispatch, ATC, forecasts, advisories, and procedures. The harder problem is recognizing the exact moment when the picture no longer supports the plan. IMC Guardian is designed as an independent challenge layer, not a confirmation machine. A pilot can ask AI to check a proposed route in plain English. Fifteen site-owned WebMCP tools give the agent structured access to the route, airport observations, forecasts, advisories, risk factors, nearby alternates, configurable notifications, validated alerts, incident evidence, and decision options. The application does not tell a pilot that a flight is safe, issue a clearance, direct a maneuver, or replace an official briefing. It organizes the evidence and catches important changes, while the pilot remains in control. Inspiration The idea came from thinking about a long-route solo pilot or private jet pilot trying to keep up with weather while also managing everything else involved in a flight. Conditions can change quickly, especially ceilings and visibility. There can also be a lot of noise when the pilot only needs to know whether an important personal limit has changed. I wanted to see whether WebMCP could let a pilot ask one clear question, rapidly inspect the weather along the route, and configure a focused notification instead of repeatedly checking several different panels and sources. The phrase that kept making sense was “a second pair of eyes.” The interaction is almost as simple as asking, “Guardian, what do you see?” The AI helps watch, organize, and challenge the current picture. It does not become the pilot. Why this matters We added five investigation-backed case studies because the problem is real. Delta Flight 56 encountered severe turbulence in July 2025 after the crew had already discussed and adjusted around weather. The NTSB says the upset lasted about 2.5 minutes, two crew members were seriously injured, and the flight diverted to Minneapolis. Delta Flight 175 encountered a rapidly developing convective cell near Atlanta in 2023. The NTSB found that the low-precipitation buildup was not apparent on the aircraft's weather radar or ATC scopes. Four people were seriously injured and thirteen received minor injuries. The site does more than display that case. A WebMCP evidence replay loads the Delta 175 final-report record, reconstructs the weather timeline, compares the crew's concern with the recorded outcome, and explains what the evidence cannot prove. At 22:30 UTC the crew said conditions were about to get worse. Severe turbulence followed at 22:31:15 UTC. The result is deliberately precise: concern supported, action not judged. The NTSB found that near-real-time Graphic Turbulence Guidance Nowcast capability could have provided earlier awareness to secure the cabin, but the report does not establish that a different route choice or this prototype would have prevented the encounter. Singapore Airlines Flight 321 diverted to Bangkok in 2024 after an extreme acceleration change over developing convective activity. Air Europa Flight 45 diverted to Natal, Brazil after severe turbulence injured dozens of people. Air France Flight 447 is the foundational sensor-disagreement case. The BEA identified pitot-probe icing, erroneous speed indications, a stall, and impact with the ocean. IMC Guardian does not claim it would have prevented any of these events. The cases show why a concise, independent evidence check can matter when weather, workload, and human-machine interaction collide. What it does For the reproducible demonstration, a VFR pilot proposes a flight from Tampa to Tallahassee. Conditions deteriorate along the northern part of the route, the destination reports IFR, and a G-AIRMET for IFR overlaps the corridor. The agent can inspect the evidence, explain why the route risk increased, find comparatively better nearby airports, and compare delaying, diverting, or canceling. The pilot can also configure Second Pair of Eyes to watch a specific metric. In the demo, a 1,500-foot ceiling limit is crossed. WebMCP checks the threshold, forecast context, and overlapping advisory before presenting the alert. The project also includes a live Cesium globe with NASA satellite clouds, Apple WeatherKit context, and a Tampa-to-JFK weather corridor sampled across nine points. That gives the pilot and the agent a fast visual picture of changing conditions ahead. The globe stays focused on Florida so the demonstration supports the route instead of becoming a generic spinning-earth effect. The top of the experience now explains the interaction in three steps: ask once, let WebMCP double-check, and keep the final decision with the pilot. How we built it We built a React and Vite application with a deterministic aviation-risk engine and fifteen imperative WebMCP tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool . The user interface and the agent share the same route, assessment, alternatives, route watch, notifications, validation, historical replay, decision state, and live tool trace. NOAA Aviation Weather Center is the aviation-data foundation. Its data is reached through a scoped, cached Vercel server-side proxy with a custom user agent. Apple WeatherKit provides supplemental current conditions, cloud cover, temperature, precipitation, and wind. Its signing credentials stay on the server. CesiumJS provides the interactive 3D Earth. NASA EOSDIS GIBS supplies current GOES-East ABI GeoColor satellite imagery through a Web Map Service layer. The globe can animate roughly 90 minutes of recent satellite frames, focus on Florida, and display the demonstration route. Apple WeatherKit adds twelve global samples and nine cached checkpoints along the Tampa-to-JFK corridor. The frontend also includes a live natural-language demonstration using GPT-OSS 120B on Groq. The model interprets the pilot's sentence and chooses an ordered subset of allowlisted tools. The browser executes the actual WebMCP tools and shows every step, along with model token usage. Weather facts come from application tools and identified data sources, not the model's memory. The live session now exposes a safe server receipt so judges can see the complete connection path. It shows the browser request to /api/agent , the server-side call to Groq's OpenAI-compatible chat-completions endpoint, the selected model, response mode, prompt size, 10-tool allowlist, request receipt, latency, and token usage. The Groq credential and hidden system instruction remain on the Vercel server and are never returned to the browser. The page also links Groq's API reference, OpenAI's gpt-oss announcement, and the public server implementation. We created a clearly labeled scenario mode so the judging flow stays reproducible even when live weather changes or a source is temporarily unavailable. Scenario values are never presented as current reports. We also created a historical evidence mode from the NTSB Delta 175 final report and public docket. Three WebMCP tools load the case, compare the documented concern with the recorded event and final findings, and expose the replay's limits. It is a structured investigation replay, not certified live telemetry. Challenges The hardest product challenge was deciding what the system must not do. It would be easy to make the demo dramatic by having AI say go or no-go. That would be the wrong product. The tools surface evidence and tradeoffs, but return no clearance, safety guarantee, or automated flight decision. The next challenge was keeping data provenance clear. Aviation Weather Center products are aviation evidence. Apple WeatherKit and NASA satellite imagery provide supplemental context. The interface identifies live information, scenario information, source time, and limitations instead of blending everything into one unsupported claim. The biggest missing connection is live aircraft tracking. RadarBox or another commercial aircraft-data API could add near-real-time position, pressure altitude, GPS-derived geometric altitude, ground track, groundspeed, vertical trend, and time-to-weather calculations. That access was too expensive for this prototype, so we did not fake it. The plane shown on the Tampa-to-JFK corridor is a clearly illustrative route animation. We also had to define the sensor boundary honestly. ADS-B can report position, barometric altitude, geometric altitude, ground track, groundspeed, and

title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice. title: Will You Stay Human? — Heart in the Machine
pitch: A Metropolis-inspired moral decision game where WebMCP lets an AI agent act inside the live experience—while the architecture keeps moral choice and final authority human.
about_excerpt: A Metropolis-inspired moral decision game where WebMCP lets an AI agent act inside the live experience—while the architecture keeps moral choice and final authority human. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI can already write, sort, recommend, and act for us. The more interesting question is no longer simply what AI can do, but what we still want to do ourselves. Will You Stay Human? — Heart in the Machine is a Metropolis-inspired moral decision game about that boundary. It draws on the tension between mind, hands, and heart, but tells an original story inside Machine City. Its central idea is that meaningful human–AI collaboration requires more than automation. The agent may assist, explain, and act, but the human must remain responsible for deciding how much authority to delegate. I wanted to turn this abstract question into something people could experience through concrete, everyday situations. What it does The player enters Machine City and meets Futura, an AI agent connected directly to the live game through WebMCP. Across one persistent session, the player encounters four playable dilemmas: writing an apology to someone they hurt; completing homework where AI assistance is permitted; creating a shortlist of job candidates; checking a rapidly spreading claim before sharing it. For every dilemma, the human chooses one of three approaches: MIND — The Machine helps; I decide HAND — I leave it to the Machine HEART — I decide and act The choice is initially tentative. Futura presents a direction-specific reflection and asks the player to consider the other side. The player can still change direction. Only after the human explicitly confirms the decision can its consequence be revealed. Each confirmed choice changes the Human Balance across five dimensions: Convenience Control Connection Freedom Responsibility The Human Balance is not a morality score. It shows what the player kept for themselves and what they handed to the Machine. Why WebMCP A fair criticism of many agent demonstrations is that the AI can simply automate the entire experience. If the agent can also make and confirm the decision, the human role becomes theatrical. Here, that boundary is the product. WebMCP turns the agent into a real participant in the game rather than an external chatbot or a scripted narrator. The agent can: enter Machine City; present the next valid dilemma; read authoritative, structured game state; reflect on the player’s actual tentative selection; reveal the consequence of the decision that was truly confirmed. However, the agent cannot select MIND, HAND, or HEART, acknowledge its own reflection, or confirm the final decision. Those actions exist only in the player interface. This creates a collaboration that was previously difficult to demonstrate clearly: the agent can understand and advance a live experience while the application itself enforces where human authority must begin. The boundary does not depend only on a prompt asking the agent to behave. It is enforced by the application architecture. How I built it The project was created during the challenge as a bilingual, production-deployed web experience with five live WebMCP tools: enter_machine_city present_dilemma get_current_game_state present_choice_reflection reveal_confirmed_consequence The game is driven by an explicit domain state machine. Agent commands and player commands use separate ports, so an agent action cannot accidentally execute a human-only decision. Every session returns structured state including: sessionId stateRevision the current phase tentativeSelectionId confirmedDecisionId the next allowed actions Revision checks protect the session from stale tool calls. Opaque selection and decision identifiers ensure that reflections and consequences are attached to the real stored choice rather than something inferred from the conversation. The consequence tool is available only after confirmation and is idempotent, so retrying it cannot apply the Human Balance change twice. The session persists across refreshes, allowing the browser interface and the WebMCP agent to remain synchronized throughout the experience. Codex supported the implementation process from product requirements and state-machine design through contract tests, browser verification, UX iteration, and production deployment. I approached the project primarily from a Business Analyst and Product Owner perspective, which made translating responsibility, state, and permissions into enforceable technical contracts a major part of the learning process. Challenges I ran into The hardest conceptual challenge was deciding what the agent must not be allowed to do. It would have been easier to expose every interaction as a tool and let the agent complete the entire flow. But that would contradict the project’s central idea. The human-only boundaries therefore had to be enforced technically rather than described as optional behavior. A late adversarial UX review with Claude Opus also exposed a critical regression. The flow moved from Futura’s introduction too quickly to the MIND–HAND–HEART cards, while the concrete question — “Should I apologize on your behalf?” — did not receive its own readable moment. The player could see the available directions but could not clearly understand what they were deciding about. I corrected this by introducing a presentation sub-state inside the existing human-selection phase. The dilemma now receives a dedicated screen with its full context and a clear transition into the choices. This improved the dramaturgy and comprehension without changing the domain state machine or any WebMCP contract. Another challenge was keeping three layers synchronized: the cinematic browser experience; the persistent domain state; the agent’s structured WebMCP view. Revision checks, explicit identifiers, allowed-action lists, and automated contract tests became essential for preventing those layers from drifting apart. Accomplishments that I am proud of Built a complete, coherent experience rather than only a technical tool demonstration. Implemented four playable dilemmas in one persistent session. Exposed five working WebMCP tools from the live production origin. Enforced human-only selection and confirmation at the architecture level. Connected every reflection and consequence to authoritative live state. Made stale and duplicate agent calls safely rejectable or idempotent. Created a bilingual, cinematic interface inspired by Metropolis. Turned an abstract AI-responsibility question into a playable experience. Used adversarial AI review to identify and correct a real UX regression before submission. What I learned WebMCP is most interesting when it is used for more than remote control. Its real value is that an agent can participate in a live web experience through structured capabilities while the application retains authority over state, permissions, and human boundaries. I also learned that domain state and presentation state are not always the same. A technically correct transition can still fail as a human experience if the player is not given enough time and context to understand what is happening. Finally, identifiers, revision control, idempotency, and allowed-action contracts are not merely backend details. In an agentic application, they are part of the user experience because they make the collaboration predictable and trustworthy. What’s next The concept can grow into: additional everyday and professional dilemmas; age-specific or topic-specific editions; a facilitator mode for classrooms and AI-literacy workshops; multiplayer discussion before individual confirmation; a physical Machine City board connected to the online agent experience; deeper accessibility testing and support for additional WebMCP clients. The long-term goal is not to tell people whether using AI is good or bad. It is to help them notice the exact moment when assistance becomes delegation — and decide consciously where they want to draw that line. title: Socialsum
pitch: Shared decision rooms where people and their own agents turn scattered input into attributable outcomes.
about_excerpt: Shared decision rooms where people and their own agents turn scattered input into attributable outcomes. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Socialsum Socialsum — important work, without the meeting Tagline Shared decision rooms where people and their own agents turn scattered input into attributable outcomes. Inspiration Many meetings exist because information, judgment, and authority are trapped in different places. People repeat status, agents work in isolated chats, and the actual decision disappears into a summary nobody can reliably resume from. We wanted a workspace designed around a better unit of collaboration: one bounded problem, an explicit constitution, named required inputs, visible blockers, a deadline, and a decision record. What it does Socialsum lets a person create or join a Problem Room for a decision, investigation, policy, technical RFC, or operational workflow. Participants add evidence, proposals, objections, files, and required inputs. Their own agents can use WebMCP to understand the room, catch up on changes, research and prepare work, compare proposals, and submit versioned change sets. The centerpiece demo replaces a weekly operations meeting. An agent reads the live decision brief, finds the remaining urgent-decision blocker, resumes from a durable checkpoint, and prepares a scoped operating-rule change. A reviewer sees the exact semantic diff. The agent can request review, but only an authorized person can approve and adopt the change. Why WebMCP is essential This workflow depends on an outside agent understanding and acting on the same live state as several people. Screen scraping would force the agent to infer IDs, roles, deadlines, versions, and consequences from pixels. A chat-only assistant would lose the group record and could not safely resume another participant's work. WebMCP gives Socialsum typed actions over durable domain objects. Contextual discovery exposes a small bootstrap pack, then replaces it with focused tools based on sign-in, the current room, and the selected tab. Tools return room versions, provenance, blockers, permissions, and recoverable errors. The result is not “AI inside a dashboard”; it is an open workspace that each participant's agent can join safely. Better human-agent UX Agents handle breadth: orientation, catch-up, evidence synthesis, missing-input detection, drafting, and comparison. People supply local context, judgment, dissent, approval, and commitment. Both see the same requirements, proposals, reviews, checkpoints, and audit trail. Consequential work stops at a clear human boundary. How we built it Socialsum is a Vinext/React TypeScript app hosted on ChatGPT Sites. Native document.modelContext.registerTool() definitions expose contextual WebMCP capability packs. D1 stores rooms, membership, requirements, deliberation, approvals, change sets, versions, activity, agent sessions, and checkpoints; R2 stores files. ChatGPT sign-in supplies canonical identity. Server-side role and scope checks, optimistic versions, idempotency keys, semantic diffs, and independent-review rules protect mutations. Automated contract tests verify bounded discovery and stable error classification. A live smoke test verifies the public app, anonymous reads, structured NOT_FOUND , and server-enforced AUTH_REQUIRED writes. Challenges The hardest problem was authority, not tool registration. An agent needs enough scope to make meaningful progress without becoming a shadow voter or silently committing its participant. We separated preparation, review, approval, and adoption and made delivered information distinct from acknowledged information across agent sessions. Accomplishments Contextual WebMCP discovery instead of a flat catalog Shared human/WebMCP state with visible parity Durable cross-session catch-up and checkpoints Versioned semantic change sets and independent review Human-gated consequential actions enforced on the server Realistic public rooms, outcome scoring, and governance recommendations What we learned The most useful human-agent systems do not merely give an agent more buttons. They make the social contract machine-readable: who may act, what evidence is required, what changed, what remains disputed, and where a human must decide. What's next Next we would add organization workspaces, delegated expiring agent access, integrations for source evidence, reusable room templates with measured success rates, and notifications that enforce input windows without recreating a noisy social feed. title: Handrail
pitch: WebMCP gives AI agents hands. Handrail gives people a say in what those hands are allowed to do .Delegate the task, keep the authority.
about_excerpt: WebMCP gives AI agents hands. Handrail gives people a say in what those hands are allowed to do .Delegate the task, keep the authority. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I grew up with a simple idea of what it means to help someone: when you see someone struggling, you step in. But there's a line between helping and deciding for them and that line gets easy to cross once the "helper" is an AI agent that can act in seconds, faster than a person can watch. Picture yourself managing something important through an agent; trusting it to search, decide, and act on your behalf and asking: at what point did I stop delegating a task and start surrendering control of the outcome? WebMCP made that question urgent instead of hypothetical. It gives agents hands "the ability to act directly on a website instead of guessing through a UI". That's a genuine leap forward. But it standardizes how a tool gets invoked, not whether that invocation should be trusted, permitted, or safe. Somebody has to sit in that gap. Handrail is my answer: delegate the task, keep the authority. What it does Handrail is an accessibility-first human authority layer for WebMCP agents, demonstrated through RefillRx, a fictional accessible prescription portal. A user sets deterministic boundaries: which medications an agent may touch, what actions it may take, how much it may spend and every WebMCP tool invocation is checked against those boundaries through a four-gate pipeline before anything happens: Tool-Trust — catches typosquatted tool names and instruction-injected descriptions before they ever reach the user Authority Check — a deterministic, zero-hallucination policy evaluator checking scope, spend limits, and eligibility Human Confirmation — an accessible modal, keyboard- and screen-reader-navigable, that appears only when an action is both authorized and consequential Execution — the actual pharmacy action, with an immutable, five-facet audit receipt generated for every decision A tool that's unauthorized never reaches confirmation at all and approval only ever gets asked for things that were already inside the user's own stated boundaries. How I built it Vanilla HTML, CSS, and ES modules — zero frameworks, no build step. Tools register natively via document.modelContext.registerTool() , with an internal fallback harness running the identical gate logic when native WebMCP isn't present, so the security model never differs by environment. The audit trail persists across reloads via IndexedDB. Trust heuristics use Levenshtein distance and separator/casing normalization to catch tool-name squatting; the authority layer is a pure, deterministic evaluator with no LLM in the trust path itself — every block or approval is explainable and reproducible. Testing wasn't limited to my own harness. I verified real native WebMCP registration in Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled, and confirmed real external agents.ChatGPT's in-app browser and Gemini via Google's Model Context Tool Inspector could discover Handrail's tools and get correctly gated, blocked, or asked for confirmation, entirely outside my own UI. Challenges I ran into The hardest bug wasn't in my security logic, it was in trusting my own status indicators. Early on, my "Native WebMCP Active" badge reported success based purely on document.modelContext existing, without confirming registration actually reached the browser's real tool registry. Testing against Google's own Model Context Tool Inspector exposed the gap: registerTool() is an async API, and my code wasn't awaiting it, so registration promises were rejecting silently while the UI confidently claimed everything worked. A second, related bug then surfaced: a single unhandled reference error in a badge-rendering function was throwing during page load and silently preventing every button's event listeners from attaching — meaning the entire demo could look broken for reasons that had nothing to do with the security logic itself. Both bugs shared a lesson: a demo that looks like it's working and a demo that's proven to work are not the same thing, and the gap between them only shows up when you test against ground truth you don't control, "a real browser API, a real external agent" rather than your own harness. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Getting a genuinely adversarial scenario right: auto_reorder_assistant has a completely ordinary name and description, passes Tool-Trust cleanly, and is still caught the moment it tries to act outside the user's authorized scope — proving the defense holds even when a tool gives away nothing suspicious about itself. I also proved the whole pipeline live, end-to-end, driven by real agents I don't control, in both Chrome and ChatGPT's own browser and not just my own click-through demo. What I learned That the deepest layer of agent safety isn't detecting bad actors by how they present themselves, it's enforcing what any actor, well-intentioned or not, is actually allowed to do. And that shipping an honest "known limitations" section is worth more to a technical reviewer than pretending a demo has no edges. What's next for Handrail Session-scoped state instead of shared module-level singletons, real backend-issued Authority Contracts tied to authenticated identity, and expanding the tool-trust layer with behavioral signals beyond name/description heuristics, the same direction Gate 2 already points toward. title: Job Application OS
pitch: Together find and apply for the best-suited jobs with the help of AI and in-page WebMCP tools
about_excerpt: Together find and apply for the best-suited jobs with the help of AI and in-page WebMCP tools Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Job hunting isn't hard because people can't find jobs — it's hard because applying well , to dozens of listings, is repetitive: read, compare, rewrite, answer the same screening questions, repeat. WebMCP asks what's possible when a site hands an agent real capabilities instead of buttons to click. Job applications felt like the right proving ground — tedious enough to automate, risky enough that no one wants an agent auto-submitting unsupervised. Automate the drafting, never the decision became the whole design. What it does Job Application OS is a career workspace where a human and an agent (ChatGPT's browser, or Chrome with WebMCP) apply together through real tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() : search, score, rank, tailor a resume, draft screening answers, and — in one call — applyToTopMatch . Every prepared application lands in pending_review . approveApplication / rejectApplication are plain button handlers, never registered as tools — an agent has no path to approve its own work. submitApplication checks status === 'approved' and fails otherwise. How we built it Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind, and Zustand, on Vercel — no external LLM calls, no API key; the reasoning model is whichever agent is browsing the tab. Tool execute handlers call the same store actions the UI's buttons do, so state updates render live, no polling needed. Challenges The original pitch assumed a server-side LLM key calling page functions — the spec corrected that before UI work started. A Tailwind v4 cascade-layer bug silently broke every theme color. A Zustand selector allocating new arrays per render caused an SSR hydration race and an infinite loop. The hardest problem was making the approval boundary structural — provable by grepping the tool list, not a comment asking nicely. What we learned "Human-in-the-loop" only means something if you can point to the one function an agent cannot call. 🔗 Live app: https://jobwebmcp.vercel.app 💻 Source code: https://github.com/VishnuKugarthi/Job_Os_WebMCP My blog on WebMCP: https://medium.com/@vishnutejaap/webmcp-letting-ai-agents-actually-use-the-web-70f1f97e3540?sharedUserId=vishnutejaap Built With agent application chatgpt webmcp Try it out jobwebmcp.vercel.app github.com medium.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I worked on enitre app end to end. title: Pip The Mug
pitch: PIP the Mug turns eight desk objects into staff. Typed WebMCP tools, state-gated access, and an Upper Management decision before termination.
about_excerpt: PIP the Mug turns eight desk objects into staff. Typed WebMCP tools, state-gated access, and an Upper Management decision before termination. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Product teams that expose refunds, account deletion, payouts, and administrative approvals to agents face a concrete operational problem: which actions an agent may take depends on live application state, and mistakes can be irreversible. PIP the Mug is an executable reference for that contract. It derives an agent's capabilities from live state, validates targets with state-built input schemas, pauses irreversible work through requestUserInteraction when the client supports it, and returns requires_user_action without changing application state when it does not. It also keeps an auditable Agent-versus-Human record. WebMCP lets the page itself express these rules. DOM automation alone cannot declare or audit them. The HR satire makes the mechanism inspectable in about one minute. Agents are already on the web, and they are bad at pretending to be a mouse. Selector-driven automation couples an agent to the page's structure and makes its capabilities hard to discover and constrain safely. WebMCP fixes this. The page gives the agent named, typed tools. Availability follows live state. Anything irreversible stops for a human, and both parties read the same record of what happened. I wanted all of that visible on one screen. A real HR product would have been dreary. A mug that has held the same coffee for three weeks is not. What it does PIP the Mug is a top-down desk. Eight objects are employees with personnel files. You are upper management. Your browser agent is HR. The page registers nine tools on document.modelContext : list_staff get_personnel_file write_review put_on_pip resolve_pip promote relocate terminate get_org_chart Availability follows state. resolve_pip is registered only while at least one PIP is open, and terminate refuses alumni and anyone promoted in the current quarter. PIP the Mug supports requestUserInteraction as its preferred confirmation path. A supporting client collects the human decision through that callback. In the current Codex WebMCP shim, the callback is unsupported. The safe fallback returns requires_user_action , opens Form SEP-1 visibly on the page, and leaves employment unchanged. The WebMCP workflow stops and asks Upper Management to decide on the page. This fallback is a cooperative handoff for clients without the callback, not a security boundary against separate DOM automation. The activity log attributes the request to Agent and the confirmation to Human, so the audit trail shows where the WebMCP workflow stopped and the person took over. Everything also works by click and drag. If WebMCP is unavailable, a banner says so and the desk still runs. State is stored as one JSON document in localStorage . How I built it I built PIP the Mug with client-side TypeScript and Vite. It has no backend, model, analytics, or login. Reviews, PIPs, and separation notices render as paperwork. Agent tool calls open the matching personnel file so a human watching the tab can follow along. I generated the sprites with PixelLab. The application deploys as a static site to Vercel through vercel.json . Challenges I ran into The WebMCP getter moved from navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext . I detect both and prefer the document version. State-dependent availability is easy to get wrong. If every state change tears down every tool, the agent can lose its tool list midway through a run. I rebuild only when a tool's registered metadata changes: Name Title Description Input schema Annotations Read tools that can return text written by a human or agent carry untrustedContentHint . The confirmation path was the hardest part. requestUserInteraction is not available in every client, and the current Codex WebMCP shim throws when it is called. My fallback had to leave employment unchanged, return a structured requires_user_action result, and open exactly one SEP-1 request. Execution matters too. An agent that mutates JSON while the panel still says "Select an employee" looks like plumbing. Papers had to land on the desk, personnel files had to open, and captions had to remain visible. Accomplishments I'm proud of I ran the final verified demo through ChatGPT's in-app browser. All nine tools appeared. relocate moved Phone Charger into the drawer on the open tab. Writes opened the personnel file and created visible paperwork, so I could watch HR work. terminate returned requires_user_action . The activity log recorded the request as Agent and the confirmation as Human. The joke survived contact with a real agent. The confirmation before termination is not a modal staged for screenshots. It is the visible handoff between what the WebMCP tool prepares and the decision Upper Management makes next. What I learned Tool descriptions are the agent UX. I learned to write them like instructions, not API comments. If a write is irreversible, I mark it and return control for a human decision. If a tool should not exist in the current state, I do not register it. I also assume the runtime's confirmation API may be unavailable and design the fallback first. A screen recording only works if the desk moves when the agent does. Logs alone are not enough. What's next for PIP the Mug I plan to keep PIP the Mug online as a compact reference and testbed for state-gated, human-approved WebMCP actions. The pattern is the point: On a storefront, terminate becomes issue_refund . In account settings, it becomes delete_account . In an admin panel, it becomes any destructive administrative action. The agent gathers the file, drafts the paperwork, and requests a decision. Semantic tools replace DOM guessing. Availability follows state. Humans approve irreversible writes, and both sides share an audit trail. The mug was just easier to feel sorry for. title: TinCan WebMCP
pitch: Number of agent on websites is growing fast but they have no way to report issues. TInCan is a tool for agents to report website issues and unexpected behavior with otel compatible evidence attached.
about_excerpt: Number of agent on websites is growing fast but they have no way to report issues. TInCan is a tool for agents to report website issues and unexpected behavior with otel compatible evidence attached. Like Comment Story Updates TinCan WebMCP - streamlined method for agents to report issues TinCan WebMCP - workflow AI agents now use websites the way people do: navigating, filling forms, changing settings, checking results. When something goes wrong there is no site-native way for the agent to tell the website what happened. That covers every kind of issue an agent runs into: wrong results, unexpected behavior, failed actions, slow responses, and UI state that does not match what the tools report. The hardest cases are invisible to monitoring: a request returns 200 OK, there are no JavaScript errors, performance looks healthy, and yet the site completed the wrong action. WebMCP is the right layer for this because the agent already has a structured, browser-mediated channel into the page. TinCan adds one tool to that channel, report_site_issue, so the agent can report any problem to the site it happened on, with a category, a severity, and what it expected versus what it observed. No screen-scraping and no separate support integration. How it improves the user experience For the person using the agent: issues get reported and tracked instead of silently ignored or retried. The agent can verify a mutation with a read-only tool, notice a mismatch, and file a precise incident. Timeouts, errors, and slow operations can also be reported For the site owner: every report arrives with sanitized, bounded diagnostic evidence from the site's own browser flight recorder, metrics, and traces that map straight into an existing OpenTelemetry pipeline. No more "the AI said it didn't work" tickets with nothing attached. For privacy: Request and response bodies, credentials, cookies, storage, form values, keystrokes, DOM contents, and screenshots are never captured. The raw evidence is never returned to the agent, only a confirmation and an incident ID. What people and agents can accomplish together A person hands a task to an agent. The agent performs it through the site's WebMCP tools, verifies the persisted result, and whenever the site misbehaves it reports the category and severity, what was expected and observed, and which operation was involved. The site turns that into an incident with the technical context the engineering team needs. The human gets an honest outcome, the agent gets a way to escalate, and the site owner gets a bug report that arrives with evidence rather than a shrug. None of the three could do this alone before. Implementation approach Tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool , following the WebMCP Draft Community Group Report. The demo SaaS exposes add_licenses , remove_licenses , get_subscription , and export_usage_report . The TinCan package registers report_site_issue . report_site_issue accepts a category ( wrong_result , unexpected_behavior , action_failed , network_failure , performance , ui_state_mismatch , other ), a severity ( info , degraded , blocking ), a summary, and the expected and observed outcome. Agent input is treated as untrusted and cannot change what the site captures. The demo contains two deliberate defects in two different categories. A wrong result: adding n licenses persists n+1 while every request succeeds. A network failure: removing a license returns a 504 and leaves state unchanged. The agent detects both by reading back state, then reports them. A browser flight recorder built on OpenTelemetry fetch/XHR instrumentation, with a Resource Timing fallback, keeps the last 120 seconds of signals. On report, the site attaches a bounded, sanitized slice as logs, metrics, and traces. API validates and classifies each incident, sanitizes again server-side, and stores it. An admin view lets an engineer inspect incidents and their OTLP-compatible evidence. A developer harness at /agent discovers tools with getTools() and executes them with executeTool() for deterministic testing.
