title: GuacaDoc
pitch: GuacaDoc lets an AI agent work on a confidential document without ever receiving a single name, account number or address from it.
about_excerpt: GuacaDoc lets an AI agent work on a confidential document without ever receiving a single name, account number or address from it. Like 1 Comment Story Updates GuacaDoc Homepage GuacaDoc — Devpost submission text Inspiration There is a whole class of documents you cannot hand to an AI. A client contract, a patient record, an unsigned deal. You have the analysis problem, the tool that could solve it, and no right to hand over the file. What struck me is that the constraint is not really about privacy. It is about what an agent actually needs in order to be useful . An agent reasoning about a liability clause does not need to know the counterparty is Marceline Dubreuil. It needs to know that the party in section 2 is the party in section 7. That is a structural fact, not an identity. Separate those two and the impossible task becomes possible: the agent gets the substance, never the identities. WebMCP is what makes that separation enforceable rather than aspirational, because the tools run in the page, next to the person who owns the document. What it does GuacaDoc opens a document in your tab, parses it there (TXT, MD, PDF, DOCX), scans it locally for identifying values, and turns it into five WebMCP tools an agent can call. The agent outlines, searches and reads the document, and never receives a name, an account number or an address from it. You review what was found and choose, per value or per type, whether it goes out as written , as a stable token , or never . Bank details default to never, because an account number carries no analytical value. Names come back as [PERSON_01] , stable across the whole document. That stability is what keeps the analysis useful: the agent can reason that the signatory of section 2 is the person named in section 7 without knowing who either is. When it answers in tokens, you paste its answer into a decode panel and get the real names back, assembled in your tab from your key. Withheld values have no token, so they are not reversible by construction. A running counter shows exactly how many characters the agent has read, and a strip lists every chunk that left the tab, in order, with its tool and timestamp. How we built it Static Next.js export, React, TypeScript, no backend and no network access at all . Five layers, and the boundary between them is enforced by which module is allowed to talk to the agent. extract file → text, in the tab (pdf.js, mammoth) sections text → addressable sections (s01…sNN) detect text → entities (regex rules + capitalisation heuristic + aliases) ↓ the user marks: shown | token | withheld policy substitute · verify · confirm · record webmcp document.modelContext.registerTool() The load-bearing decision is the one-door rule: exactly one function in the project hands a tool to the browser, and it scrubs the entire result tree after the handler returns. The handler has no say in it. The alternative, asking every handler to remember to redact, is a design that fails the first time someone adds a sixth tool at 2 a.m. Here a leak requires defeating the scrubber, not forgetting to call it. The second decision was to make the strongest guarantee one I did not write myself. The page ships connect-src 'none' , so it cannot open a network connection: no fetch, no XHR, no WebSocket, no beacon. Anyone can confirm that from the Network tab in seconds, which is stronger than any sentence in a README. Runtime traps sit behind the CSP so an attempt shows up in the interface instead of in a console nobody opens. Detection is local and deliberately blunt: regex plus a capitalisation heuristic, tuned to over-detect, because a false positive costs one click and a false negative silently leaves a name in the outbound text. Sending the document to a remote recogniser would have recreated the exact leak the app exists to prevent. Challenges we ran into The search oracle. Search first ran over the source text and returned redacted snippets, which looks correct and is completely broken. An agent could query Dubreuil and learn from a hit or a miss whether that name is in the document, without one byte of it being returned. The channel leaks through its own metadata. Search now runs over the redacted text, never the source, and the cost is real: withheld values are genuinely unfindable, even by their owner. There is a test named searching a redacted name returns nothing (no oracle) because I wanted the property pinned down, not remembered. Anonymisation that survives a real document. Substituting a name once is trivial; substituting it everywhere is not. A document introduces Marceline Dubreuil on page one and says Dubreuil for twelve pages after, so surname aliases are derived and mapped to the same token, but kept only when they actually occur outside the full form, otherwise the counts start lying . Phone numbers appear as +33 6 41 88 07 23 and 06 41 88 07 23 , so token identity is decided on a normalised key, not the surface string . Addresses are matched as one entity across number, street and postcode, and a longer hand-marked span absorbs the town entity inside it rather than minting two tokens for one place. Accented names break word boundaries, so substitution uses Unicode letter lookarounds instead of \b . And after all that, the scrubber verifies its own output and hardens anything that survived, because the honest assumption is that the detector missed something. No unregisterTool() in the API. A tool is withdrawn by aborting the signal it was registered with. Without handling that, a second mount re-offers five names the browser already holds, every call is rejected, and the page advertises tools while the browser answers an older set of closures. Registration is therefore generational. Trusting the browser over myself. I keep my own registry of tools and I do not believe it. The header count comes from the browser's own getTools() , because the browser's answer is the only one that cannot be wrong. "5 tools" above an empty record is made structurally impossible. The screen is a channel WebMCP does not govern. My tool surface is sealed, but an agent that can screenshot the tab is not reading through my tools at all. So the token map is absent from the DOM by default rather than blurred , revealed on demand for 45 seconds with a visible countdown, ending immediately on blur , pagehide or visibilitychange , which are facts the browser states rather than infers. The activity bar deliberately does not claim the page is being read, because a screenshot is invisible to the page and a bar that lit up for it would be guessing. Tool-mediated disclosure is what WebMCP governs, and that is what this enforces. The rest is written into the interface itself, because a threat model you hide is not a threat model. Accomplishments that we're proud of It works end to end in a real WebMCP browser. You ask ChatGPT to find the liability clauses, it calls search_document then get_section , and comes back with a correct answer in which every party is a token and the bank details simply are not there. 28 assertions turn the README into something executable. npm run verify re-derives every claim from the real modules and exits non-zero on failure. The ones that matter are adversarial: the search oracle is closed, a surname used alone is still substituted, decode does not restore withheld values, and no section leaks after scrubbing. Every refusal is a structured answer, never an exception , so an agent that hits a wall learns why and adapts instead of retrying blind. Session boundaries are marked, not erased. Opening a new document restarts the token registry but keeps the record, with a boundary row at the seam. An agent's first probes cannot vanish from a trail that claims to be gapless. The export contains not one source value , because exporting the key would put the protected data on a disk. There is no red anywhere in the interface. A refusal is the policy working, and colouring it as an error teaches people the wrong thing about their own tool. What we learned WebMCP, properly. The imperative API, JSON Schema declarations, abort-signal lifecycle, and why Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 is mandatory: the API is exposed only to origin-isolated documents, so without the header registerTool() rejects and your page advertises nothing. That tool descriptions are the real interface. More time went into the wording of five descriptions and their error hints than into the code behind them. An empty search returns a hint explaining that search runs on redacted text, so real names are not findable by design. Those sentences changed agent behaviour more than any handler I wrote. That the interesting question is not "what did I hide" but "what can be inferred". Substitution shrinks the exposed surface, it does not remove it. A pseudonym protects a name while someone with distinctive behaviour stays recognisable by inference. Naming that limit turned out to be more useful than pretending to have closed it , which is why

title: Campaign Arena
pitch: AI agent searches KOC creators and proposes deals via WebMCP Site tools. Policy violations pause the tool call until you decide — approve, reject, or let it self-correct.
about_excerpt: AI agent searches KOC creators and proposes deals via WebMCP Site tools. Policy violations pause the tool call until you decide — approve, reject, or let it self-correct. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Influencer marketing is a $32.5 billion industry growing at 33% annually — and the #1 investment priority for marketers in 2026 is AI-powered creator matching. Yet most campaign tools still treat the agent and the human as two separate systems: the agent guesses through a UI, the human reviews a report afterward, out of context and too late to change anything. Influencer campaigns have a split-second problem: the agent that's fast enough to search hundreds of creators and score them against policy is the same agent you don't trust to commit ¥12,000,000 without asking. We built Campaign Arena to close that gap — not by slowing the agent down, but by giving it a shared workspace where both agent and person operate on the same live page. What it does Campaign Arena is a KOC (Key Opinion Consumer) campaign workspace where an AI agent and a human operator work side-by-side through four WebMCP Site tools: searchKOCs(platform?, category?) — filters the creator roster and updates the dashboard KOC grid in real time proposeDeliverable(kocKey) — proposes a deal; auto-confirms if safe, or blocks until the human decides if a policy violation is detected getTrustScore() — returns the current AEGIS trust score, autonomy tier, and factor breakdown endSession() — closes the session, locks all mutations, and writes the final trust report A policy engine enforces five rules: blacklist, platform allowlist, campaign budget ceiling (hard limit), split-deal detection, and single-deal approval threshold. An AEGIS trust score tracks the agent's behavior across the session — LOW, MEDIUM, and HIGH autonomy tiers control how much the agent can auto-confirm without asking. Every event — proposed, blocked, rejected, corrected, confirmed — is recorded in order in the Session Ledger. After a rejection, the agent suggests a policy-safe alternative. That suggestion is a nudge, not an automatic commit. How we built it Single HTML page using React 18 (via CDN) and JSX compiled to vanilla JS at build time — no framework build chain, no server. All WebMCP tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool directly in the top-level page. The production build strips runtime Babel using esbuild and is served as a fully static site on Vercel. The core of proposeDeliverable is a Promise-based human-in-the-loop gate: waitForDecision(kocKey) stores a resolver in a Map . The tool await s that Promise. The human's Approve or Reject button resolves it — and only then does the tool return its result to the agent. ChatGPT is correctly suspended while the dialog is open and cannot proceed until the person has acted. Challenges we ran into Making the approval flow genuinely transactional was the hardest part. The tool result must be truthful about what happened — not what was intended — so the agent's next action is always correct. Concurrency edge cases required the most attention: double-clicking Approve or Reject, closing the session while a simulation is mid-flight, an orphaned Promise resolver when an intermediate await throws. Each of these could silently corrupt the ledger or committed spend. We addressed them with synchronous instance flags and careful finally cleanup — the part that took longest to get right. The policy engine also required precision: split-deal detection depends on cumulative confirmed spend across proposals, which must account for prior session history to trigger correctly. Accomplishments that we're proud of The proposeDeliverable tool genuinely blocks as a Promise until the human decides. This means the agent's next tool call is always based on the real outcome. Agents using Campaign Arena cannot accidentally double-spend, propose the same creator twice, or close the session while a decision is pending — these return bounded error objects instead of hanging or corrupting state. The shared-page model is the real accomplishment: the agent does not guess through visual controls, and the person never loses context or authority. Both see the same ledger, the same trust score, the same mission progress — in real time. What we learned Designing for agents and people simultaneously forces contract clarity that is easy to skip in ordinary apps. Every tool needs a precise description, strict input schema ( additionalProperties: false , enum for allowed values), and a result that accurately reflects state — not just the happy path. We also learned that the shared-page model is fundamentally different from building an API. The tool and the UI must stay in sync: what the ledger shows and what the tool returns must always agree. Getting that right is a design problem as much as an engineering one. What's next for Campaign Arena Persistent session ledger so campaigns survive a reload Multi-agent support: a planning agent hands deals to an execution agent, with the human overseeing both Audit export: the session ledger as a signed, timestamped record for compliance review Expanded policy rules: geo restrictions, budget pacing, and creator exclusivity windows Built With css html javascript react vercel webmcp Try it out campaign-arena-webmcp.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I led the WebMCP integration and policy engine design, built the human-in-the-loop approval flow, and handled all bug fixes and hardening before submission. My teammate handled UI design, character design, and initial project scaffolding with ChatGPT. title: Arcana Table: RPG with an AI DM: Do push-ups for natural 20s
pitch: Everyone wants to play tabletop RPGs (50 million people) but nobody wants to run them, and everyone wants to exercise but the couch is winning. Arcana Table brings the dungeon; you bring the muscle.
about_excerpt: Everyone wants to play tabletop RPGs (50 million people) but nobody wants to run them, and everyone wants to exercise but the couch is winning. Arcana Table brings the dungeon; you bring the muscle. Like Comment Story Updates Instructions Explore the Area - Encounter Monsters Real World Exercise to Get bonus points on the roll. Timed Goals for Extra Bonus Points on rolls Use real world activities as micro goals to get done. Break cleaning a room into 5 minute or ten minute bursts. Fight Monsters Leveling Up - Micro Reward in Game - Hit those Endorphins Diagram Inspiration Literally, there are multiple influencers with millions of followers who act as DM while their clients lose weight and get in shape. ie link The first version of this was just a board that exposed some WebMCP tools and waited for you to bring your own agent. It was dead on arrival. You opened it and clicked buttons at yourself. What made it a game was putting an actual Dungeon Master in the seat, but making it go through the exact same tools an outside agent would have to use. Now when I say the tool surface is real, the DM playing the game is the evidence. What it does You open the URL and you're playing. The DM (GPT with function calling, talking through OpenAI TTS) sets the scene. You type or say what you do. It answers on a cartoon battle map: narrates, moves the tokens, lifts the fog, drops monsters in, runs initiative, rolls dice where you can see them. Click the map and your party walks there. There's a five-beat quest called The Ember Crown so a session has an ending. Each beat you clear levels the party up, hands out loot, and heals everyone. The last one is a boss called the Cinder Wight. The thing I actually care about is Heroic Effort. When a roll matters, the DM offers you a deal. Ten push-ups gets you +5 on the roll. Twenty-five gets you a natural 20. You count them on a big tap ring, or out loud if you're in hands-free mode because your hands are on the floor. There are timed holds too (a 30-second plank counts itself down), and a task list where it puts up three small things at once and you tick off whichever ones you did. Two out of three still pays. And there's the Oath. If you can't exercise, or just don't want to today, you can pay with something real that the page can't see. Clear the sink. Twenty minutes of studying. The email you've been avoiding. The whole table locks for however many minutes you agreed to, and when you come back you click "I kept it" on your honour. It pays the same as push-ups. You can also set the table to "Oaths only" in the party panel and it will never ask you for anything physical, so the game works for people who can't do any of this. If a hero drops to 0 HP, time stops. The board freezes and almost none of the tools work, including for the DM. You get out with a death save on a d20, or by doing a Heroic Effort, which always works. I like that effort is the guaranteed way out of dying. That's kind of the point of the whole thing. How we built it It's plain JavaScript with no build step. Canvas for the board, localStorage for state. There's one Cloudflare Worker, about 200 lines, that holds the OpenAI key so it never ends up in a browser. It's locked to the site's origin and rate-limited per IP. The page ships the @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill (MIT) so document.modelContext exists in any browser without a flag. If the browser has WebMCP natively, that takes over and the badge in the header says so. There are 25 tools on document.modelContext. 21 are always there. Three more (advance_turn, update_hp, apply_condition) get registered when combat starts and unregistered when it ends. death_save only exists while somebody is bleeding out. Every tool is registered with an AbortController and removed with abort(), which fires toolchange the way the spec says. Read tools have readOnlyHint. The destructive ones, like deleting a token or damaging a player character, pause inside execute() until the player clicks approve. There's a 45-second timeout on that so a judge who walks away doesn't leave the DM hung forever. The DM loop is about 180 lines. It calls getTools(), turns the result into OpenAI function specs, sends the conversation to the Worker, runs whatever tool calls come back through executeTool(), feeds the results back in, and repeats up to seven times before it has to say something. There's no other path for it to change the game. The DM Panel tab in the app shows you the same registry live, every tool with a form built from its JSON schema, and running one goes through the same executeTool() and shows up in the same log. There's a Playwright test suite, 435 assertions in eleven files, that drives everything through the real document.modelContext in headless Chromium. It checks the registry growing and shrinking with combat, both approval paths, all the effort modes, a full five-beat run, and it samples pixels off the canvas. That last part exists because I once shipped a scope bug that made every monster disappear from the board and all 196 tests at the time still passed. I used Claude (in Cowork) as a pair programmer for most of the build. A lot of the test suite and the refactoring described below came out of that. Challenges we ran into Wiring up tools was the easy part. The hard part was that the model is a great storyteller and a bad referee. I'd put a rule in the system prompt, it would follow it for a few turns, and then it would drift. I told it to offer push-ups often. It didn't. I told it to move the tokens when the party moved. It described the walk and left everyone standing there. I told it not to change maps with set_scene. It walked the party into the forest that way, never called advance_quest, and the beat never paid out. Every one of those got fixed the same way, and it turned into the rule for the whole project: if it matters, the tool enforces it. The attack tool checks reach, so if you swing from across the room it refuses and tells you which square to move to. The dice enforce pacing now. Two rolls without anything staked and roll_dice refuses once and tells the DM to make an offer first. The map only changes through advance_quest. Monsters take their own turn when initiative gets to them instead of waiting to be asked. The player's effort preference gates the effort tools directly, and there is on purpose no tool to change it, because an agent that can decide what it's allowed to ask of your body isn't respecting a preference. The other big one was hands-free mode hearing itself. The DM would talk, the mic would pick it up, and it would come back as the player's turn. That took three separate layers of echo suppression and a test that fakes the SpeechRecognition API to replay the exact failure, since headless Chrome has no microphone. Accomplishments that we're proud of Someone who has never seen this can open the link and play a real ten-minute dungeon with zero explanation. And when the DM offers push-ups for a natural 20, people stand up. Everyone I've tested it on has stood up. The DM has no special access. It finds its tools with getTools() and uses them with executeTool() exactly like a ChatGPT or Claude agent would from outside. You can watch every single call in the log while you play. I'm also glad I didn't fake verification on the Oath. The card literally says "Nothing here can check, which is rather the point." I could have added a webcam check. It would have limited the whole mechanic to things a camera can see, and the things people most need a push on (reading, practicing, that email) aren't those. What we learned Rules belong in the tools, not the prompt. Every time I tried to fix behaviour with better wording it worked for a while. Every time I turned it into a counter or a refusal it stayed fixed. A good refusal that says what went wrong and what to call instead does more than a paragraph of instructions. Passing tests don't mean the game works. I had 196 green assertions and no monsters on the screen. Now the suite looks at pixels, and I don't trust anything I haven't watched. And accessibility turned out not to be a separate feature. Once the Oath paid the same as push-ups, "I can't exercise" stopped being a reason you couldn't play. It's a setting now. What's next for Arcana Table Webcam rep counting with MediaPipe Pose, running in the browser, so push-ups count themselves. The Oath stays unverified on purpose. Multiplayer, with a few people sharing one DM. Campaign art generated per run from my ComfyUI setup. And I want to record a Claude or ChatGPT browser agent running the same dungeon through the same 25 tools, next to the built-in DM, because that comparison is the thing WebMCP makes possible and I haven't shown it yet. title: AriaLens: WebMCP Accessibility Studio
pitch: A developer studio enabling LLM agents to safely audit and remediate live DOM accessibility violations via WebMCP, featuring optimistic concurrency locks and security honeypots.
about_excerpt: A developer studio enabling LLM agents to safely audit and remediate live DOM accessibility violations via WebMCP, featuring optimistic concurrency locks and security honeypots. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Over 96% of the world's top one million websites fail basic WCAG accessibility tests . For developers, retrofitting unsemantic <div> elements with complex ARIA attributes ( aria-expanded , aria-controls , role="combobox" , keyboard focus traps) is tedious, manual, and error-prone. With the advent of the Web Model Context Protocol (WebMCP) , web applications can finally expose structured tools directly to AI agents. But giving an autonomous LLM write access to a live DOM is inherently dangerous: Hallucination & Prompt Injection: Agents might apply unvetted, destructive mutations across the entire page. Race Conditions (TOCTOU): If an agent takes 10 seconds to analyze a component while a user is actively clicking and mutating the DOM, applying the patch blindly will corrupt UI state. We built AriaLens to solve this: an agent-native developer studio where humans and AI agents collaborate safely on live DOM accessibility remediation with strict Human-in-the-Loop Authority Boundaries , Optimistic Concurrency Locks , and Adversarial Honeypots . What it does AriaLens turns the browser into an interactive, agent-guided accessibility workbench: Live Accessibility Introspection: Using WebMCP, the agent inspects computed accessibility trees, AccName 1.1 calculations, and keyboard focus trap boundaries directly through audit_accessibility_tree . Human-in-the-Loop Authority Boundary: Destructive mutation tools ( commit_a11y_fix ) are never exposed upfront . The agent can only stage speculative changes via stage_aria_remediation . Staged changes render in an IDE-style visual code diff awaiting human sign-off. Optimistic Concurrency Lock (W3C § 6.3): Patches are cryptographically bound to an Epoch Lock recorded at audit time. If a user interacts with or mutates the DOM before commit, the epoch advances and the patch is safely rejected with a STALE_EPOCH_CONFLICT . The Honeypot Gauntlet (W3C § 6.4): To guard against rogue or jailbroken behavior, AriaLens mounts hidden bypass tools ( bulk_apply_all_fixes ). Any agent attempting to bypass human approval is intercepted, blocked, and flagged in the live audit log. Export as Git Patch: Staged remediations can be downloaded with one click as standard unified .patch files, enabling developers to review in browser and commit directly to their local Git repositories. How we built it WebMCP Protocol Integration: Built directly against the emerging W3C WebMCP draft specification using document.modelContext.registerTool() . We implemented ephemeral capability mounting via AbortController lifecycles to dynamically attach and detach tools based on human gate approval. Architecture & State Machine: Powered by React 19 , TypeScript , and Vite , with Zustand orchestrating the optimistic concurrency state machine and telemetry logs. Accessibility Evaluation: Backed by axe-core 4.10 , AccName 1.1 computation models, and automated WCAG 2.2 AA heuristics. Developer Interface: Designed with a high-density, dark-mode developer experience inspired by Linear and Vercel, featuring real-time latency badges, sub-pixel antialiasing, and structured code diff views. Challenges we ran into Solving TOCTOU Concurrency: Bridging the gap between asynchronous LLM inference (5–15 seconds) and synchronous DOM events required architecting a zero-overhead optimistic locking protocol (Epoch Locks) that cleanly rejects stale mutations without freezing the browser. Ephemeral Tool Lifecycle: Designing tool registration so that commit capabilities remain invisible to LLM tool discovery until explicitly authorized by a human, and immediately unregister after single execution. Clean Agent Steering: Calibrating tool descriptions and input schemas so that models prioritize structured attribute staging rather than attempting raw HTML string rewrites. Accomplishments that we're proud of Strict W3C WebMCP Compliance: Directly implemented and validated Sections 6.3 (Concurrency) and 6.4 (Untrusted Content) of the WebMCP draft specification. Enterprise-Grade Utility: Going beyond a toy demo by enabling instant .patch unified diff generation for real-world engineering workflows. Security-First Agent Design: Proving that agent-native web applications can grant high-level reasoning capabilities to AI without ever compromising runtime safety or human authority. What we learned Agents perform exponentially better when constrained by formal capability state machines rather than natural language prompt boundaries. WebMCP represents a paradigm shift: websites are no longer passive documents for LLMs to scrape, but active APIs where humans and agents co-operate with cryptographic guarantees. What's next for AriaLens Headless CI/CD WebMCP Runner: An automated GitHub Action that spins up headless Chrome with WebMCP enabled to audit staging deployments and open pull requests automatically. Support for Complex APG Patterns: Expanding fixture coverage to ARIA 1.3 TreeGrids, MenuBars, and complex multi-select comboboxes. Framework Code Generators: Generating native JSX/TSX component patches for Tailwind, Radix UI, and Shadcn components. title: Kern
pitch: A kerning workbench that an AI agent operates through WebMCP. Load a font, give it one line of instruction, and it looks at every letter pair and fixes the spacing — then exports a real font file.
about_excerpt: A kerning workbench that an AI agent operates through WebMCP. Load a font, give it one line of instruction, and it looks at every letter pair and fixes the spacing — then exports a real font file. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Kerning is the space between two letters. AV needs less space. nn needs no change. There is no formula. The eye judges the shape of the white space, not the distance. A person must look at every pair. A typeface has hundreds of pairs. Thomas Phinney kerned one weight of one typeface. He made 632 adjustments. The work took about one week. Nobody can automate this with a formula. So the question was whether an agent could do it by looking instead — and whether it would know when a pair was already fine. What it does Kern is a kerning tool. It shows every pair in a font, and an agent fixes the spacing. Load any .ttf or .otf , give the agent one sentence, and it will: Survey every pair as a labelled contact sheet, up to 36 pairs in one image Compare candidate values side by side, one row per pair Apply the values it chooses, and mark the pairs it leaves alone Check the result in real words, shipped against kerned Export a .ttf with real GPOS and kern tables written into it Six of the eight tools return an image. The agent does not read a score and act on it. It looks at the render and decides. The person keeps control. Every value is visible on the page. Hover a pair to see the old value. Use the arrow keys to change any value. The agent and the person share one state, so nothing is locked. Why this fits WebMCP The agent must see the letters. It cannot decide from a number or a database row. The page already holds the font and the canvas. WebMCP lets the page draw the pair and give the picture to the agent. A tool can also answer a question that no interface asks. preview_pairs takes eight pairs and four candidate values, and returns one labelled image. No button on the page does this. Only an agent needs it. The tool list follows the page state. The tools register when you load a font. They unregister when you load a different font. This fires toolchange . An agent that arrives before a font is loaded finds no tools. What people and agents can do together Before, you kerned a font by hand, one pair at a time, or you shipped it unkerned. There was no middle option. Now the agent can also say that a pair is already correct: typeface shipped state reviewed changed left alone EB Garamond no kerning 51 46 5 Comic Relief no kerning 51 39 12 Roboto Condensed professionally kerned 51 10 41 The tools and the instruction were the same for all three fonts. The results are different. On Roboto the agent corrected only the L pairs and the punctuation. It kept the other 41 values. A tool that always finds a change has not looked. How we built it Vite, React 19, TypeScript, on Cloudflare Workers. opentype.js reads the font. Kern uses no MCP library. I removed the one I started with, so the specification call is visible in the source: document.modelContext.registerTool( { name, description, inputSchema, annotations, execute }, { signal: controller.signal }, ) Each registration holds an AbortController . The signal unregisters the tool. getTools() fills the tools panel in the app, so the page shows what is really registered. The annotations are the two that WebMCP defines: readOnlyHint on the four read tools, and untrustedContentHint on all eight. Every answer repeats the font family name, and that name comes from a file the user supplied. The export is real. opentype.js drops kerning when it writes a font. So Kern builds the GPOS and kern tables by hand and splices them into the original bytes. Every deploy runs a test that reads the exported font back. The build fails if the values are missing. Challenges we ran into The agent needed to know how to do the job. Look at every pair first. Compare a few values. Apply them together. Then check the result in real words. That is a short set of instructions, but WebMCP has nowhere to put it. You can describe each tool. You cannot describe the page. So there is no way to tell an agent how the work should go before it starts. I tried adding a help tool. That did not work. The agent that needs help is the agent that never calls it. What worked was attaching the instructions to the first answer the agent gets, whatever tool it happened to call first. A full run went from 4 minutes 17 seconds to 2 minutes 34 seconds . MCP, the protocol underneath, already has a field for this. WebMCP does not expose it yet. video_transcript_excerpt: You know something's wrong. The letters are right. The spaces aren't. That's kerning. And one typeface can have hundreds of pairs. Type designers do this by hand, one pair at a time. Look, adjust, look again, then move to the next one. There are 632 pairs. It takes about a week. So, I built Kern. A kerning tool which shows every pair in a font, and an agent fixes the spacing. An agent drives it through Web MCP. Eight tools registered on the page itself. title: DiscoveryHub
pitch: DiscoveryHub turns “where do I start with open source?” into action, matching your skills to active projects, finding available issues, and tracking contributions through tools a human would use.
about_excerpt: DiscoveryHub turns “where do I start with open source?” into action, matching your skills to active projects, finding available issues, and tracking contributions through tools a human would use. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Tell the agent your skills once, and it remembers you for next time. Ask for matches and the agent maps projects to your skills as a live graph. Say "highlight the starred one" and the agent makes that graph node glow — it drives the UI. The agent checks an issue's availability and requirements, then saves it to your dashboard. Your tracked contributions, laid out as a journey from Interested to Merged. Ask "will my PR get reviewed?" and the agent reports real response and merge times. Inspiration Almost every developer wants to contribute to open source but stalls at the same wall: where do I start? With 200M+ repos, and endless follow up questions like whether the project is active, whether a PR will get reviewed, or whether an issue is already taken, the research takes hours, and most first contributions never happen. WebMCP made us realize the tedious digging is exactly what an agent is good at, while the judgment is what a human is good at. So we built an app that is better when a person and their agent use it together. What it does DiscoveryHub turns "I want to contribute" into "here is a specific, unclaimed, doable issue in a responsive project, plus a plan to fix it." It exposes 19 WebMCP tools and a built in "Ask the Agent" chatbox. You type a goal in plain English, and the agent chains tools to match projects to your skills, measure how responsive a project is, find issues, check if they are actually free, assess their real difficulty beyond the label, draft a contribution plan, and track your progress. Some tools even drive the UI live, so when the agent highlights a project the on screen skill graph reacts, and the human and agent share the same page. How we built it Next.js 14, React, and TypeScript, with Tailwind, live GitHub data via Octokit, D3, React Flow, and Recharts for visuals, and the OpenAI API for the agent. The core is a three role split: the WebMCP tools run in the browser, the OpenAI key stays server side behind /api/agent, and a chat loop shuttles between them, which is what lets one sentence trigger a whole chain of tool calls. A couple of tools also think, like draft_contribution_plan, which synthesizes a plan from a repo's README and contributing guide, and we kept the scoring honest and explainable rather than a black box. Challenges we ran into Building on an unreleased standard was the hardest part. WebMCP runs behind an experimental browser flag, and we discovered its exact contract by trial: executeTool needs the tool object plus JSON string arguments. React Strict Mode double registered our tools, so we made registration idempotent. We also had to be honest about data limits, since GitHub has no difficulty qualifier, so project search uses a maturity proxy while the real difficulty signal lives per issue. Accomplishments that we're proud of One plain English request now carries a user from "I want to contribute" to a concrete plan, with the agent chaining tools on its own. We are proudest of the agent driving the UI, something a normal API cannot do, and of tools that add real value: catching mislabeled "good first issues," flagging already claimed ones, and measuring whether a project will even review your PR. And it stays honest, saying "unknown" when it lacks data instead of guessing. What we learned WebMCP shifts the mental model. The agent never touches your app directly. It emits a structured request and your code executes it, so keeping the model on the server and execution in the browser is the key unlock. Good schemas do the heavy lifting, so the user never needs to know a repo is written as owner/repo, because the agent translates. And honesty beats cleverness: the best moments are not just better answers, but shared state the agent can change. What's next for DiscoveryHub Next: a draft_pr_description tool and more "act on my behalf" features, expanding beyond GitHub to GitLab with a platform aware data layer, sharper difficulty and responsiveness signals such as filtering out bots and calibrating to a contributor's history, and being ready out of the box as WebMCP graduates from experimental flags into mainstream browsers. title: Tether
pitch: Teach one site, and a site that has never met you is already configured. A shared memory layer for the agent-native web, built on WebMCP. Delete a memory, and the next build forgets it.
about_excerpt: Teach one site, and a site that has never met you is already configured. A shared memory layer for the agent-native web, built on WebMCP. Delete a memory, and the next build forgets it. Like Comment Story Updates Logo Inspiration You tell one site you want dark interfaces, compact layouts, and TypeScript. Then you open the next tool and type all of it again. And again. Agents were supposed to remove that friction, but each one starts cold at the tab boundary, so the person ends up carrying context from site to site by hand. Being the integration layer is the last unautomated job on the web, and nobody was treating it as a problem. WebMCP changes what a website can hand an agent: real capabilities the page declares, instead of a DOM that was never built to be driven. That made one question worth answering. If every site can expose genuine tools, what is the single shared capability that would make all of them better at once? Memory. Not an assistant's private chat history sealed in a vendor cloud, but structured context that any participating site can read and write, with the person holding the delete key. What it does Tether is a shared memory layer for the agent-native web, plus two working sites that prove context survives the jump between them. DesignLab is the producer, a small design studio. Ask the agent to remember your preferences and its save_preference tool applies them to the canvas and writes them to Tether in the same call. DevForge is the consumer, a project scaffolder whose form has a project-name field and nothing else. Its create_project tool asks Tether what you prefer, then configures six things it never asked about: language, theme, layout density, framework, package manager, and styling, down to the lock file and the install command. The Tether control plane shows every memory with its source site, the tool that wrote it, tags, a confidence score, and a timestamp. Inspect, search, edit, add, or permanently delete any of it. Try it in 30 seconds Open DesignLab and ask the agent: "Remember that I prefer dark interfaces, compact layouts, and TypeScript." The studio turns dark and compact, and three structured memories land in Tether. Open the dashboard . They are already there, each carrying its full lineage. Open DevForge and ask for a starter project. It comes back TypeScript, dark, compact, with every value tracing back to the memory that produced it. Now delete the TypeScript memory and scaffold again. The language falls back to JavaScript. The others hold. Step 4 is the whole project. A cross-site demo can be faked with a hardcoded path, and a judge should assume it was until shown otherwise. So deletion is part of the demo: pull one row out of the layer, and a different site's output changes in front of you. None of this is limited to a fixed set of toggles. Both DesignLab and the control plane accept context in your own words through the same validated path. Say "I prefer pnpm over npm" or "I prefer Tailwind CSS for styling" , and the next scaffold picks it up, install command included. How we built it Next.js 15 App Router and TypeScript. Tailwind for a dark, high-density developer-tool surface. Zod on every boundary. Supabase Postgres for persistence, behind a pluggable store: with no environment variables at all, a fresh clone runs immediately on an in-process driver. Memories are structured rather than free text: content, category, tags, source, confidence, scope, timestamps. That schema is what makes the whole thing work. A pile of chat transcripts cannot be filtered, ranked, explained, or selectively deleted. Security got real attention for a hackathon MVP. The service-role key lives only in server-only modules, so an accidental client import fails the build instead of leaking a credential. Row-level security is enabled on both tables with no permissive policies. Memory content is rendered as text by React and never injected as HTML. Sessions are opaque random ids in an httpOnly first-party cookie, with no accounts and no PII. Challenges we ran into Making the memory falsifiable. The cross-site moment only convinces if it can visibly fail. Building deletion into the demo, and making the fallback path genuinely fall back rather than run a second hardcoded branch, is what turned a nice animation into evidence. Refusing to simulate. It would have been easy to fake tool calls when no agent is present and let the video imply otherwise. Detecting the absence and labelling every manual invocation cost a day and made the architecture clearer, because you can now see that the agent path and the button path run the same handler. Keeping retrieval interpretable end to end. Carrying matchedOn reasons from the matcher through the API into the UI constrained the entire pipeline. It ruled out the easy embedding approach, and it is the reason the product can show its work. Serverless state. The in-process store is perfect locally and wrong in production, because serverless functions do not share memory between invocations. The /api/health endpoint reports which driver is live specifically so a misconfigured deploy looks like a misconfiguration instead of a broken app. Accomplishments that we're proud of The delete-and-rescaffold moment. It is the rare demo that proves itself by breaking on purpose. You can verify our claims in ninety seconds. The test suite runs against the live deployment: curl https://tether-swart.vercel.app/api/health # {"status":"online","driver":"supabase"} git clone https://github.com/Dotman-Bei/Tether && cd Tether && npm install BASE_URL=https://tether-swart.vercel.app npm test It scopes itself to its own session cookie and cleans up after itself, so it is safe to point at production. It covers every route handler and, through them, the configured store driver: creation and defaults, numeric coercion, tag round-tripping, the duplicate guard, list ordering and filters, ranked retrieval with match reasons, update persistence, input validation, 404s, activity logging, session isolation, delete, and reset. No test framework and no dependencies. **A fresh clone runs with zero environment variables.** `npm install && npm run dev` and the whole demo works. **We did not overclaim the protocol.** WebMCP does not carry memory between unrelated sites on its own. It is the tool interface on each page, and Tether is the shared backplane those tools read from and write to. Saying otherwise would have been an easier pitch and a false one. ## What we learned **Structure is what makes memory shareable.** Category, tags, source, and confidence are what let a second site retrieve something specific, apply it, show its work, and let a person govern the result. Unstructured recall cannot do any of those four things. **Trust surfaces are product features, not compliance overhead.** The lineage drawer and the labelled telemetry stream are what make people believe the rest of it, and they were among the cheapest things in the build. **Explainability is a design constraint, not a feature you add later.** Choosing lexical matching over embeddings looked like a downgrade until we tried to render *why* a memory was applied. The interpretable pipeline turned out to be the product. ## What's next for Tether **Per-site scoped consent and real accounts.** The cross-origin story above, which is the difference between a demo and infrastructure. - **A small client library** so a site joins in a few lines instead of reimplementing the contract. - **Memory decay and conflict resolution.** Preferences change, and the layer should notice when a new statement contradicts an old one instead of accumulating both. - **Richer context types past preferences:** working conventions, project constraints, domain vocabulary. The two demo sites are an illustration. The direction is a shared memory layer that any experience can build on, where the person keeps the keys. Built With javascript lucide-react model-context-protocol next.js node.js postgresql react rest-api serverless supabase tailwindcss typescript vercel webmcp zod Try it out tether-swart.vercel.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Heisbei: Solo build. The thesis, the product design, the ten WebMCP tools, the memory layer and the API underneath are mine, with Claude Code as implementation partner. The decision I would defend hardest is the delete step. A clean cross-site handoff would have demoed fine, but a demo that cannot visibly fail proves nothing, so I made deletion part of the flow and let the scaffold fall back on camera. The second is making the app admit when no agent is present instead of faking the call. That cost a day, and it is the reason you can trust anything else on the screen. pitch: Turn a conversation into a live itinerary that people and AI agents can plan, validate, review, save, and share together.

 Inspiration 

 This August one of my best friends visited me from Sevilla, I live in Buenos Aires. We've known each other since high school and both moved abroad 10 years ago. Since then we've lived an ocean apart, but connected. Last moth I got the joy of being physically in the same space as me, for two weeks. Me as a good Leo planned the whole itinerary for each day. I was hesitant at first but I gave ChatGPT the chance to build an itinerary based on: places I wanted them to visit, places they wanted to visit, some underground recommendations I asked for. I was quite surprised with the result, it managed to gave me a very details and packed itinerary that made sense, it managed every constraint I gave it, and it even took the weather into consideration. But the cerry on top was, every event or place that required a ticket or a reservation, it told me. I was so happy I couldn't wait to share it with them. But then that moment came, and the only thing I had was a nice itinerary in marked up language that couldn't be understood when read through a WhatsApp message bubble. A bit salty about it and the fact that they made a little fun of that (don't get me wrong I enjoyed the humor but my ego wanted to prove me right) I decided to make a website so they can navigate the whole itinerary. My friend was impressed, but we couldn't actually get to used because I was too busy and tired to finish and publish the site, since we were always out, playing video games or taking or anything (catching up 10 years of being apart in two weeks). Then I learned about this challenge, I don't remember how. And the idea sparked, use this challenge as fuel to complete the website, make it better, throw it to the public, and be grateful to my best friend for even inspiring me to do this kinds of things, thanks to his visiting. 

 What it does 

 Sendero provides an structured way for ChatGPT to build an itinerary and the UI to present them in a more beautiful and accessible way (not to say better than and copied message from the chat). Also expands its capability by giving the user 3 types of viewing the itinerary: Activities by days listed 2) Activities by days in a calendar 3) Routes in maps per day. Also you have a centralized sections of all the reservations. It takes in account weather and local activities happening in the place your're visiting, making it a very well rounded itinerary. 

 How we built it 

 I built Sendero as a bridge between the conversation and the actual travel app. The traveler describes the trip normally, and ChatGPT uses eight WebMCP tools exposed by the page to load Sendero’s planning rules, pass the trip details, validate the result, and place a real draft in the browser. The traveler can review it as a list, calendar, map, or reservation checklist, and nothing is saved or shared until they explicitly request it. 
The tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool, use closed JSON schemas, and connect to the same state and actions as the visible React interface. The public shared-trip page exposes six additional tools for navigating the itinerary without modifying the original trip. I still let myself vibe code it. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Motion and transitions in the landing page. It's ok, but there is still some road to go. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I had fun. I was happy. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP, literally. I had no idea it existed until this challenge. Now I am in love. 

 What's next for Sendero 

 Itinerary searching liking and... disliking?
Notifications
Sendero badge for your website
Sendero for business
Real time collaboration?

title: ConstraintLab
pitch: Describe the constraints. Let the solver prove the schedule.
about_excerpt: Describe the constraints. Let the solver prove the schedule. Like 1 Comment Story Updates logo main operating screen scheduling screen About the Project Inspiration Scheduling sounds simple until real-world constraints begin interacting: machines become unavailable, urgent jobs receive deadlines, tasks depend on one another, and operators override assignments. Traditional optimization software can solve these problems, but describing a model often requires specialized mathematical knowledge. AI assistants make natural-language interaction easier, but an LLM should not be trusted to invent a schedule and claim it is valid. ConstraintLab combines the strengths of both: Humans express goals and judge trade-offs. AI agents translate intent into structured actions. A deterministic solver computes and validates the schedule. We built ConstraintLab to explore what an agent-native optimization workspace could look like—one where the human interface, AI agent, solver, and audit history all operate on the same canonical application state. What It Does ConstraintLab is a browser-based job-shop scheduling workspace. Users can: View jobs, machines, dependencies, deadlines, and downtime windows. Inspect schedules through an interactive Gantt chart. Add or edit scheduling constraints manually. Ask a WebMCP-capable AI agent to inspect and modify the model. Run a real mixed-integer linear programming solver in the browser. Detect when a solved schedule becomes stale after the model changes. Receive deterministic explanations when a model is infeasible. Review every human, agent, and solver action in an audit timeline. A typical interaction looks like this: “Machine 2 will be unavailable between 1 PM and 3 PM, and Job 7 must finish before noon.” The agent discovers ConstraintLab’s site tools, adds typed constraints, and requests a solve. The HiGHS solver—not the language model—computes the resulting schedule. If another request creates a contradiction, ConstraintLab reports the genuine infeasible result and identifies the relevant constraints using deterministic conflict analysis. How We Built It ConstraintLab is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, Zod, Web Workers, WebAssembly, HiGHS, WebMCP, Vitest, and Netlify. The most important architectural decision was to maintain one canonical application state. Human interface ──┐ ▼ Domain actions ▲ AI agent ─────────┘ │ Canonical Zustand store ├── Solver ├── Gantt chart └── Audit timeline The interface and WebMCP handlers call the exact same domain actions. There is no separate “agent state” or hidden model that can drift away from what the user sees. ConstraintLab exposes nine typed site tools: get_problem_state add_job update_job add_constraint remove_constraint set_objective solve_problem get_solution analyze_infeasibility Every tool input is validated with Zod, and write operations are validated again inside the domain layer. Agent arguments are treated as requests—not as trusted data. For optimization, we compile the scheduling problem into a CPLEX LP-format model and send it to HiGHS running inside a Web Worker. This prevents the WebAssembly solver from blocking the interface. The objective is to minimize makespan: $$ \min C_{\max} $$ For every job (j), completion must satisfy: $$ C_{\max} \geq S_j + p_j $$ where (S_j) is its start time and (p_j) is its duration. Precedence, deadlines, machine assignments, availability windows, and non-overlapping jobs are represented as linear constraints. Binary ordering variables handle jobs that may compete for the same machine. The resulting assignments are translated back into application objects and applied through a single solver-result domain action. We also track a modelVersion . Every structural edit increments this version, and every solution records which version it solved. If the two differ, the interface immediately displays: Model changed — re-solve required. Challenges We Ran Into One major challenge was correctly separating language understanding from mathematical correctness. The agent is useful for translating a human request into typed tool calls, but it must never become the scheduling engine. Keeping that boundary strict influenced the entire architecture. The solver integration was another challenge. HiGHS accepts LP-format text rather than a convenient JavaScript model object, so we built an explicit model compiler and solution translator. Variable names had to remain stable enough to map solver columns back to jobs and resources. Scheduling downtime is more complicated than adding a simple bound. A job must occur either before or after an unavailable window, which requires additional binary decisions and big-(M) constraints. Infeasibility explanations were also difficult. A solver can report that a model is infeasible without producing an explanation suitable for a user. Instead of asking an LLM to guess, we built typed, rule-based checkers that examine deadlines, precedence chains, locked starts, resource assignments, and machine availability. The generated summaries are based on computed scheduling facts. Finally, WebMCP is still an emerging browser capability. We needed feature detection, top-level tool registration, a fallback path, and a clear unavailable state so that the human scheduling interface remains functional even when WebMCP is not enabled. Accomplishments That We’re Proud Of We are especially proud that ConstraintLab demonstrates a complete agent-to-solver loop rather than a simulated AI demo. The AI agent modifies the same state that the human sees. The schedule is computed by a real deterministic MILP solver. Constraints have stable IDs and structured types. Invalid agent inputs are rejected safely. Solver work runs outside the main browser thread. Model edits automatically invalidate stale solutions. Infeasibility explanations come from deterministic analysis. Every human, agent, and solver action is auditable. The entire application works without an AI agent. The complete optimization stack runs inside the browser and can be deployed as a static application. Our headline demo intentionally creates a real contradiction involving Job 4, Machine 2, machine downtime, and a deadline. The solver returns an actual infeasible status, and ConstraintLab identifies the relevant conflict instead of showing a scripted response. What We Learned We learned that the most valuable role for an AI agent in optimization is not solving the mathematics itself. Its value is translating intent, operating tools, and helping users navigate the model. Typed tools are essential. Allowing an agent to submit arbitrary mathematical expressions would make validation, auditing, and explanations significantly less reliable. A deliberately small vocabulary of structured constraints creates a much safer system. We also learned that shared state is more important than chat history. The collaboration feels trustworthy because every agent action appears immediately in the visual workspace, and every human edit is visible to the agent during its next inspection. Finally, infeasibility is not merely an error state. In real optimization work, discovering why requirements conflict can be as valuable as finding an optimal schedule. What’s Next for ConstraintLab The current version deliberately focuses on one excellent scheduling loop. Future versions could expand that foundation with: Multiple optimization objectives, including lateness and utilization. Saved scenarios and side-by-side solution comparison. Checkpoints and reversible model changes. Transactional batches of agent-proposed changes. Interactive rescheduling and assignment locking. Richer deterministic conflict analysis. Larger industrial scheduling models. Import and export support for operational datasets. Additional optimization domains such as workforce, classroom, and logistics planning. Collaboration features for teams reviewing the same model. The longer-term vision is for ConstraintLab to become a general agent-native optimization workspace: natural enough for anyone to describe a problem, rigorous enough for experts to trust the answer, and transparent enough for humans to remain in control.  What it does 

 MatchRV is an AI-native RV marketplace built to make complex RV shopping simple, trustworthy, and actionable. 

 Most RV shoppers do not search in clean filters. They ask things like: “I need a bunkhouse under 30 feet, less than 7,000 lbs, with two entry doors, a private bedroom, under my budget, and close to Tacoma.” Traditional marketplaces struggle with requests like that because the information is scattered across inconsistent dealer listings. 

 MatchRV uses WebMCP to turn those messy real-world shopping requests into structured requirements and match them against normalized RV inventory. 

 Our challenge entry focuses on three things: 

 Search: MatchRV converts multi-condition natural-language requests into precise structured matching across RV inventory. 

 Trust: Every result explains why it matched, which requirements were verified, what information is still unknown, and how fresh the inventory data appears. 

 Action: Once the shopper finds the right RV, the agent can prepare dealer contact and show the user exactly what will happen before requiring explicit human approval. 

 This demonstrates how WebMCP can transform an ordinary dealer inventory website into something an AI agent can understand and act on safely. 

 Our larger vision is to make RV inventory AI-readable across the industry, allowing shoppers to find the right RV through ChatGPT and other AI agents instead of manually searching hundreds of listings.

title: Kinstead
pitch: A shared family care plan where people and their AI agents work side by side — and a human always confirms anything that can't be undone.
about_excerpt:
A shared family care plan where people and their AI agents work side by side — and a human always confirms anything that can't be undone.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 



 
 Inspiration 

 Family caregivers manage an overwhelming amount of life-admin for a relative
who can't manage it alone — medications, appointments, insurance and
benefits paperwork, provider calls. Most of it is tedious. Some of it is
genuinely high-stakes: a dosage change, an official form submitted to a
government agency. Today, an AI agent trying to help has to either guess its
way through a UI built for humans, or get locked out of anything that
actually matters. We wanted to see what changes when a page can tell an
agent exactly what it's allowed to do — and, just as importantly, what it
has to ask a human about first. 

 What it does 

 Kinstead is a shared "care circle" dashboard for a family managing a
relative's care. It exposes seven real WebMCP tools that an agent can call:
adding tasks, logging appointments, and drafting benefits forms happen
instantly. Proposing a medication change and submitting an official form are
different — they're irreversible or safety-relevant, so those tools pause
using WebMCP's requestUserInteraction() and put the exact proposed action
in front of a real person on the page before anything actually happens.
Every action, whether a family member clicked it or an agent called it,
lands in one shared activity log, so the whole family can see what their
agent did on their behalf. 

 How we built it 

 The app is a small Express backend serving as the shared source of truth for
the care circle, paired with a vanilla HTML/CSS/JS frontend — no framework,
no build step, so the WebMCP implementation stays fully auditable in a few
files. Tools are registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() in
 public/app.js . Low-risk tools call the backend and return immediately.
High-risk tools call client.requestUserInteraction() to pause for a
same-page confirmation modal, with a fallback path for hosts that haven't
implemented that part of the spec yet, so the human-in-the-loop guarantee
holds regardless of host support. We used Claude to design and build the
core app and the risk-tiered tool architecture, then Google AI Studio to
give the dashboard a warmer, more distinctive visual design without
touching the underlying tool logic. It's deployed on Render. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 WebMCP is genuinely early — the API surface, and even which global it's
exposed on, is still moving. We built in feature detection and a fallback
path so the tools work whether a host exposes document.modelContext or
 navigator.modelContext . We also had to be deliberate about not letting
every tool behave the same way: it would have been easy to make everything
execute instantly, but the actual point of the project was making the
irreversible tools genuinely pause for a human, which meant designing the
confirmation flow carefully so it works the same way whether triggered by
a live agent or by someone testing the flow directly on the page. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Every one of the three real "you can't undo this" actions in the app —
medication changes and form submissions — is provably gated behind a human
click, not just a prompt suggesting the agent should ask first. We also
added on-page "simulate agent" triggers for every tool, so anyone (a judge,
a family member, us recording the demo) can see the full tiered-risk flow
without needing a specific WebMCP-capable browser or extension installed. 

 What we learned 

 The interesting design problem in agent-facing tools isn't "what can the
agent do" — it's "what should never happen without a person seeing it
first." WebMCP's page-defined tool model turns that from a prompt-engineering
problem into an actual enforced mechanism, which feels like the right layer
for it to live at. 

 What's next for Kinstead 

 Real multi-user accounts instead of a single demo care circle, a
notifications layer so family members get pinged when something needs their
approval instead of having to check the dashboard, and expanding the
benefits-form drafting to pull from real program requirements rather than a
generic template.

title: Captain Claw
pitch: A gaming platform where an AI agent can turn "what should we play?" into a real multiplayer session.
about_excerpt: A gaming platform where an AI agent can turn "what should we play?" into a real multiplayer session. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI gaming demos stop at recommending a game. But when my friends and I actually want to play something together, finding the game is only part of the problem. Someone still has to figure out who's online, what everyone owns, how many players a game supports, whether we've already played it, and whether it fits the time we have. Then someone has to create the party and invite everyone. I wanted to see what this would look like if an agent could work inside the gaming platform itself instead of just giving recommendations in chat. That's what led to Captain Claw . What it does Captain Claw is a fictional gaming platform with a Store, Library, Friends system, and multiplayer Parties. A player can give an agent a request like: "Alex, Sam and Maya are online. We have 75 minutes. Find a co-op game all four of us can play, preferably something none of us has finished." Using WebMCP, the agent can check who's online, compare player libraries, search the catalog, inspect game details, consider session length, and find a game that works for the group. If the player wants to continue, the agent can create a party and send invitations. Those aren't simulated chat responses. They change the actual state of Captain Claw. The party appears in the normal UI, and an invitation sent to another player can appear in that player's browser session. The agent handles the coordination. The player still decides what to play and presses Launch. How I built it Captain Claw is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and WebMCP , and is deployed on Netlify. The platform uses a synthetic but internally consistent dataset of games, players, friendships, libraries, presence, and play history. This keeps the demo self-contained while still giving the agent enough connected data to solve realistic requests. Captain Claw exposes 13 WebMCP tools for things such as checking online friends, comparing libraries, searching games, reading the current browser view, applying Store filters, creating parties, sending invitations, checking party status, and launching a session. Some tools are tied directly to browser context. For example, the agent can inspect the Store view the player is currently looking at and work with filters the player already applied. Tools can also appear based on application state, such as the ability to respond to an invitation when one is pending. One thing I tried to keep consistent throughout the project was that the agent should not have a separate version of the product. Agent actions use the same application logic as human actions. Game filtering uses the same filtering code as the Store, and party actions update the same party state used by the UI. Shared party state is handled through a Netlify Function and Netlify Blobs, which also lets party invitations work across browser sessions. Challenges I ran into The hardest part wasn't registering tools. It was making them feel like they belonged to a real application. Browser state matters. If a player has already filtered the Store, the agent should be able to understand that context instead of starting over. If an invitation is sent, another player should actually be able to receive it. I also ran into smaller problems that exposed bigger design questions. Session length was one example. "We have 75 minutes" sounds simple, but treating 75 minutes as a hard maximum can remove games that are still reasonable choices. The Store and WebMCP tools now share the same session-fit rule so they can't disagree with each other. Testing multi-user party state was another challenge. Each demo room needed isolated state so different users or judges wouldn't accidentally overwrite each other's party. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm most proud that WebMCP isn't just sitting beside the application as a demo API. The agent can operate the same product the player is looking at. It can use the current Store context, open a game, change visible filters, create a party, and send an invitation that another browser session can receive. The results of agent actions show up through the normal Captain Claw interface. I also built automated checks around the main recommendation funnel and WebMCP flows so the demo isn't dependent on one lucky prompt. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is that useful agent tools aren't always the same thing as backend API endpoints. Giving an agent a pile of raw data isn't necessarily helpful. Tools should represent useful capabilities and expose enough context for the agent to make a good decision. I also learned how important shared context is. When the player changes something and the agent can work from it - or the agent changes something and the player immediately sees it - the interaction feels much more natural than passing information back and forth through chat. WebMCP made that idea much more concrete because the browser isn't just displaying the application anymore. It can expose the application's capabilities to the agent as well. What's next for Captain Claw Captain Claw currently uses a fictional gaming ecosystem so the demo stays deterministic and doesn't depend on external gaming APIs. The next step would be exploring how the same approach could work with real gaming services and richer social data. I'd also like to expand the session-planning side: more player preferences, scheduling, better group matching, and longer-term questions like "what should our group play this weekend?" There are also interesting actions that should require stronger human confirmation, especially purchases or other account-level changes. That's an area I'd like to explore further as agent-operated web applications become more capable. title: UITester
pitch: AI agent that tests web UIs via WebMCP tool calls, not brittle selectors—catches regressions.
about_excerpt:
AI agent that tests web UIs via WebMCP tool calls, not brittle selectors—catches regressions.

 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most "AI test agents" still drive the UI the old way: guess a CSS selector, click, hope it doesn't break on the next redesign. When we saw the emerging WebMCP standard — pages exposing their own actions through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) , with a proper JSON Schema instead of a DOM tree to guess at — it looked like the missing layer for reliable, AI-native UI testing. If a page tells an agent exactly what it can do and what valid input looks like, testing stops being "click and pray" and becomes "call the tool and check the contract." 

 What it does 

 ToolProof is a small Electron "browser" built for one job: point it at any web page and it will test that page through its own tools. 

 
 Load — a target URL opens inside an embedded <webview> , just like a normal browser tab. 
 Discover — it checks the page for a native document.modelContext . If the site doesn't support WebMCP yet, a fallback pass reads the page's own HTML5 form constraints ( pattern , required , min / max , type=email , …) and synthesizes an equivalent modelContext on the fly, so any site can be exercised the same way. 
 Generate scenarios — the discovered tool's JSON Schema is sent to Gemini, which proposes 6–10 realistic test cases: happy path plus boundary and invalid-input cases. If there's no API key, or Gemini fails, a deterministic rule-based generator takes over (missing required fields, out-of-range numbers, regex-violating strings via randexp , invalid enum values) — so the tool never dead-ends. 
 Run — each scenario is executed live, inside the real page, via document.modelContext.executeTool(...) — not simulated clicks. 
 Report — pass/fail is compared against the scenario's expected outcome and shown per-scenario plus a summary. 
 

 A companion demo page implements a real, native document.modelContext.registerTool flow, used to validate the agent against an actual WebMCP-compliant target instead of only the DOM-inference fallback. 

 How we built it 

 
 Electron , with a strict main / preload / renderer split ( contextIsolation: true , no nodeIntegration ) — the renderer never touches Node directly, everything goes through an IPC bridge exposed in preload.js . 
 The target site itself runs in a <webview> , so the agent's "browser" is a real Chromium instance, not a headless stub. 
 A hand-rolled document.modelContext polyfill is injected into pages without native WebMCP support, so the discovery → generate → run pipeline is identical whether the tools are real or inferred. 
 Gemini ( gemini-2.5-flash ) turns a tool's inputSchema into concrete test data; a local, dependency-free rule engine ( scenario-utils.js ) mirrors the same scenario shape as a deterministic fallback. 
 A separate agent-runner (Node + Playwright) explores the same idea headlessly, for CI-style runs outside the Electron shell. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 IPC serialization : document.modelContext.getTools() can return live objects with circular/non-cloneable references (e.g. a window handle) — Electron's executeJavaScript bridge threw "object could not be cloned" until we normalized every tool down to { name, description, inputSchema } before it crosses the IPC boundary. 
 Timing : tools registered after client-side hydration weren't visible on first check, so discovery needed to poll getTools() for up to ~8s rather than assume readiness on page load. 
 Schema shape drift : some pages return inputSchema as a JSON string rather than an object — discovery normalizes both shapes before generating scenarios. 
 LLM reliability : an LLM won't always return valid JSON or field names that match the schema exactly, so the rule-based generator exists as a hard fallback, not just a nice-to-have. 
 

 What we learned 

 That WebMCP's registerTool / getTools / executeTool contract is a genuinely better testing surface than the DOM — it turns "does the UI still look right" into "does the underlying capability still honor its own contract," which is both more robust to redesigns and closer to what a QA engineer actually cares about.
