title: RESCASAP.UY
pitch: RESCASAP.UY uses WebMCP to let AI agents discover, compare and prepare discounted surplus-food reservations, while people keep control of the final confirmation.
about_excerpt: RESCASAP.UY uses WebMCP to let AI agents discover, compare and prepare discounted surplus-food reservations, while people keep control of the final confirmation. Like Comment Story Updates RESCASAP.UY WebMCP experience: AI agents discover, compare and prepare surplus-food reservations while humans keep final control. Inspiration Every day, local businesses end up with perfectly good food that must be sold quickly or goes to waste. At the same time, people are looking for more affordable ways to buy food. RESCASAP.UY was created to connect those two realities: helping businesses recover value from same-day surplus while giving people nearby access to food at reduced prices. The WebMCP challenge gave us the opportunity to take that idea one step further: instead of making people manually browse, filter and compare every option, we asked what would happen if an AI agent could interact directly with the marketplace on their behalf. What it does RESCASAP.UY is a surplus-food rescue marketplace built for Uruguay. Businesses can offer discounted rescue packs before food goes to waste, while users can discover available options and choose what works best for them. For the WebMCP experience, RESCASAP exposes a small set of purpose-built tools that allow an AI agent to: Find and rank available rescue packs using constraints such as price, food weight, category and urgency. Compare multiple packs by price, savings, estimated weight, pickup window and neighborhood. Prepare a selected pack for reservation by opening the checkout experience for human review. The agent handles the repetitive discovery and comparison work, but the consequential action remains human-controlled: it never completes the final reservation or initiates a payment by itself. How we built it The WebMCP integration is implemented directly inside the RESCASAP web application through typed, imperative site tools. Three WebMCP tools power the challenge experience: find_rescue_packs compare_rescue_packs prepare_pack_reservation Their inputs use bounded schemas, their outputs are concise and verifiable, and every agent action is reflected visibly in the interface. The application is built with TypeScript, React, Vinext and Cloudflare infrastructure. The production architecture includes Cloudflare D1/SQLite with Drizzle ORM, Supabase authentication and Mercado Pago marketplace payments. For judging, we created a dedicated /demo route that requires no account, API keys, database setup or payment method. It uses an isolated in-memory dataset while running the same product interface and WebMCP tool implementation. This makes the complete agent experience immediately testable by evaluators without touching real customer, merchant or payment data. Human–agent collaboration A core principle of the project is that AI should remove mechanical work without hiding important decisions from the person using it. The agent can search, filter, rank, compare and prepare an action, while the user remains in control of the final commitment. The demo itself was produced through human–agent collaboration: while I recorded the experience, an AI agent operated the web workflow being demonstrated. Challenges One of the biggest challenges was deciding where agent autonomy should stop. A food marketplace contains time-sensitive inventory and potentially consequential actions such as reservations and payments. Instead of giving the agent unrestricted control, we designed a clear boundary: discovery and preparation can be automated, while the final reservation remains a human decision. Another challenge was making the experience easy for judges to reproduce. The WebMCP demo therefore runs without authentication, secrets or payment credentials and resets automatically with the browser session. We also had to make agent actions visible in the actual interface so users can verify what the agent found, compared or prepared instead of trusting an invisible automation. What we learned WebMCP changes the relationship between an AI agent and a website. Instead of relying on visual interpretation or fragile browser automation, a website can expose a small set of intentional, structured capabilities designed specifically for agents. We learned that the most useful agent experience is not necessarily the one that automates everything. It is the one that gives the agent enough capability to remove repetitive work while preserving transparency and human control where it matters. What's next The next step for RESCASAP.UY is to continue developing the real marketplace in Uruguay: onboarding more local businesses, increasing available rescue inventory and improving location-aware discovery. The WebMCP layer can evolve alongside the marketplace, giving people an increasingly natural way to discover and compare surplus food through AI while keeping reservations and payments safe and user-controlled. RESCASAP.UY turns a simple idea — rescue food before it becomes waste — into an experience that humans and AI agents can navigate together. title: Tour De Controle
pitch: A deterministic front door for a fleet of 21 agents. Known request: a circuit answers, zero model calls. New request: Gemini 3.5 decides. 10 model calls instead of 200, measured live on Cloud Run.
about_excerpt:
A deterministic front door for a fleet of 21 agents. Known request: a circuit answers, zero model calls. New request: Gemini 3.5 decides. 10 model calls instead of 200, measured live on Cloud Run.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 



 
 Control Tower — a deterministic front door for an agent fleet 

 10 model calls instead of 200. A 95% reduction, measured on Google Cloud Run. 

 The friction 

 I ran out of credit on a paid model. Mid-project. The agents stopped thinking and the work stopped. 

 That accident exposed something I had never questioned: every single agent action was going through a large model — including the actions we already knew by heart. Read the inventory. Give the status. Run a written procedure. Each one cost money, took seconds, and could answer differently twice in a row. For work that is not speculative at all. 

 What we built 

 A deterministic front door that decides before the model. 
 request → guardrails (pure code)
 ├── known capability → circuit runs, ZERO model calls
 └── no match → Gemini 3.5 Flash decides, explicitly
 
 The model is not removed. It is moved to where it earns its cost . 

 Measured, not claimed 

 200 mixed agent requests, handed over as one asynchronous batch. The caller gets a job id in ~100 ms and walks away. 

 
 
 path 
 count 
 median 
 model calls 
 
 
 
 answered by a circuit 
 180 
 9 ms 
 0 
 
 
 refused by a guardrail 
 10 
 0 ms 
 0 
 
 
 escalated to Gemini 3.5 Flash 
 10 
 5 899 ms 
 10 
 
 

 10 model calls instead of 200. That figure is a count , not a timing: it does not move with hardware, network or load. GET /metrics publishes both counters live, so the claim is a measurement anyone can reproduce. 

 A fleet, not one agent with many prompts 

 21 agents, each with a written specification, a declared scope and an engine. 9 of them are bound to no model at all — deterministic code only. 

 POST /delegate splits a broad request across the agents whose specifications cover each piece: 

 
 
 agent 
 piece 
 outcome 
 
 
 
 Jimmy — the test bench 
 run the regression tests 
 done, no model 
 
 
 Victor — security 
 audit the secrets 
 done, no model 
 
 
 Lois — review 
 review the wording 
 done, no model 
 
 
 Chloe — assistant 
 publish the article 
 refused 
 
 

 The refusal names its own cause: "Chloe may not publish: its specification grants may_publish = false." Separation of concerns is enforced in code, not suggested in a prompt. A failing sub-agent marks only its own piece; the rest continue. 

 Guardrails that actually refuse 

 A safety check must return the same verdict twice in a row. A check whose answer varies is an opinion, not a control. So the guardrails are plain Python: a deny list that does not negotiate, and writes that refuse unless explicitly confirmed. 

 An independent oracle recomputes every expected value in a separate program. It caught a real fabrication in our own repository: a dataset claimed 5468 , the oracle computed 712 , and the reasoning code had 5468 hard-coded so it "agreed" with the fake. Two lies confirming each other. A checker that shares code with the thing it checks is not a checker. 

 Architecture 

 
 Model : Gemini 3.5 Flash through Vertex AI, via the Google GenAI SDK 
 Serving : FastAPI on Google Cloud Run 
 Second deployment : the governed platform itself on Compute Engine — 93 Odoo modules, 21 circuit templates, 67 control gates, 58 skills 
 

 Mandatory disclosures 

 Pre-existing. The Living Map discovery mechanism and the Circuit orchestration model come from an earlier Odoo-based project that has been running in production for a month: 1 580 circuit runs, 2 912 gate crossings, 2 130 human decisions of which 513 were refused . 

 Built during the submission period. The deterministic router, the Gemini fallback through the GenAI SDK, the asynchronous batch endpoint, the delegation to sub-agents, the independent-oracle wiring, /metrics observability, both Cloud deployments, and an audit script that fails the build when a claim in the README is not corroborated by the files on disk. 

 Honest limits. The circuit used in the demo reads a 478-entry living map — real work, but modest. A circuit querying a business database would be slower and the ratio smaller. The "small reasoning model" is a prototype: it selects among hand-written strategies. It is not a trained model, and calling it one would repeat exactly the overclaim the oracle exists to catch. 

 What I learned 

 Constraints are a filter, not only a loss. Running out of credit removed the solutions I could previously afford, and left the ones that stand on their own. I would never have built this with money in the account.

title: Agent-Native Newsroom Portal
pitch: An agent-native newsroom where editors and browser agents collaboratively move stories from draft to publication through 22 real WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: An agent-native newsroom where editors and browser agents collaboratively move stories from draft to publication through 22 real WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates The Story Desk gives editors a complete view of the editorial pipeline, from draft and review through approval and publication. The Media Vault combines image discovery with licensing, allowed channels, attribution, expiration, and accessibility metadata. An approved story is blocked by an expired image license—a real newsroom problem that a WebMCP agent can detect and resolve. The Handoff Engine validates editorial, media-rights, attribution, accessibility, and publishing requirements before generating the handoff. A publishing payload is prepared through WebMCP and delivered only after the workflow passes validation and receives human approval. List of WebMCP tools available Inspiration A newsroom is a coordination machine. A story moves through many steps before it becomes publishable: assignment, drafting, editing, review, approval, media selection, rights verification, and finally handoff to a publishing system. Humans are good at navigating these workflows through interfaces. Agents face a different problem: a traditional website tells them what the interface looks like , but not necessarily what the application can do in a structured way. That led to a simple question: What would a newsroom look like if the website itself were designed for both people and agents? That question became Agent-Native Newsroom Portal . Instead of adding a chatbot to a newsroom, I built a newsroom whose actual capabilities can be exposed directly to external browser agents through WebMCP . What it does Agent-Native Newsroom Portal is an internal newsroom workspace built around three connected areas. Story Desk The Story Desk manages the editorial lifecycle from draft to publication. Editors can: Create and edit stories Assign stories to editors Submit stories for review Approve or request revisions Reorder the editorial run Track the complete story history The application enforces valid editorial state transitions instead of allowing arbitrary status changes. Media Vault The Media Vault manages newsroom images together with the metadata required to publish them safely. Each asset can contain: License information Allowed publishing channels Expiration dates Attribution requirements Photographer/source information Alt text This makes the workflow more useful than simply searching for an image. Can this image actually be used for this publication? The system can detect expired rights and identify usable replacement assets. Handoff Engine The Handoff Engine turns approved editorial content into publication-ready output. Before a story can be handed off, it validates: Editorial approval Editor assignment Headline and body content Media attachment Lead image Media rights Attribution Web publishing permissions Alt text Once the checks pass, the system generates a structured web publishing payload and can execute the simulated handoff. WebMCP The WebMCP layer is the core experiment. The application exposes 22 structured WebMCP tools covering newsroom operations such as: Finding and reading stories Creating and updating stories Approving stories Reordering stories Searching and inspecting media Checking media rights Replacing media Updating captions and alt text Renewing media licenses Validating publication readiness Preparing publishing payloads Executing the handoff There is deliberately no in-app chatbot . The website itself becomes agent-operable. A human editor can use the normal interface, while an external browser agent can use the same application capabilities through WebMCP. Both interact with the same underlying newsroom state. How we built it I built the application as a full-stack web product using: Next.js 16 React 19 TypeScript Tailwind CSS shadcn/ui Prisma SQLite for local development PostgreSQL in production Zustand The application is deployed on Vercel . The architecture separates the user interface, REST API routes, business logic, database, and WebMCP integration. One of the most important design decisions was to make the WebMCP tools use the same business-logic layer as the human UI . For example, approve_story , replace_story_media , and execute_web_handoff are not special demo-only operations. They perform real application operations and follow the same validation and workflow rules used by the normal interface. WebMCP tools are registered through the browser API: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) Each tool exposes structured inputs and structured results. I also seeded the application with realistic newsroom data, including expired media rights and valid replacement assets, so the agent workflow has real problems to discover and resolve. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not registering WebMCP tools. It was making them trustworthy . Once an external agent can change application state, the application needs strong rules around what the agent is allowed to do and when an operation should fail. For example: Editing an approved story should invalidate its previous approval. Expired media should not pass publication validation. Missing alt text should block publication. Invalid editorial transitions should be rejected. The final handoff should be validated again on the server. Another challenge was keeping human and agent interaction synchronized. When an agent changes the application, the human-facing UI must immediately reflect that change. Both paths therefore operate on the same underlying application state. Testing also uncovered a subtle bug in the media attachment flow. When isPrimary was omitted, it was being treated as false , which prevented the first attached image from automatically becoming the lead image. I fixed the API and WebMCP tool behavior and re-tested the workflow. For WebMCP testing, I used the Brave browser and the Chrome extension WebMCP - Model Context Tool Inspector while its free credits were available. I also used ChatGPT to help prepare the demo and GLM for additional WebMCP QA. I focused that external testing on the main workflow tools. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that the project became more than a visual WebMCP demonstration. The application exposes a real, stateful agent workflow across the newsroom. The main publication path is: Create Story ↓ Update Story ↓ Editorial Review ↓ Approve ↓ Attach / Replace Media ↓ Check Rights ↓ Validate Publication ↓ Prepare Web Handoff ↓ Execute Handoff ↓ Published The agent can perform these operations through WebMCP without having to guess its way through the visual interface. We are also proud of the guardrails around agent actions. WebMCP is not treated as a back door around newsroom rules. Agent operations go through the same application logic and validation as human actions. The repository also includes an end-to-end WebMCP validation report covering the project's tool surface and failure handling. What we learned The biggest lesson was that building an agent-native application is different from adding AI to an existing application . The difficult question is not: “Where should I put the chatbot?” It is: “What should the agent actually be able to do?” Good WebMCP tools need meaningful boundaries, clear inputs, predictable outputs, validation, and safe failure behavior. I also learned that useful human-agent systems do not need to be completely autonomous. For a newsroom, the agent can investigate, prepare, validate, and execute structured work, while the human retains editorial judgment and final authority. That led to the interaction model at the heart of this project: The agent handles structured work. The human remains the decision-maker. Building the project also changed how I think about web applications. A website is not only a collection of screens and buttons. It can also expose a structured set of capabilities that other intelligent systems can understand and use. What's next for Agent-Native Newsroom Portal This project is a starting point for a larger agent-native newsroom. The next step would be to move beyond individual publishing tasks and let agents help coordinate the wider editorial operation. For example, a newsroom agent could: Monitor upcoming deadlines Identify stories at risk of missing publication Detect missing media or metadata Find unresolved workflow blockers Prepare recommended actions for editors Coordinate handoffs across publishing channels I would also like to connect the Handoff Engine to real publishing systems instead of the current simulated delivery flow. Another area I want to explore is agent permissions : allowing a newsroom to define which actions an agent can perform automatically and which actions always require explicit human approval. The long-term idea is simple: Don't build AI around the newsroom. Build the newsroom so humans and agents can work together inside it. That is the experiment behind Agent-Native Newsr

title: Poll
pitch: Poll is a shared survey studio where people and AI agents build, launch, and analyze studies together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Poll is a shared survey studio where people and AI agents build, launch, and analyze studies together through WebMCP. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Home GIF WebMCP in action Results Inspiration The inspiration came from a routine observation of our friend, a PHD student. She rushed home to her laptop because she had to check in with her research participants and see how many had responded by a certain time. We remember thinking to ourselves what a tedious task, what if she could get a summary of her results and a summary of her participants feedback by asking an agent. That brought to mind the hours she spent in Qualtrics and Prolific and did the same tedious task: create a new page, pick a question type, click, type, repeat. She already knew her research questions. What if she could tell an agent to build the survey, and all she has to do is approve it. Later she can ask for a summary of results across her studies without needing to rush home. That is Poll: a survey studio where a researcher and their agent share one workspace, and a person still decides what goes out. What it does Poll is a survey research studio. A researcher works with an agent to build, share, and report results of the survey. The human has to give explicit approval for all participants facing tasks while the agent can help them get to the final draft quicker. In a WebMCP-capable browser, an authenticated user can use their favorite agent tool like Codex to interact with Poll to create a draft from a research goal, edit questions, preview, share, and summarize results or feedback. Tools call the same APIs as the buttons on the screen, allowing humans and agents to make edits the same way. Participant routes register no tools: people still consent and answer for themselves. How we built it We started by mapping out a researcher workflow and where an agent can help them. We wanted to see what the user workflow looks like end-to-end should a user choose to manually create a survey, edit the questions, and launch it. The majority of the tedious work came from survey building, so that became the focus of our first tool. We spent time in the documentation reading the example repos and WebMCP docs from Google, OpenAI's Site tools notes, and Cloudflare's WebMCP React starter. What we wanted was a survey studio that still works in a normal browser, and then researcher tools if WebMCP is there. Codex then did the majority of the implementation. We used Codex agents for most of the coding and also used automations to run long running PRs overnight that could be merged in parallel. We reviewed every open PR, no agent was allowed to merge their own work. We tested WebMCP with Codex's Chrome plugin, in-app browser and also the Chrome DevTools MCP. The gif on our landing page was entirely created by Codex and DevTools MCP . We used Cloudflare MCP directly as well to help with db configuration, setup and automated release pipelines. Stack : Our app uses React 19, React Router and TanStack Query with a Hono powering the api. We use D1 and Drizzle for the database. The UI, api and the WebMCP tools all share the same Zod contracts as well. Finally we are using Better Auth for authentication and Resend for email through a Cloudflare Worker cron. WebMCP implementation. Tools are registered imperatively with document.modelContext.registerTool through a small React hook ( useWebMCPTool ). Registration is keyed on the public metadata (name, description, schema, annotations) while the handler is swapped in a ref, so navigating between Build, Share, and Responses does not tear the catalog down. Every tool carries annotations: readOnlyHint , idempotentHint , destructiveHint: false , and untrustedContentHint wherever participant-authored text appears. All of our tools are aware of the role of the logged in user as well to always allow authenticated access. edit_survey is a the core tools, it is a single transactional batch (add, update, move, replace, delete pages and questions, with same-call ref names for branching). Every write that the agent does returns the new revision, an outline, and a validation check, so the agent can see whether it broke anything without another tool call. The /demo route swaps the network transport for a browser local one behind the same tool code, so the entire app is usable without signup Stack. React 19, React Router, TanStack Query, Tailwind on the client; Hono on Cloudflare Workers; D1 with Drizzle; Better Auth; Resend for invitation email from a durable outbox drained after approval; Vitest with 250+ tests across jsdom and the Workers runtime. MIT licensed. Challenges we ran into The agent could not see the tools - In production Chrome refused the page: "WebMCP is disabled for this page because the site's WebMCP configuration exceeds supported limits." We could not find any published limit in the webmcp spec. Our first edit_survey schema, generated from Zod with every question type inlined wherever it appeared, and was close to 100 KB and about 30 levels deep. We rewrote it to define each question type and condition once and point to it with $ref , and hand-tuned the public shape. The same operations, same validation, now under 11 KB and 11 levels deep. The tools kept vanishing mid task - Poll is an SPA and moving from Build to Share rebuilds component state. Our hook treated every new tool object as a new catalog, unregistering everything. To the agent, the tools disappeared between calls. We split "what the tool is" (registered once) from "what it does right now" (a ref that always sees the current survey). Drawing the line between agent work and human approval - One of the hardest decisions to make while building this was what should an agent be unable to do even if asked? We debated this decision a lot because, as models are getting better, they are able to do much more work autonomously and correctly but on the other hand we thought from a researcher's POV and landed on prepare only approach. Anything that reaches other humans has to be explicity approved through the web interface. title: ThreatWeaver
pitch: Humans sketch a cloud architecture. Agents read the live graph, draw STRIDE attacks, and patch the same canvas via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Humans sketch a cloud architecture. Agents read the live graph, draw STRIDE attacks, and patch the same canvas via WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates simulate_attack — attacker and STRIDE threat edges on the live graph Eight document.modelContext tools discovered in ChatGPT apply_security_patch (patchType: waf, target: api-gateway-1) — WAF inline on the shared ThreatWeaver canvas, verified in the activity log. Inspiration Threat modeling usually lives in a spreadsheet or a chat reply that says “add a WAF.” You still redraw the system by hand. I joined the WebMCP Challenge because architecture work is spatial: if an agent is going to help, it should operate the same live graph the human is looking at—not guess from a screenshot or a text memo. I evaluated a few directions (generic architecture canvases, workflow builders) and chose a narrow B2B technical niche: security-by-design cloud diagrams where the agent can read topology, simulate STRIDE findings, and patch the canvas in place. What it does ThreatWeaver is a security-by-design architecture canvas for cloud systems. The page loads an insecure 3-tier starter: Internet → Web Server → API Gateway → Backend → Database + Object Storage. The human can drag components onto the canvas, toggle public / encrypted / rate-limit flags, or ask the agent to add and connect nodes. The agent uses eight WebMCP site tools on the open page. A typical flow: get_architecture_state → simulate_attack on api-gateway-1 (denial of service) and database-1 (information disclosure), which draws an Attacker node, animated red threat edges, and STRIDE badges → apply_security_patch to insert a WAF in front of the gateway, encrypt the database, and remove public access → get_threat_report for what is still open vs secured vs misconfigured. Every tool call is recorded in the activity log so the human can audit what the agent did. Live demo: https://t-weaver.vercel.app/ This is a graph visualizer and mutator with deterministic tool handlers. The LLM reasons about STRIDE; the app applies consistent canvas changes. It is not a production vulnerability scanner or pentest tool. How we built it Stack: React 19, Vite, TypeScript, xyflow, Zustand, Tailwind CSS v4. Frontend only—no backend MCP server. WebMCP: Eight tools register with await document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) in client/src/hooks/useWebMCP.ts . Each tool has JSON Schema with additionalProperties: false , a title, and readOnlyHint where appropriate. Cleanup uses AbortSignal on unmount. Agent-facing data: Read tools return semantic kind values ( apigateway , database , waf , …) and stable ids like api-gateway-1 , not React Flow internals such as architectureNode . Write path: Tool handlers mutate a Zustand store; React Flow re-renders. The WAF patch inserts a real WAF node and rewires incoming data edges to the target gateway—not just a badge on the card. Deploy: Static Vite build on Vercel; Root Directory is client/ . Scope: New project built during the submission period, not a pre-existing product extended with a thin WebMCP layer. Challenges we ran into Discovering the real WebMCP path: Site tools appear in ChatGPT desktop on Work or Codex with models like Terra / Terra Light. The Chat tab and Luna do not expose site tools the same way. The in-page badge “WebMCP ready · 8 tools” only means tools registered—it does not mean an agent has called them yet. Keeping the agent on the page: The agent sometimes tried to open GitHub or leave the live URL. Tighter prompts (“Stay on this page. Use site tools only.”) were required for reliable demos. Separating reasoning from mutations: STRIDE narrative belongs to the LLM; canvas changes must be deterministic. Each write tool has explicit validation and predictable graph effects so the UI always matches what the tool contract promises. From thin PoC to demo-ready product: An early version was too shallow. I refactored toward an insecure starter graph, topology-changing patches, and an activity log so judges could see tool leverage, not just chat text. Accomplishments that we're proud of A single-canvas red-team / blue-team story: attack paths appear on the graph, then WAF insertion, encryption, and private access clear the relevant threat edges—visible in one session and in the demo video. Eight non-trivial tools with clear read vs write roles and schema descriptions agents can follow. WAF mitigation that mutates topology (node + edge rewire), matching what architects expect from “put a WAF in front of the gateway.” Shipping frontend-only on document.modelContext without standing up a separate MCP server. What we learned WebMCP leverage comes from tools against live application state , not from describing UI in chat. Agent APIs should expose stable semantic ids and kinds, not framework implementation details. await registerTool and AbortSignal matter for correct registration and teardown. For this hackathon, the demo video and written description are what help a submission land—show the canvas move when tools fire, not only the agent’s prose. What's next for ThreatWeaver Richer component library and optional import hints from IaC snippets (still scoped as design-time, not auto-deploy). Sharper in-page guidance for agents (copy-ready prompts, clearer misconfiguration rules in get_threat_report ). Shareable threat-report exports for review sessions. Out of scope for the MVP: claiming enterprise SecOps scanning, multiplayer collaboration, or real infrastructure apply from the canvas. Built With javascript react react-flow tailwindcss typescript vercel vite webmcp zustand Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Solo submission. I owned the product direction, scope, and final delivery for ThreatWeaver. What I did: - Chose the ThreatWeaver concept (security-by-design architecture canvas with agent red/blue team on a shared graph) and locked scope: frontend-only WebMCP, eight tools, insecure starter graph, no backend MCP server. - Defined the WebMCP tool contract (read vs write tools, semantic node kinds, JSON Schema, simulate_attack / apply_security_patch behavior including WAF topology changes). - Directed implementation and refactors after an early thin PoC—toward demo-ready behavior: activity log, inspector payloads, threat report, and judge-friendly sample prompts. - Tested WebMCP end-to-end with ChatGPT desktop (Work/Codex, Terra Light) and Chrome (WebMCP flag + Model Context Tool Inspector). - Deployed the static app to Vercel ( https://t-weaver.vercel.app/ ), recorded the demo video, and prepared Devpost/README submission materials. title: Scholarship Scout
pitch: A source-transparent WebMCP workspace where students and agents find, explain, compare, and plan scholarship applications together.
about_excerpt: A source-transparent WebMCP workspace where students and agents find, explain, compare, and plan scholarship applications together. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Scholarship Scout turns fragmented scholarship research into a structured human-and-agent workflow. Students provide a lightweight profile, search a curated catalog of 30 named programme records, inspect match, mismatch, and unknown evidence, compare up to three candidates, and turn a selected route into a planning checklist. A catalog record is not automatically presented as an open application or a verified match: each result exposes its official provider link, review date, evidence scope, cycle status, and unresolved facts. WebMCP is central to the experience. Six typed page-defined tools expose search, eligibility, comparison, shortlisting, checklist generation, and checklist updates to an agent. The tools use the same deterministic TypeScript domain layer and browser-local state as the visible interface, so agent actions and student actions stay synchronized. State-changing tools require explicit student confirmation, and the app never submits a scholarship application. This improves scholarship research because agents can filter and normalize structured evidence while students retain the judgment calls: resolving country or course rules, choosing among tied candidates, verifying the official source, and approving saved work. Unknown facts add no ranking points, so missing evidence cannot silently become a recommendation. The release was tested on the live Vercel deployment in ChatGPT’s in-app browser. All six tools were discovered. A clean Nigeria + Computer Science + any-level + any-funding run returned 25 candidates, preserved unknown criteria in the top-three eligibility checks, populated a three-way comparison, and generated three source-aware Chevening planning tasks. Built with Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, browser-native document.modelContext.registerTool registration, deterministic domain functions, local browser persistence, and Vercel. The public repository contains the complete source, demo assets, setup instructions, automated tests, and MIT license. Codex helped scope the product, implement and test WebMCP, audit all 30 catalog records against official-source evidence, correct high-risk facts, harden persistence and confirmation boundaries, verify the live workflow, and render the narrated demo. title: Adamastor
pitch: The agent's output stops being a message and becomes something you can pick up and move.
about_excerpt: The agent's output stops being a message and becomes something you can pick up and move. Like Comment Story Updates Adamastor dashboard InspirationFor judges: the WebMCP tools require the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser (model GPT-5.6 Sol or Terra — Luna has WebMCP disabled), or Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing. The site works normally in any browser; the agent tools only appear in those. No credentials required — you get your own private workspace automatically. Signing in with ChatGPT is optional. Inspiration I have about 2,500 photographs from six years of hiking in the Western Cape — birds, fynbos, mountains, the sea — and I want to make a YouTube channel out of them. I am not a developer. So I asked an AI to help me plan it. It gave me nine hundred words. I read them once, and I never found them again. That is the whole problem in one sentence. An answer in a chat window is linear and undifferentiated, and it scrolls away. You cannot pick up idea four and put it beside idea eleven. You cannot fix line three and keep line four — you can only ask for the whole thing again and hope the new version's flaw is somewhere you'll notice. When the conversation ends, it is gone. Chat memory belongs to the AI. It is not yours, and you cannot rearrange it. I wanted the answer to be an object instead of a message. What it does Adamastor is a spatial canvas — notes, tasks, links, columns and files placed freely on a board. WebMCP lets an agent work on that board alongside you. The agent's output stops being a message and becomes something that stays where you put it, that you can move, edit, group and keep — and that the agent can read back later. Four things follow from that: You keep 90% and fix 10%. The agent lays out twenty shots for a film. You disagree with one. You drag it out and retype it, and the other nineteen don't move. In a chat window the equivalent is asking for the whole list again. The board is the briefing. Come back a week later, in a conversation that has never seen you, and ask what you'd done. The agent reads the board — your ticked tasks, your own edits — and picks up from there. You explain nothing. Structure survives. Ask it to re-cut twenty shots by what you could film this weekend versus what needs a trip, and it doesn't hand you a list you read once. It rebuilds the board. That structure is still there next month. Arranging stays yours. The agent composes; you place. Why this fits WebMCP A chat interface is the wrong shape for planning work, because planning work is spatial. But a spatial canvas has always been the wrong shape for AI help, because there was no way for a model to act on it without pretending to be a mouse. WebMCP closes that gap in the only place it can be closed — inside the page, where the application already knows what a board is, where the cards are, and how wide a column should be. The agent doesn't need to see pixels or guess coordinates. It says these items belong together and this group is called "This weekend", and the application does the geometry. The eight tools list-boards · read-board · search-items · create-board · open-board · add-items · update-item · group-items group-items takes meaning, not coordinates. The agent supplies groupings and labels; the application measures each card, sizes the columns to fit their contents, and grows the canvas to hold them. Chrome's WebMCP guidance is explicit that tools should not ask an agent to perform maths, and it produces a better result — the layout is consistent however the agent chooses to group things. add-items is batched, so one call can populate an entire board rather than twenty round trips. create-board opens the board in the same state update that creates it — no second call, no race, and the new board is on screen before the agent has finished speaking. Eight tools, not eighty. Each maps to one thing the product actually does — and one more was deliberately left out. What the agent deliberately cannot do It cannot delete your content. Notes, tasks, links and files are never removed by an agent, only regrouped. Column headings are structural labels and are replaced when a board is reorganised. There is no confirmation step in the WebMCP specification yet, and the read tools return user-generated content flagged untrustedContentHint — content the model then acts on. A delete tool in that context is a prompt-injection hazard, so it wasn't shipped. The agent groups what it suggests removing; the person removes it. It also cannot reposition individual cards. Composition is the agent's half of this product; arrangement is mine. What happened when I left a gap — and why it makes the case While testing, I asked the agent to move an image. There is no tool for that. Instead of refusing, it read the page, added a new image card through the toolbar, and pasted in a blob: address it had scraped from the rendered photograph. Then it reported: "Done — the bird image is now at the top of the board and synced." Nothing had moved. The new card was permanently broken — a blob: address dies with the page that made it. And "synced" was read off the interface, not returned by anything. That is what an agent does when it has no tool: it improvises with your interface and tells you it worked. With tools, every result across nineteen deployed versions was real, because a tool returned it. Without one, it scraped, clicked, and lied confidently. Every tool in this project exists to make that unnecessary — and update-item now says plainly when it has been asked to do something it cannot do, instead of reporting a success it never achieved. How I built it Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Cloudflare D1 and R2, deployed on ChatGPT Sites. The WebMCP layer is deliberately boring: the eight tool handlers are pure functions over the board array, in a file that imports no React and touches no browser API. That means they're unit-testable without a DOM, and the React layer only has to apply the result. Tool handlers read current state through a ref synced on every render, so they never act on a stale copy of the boards. Tools are registered with the imperative API on the top-level document. ChatGPT's browser does not discover tools inside iframes and does not support the declarative form API, so this approach runs in both browsers. readOnlyHint on all three read tools, untrustedContentHint on the two that return user content, outputs truncated to the recommended 1.5K budget, and errors written so the agent can recover on its own — "No board with that id. Call list-boards to see the available boards." Nineteen automated tests, including the output budget and the layout geometry. Challenges The thing I started from was broken in ways it did not admit to. This began as an AI-generated app that looked finished. It had one workspace, hardcoded, shared by every visitor — no concept of a user at all. The entire application state lived in a single database row. The file upload had never once worked in production, because of an undocumented ~1 MB request-body limit that nobody had measured. It was audited file by file before a single tool was written. Per-user workspaces had to come first. There was no point giving an agent tools to write into a workspace everyone shared. Authentication was added using a sign-in helper the original build had shipped and never called. Everything I guessed about behaviour, I got wrong. Not the structure — the behaviour. I guessed at the cause of a Safari error and was wrong. I guessed a storage binding was missing and was wrong. I predicted the agent would produce a scattered grid and it chained a second tool unprompted and produced a clean one. The lesson held every time: measure it, don't reason about it. A cached JavaScript bundle produced three false bug reports before I worked out that the embedded browser had to be quit entirely between deploys. What I learned That the interesting question isn't what tools to give an agent. It's what to withhold, and how a tool should behave when it's asked for something outside its remit. An agent with no tool doesn't stop. It improvises with your interface and reports success. So the honest failure message — "Items cannot be repositioned by a tool; a person drags them" — turned out to matter as much as any capability I added. And that latency belongs to the model, not the page. The tool calls return in milliseconds. The wait is the agent working out what to say — which is worth knowing before you design around it. What's next Per-item history, so you can see what the agent changed and undo one thing rather than everything. A read tool that returns a compact board summary for very large boards. And a delete tool, the day WebMCP has a confirmation step to hang it on. title: Stack Blueprint
pitch: Describe your project. Stack Blueprint uses WebMCP to draft the software stack, equip your coding agent with the right skills and MCPs, and then explain every choice as the blueprint is drawn.
about_excerpt: Describe your project. Stack Blueprint uses WebMCP to draft the software stack, equip your coding agent with the right skills and MCPs, and then explain every choice as the blueprint is drawn. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI coding agents are good at naming a familiar framework, database, and host. That answer is rarely enough to make them excellent at building with those choices. A React Native project may need Expo-specific skills, device automation, React diagnostics, and a native-quality design pass. A Supabase project benefits from its MCP and explicit database and RLS guidance. Builders should not have to know this entire ecosystem before they begin. We built Stack Blueprint to answer the harder question: “How do I fully equip my agent to execute this stack well?” What it does Describe any software idea in ordinary language. Stack Blueprint infers the project shape, stage, and priorities; selects a focused product stack; applies curated technology-to-tool mappings; verifies matching workspace picks against VibeLeaderboard's maintained public index; and converts relevant engineering Intel into project-specific instructions. The result draws itself as an architectural blueprint. The equipped AI workspace appears first, grouped into harness and model, connected MCPs, diagnostics and QA, project skills, and an execution playbook. The application and delivery layers follow. Click any logo to see its role, why it was chosen, and its official source. The overview stays deliberately simple, while the browser agent can inspect, refine, and render the same structured plan through WebMCP. Why WebMCP This is shared work, not a static recommendation. The user needs a visible plan they can understand and question; the agent needs structured tools it can call, inspect, and revise. WebMCP lets one project description trigger the real product workflow, update visible page state, and return the same evidence-backed blueprint to the agent. The page registers seven tools: build, inspect, apply a constraint, refine, survey, consult, and render. Together, a person and agent can create and improve one inspectable execution system instead of passing disconnected lists between a chat and a website. An agent can explain why Expo was selected, open that same explanation for the person, then apply an offline-first requirement and visibly record which choices stayed or changed. How we built it Stack Blueprint is an open-source Next.js and TypeScript application hosted on Vercel. Its client registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) ; tool calls update the same React state as the manual interface. A bounded same-origin API proxy calls only VibeLeaderboard's public, read-only catalog and Intel tools. No private source code, credentials, transcripts, or article bodies are shipped. Recommendations are conditional. Selecting Expo activates Expo MCP, exact Expo project/design/router skills, React and Expo diagnostics, and device automation. Selecting Supabase activates Supabase MCP and database guidance. Live catalog matches are marked as verified; curated fallbacks remain linked to their official sources. Prototype briefs intentionally defer production-only services. Intel results are filtered to the project's risks and rewritten as imperative build instructions rather than displayed as a generic reading feed. Challenges The hardest problem was resisting a template-driven stack picker. Similar apps do not prove that their choices were correct, and a dense alternatives grid made the result harder to use. We removed automatic product matching and focused the consultation on the more defensible value: a maintained, stack-specific AI workspace. We also had to make external evidence useful without making it authoritative. Catalog and Intel results are bounded, sanitized, cited, and treated as untrusted inputs. The initial blueprint remains a first draft that the calling agent can refine only with a complete replacement plan and explicit reasoning. What we learned The framework decision is often the easy part. Execution quality improves when a stack selection automatically brings along its official MCPs, exact implementation skills, deterministic diagnostics, and proof requirements. WebMCP is especially useful when the browser experience and the agent's structured state are the same object instead of two approximations. What's next Next we want to expand the maintained tool mappings, add repeatable browser evals for more project types, and let teams export the final blueprint directly into repository instructions and agent workspace configuration. title: Package-G WebMCP
pitch: Package-G lets ChatGPT inspect, run, and explain deterministic evidence audits through WebMCP—without letting the agent decide the verdict.
about_excerpt: Package-G lets ChatGPT inspect, run, and explain deterministic evidence audits through WebMCP—without letting the agent decide the verdict. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration: AI agents are increasingly capable of navigating interfaces, collecting information, and helping humans complete complex workflows. But in evidence-sensitive work, there is an important boundary: the agent helping with the process should not automatically become the authority that decides what is true. That idea inspired Package-G WebMCP. Package-G is a deterministic, browser-local evidence auditor. A human defines and confirms the audit semantics, while claims, evidence, provenance, gaps, findings, and results remain explicitly inspectable. ChatGPT can navigate and operate that workflow through WebMCP, but the authoritative verdict is produced by Package-G's deterministic auditor. The core principle is simple: ChatGPT navigates. Package-G decides. What it does: Package-G lets a user create or load an audit workspace containing claims, evidence, provenance, and an audit contract. Through WebMCP, ChatGPT can then: summarize the current workspace; read the audit contract; list and inspect claims; list and inspect evidence; identify evidence gaps; request a deterministic audit; retrieve the authoritative result; explain the resulting decision chain. The submitted application exposes exactly 10 WebMCP Site Tools. The important part is what those tools cannot do. ChatGPT cannot use them to invent authoritative findings, change evidence truth, override a verdict, or turn a rejected audit into an accepted one. For the same frozen inputs, ruleset, and auditor runtime, Package-G is designed to produce the same semantic audit result independently of the agent operating it. Why WebMCP This is a workflow where structured interaction matters much more than having an AI read text from a page. Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer application state from the visual interface and decide which buttons or text correspond to the user's intent. With WebMCP, Package-G exposes explicit, bounded operations with structured inputs and outputs. ChatGPT can understand the audit workspace as a tool-enabled application rather than approximating it from page content. We tested this using the ChatGPT desktop app and its built-in browser. ChatGPT discovered all 10 Package-G Site Tools and successfully invoked all 10. In our C09 demonstration scenario, Correct Evidence, Wrong Repository , ChatGPT requests the audit through WebMCP, while Package-G's deterministic Worker evaluates the evidence and returns: "REJECT_WITH_REPAIR_REQUIRED" ChatGPT can inspect and explain that result, but it cannot override it. How we built it: Package-G WebMCP is implemented as a browser-local TypeScript application using React and Vite. The deterministic auditor runs in a fresh Dedicated Module Worker. Runtime identity, ruleset identity, and audit inputs are explicitly bound so reproducibility can be checked rather than assumed. The application uses: WebMCP / document.modelContext for Site Tool registration; TypeBox schemas and Ajv standalone/AOT validation; Web Workers for deterministic audit execution; IndexedDB/Dexie for local persistence; Web Crypto for hashes and integrity checks; Vitest and fast-check for unit/property validation; Playwright for real-browser conformance testing; Netlify for the public production deployment. Core V1 does not require a remote application backend, remote database, or OpenAI API key. The audit itself runs locally in the browser. Challenges: One of the most useful parts of the project was discovering problems that only appeared when the system left the local test environment. Our first production pipeline revealed that a clean Netlify build did not reproduce the same finalized D11 verification artifact as our audited local release. We changed the release pipeline so that a production build validates a closed, cryptographically bound scenario corpus and fails transactionally instead of leaving stale release artifacts behind. A later live-browser test exposed another issue: our strict production Content Security Policy blocked Ajv's runtime schema compilation because it relied on dynamic code generation. Instead of weakening the CSP with unsafe-eval , we changed the validation architecture to compile the runtime validators ahead of time with Ajv standalone generation. We independently compared the new AOT validators against reference Ajv behavior across more than 15,000 validation cases with zero mismatches. The final production application runs successfully with the strict CSP and without runtime "eval" or "Function" construction. What we learned: The biggest lesson was that WebMCP is not only about making websites easier for agents to operate. It can also be used to define authority boundaries between an agent and the application it operates. We learned how important lifecycle-scoped tools, bounded schemas, deterministic execution, runtime identity, production CSP behavior, and real in-app ChatGPT discovery are when moving from a WebMCP prototype to something independently testable. We also learned that browser-local deterministic systems and AI agents do not have to compete for authority. They can complement each other. What's next: Package-G can operate without an LLM, which opens an interesting next step: exposing the same deterministic audit core through human-only, agent-operated, and hybrid workflows. WebMCP demonstrates that an AI agent can participate deeply in a high-integrity application without becoming its final source of truth. title: Drishti
pitch: Drishti is an AI accessibility lens that sees, understands, and narrates the world around you for greater digital and visual accessibility.
about_excerpt:
Drishti is an AI accessibility lens that sees, understands, and narrates the world around you for greater digital and visual accessibility.

 Inspiration 

 Accessibility should not depend on whether someone can see, read, or interpret digital and physical environments easily. I was inspired by the idea of creating a universal AI lens that can turn visual information into useful, understandable guidance. Drishti was built to make technology and the world around us more accessible through AI-powered vision and narration. 

 What it does 

 Drishti is an AI-powered accessibility lens that analyzes visual environments and explains what it sees in a clear, useful way. It can identify objects, describe scenes, extract relevant information, and provide accessibility-focused insights.
With WebMCP, Drishti can also expose its accessibility capabilities as tools that AI agents can discover and use, allowing agents to request visual analysis, accessibility summaries, barrier details, recommendations, and reports. 

 How we built it 

 Drishti was built with React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and the Google GenAI SDK. Gemini vision models power the visual analysis, while the Web Speech API provides voice narration.
We added WebMCP tool registration so supported AI agents can interact with Drishti's accessibility capabilities programmatically. The interface remains usable normally even when WebMCP is unavailable. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of my biggest challenges was designing AI-powered accessibility features that are genuinely useful rather than simply generating descriptions. We had to consider clarity, uncertainty, and how information should be presented to someone who may depend on the output.
Integrating WebMCP also required us to think about how existing application functionality could be exposed as agent-accessible tools without compromising the normal user experience. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I'm proud of turning an accessibility concept into a working product that combines computer vision, narration, and agent interoperability.
Adding WebMCP makes Drishti more than an accessibility interface. Its capabilities can become part of larger agent workflows, giving AI agents a structured way to access visual accessibility information. 

 What we learned 

 I learned that accessibility is not only about adding assistive features. It is about designing information around the needs of the person using it.
We also learned how emerging web standards such as WebMCP can make web applications more useful to AI agents by exposing meaningful capabilities as structured tools rather than relying only on traditional interfaces. 

 What's next for Drishti 

 I want to expand Drishti beyond individual visual analysis into a more complete accessibility assistant.
Next, i plan to improve real-time scene understanding, add more accessibility-specific detection, support richer agent workflows through WebMCP, improve multilingual narration, and explore integrations that allow Drishti to assist users across more environments and devices.

title: Tengu and Boykot web mcp the art of interact with agents
pitch: A real Santiago restaurant and a real art-supply store expose menu, catalog, live stock and forms as WebMCP tools. The agent does the tedious part and stops: you send, you pay.
about_excerpt: A real Santiago restaurant and a real art-supply store expose menu, catalog, live stock and forms as WebMCP tools. The agent does the tedious part and stops: you send, you pay. Like Comment Story Updates Tengu Swag Boykot Flow Restaurants and small shops are the most-attempted and worst-served agent task on the web. Every assistant can find a restaurant. Almost none can do anything with one. The menu lives in a PDF or a photo, the prices are stale, and the booking widget is a third-party iframe an agent cannot reason about. So the agent guesses — and it guesses wrong about the one thing the diner is paying for. We run two real businesses in Santiago, Chile, and we felt this from the other side. Agents were already describing our menu and our catalog to people, from blog posts written years ago. We had no way to be the author of what agents said about us. But the thing that actually kept us from opening the door was not the reading. It was the booking. Nobody wants an agent that reserves a table, or buys $80,000 CLP of paint, on their behalf while they are looking away. So we built for the opposite: the agent does the tedious part and stops. What it does Two businesses that have nothing in common expose the same pattern. Tengu — a kappo omakase restaurant, average table $300–400k CLP. Five tools on the page: get_carta (the live menu with real prices, by section), buscar_plato (search dishes, cocktails, wines and sake), get_guia (long-form guides the restaurant wrote about bluefin, sake and kappo cooking), get_info, and the one that matters — preparar_reserva. Boykot — an art and graffiti supply store, about 3.000 SKUs. Thirteen tools: catalog search, product detail, brand list, quotes, stock subscriptions, promotions, project planning, colour cards — plus agregar_al_carro, ver_mi_carro and guardar_en_lista. preparar_reserva fills the reservation form on the page with the party size, date, time and name the agent gathered in conversation — and then stops. It does not submit. The form is left visible, filled, scrolled into view, with the fields the agent touched marked, and a notice above it that says so and offers to discard. The human checks it and sends it. agregar_al_carro does the same on the store side. The cart gets built. Nobody pays. That is the division of labour we wanted. The agent parses "a table for four next Friday, somewhere quiet, my wife doesn't eat raw fish". The human keeps the part that costs money and social capital. The restaurant's host still sees a normal booking arrive. The read tools matter for a subtler reason: grounding. An agent asked "what's the sake situation at Tengu" now answers from the restaurant's own words and tonight's actual list, instead of from a 2023 blog post. For the first time, the business is the author of what agents say about it. How we built it Eighteen tools across the two sites — five on Tengu, thirteen on Boykot — registered on document.modelContext (with navigator.modelContext as the deprecated alias), feature-detected so each page degrades to an ordinary website when the API is absent: var mc = document.modelContext || navigator.modelContext; if (!mc || typeof mc.registerTool !== 'function') return; Both sites carry origin trial tokens, so the API is native — no ?webmcp flag, no polyfill, nothing for the judge to enable. Open the URL and the tools are there. The in-page tools are deliberately thin: they proxy to the same /api/mcp JSON-RPC server each business already runs for out-of-page agents. A browser agent and a server-side agent get the same answers from the same source. One truth, two transports. The exception is the write-side tools — preparar_reserva and agregar_al_carro only exist in the page, because their whole job is to touch the DOM in front of a human and leave it there. Tengu is static HTML and vanilla JS on Vercel with zero npm dependencies on the page — the smallest attack surface we could manage for something that hands tools to an autonomous caller. Reservations persist to Postgres through SECURITY DEFINER functions behind row-level security that denies all direct access; the page never holds a database credential. Boykot is Next.js, backed by the store's live inventory. Deliberately not exposed: anything that spends money or commits the business. No payment, no confirmation, no cancellation, no order modification. The reservation engine has its own caps underneath — 8 tables per slot, rate limit per name and phone — and the agent surface sits strictly inside them. A tool we don't register is a tool that can't be jailbroken. Thnks For Reading :) Built With chrome edge html javascript json-rpc model-context-protocol nextjs origin-trial postgresql rest-api supabase vanilla-js vercel webmcp woocommerce Try it out boykot-nu.vercel.app tengu-deploy.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Everything: the WebMCP tool surface on both sites, the reservation engine behind Tengu, the catalog and cart tools on Boykot, the write-up and the video. — Tengu's site is work I do for the restaurant, Boykot is my shop — so the decision about what NOT to expose was mine to make and mine to live with. pitch: Mutual-aid dispatch for a flood. Coordinators drag pins and set urgency; the agent logs, matches and broadcasts on the same live map through WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
Mutual-aid dispatch for a flood. Coordinators drag pins and set urgency; the agent logs, matches and broadcasts on the same live map through WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 What it is 

 When the Grand River comes up, help is a group chat: forty unread messages, a spreadsheet nobody updates, and a volunteer with a truck who doesn't know where to go. Highwater is one map. Requests and volunteers are pins. The coordinator drags pins, bumps urgency and marks things done by hand. The dispatch agent reads the same board through WebMCP, logs what comes in, matches the nearest suitable volunteer, draws the dispatch line, and broadcasts what's still unmet. 

 Live: https://highwater-six.vercel.app · Code: https://github.com/chinesepowered/highwater 

 Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP 

 Dispatch is a shared-state problem. An agent that only sees a screenshot of a map cannot know that the coordinator just moved Jamal's truck to the far side of the closed bridge. Highwater exposes the board as eleven structured tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool : 

 get_situation , get_stats , add_request , add_offer , find_volunteers_for , match , unmatch , update_request , update_volunteer , broadcast , focus_map 

 add_request accepts a street name and places it on the map through a small gazetteer, so the agent can work from raw text messages. find_volunteers_for returns capable volunteers nearest-first with distance in km and availability, and match draws the dispatch line. Every human edit (a dragged pin, an urgency click) changes the same model the tools read; every agent edit lands in the event feed with a 🤖 mark. 

 How it creates a better experience 

 
 Paste, don't transcribe. Three incoming texts become two requests, one volunteer, two matches, dispatch lines on the map, and a broadcast for what is still unmet. Eight tool calls, one paste. 
 Human corrections are first-class. Drag Priya's boat across the river because the bridge closed, say "Priya is stuck", and the agent re-reads the board, sees her new position, releases her, and re-matches the seniors' residence to the accessible van. The map flies to it with focus_map . 
 Triage you can see. Urgency 1–5 colours the pins; open-and-urgent requests sort to the top; stats show people waiting and volunteers free. 
 

 What people and agents can do together that was hard before 

 Before: one exhausted coordinator reading messages aloud while someone else types into a sheet, and matching by memory. Now: the coordinator keeps judgment and local knowledge (which bridge is closed, who is reliable) and expresses it by moving pins and setting urgency; the agent keeps the bookkeeping and the distance math, and never acts on stale state because it reads the board before every action. 

 How WebMCP is implemented 

 
 lib/webmcp.ts : registry that calls document.modelContext.registerTool(..., { signal }) for each tool and unregisters via AbortController on unmount. Native browser-agent calls and in-page agent calls share one execute path and one activity log. 
 lib/tools.ts : the eleven tools with JSON Schema inputs and read-only / destructive annotations. 
 lib/aid.ts : the shared store (requests, offers, events, map focus), haversine distances, the street gazetteer, and match/unmatch bookkeeping. Dragging a Leaflet marker calls the same store the tools mutate. 
 components/AidMap.tsx : react-leaflet map with draggable pins, dispatch polylines, and a fly-to controller driven by focus_map . 
 components/AgentPanel.tsx + app/api/agent/route.ts : a Gemini function-calling loop that discovers the registered tools and dispatches through WebMCP, with a model fallback chain for free-tier limits. 
 

 Tested in Chrome 153 with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing (DevTools → Application → WebMCP lists all eleven tools) and with the in-page Gemini dispatch agent. 

 Fictional scenario and people; not an emergency service.

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 I grew up playing pokemon emerald and I loved it, this is an homage to a game that has meant a lot to me. there's a whole community of people who mod old gameboy games and create "rom-hacks", this is something along a similar vein, I'd like for people to be able to experience the beauty of the game design that went into crafting pokemon emerald. for a game released in 2004, I think it's astounding how well it holds up even today and how intricate the map is. 

 What it does 

 it's a faithful adaptation of pokemon emerald, built to simulate what the game feels like on the actual gameboy. unlike emulation, this isn't just running the ROM, it instead lets you zoom out and explore the world. think of this as "creative mode" in minecraft. 

 How we built it 

 there is a big rom-hacking pokemon community, and it is due to the incredible work of this community that building this game was so easy (relatively). just a few years ago this would've been a weeks-long, if not month long project. I took the decompiled works of pokemon emerald (pokeemerald-decomp), and asked codex to reimplement it in JS. I then asked it to make a parity list, and thought about what I want to preserve and what I'd like to change. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 making the map feel responsive was a big issue, especially when zooming out. I also had to match the exact ticks that a gameboy uses, because I want the site to feel realistic. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I'm really happy with how the zoomed out view looks, and the fact that you can still walk around and explore the region whilst having a "god view". 

 What we learned 

 webmcp in my opinion is currently constrained, I look forward to contributing to the standard. it needs bidirectional communication - the website needs to have a callback / some way to tell the agent when a task is done or ready instead of just polling. 

 What's next for overworld-webmcp 

 I'd love to make it multiplayer, and add secret bases. I might add battling capabilities as well, but it would be okay to leave it out since there are plenty of battle simulators, and this is more of an artistic project instead of a faithful simulation of the game.

Political purview is a centralized hub for chatting and researching elections, running candidates, the policies they support, and how those policies relate to their donors.

 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 The inspiration for this project is from a long-standing issue that I had with the political process. In California, in the last election, over 30 candidates were running for governor, and a laundry list of gubernatorial positions for local needs. It's an arduous task to research all the candidates to find one you can trust. Relying on corporate-owned media and/or commercials, or on sites like Ballotpedia and Vote Smart, only skims the surface of who each candidate is, so I often had to do additional research through videos, C-SPAN, etc., to get a full understanding of each person. With U9itus, I wanted to bring all of these issues together in one place. 

 What it does 

 U9itus is a resource network that brings all data sources together in one place, allowing users to "date" their potential leader by accessing their history like a dating profile. Users can save their favorite candidates and use the Map feature to explore districts across America. With the added WebMCP functionality, users can connect AI systems to find relevant data connections and scale knowledge about each candidate. 

 How we built it 

 I built the system using Laravel and Next.js; these additional components of WebMCP expand on the functions already used in models and views, exposing specific data points via the browser. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The most challenging aspect of this app's creation, beyond the countless errors and adjustments required to develop the monolith, was how data was collected. Using third-party APIs dedicated to political needs often required payment. So I had to creatively use tools such as RSS feeds, Google Civics, and Congress.gov, along with backend data matching and AI services to query and clean up data as it arrives through our Workflow services within GitHub. I also ran into issues with configuring the WebMCP tools. At first, the API were not properly designed to be accepted, and the data was pulled using Playwright functionality. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Following through even with all the adversities. After all the struggles, the application works. 

 What we learned 

 There are a lot of things I learned in the process. One notable aspect is the use of GitHub workflows and how data connects with AI WebMCPs. 

 What's next for U9itus: Political purview 

 I would love to get more users into the app, so I can learn how they use it. Also, I would love to work with the PACs and Non-profits to incorporate more dialed-in features that can help users with the voting process.
