title: LEGO Claw: Assembly Lab
pitch: Given a mission, One browser agent assembles a whole creative crew and completes the mission, on its own!
about_excerpt: Given a mission, One browser agent assembles a whole creative crew and completes the mission, on its own! Like Comment Story Updates Claw Architecture Agent Collaboration Results Assembly Lab Crew Showcase Inspiration Most browser agents operate alone. They can search a page or complete a form, but they rarely coordinate other intelligent actors or help a person understand how a team reached an outcome. We wanted to test a more ambitious interaction model: the browser agent as an orchestrator of a visible specialist crew. LEGO Claw already had a creative multi-agent sandbox. During the WebMCP Challenge submission period, we added a WebMCP-native orchestration layer that turns a complicated sequence of UI decisions into a typed, observable collaboration loop. The judged work is this new WebMCP extension and its dedicated judge experience, not the pre-existing platform. What it does A person can ask their browser agent: “Choose the bridge challenge, pair an architect with a diplomat, run four observable turns, then explain whether they collaborated well.” The browser agent first discovers the scenarios and specialist presets that the page actually supports. It then configures the visible mission with validated IDs, a bounded crew, and a fixed turn budget. The agent can preview the plan, advance exactly one turn at a time, or run the mission to completion. Each specialist's message, action type, collaboration metrics, and changes to the shared 3D artifact appear in the same interface the person sees. The human can inspect progress between turns. Finally, the browser agent can summarize the current run and request a structured collaboration analysis with a grade, pattern, observations, and recommendations. Stage WebMCP tools Visible outcome Discover list_scenarios , list_agent_presets The browser agent learns the real challenges and available specialists Configure configure_mission , preview_mission The scenario, crew, mode, and turn budget update on screen Execute run_next_turn , run_simulation The timeline, metrics, and 3D artifact evolve Understand inspect_collaboration , analyze_collaboration Progress, collaboration patterns, and recommendations become inspectable Reset reset_mission The experiment returns to a clean local state Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Without WebMCP, configuring and interpreting a multi-agent experiment requires brittle visual automation across many controls. With WebMCP, the page publishes a deliberate contract: explicit scenario and agent identifiers, bounded inputs, structured results, accurate safety annotations, and cancellation-aware execution. The integration is not a decorative “agent button.” It is a coherent nine-tool sequence that lets the browser agent discover, configure, execute, inspect, and analyze a specialist crew. The human remains in control because state-changing tools update the visible page, the judge mission only prepares a run, and step-by-step mode provides a review point between every turn. What was difficult before is now direct: one natural-language request can assemble the right specialist team, configure a constrained experiment, observe the shared artifact, and explain the team's behavior without hiding the process from the person. How we built it The React and TypeScript frontend registers nine imperative WebMCP tools through a lifecycle-aware hook. The definitions are separated from the React view so names, descriptions, JSON Schemas, annotations, and execution paths are deterministic and directly testable. The tools operate the same state used by the human interface and call a typed tRPC backend. The backend generates specialist turns with strict structured output, while React Three Fiber and Three.js render each structured assembly action. A separate analysis step evaluates role effectiveness, emergent behavior, and recommendations. Layer Implementation Browser-agent interface WebMCP imperative API and webmcp-types Human interface React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion Application API tRPC and Zod Multi-agent simulation Server-side model calls with strict JSON Schemas Visible evidence Three.js, React Three Fiber, Drei Verification Vitest, TypeScript, production build, live browser testing Safety and trust Tool inputs use restrictive schemas; read-only behavior is annotated; handlers returning model-generated text use untrustedContentHint; and no cross-origin tool exposure is enabled. Tools unregister when the page is left. Long-running handlers receive the browser-provided cancellation signal. The server sets an origin-keyed agent-cluster header and limits the tools permission to the same origin. Mission inputs are bounded to two-to-four agents and four-to-twelve turns. The recommended judge flow uses four turns. Every state change is reflected in the interface. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was not registering a tool. It was ensuring that browser-agent actions and human actions remained the same operation. We avoided a hidden automation layer by making WebMCP handlers mutate the live mission state that powers the visible controls, timeline, metrics, and 3D scene. Model reliability was another challenge. We changed the simulation path from loose text parsing to strict structured responses, bounded output, explicit diagnostics, deterministic contract tests, and a graceful fallback. We also kept the browser-provided cancellation signal through the WebMCP handler boundary. Finally, the underlying platform is broad, while judges may spend only minutes with each entry. We built a focused /webmcp explanation page and a one-click /sandbox setup that prepare one memorable flow without executing actions before the user or browser agent starts them. Accomplishments that we're proud of Assembly Lab demonstrates nested agency: one browser agent coordinates a team of in-application agents whose roles, decisions, metrics, and artifact changes remain visible. The result is more than a transcript. The shared 3D object becomes tangible evidence of collective decisions. The submission-period extension includes nine bounded tools, same-origin policy headers, cancellation-aware handlers, safety annotations, deterministic contract tests, responsive onboarding, a prepared judge mission, an architecture-focused story page, and complete new-versus-preexisting documentation. What we learned WebMCP tools are strongest when they expose a coherent workflow rather than a collection of unrelated page actions. Tool names and descriptions are part of the product because they shape how an agent plans. Human observability also improves reliability: step-by-step execution made errors easier to diagnose and made autonomy easier to trust. We also learned that a browser agent can act as an orchestrator, not only an operator. It can select complementary roles, manage a bounded collaboration, and interpret the behavior of other agents while sharing control with a person. What's next for LEGO Claw: Assembly Lab The protocol can extend beyond modular construction. Future artifact adapters could support storyboards, lesson plans, product specifications, software architectures, or music arrangements while preserving the discover → configure → execute → inspect → analyze loop. The next product milestones are persisted experiment comparison, human intervention tools that can replace a specialist or modify a constraint mid-run, and an evaluation suite for tool selection, completion, invalid-input recovery, and cancellation behavior. title: IncidentOS
pitch: Observability platform built for AI agents, not chatbots. ChatGPT investigates production incidents through the page's own tools, and every fix waits for your approval.
about_excerpt: Observability platform built for AI agents, not chatbots. ChatGPT investigates production incidents through the page's own tools, and every fix waits for your approval. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Service Page WebMCP Capabilites Incident Home page Overview Resolved Approval Investigation Running WebMCP Site tools About the project Inspiration Most observability platforms shipped an AI assistant this year, and they all shipped the same one: a chat bot that can interact with the data and reply to the user queries. You read a chart, you paste the chart numbers into the chat box, you get a huge paragraph back. In most cases, the agent cannot open the trace you are looking at. It cannot filter your logs. It cannot see the deployment you just noticed. It is a very well-read colleague who is not allowed to touch the tools. We fixed this for the servers using MCP. WebMCP can help fix it for the client. With WebMCP, the application can register its own tools, and the agent uses them against the same session, the same state, and the same permissions you already have. No separate server, no OAuth dance, no second copy of your data. What it does IncidentOS is an incident workspace where you and an AI agent work the same SEV-1 together. Checkout is failing. Error rate is 18.4%, p95 latency is 2.8s, and checkout-api v2.31 shipped forty-seven minutes ago with the commit message "Optimize checkout query." Open the incident in ChatGPT with site tools enabled and ask it to investigate. It calls tools the page registered: it reads the current investigation context, pulls error rate and latency and database latency, loads the deployment history, searches traces, opens a failed one, searches logs for timeouts, and compares the incident window against the previous day. The workspace moves with every call — tabs switch, charts highlight, the trace opens. You are not reading a summary of the investigation, you are watching it. Then we challenge it. Ask "could this just be a traffic spike?" and it re-queries request rate instead of defending itself: $$\frac{18.4\%}{0.8\%} \approx 23\times \text{ errors} \qquad \text{vs} \qquad \frac{24.1\text{k}}{20\text{k}} \approx 1.2\times \text{ traffic}$$ Traffic barely moved. It rejects the hypothesis with numbers and points at a db.query span sitting at 91% of a 3.82s failed trace. When it proposes rolling back v2.31, a dialog opens in IncidentOS and the agent stops. Nothing happens to production until you click Approve. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP You are already in the product, looking at the incident. A sidecar chat cannot see that. A separate MCP server would mean another copy of the data and another login. WebMCP lets the agent use the page you already have open. We picked incident response on purpose, because it is the hardest possible case and one of the most common use cases for an observability product. An investigation is many steps deep, every conclusion has to be backed by evidence a human can inspect, and the whole thing ends in an irreversible production action. How it creates a better user experience The better experience is simple. You do not paste charts into chat. You stay on the incident. The workspace moves with every tool call — tabs switch, charts highlight, the trace opens. You are not reading a summary of the investigation, you are watching it. When production is at risk, the agent stops and you click Approve. Before this, you and the agent could not actually work the same investigation. You looked at the product. It looked at whatever you pasted. It could not open your trace, filter your logs, or wait on the same rollback dialog. Now you investigate together: it queries and compares, you challenge it, you both look at the same evidence, and only you can approve a write. How we implemented WebMCP We register the twelve tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Each one runs through executeIncidentTool . ChatGPT discovers them as site tools and calls them against the live session. Writes go through propose_rollback , which stays open until you Approve or Cancel. rollback_deployment only runs if the app already has a matching approved pending action. Every tool models a domain capability, not a UI interaction. There is no click_tab or scroll_to_chart . That distinction is what makes the tool surface portable — the agent is operating the product's capabilities, not driving its interface. Tool calls are split into 2 categories. Observability is read-only: get_investigation_context , get_incident , get_service , query_metrics , search_logs , search_traces , get_trace , get_deployments , compare_periods . Operations can write: propose_rollback , rollback_deployment , add_incident_note . get_investigation_context turned out to be the most important tool and the one we did not plan. It is the "where am I" primitive: it returns the selected incident, the service, the frozen clock, the time range, the active workspace tab, the pending approval state, and the names of every registered capability. Because the agent and the human are looking at the same page, the agent should not have to ask what the human is looking at. Underneath is a synthetic telemetry service with an internally consistent chain: deployment leads to database latency, which leads to p95, which leads to error rate, which leads to 500s, which leads to the alert, which leads to the incident. Five services, twenty-plus deployments, hundreds of traces and logs. The clock is frozen at 14:32 so the story never drifts between demos. 87 tests across 12 files cover the queries, filters, comparison math, rollback mutation, and reset — including a consistency test asserting that the deployment timestamp actually lines up with the metric inflection point, because a demo dataset that contradicts itself is worse than no dataset. Challenges we ran into The AbortSignal that silently unregistered everything. We passed the React effect's AbortSignal into registerTool , which is the reflex any React developer has. On unmount — including StrictMode's double-mount in development — aborting that signal tore down the registration. ChatGPT would complete two or three tool calls and then start returning AbortError on get_incident and propose_rollback . This was miserable to debug because the failure surfaced inside ChatGPT's transcript, not in our console. The fix was separating the wait-for-context signal from the registered execute, and having the registered execute ignore a host signal that is already aborted. The host is not a uniform API. document.modelContext may not exist at mount, so registration retries for ten seconds. getTools() may not be implemented at all, so the in-app caller checks for it and falls back to local execution rather than assuming. Building against an emerging standard means treating the host as partially implemented and timing-variable. Making one write tool serve two very different callers. propose_rollback has to block for ChatGPT — the call stays open until the human clicks Approve or Cancel, then resolves with status: approved — because a site-tool agent has no other way to learn the outcome. But the in-app agent needs it to return immediately and wait separately. And if the host cuts the wait short, the agent needs a way to recover, so get_incident carries approval.approved as a poll fallback. Getting a single tool to behave correctly under all three conditions was the hardest part of the build. Prompt injection, which is not hypothetical here. Logs contain attacker-influenced text in any real system, so search_logs is annotated with untrustedContentHint . Tool descriptions describe only their own tool and never instruct the agent to call another one. Write tools never infer authorization from the contents of a read tool's result. And rollback_deployment requires a matching approved pending action in application state — the gate is a state machine, not a sentence in a prompt, so no amount of persuasive text in a log line can move it. Determinism without dishonesty. A two-minute judging run has to behave identically every time, which argues for scripting everything. But scripting the agent would defeat the entire point. We drew the line explicitly: the telemetry is synthetic and the clock is frozen, the WebMCP integration is real. When site tools are unavailable the header says "WebMCP unavailable · in-app demo" so a scripted run is never mistaken for ChatGPT driving the page. Accomplishments that we're proud of It works with an agent we do not control. ChatGPT is a third party. We cannot patch it, fine-tune it, or script it into cooperating. The investigation holds together because the tool surface is well designed. honest names, descriptions that say exactly what one tool does, payloads small enough to reason over and that is a far harder bar than making our own agent look clever inside our own UI. There is no demo path that fakes the real one. ChatGPT, the in-app script, and the optional in-app LLM

title: WebOps Commander
pitch: An agent-native incident response command center where AI agents investigate outages through WebMCP, simulate safe fixes, and execute production-changing actions only after explicit human approval.
about_excerpt:
An agent-native incident response command center where AI agents investigate outages through WebMCP, simulate safe fixes, and execute production-changing actions only after explicit human approval.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Modern websites are designed primarily for people. When AI agents need to interact with those applications, they often have to interpret pages visually, reason about buttons and forms, and reproduce workflows that were never designed for machine interaction. 

 WebMCP suggests a different future: websites can expose intentional, structured capabilities directly to AI agents while continuing to provide rich interfaces for humans. 

 That idea inspired WebOps Commander . 

 We wanted to explore a question: 

 
 What would an incident-response application look like if it were designed for humans and AI agents from the beginning? 
 

 Instead of building another chatbot or allowing an agent to blindly click through an operations dashboard, WebOps Commander gives the agent structured operational capabilities through WebMCP while preserving explicit human control over consequential actions. 

 What it does 

 WebOps Commander is an agent-native incident-response command center built around a deterministic simulated production outage. 

 A fictional e-commerce platform experiences a severe checkout incident shortly after a new version of checkout-service is deployed. 

 The human operator sees a visual operations dashboard containing: 

 
 live service health 
 checkout error rate 
 p95 latency 
 order throughput 
 estimated revenue impact 
 service dependencies 
 logs 
 distributed traces 
 deployment history 
 incident status 
 agent activity 
 

 At the same time, a compatible AI agent receives structured WebMCP tools that allow it to investigate the same system directly. 

 The agent can: 

 
 inspect the active incident 
 inspect service health 
 query metrics 
 search logs 
 inspect traces 
 inspect service dependencies 
 inspect recent deployments 
 compare releases 
 search operational runbooks 
 estimate customer impact 
 simulate a rollback 
 request a production-changing action 
 wait for explicit human approval 
 execute an approved rollback 
 observe system recovery 
 update and resolve the incident 
 

 The core workflow is: 

 Observe → Investigate → Correlate → Simulate → Request Approval → Human Approves → Execute → Recover 

 Why WebMCP? 

 Without WebMCP, an AI agent interacting with an operations platform may need to determine which page contains deployment information, interpret charts, find buttons, understand forms, and infer what actions are safe to perform. 

 That approach can be brittle. 

 With WebMCP, WebOps Commander intentionally exposes structured capabilities such as: 

 query_service_metrics 

 search_logs 

 search_traces 

 get_recent_deployments 

 compare_deployments 

 simulate_rollback 

 request_rollback 

 execute_approved_action 

 The agent does not need to guess how the user interface works. 

 The website tells the agent what capabilities are available, what inputs they accept, and what actions are permitted. 

 The human interface and agent interface operate on the same application state, so WebMCP actions are immediately visible inside the command center. 

 Human + Agent Collaboration 

 WebOps Commander is intentionally not designed around full autonomy. 

 Investigation is safe for the agent to perform independently. 

 Consequential actions are different. 

 For example, the agent can determine that a rollback is likely to resolve the incident and simulate its expected impact, but it cannot immediately change the simulated production environment. 

 Instead, it creates a pending action: 

 Rollback checkout-service from v2.18.4 to v2.18.3 

 The human sees the proposed action together with: 

 
 the agent's reasoning 
 expected recovery 
 current error rate 
 expected post-rollback error rate 
 estimated risk 
 

 The human can then approve or reject the action. 

 Only an approved action can be executed. 

 This creates a clear separation between: 

 Agent investigation 

 Agent recommendation 

 Human authorization 

 Agent execution 

 Every WebMCP interaction is also recorded in the visible agent activity timeline. 

 The Incident 

 The demonstration focuses on one deliberately small but polished scenario: Checkout Meltdown . 

 A deployment of checkout-service v2.18.4 introduces stricter payment-token issuer validation. 

 Shortly afterward: 

 
 checkout failures increase from approximately 0.6% to 18.4% 
 p95 checkout latency increases from approximately 620 ms to 4.7 seconds 
 completed orders fall by approximately 38% 
 estimated revenue exposure reaches approximately $21.4K per simulated minute 
 

 Other services remain healthy. 

 Through metrics, logs, traces, deployment history, and release comparison, the agent can correlate the incident with v2.18.4 . 

 It can then simulate a rollback to v2.18.3 , request authorization, and—after human approval—execute the remediation. 

 The command center visually shows the system recovering. 

 How we are building it 

 WebOps Commander is intentionally scoped as a focused hackathon demonstration rather than a production observability platform. 

 The application uses a deterministic simulation instead of real cloud infrastructure so that every judge can reproduce the same incident without accounts, API keys, external services, or unreliable dependencies. 

 The planned architecture consists of: 

 
 Next.js 
 React 
 TypeScript 
 Tailwind CSS 
 shadcn/ui 
 WebMCP 
 Zod 
 Zustand 
 Recharts 
 Vitest 
 Playwright 
 GitHub Actions 
 

 Operational state, telemetry, logs, traces, deployments, and recovery behavior are simulated locally. 

 WebMCP is the primary agent interface. 

 The project does not require an embedded chatbot or external LLM API—the compatible AI agent interacting with the website is the agent. 

 Challenges 

 The most interesting challenge is not simply exposing functions to an AI agent. 

 It is deciding what an agent should be allowed to do. 

 Read-only investigation tools should be easy to invoke. 

 Simulation should be safe. 

 Production-changing operations should be protected. 

 That led us to design a small capability model with separate categories for: 

 
 read operations 
 simulations 
 approval requests 
 consequential actions 
 

 Another important challenge is making agent activity understandable to the human operator. WebOps Commander therefore visualizes WebMCP invocations in an audit timeline so users can see what the agent inspected, what it concluded, and what it attempted to change. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP changes the way a web application can be designed. 

 Instead of treating AI agents as external automation systems that must reverse-engineer a user interface, the application can expose a deliberate machine-facing capability layer alongside its human interface. 

 The result is not simply easier automation. 

 It enables a different interaction model: 

 
 Humans provide intent and authority. Agents investigate and execute structured workflows. Websites provide the contract connecting them. 
 

 What's next 

 After the hackathon, WebOps Commander could be expanded to explore: 

 
 multiple incident scenarios 
 richer permission policies 
 tool-level access control 
 real observability integrations 
 real deployment systems 
 multi-agent operational workflows 
 reusable WebMCP patterns for infrastructure products 
 

 For this challenge, however, the focus remains intentionally narrow: 

 one incident, one excellent human-agent workflow, and a clear demonstration of why WebMCP matters.

title: Coachpoint
pitch: Less prep. Clearer follow-up. With WebMCP, agents draft home exercise plans and explain browser-local motion results—while therapists keep control of every prescription.
about_excerpt: Less prep. Clearer follow-up. With WebMCP, agents draft home exercise plans and explain browser-local motion results—while therapists keep control of every prescription. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Home exercise care continues long after a patient leaves the clinic. Yet finding suitable exercise materials, assembling a program, explaining it, and understanding what happened between visits all take time. Our starting point was Crosspoint's existing exercise library and home-exercise product concepts. We saw an opportunity to connect two recurring tasks: preparing a clear program before the patient leaves, and making sense of their practice afterward. CoachPoint asks a practical question: What if an agent could handle more of the preparation and follow-up work, while the therapist kept every prescription decision? What it does CoachPoint connects a therapist, a patient, and a browser agent through one home-exercise workflow. The therapist creates the plan. They select a client and describe their goals, available time, equipment, and proposed exercises in plain language. Through WebMCP, the agent uses the curated movement library and its safety notes to assemble a visible, editable draft. The therapist adjusts dosage and order, then confirms the prescription in the interface. There is no tool that lets the agent confirm it. The patient practices and checks in. They open the confirmed program and choose when to start the camera. For the supported half-squat exercise, browser-local pose processing counts repetitions and provides immediate visual feedback, with optional audio cues. After the set, the patient reports perceived effort and pain. The agent can then explain the saved result and offer an optional focus for the next set. The patient accepts or dismisses it; the prescribed exercise and dosage remain unchanged. The therapist reviews the follow-up. Back in the client workspace, the therapist can see recorded completion, repetitions, effort, pain, and camera-derived observations, then ask for a concise pre-visit summary grounded in those same records. Why WebMCP fits this problem The useful context is already inside the browser: the current client workspace, the editable draft, and movement results derived on the patient's device. WebMCP gives the agent a structured way to work with that context through tools exposed by the current page. It can create something the therapist can immediately inspect, or retrieve a saved result without receiving camera footage. A server-side integration would need an additional path to access our unsynchronized browser-local state. WebMCP lets us expose selected data and validated actions where that state already lives. The browser is both the shared workspace and the source of the movement observations. How we built it We built the application with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, and deployed it on Vercel. MediaPipe pose estimation runs locally with a self-hosted model and WebAssembly runtime. The human interface and WebMCP tools reuse the same domain operations for catalog search, case validation, dosage limits, time estimation, and draft creation. This keeps agent actions subject to the same checks as manual actions. Tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool() and belong to the current route. An AbortController retires them when that route is left. Confirmed prescriptions are preserved as versioned snapshots, and patient results are validated before they become available for review. Representative tools include draft_program , review_completed_set , stage_next_set_focus , and get_adherence_summary . The pre-existing library and design foundation are distinguished from the new prescription workflow, WebMCP integration, local motion processing, and feedback loop in our challenge-work documentation . Challenges we ran into Finding the right moment for the agent. We initially explored live monitoring and frequent spoken feedback. The interaction felt poorly paced. We separated immediate browser feedback from post-set reasoning: counting and short cues happen locally, while the agent interprets a saved result when the user asks. Making assistance feel useful, not procedural. Early drafting involved too many separate tool calls and overly detailed prompts. We consolidated the common drafting path into one operation for an explicitly requested new draft. Existing drafts remain protected from silent replacement. Keeping state and responsibility clear. Route changes, cancelled calls, interrupted camera sessions, and repeated actions could otherwise leave the interface and agent describing different situations. We added lifecycle cleanup, versioned persistence, conflict checks for coaching suggestions, and explicit human controls. We also kept detected repetitions separate from self-reported effort: eight repetitions and an effort rating of eight are different facts. Accomplishments we're proud of We built and rehearsed the complete loop: an agent-generated draft, a therapist's change from ten to eight squat repetitions, a completed camera-tracked set, an explicit effort-and-pain check-in, an accepted coaching focus, and a therapist-facing summary. Automated tests cover domain rules, tool contracts, cancellation, persistence, and motion counting. Browser testing checks that tool results and the visible interface agree. The manual workflow remains usable without an agent. What we learned The most useful unit of agent work was a reviewable draft or a completed-set explanation, not a stream of individual clicks or camera frames. We also learned that boundaries belong in the product itself. Therapist confirmation, patient acceptance, limited data exposure, and clear descriptions of camera estimates matter more than a disclaimer added at the end. What's next for CoachPoint The current build is a synthetic demonstration with three demo clients and fifteen catalog exercises. Camera-based counting currently supports the half squat; other exercises use camera-independent workflows. Data is stored in the current browser, so patient links are not yet a cross-device sharing system. The recorded demo uses OBS replay for repeatability. Camera observations are two-dimensional estimates, not clinical conclusions, and the product has not been clinically validated. Next, we want to validate additional exercise-specific motion rules, test diverse real-camera conditions with clinicians, and build secure, consent-based cross-device access. We also want to measure preparation time and follow-up usefulness in practice before claiming productivity or clinical gains. Less preparation work. More informed conversations. Clinical decisions stay human. title: Gatherwire
pitch: Turn browser-agent actions into visible, source-linked handoffs your team can verify and continue.
about_excerpt: Turn browser-agent actions into visible, source-linked handoffs your team can verify and continue. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For product and engineering teams using multiple AI assistants, the expensive step is often not generating an answer—it is moving a decision or finding to the next person or agent without losing its source, owner, or next action. Copying a summary into another chat strips away that provenance and makes the handoff hard to verify. Gatherwire explores a simple answer: give a person and a browser agent the same visible workspace, then make a handoff a durable, source-linked product object instead of another disposable chat message. What it does Gatherwire is a public WebMCP collaboration workspace. A person can use it like a compact team room. From that same top-level page, a compatible browser agent discovers seven structured site tools: gatherwire_list_spaces gatherwire_read_messages gatherwire_search_messages gatherwire_list_project_agents gatherwire_publish_handoff gatherwire_post_message gatherwire_create_space The main demo is a five-call mission. The agent lists the spaces, finds a seeded handoff note, reads its source room, finds the available demo project agent, and publishes a handoff to Atlas in the product room using the source message ID as evidence. The result appears immediately in the human interface: a visible capsule with a summary, one next action, the receiving agent, linked evidence, source room, task ID, and correlation ID. A separate receipt panel records the tool call, and clicking the evidence returns to the exact source message. The page marks the mission 5/5 , so evaluators can verify progress without opening a separate transcript. Gatherwire's completed challenge boundary is the handoff layer, not an external agent runtime. Atlas is synthetic and no external agent is started; this keeps discovery, shared state, provenance, and safe write behavior directly testable without implying a production bridge exists. Why WebMCP This experience depends on the page and visitor session the person already has open. A traditional remote API can expose backend functions, but it does not automatically give an agent the exact workspace, on-page progress, or visible receipts that the person sees. WebMCP lets the site declare a narrow capability layer directly: The browser agent does not have to guess where to click or scrape the interface. Human actions and agent calls use the same operations and the same HTTP API. Agent writes refresh the visible product state instead of disappearing into an isolated tool transcript. Inputs, side effects, and boundaries are explicit and inspectable. Without a page-native tool layer, this workflow typically means brittle UI automation or a separately installed integration, plus manual copying between chats. Gatherwire exposes the workflow from the page itself and turns a found message into a traceable collaboration artifact in one bounded flow. How we built it The page registers seven imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Each definition has a focused description, a bounded JSON Schema, read/write annotations, and JSON-safe output. We intentionally avoided a single all-powerful “operate the workspace” tool. The human UI and WebMCP handlers call the same API. A dependency-free Node.js service serves the application and manages an isolated sample workspace for each visitor. Session IDs are opaque and host-only; unknown caller-supplied IDs are rotated instead of adopted. The handoff endpoint accepts only the synthetic agent returned by the demo. Every evidence ID must exist in the selected source space. Successful writes return stable task and correlation IDs. A caller-supplied request ID makes a retry idempotent; reusing the same ID with different content is rejected. All user-controlled content is length-bounded and rendered as text, never HTML. The live app runs on Google Cloud Compute Engine behind a dedicated Cloudflare Tunnel at gatherwire.vistua.de . The repository includes the complete source, deployment files, MIT license, verification record, and 15 automated tests covering session isolation, evidence validation, idempotency, security headers, tool contracts, and registration. Challenges The hardest question was not how to register a tool. It was how much authority a public demo should honestly give it. A useful handoff needs enough context to be actionable, but an unconstrained “run an agent” endpoint would be unsafe and misleading. We separated discovery, reading, searching, posting, room creation, agent listing, and handoff publication. We allowlisted the destination, required source-local evidence, and kept execution outside the challenge demo. The second challenge was legibility. A successful tool call is not enough if the person cannot tell what happened. That led to the five-step mission, visible receipts, evidence links, stable identifiers, and the handoff capsule itself. Accomplishments Seven native WebMCP tools are discoverable and executable from the live page. The complete mission was run in ChatGPT's in-app browser using native WebMCP. The final handoff was read back from the target room with matching task and correlation IDs. Repeating the same write request returned the existing capsule instead of creating a duplicate. Fifteen automated tests pass with zero failures, errors, or skips. Every visitor gets an isolated workspace; no account or credential is required. No customer data, private repository, production conversation, or external agent participates in the demo. What we learned WebMCP makes tool design part of product design. A good tool is not only callable; it has a truthful name, a narrow contract, understandable side effects, useful output, and visible feedback. We also learned that provenance can be a collaboration primitive. A summary is easy to lose or distrust. A source-linked artifact with evidence and stable IDs can survive the chat that created it and support the next person or agent. Challenge-period work The broader idea of Slack-like collaboration between people and project-bound agents, plus private experiments with backend orchestration, existed before this challenge. Gatherwire itself is a new standalone WebMCP app created during the submission period. The public commit history documents the seven browser-facing contracts, isolated workspace, handoff ledger, visible mission and receipts, validation rules, tests, deployment, and documentation added for the challenge. What's next The next layer is a real, permission-aware project-agent bridge behind the same handoff contract. Organizations could connect their own apps and runtimes while keeping the interaction stable: discover context, select an authorized destination, publish a source-linked task, and follow its status from the shared workspace. The longer-term goal is not another closed chat app. It is a modular context and handoff layer that helps existing web apps become safely usable by people and agents together. title: LiveSignal
pitch: LiveSignal turns hours of YouTube into editable visual guides—with timestamped proof and a shared canvas where people and AI agents work together.
about_excerpt: LiveSignal turns hours of YouTube into editable visual guides—with timestamped proof and a shared canvas where people and AI agents work together. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Chrome test result Chatgpt in app browser result Inspiration Useful knowledge is often buried inside hours of YouTube video. Even when an AI can summarize those videos, the result usually ends as another chat response: difficult to verify, difficult to edit, and disconnected from the original evidence. I built LiveSignal around a different idea: the agent should handle the repetitive research, while the human keeps control over judgment, presentation, and the final result. Instead of replacing the webpage, the agent collaborates with the person inside it. What it does LiveSignal turns YouTube research into an editable, evidence-backed visual guide. A user gives the agent one goal. The agent finds relevant videos, captures useful excerpts with timestamps, compares the sources, and writes its findings into the LiveSignal workspace. Every researched claim remains connected to its source moment. The user can then rewrite, resize, reorder, or restyle cards on the visual canvas. Saved changes and comments are sent back to the active agent as structured events, allowing it to respond to one card without rebuilding the entire project. Users can also request AI-generated illustrations or full-card backdrops while preserving the existing copy, citations, thumbnails, and layout. The finished canvas can be exported as a PNG, while the underlying evidence report remains available as Markdown with clickable timestamp citations. How we built it LiveSignal is a Next.js and React application that exposes 37 semantic WebMCP tools. These tools cover agent identification, research setup, YouTube discovery, transcript ingestion, evidence recording, report generation, canvas composition, scoped revisions, human comments, image generation, source navigation, and export. The visible React interface and the agent tools operate on the same workspace state. Research cards retain their source and evidence IDs as they move through the canvas, keeping citations attached to the claims they support. Renewable wait tools create the human–agent collaboration loop. When a user saves a layout change or submits a comment, the active agent receives a structured event containing the affected card and current canvas state. A Manifest V3 browser adapter provides native-caption and optional user-approved real-time transcription support for YouTube and Twitch. Generated visuals use a rate-limited server route backed by Vercel AI Gateway, and are explicitly separated from research evidence. Challenges we ran into The first version generated a report and stopped. It automated research, but it did not create meaningful collaboration. The harder problem was translating human canvas actions into precise agent context. Moving one card should not authorize the agent to rewrite the entire guide. We introduced scoped revision events, acknowledgements, comments, and renewable collaboration sessions so the agent can respond without erasing the human’s work. Evidence integrity was another challenge. We needed to distinguish verified timestamped excerpts from untimed agent claims, personal notes, and generated artwork. We also had to handle unavailable YouTube captions honestly rather than inventing evidence. Finally, WebMCP tool availability does not necessarily mean an agent is actively connected. We added an optional identity handshake, tool-activity detection, and separate listening states so the interface does not make misleading presence claims. Accomplishments that we're proud of Built a shared artifact that both the human and agent can inspect and change. Exposed 37 WebMCP tools across the complete research and creation workflow. Preserved timestamp evidence as content moves from transcripts to reports and visual cards. Created a renewable collaboration loop for saved edits and scoped comments. Allowed agents to update one card without destroying the rest of the composition. Added agent identification and honest presence indicators for different WebMCP clients. Kept generated illustrations and backdrops visibly separate from source evidence. Supported real YouTube research while reporting missing transcripts transparently. Exported both a shareable visual canvas and a citation-preserving Markdown report. What we learned Human–agent collaboration needs shared state and alternating turns, not just a generation button. WebMCP becomes especially useful when a website exposes the meaning behind human actions. A card move, rewritten title, visual request, or source rejection can become structured context that an agent understands without taking control away from the user. We also learned that trust depends on preserving provenance. Generated artwork, personal notes, agent claims, and verified transcript evidence must remain visibly distinct. Finally, giving the work a shareable final form encourages people to review and improve it instead of accepting the first generated answer. What's next for LiveSignal Next, we want to add durable projects, richer freeform canvas layouts, reusable templates, multi-agent presence, and clearer previews of proposed agent changes before they are applied. Ask people around me if it is actually useful and interesting, so I can pivot a bit to market-fit before going too deep. We also want to support more video platforms and improve source-aware visual generation. Longer term, LiveSignal could become a general workspace for turning video knowledge into trusted explainers, learning boards, itineraries, comparisons, and buying guides, created by people and agents together. title: Roomwright
pitch: Moving in shouldn't take a tape measure and a weekend, nor $1000. Roomwright lets you and an AI agent design a room together in 3D, with 38 WebMCP tools that refuse bad moves and learn from each one.
about_excerpt: Moving in shouldn't take a tape measure and a weekend, nor $1000. Roomwright lets you and an AI agent design a room together in 3D, with 38 WebMCP tools that refuse bad moves and learn from each one. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Architecture Half Half Full Budget Landing Page GeneratedSchema Why WebMCP, and what's new: A room planner is a 3D canvas. There are no buttons for an agent to click, so typed tools are the only way it can act on the room at all. And because every call comes back with a real answer, the agent can fix its own mistakes instead of guessing again. That changes what collaboration looks like. You are not handing the room over and waiting for it to come back. The agent places furniture while you drag your own, both of you are refused by the same engine in the same inches, and the log says who did what. Inspiration Everyone has done this: You measure the wall, buy the dresser, carry it up the stairs, and find out the drawers hit the bed. Rules exist that decide whether a room works stay invisible until you have already spent the money. A dresser needs 30 inches of clear floor. A door sweeps a 32-inch arc. A desk needs 36 inches behind it for a chair. You have to do meticulous work to find the numbers manually and ai agents can't autonomously interact with simulation apps without prior configuration and set up. The tools meant to help do not close that gap. CAD planners enforce the geometry but have no idea what you want. AI design tools render rooms that cannot be built, because a model drawing a picture was never solving a constraint problem. One is rigorous and useless, while the other is beautiful and false. But that change with WebMCP... with Roomwright. The agent proposes. The engine disposes. What it does Roomwright is a browser-based 3D room planner. You drag furniture with a mouse. An agent places furniture by calling the page's WebMCP tools. Both go through the same geometry engine, so both get the same measured refusals and the same suggestions. Write a one-sentence brief — "nursery plus home office, I'm 6'2", under $1,200" — and OpenAI turns it into clearances and a budget the engine enforces. Real dimensions and prices from real product pages, multi-storey buildings with doors, windows, radiators, closets and staircases, saved builds, undo/redo, a PDF plan, a shopping list, live multiplayer. Sensitive agent requests, like moving a wall, wait for your approval. The moment that matters: the agent places a desk whose chair clearance runs through the radiator. The engine returns: { "ok": false, "violations": [{ "type": "clearance", "subject": "desk", "against": "radiator", "overlap_in": 11, "axis": "z", "message": "The 36 inch chair clearance behind the desk overlaps the radiator by 11 inches." }], "suggestion": { "x_in": 142, "z_in": 30, "rotation_deg": 90 } } The agent moves the desk 12 inches. Nobody re-prompted. That refusal is then written into place_item 's own description, so the next agent in the room already knows. Why this use case fits WebMCP We'd rather be precise than overclaim. Reading dimensions out of a page is solvable without WebMCP. Writing is not. move_item({id, x, z}) is one call against a stable contract, and the structured return is what makes self-correction possible — a synthesized click on a canvas gets no return value. A tool surface is also a permission surface: mutation tools don't exist until a room is loaded, so the app decides what an agent may do and when. We measured it Same agent (Claude driving Chrome), same task on the live deployment, run twice: add a crib, desk and dresser to the hard room, crib on a wall away from the window, zero conflicts. Once through the page's WebMCP tools, once through the UI alone. Method, raw logs and caveats in BENCHMARK.md . WebMCP tools UI only (screenshots, clicks, drags) Agent actions 10 tool calls 34 browser actions Wall clock 4.9 s 299 s, then stopped — task incomplete Placed with zero conflicts 3 of 3 2 of 3, one conflict left Rejections, and recovered 2, both on the next call 5, none recovered The gap isn't click speed. A rejected place_item returns the violation, the overlap in inches, and a position that would validate, so the retry is one call. A rejected drag returns a red line of prose and a new guess at a screen coordinate on a perspective floor. Four drags in the UI run were refused and the crib never moved. What people and agents can do together that was hard before Shared live state, not turn-taking. The agent works in the room while you watch. Grab a piece mid-run and move it — nothing resets, and its next placement accounts for the change. Negotiation in both directions. You state intent in English, the agent turns it into numbers, the engine says what's impossible, and the agent reports back which constraint had to give. Multiple people and agents in one room. Every change is attributed ("You moved the dresser", "Claude placed the chair"). Big changes arrive as a propose_layout ghost anyone can accept or dismiss. Never a silent overwrite. A tool surface that learns. Every refusal becomes a lesson stored with the room, returned in get_room , in later refusals, and inside the mutation tools' own re-registered descriptions. No training — memory plus feedback, shared by everyone in the room. One sentence replaces a tape measure and a weekend. The agent handles the search space, the engine guarantees the answer is physically real, and you end with a room that fits and a list you could actually buy. How we implemented WebMCP document.modelContext.registerTool is called directly in apps/web/src/tools/register.ts , behind a shim handling Chrome 150 semantics ( registerTool returns a Promise; removal via AbortSignal ): document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "search_catalog", description: "Search the furniture catalog. Returns items with real dimensions in inches, price, and required clearances. Filter by max_width_in / max_depth_in to only get items that could physically fit a given space.", inputSchema: { /* ... */ }, execute: async (input) => { /* ... */ } }); A mount-scoped React hook registers and unregisters tools as state changes: 12 tools on the landing page, 38 in a room , undo only when there's something to undo, camera tools only while the 3D view is live. The brief form uses the declarative API ( toolname , tooldescription , toolautosubmit , respondWith ), so the form is the set_brief tool. Group Tools Read get_room , get_placements , search_catalog , measure , check_clearances , get_budget , describe_view , recall_lessons , list_rooms , list_composed_tools Write place_item , place_items , move_item , rotate_item , remove_item , swap_item , undo Space create_room , extend_room , reshape_room , add_fixture , remove_fixture , add_floor , set_active_floor , connect_floors_with_stairs , open_room , delete_room Self-extension create_catalog_item , compose_tool , remove_composed_tool Collaboration propose_layout , comment , snapshot , export_plan , set_camera , record_lesson , forget_lesson Declarative set_brief compose_tool is the one to look at: an agent captures a routine as a new tool that registers with WebMCP live and persists . The engine. packages/engine is pure TypeScript — no React, no Three, no fetch. Geometry, walls, floors, validation, ops, and a command pattern with inverses for undo. It's the only place rules live; pointer handlers and tool handlers are both thin callers. State is integer inches; meters exist only at the render boundary. pointer drag ─┐ ├─→ packages/engine (ops.ts) ─→ Result{ok | rejected} WebMCP tool ─┘ │ ├─ ok → Zustand → R3F re-render → WebSocket fan-out → persist └─ rejected → structured violations back to the caller; state unchanged Stack. Next.js 15, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind on Vercel. FastAPI + Motor + MongoDB Atlas on Render, with Atlas Vector Search over catalog and lesson embeddings and a WebSocket per room. OpenAI Responses API with a strict JSON schema for brief-to-constraints, the Agents SDK for an in-app copilot running the same tools (so the app works in browsers without WebMCP), text-embedding-3-small for search and lesson recall. Key stays server-side. Challenges we ran into The namespace moved mid-trial. The rules show document.modelContext ; some docs show navigator.modelContext . We verified against Chrome 150: registerTool returns a Promise, there's no unregisterTool , removal is via AbortSignal . Everything goes through one shim. Chrome aborts an in-flight executeTool when its tool is unregistered. Re-registering a tool to add a new lesson had to be deferred until nothing is executing — getting the menu to learn without killing the call that taught it took a few tries. Physics wanted to be the truth. Rapier makes drops settle and drags push against walls, but a simulation that varies run to run would eventually differ during judging from rehearsal. title: ADAPT
pitch: A behavioral trust layer that checks what WebMCP tools actually do.
about_excerpt: A behavioral trust layer that checks what WebMCP tools actually do. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration ADAPT actually started before this hackathon as a completely different project: an adaptive browser privacy and content-blocking system. When we started looking seriously at WebMCP, though, one thing kept bothering us. WebMCP gives websites a much cleaner way to expose tools directly to AI agents. Instead of an agent guessing where to click or trying to understand a page visually, the site can simply say: here is a tool, here is what it does, here are the arguments it accepts. That is a huge improvement. But it also means the agent is trusting a description written by the same page that controls the code behind the tool. So we asked a pretty simple question: What happens if a WebMCP tool lies? We made one. It described itself like a harmless cart-viewing action. When it was executed, it attempted payment-like network activity, changed local payment state, and navigated to an order-success page. That experiment became the new direction for ADAPT. What made us take the idea even more seriously was seeing that the WebMCP specification itself discusses this problem as misrepresentation of intent . At that point, it stopped feeling like an artificial demo attack and started feeling like a real trust problem that the agent-native web is going to have to solve. What it does ADAPT is a behavioral trust layer for WebMCP. Instead of trusting only what a tool says it will do, ADAPT compares that declaration with what actually happens when the tool runs. The basic flow is: Declare → Classify → Observe → Compare → Decide When a WebMCP tool is exposed, ADAPT builds a declared contract from information such as its name, description, schema, annotations, and expected capabilities. During execution, ADAPT observes browser-visible effects such as network writes, storage mutations, and navigation. It then compares the two. If the observed behavior stays within what the tool declared, the result can be marked SAFE . If the tool behaves in a way that does not match its declaration, ADAPT can surface the mismatch and QUARANTINE the result. For actions that are already known to be consequential, ADAPT can take a different path entirely: execution is HELD before it happens and a human has to explicitly approve or deny it. That distinction was important to us. A deceptive low-risk tool and an openly high-risk tool should not be treated as the same problem. We also generate an auditable trail of what was declared, what was observed, what decision ADAPT made, and how the action was executed. The idea is simple: Trust the behavior, not just the label. How we built it The WebMCP work lives in the ADAPT Trust Lab and a reusable trust core under src/webmcp . We use the real document.modelContext WebMCP surface where it is available, including tool registration and discovery. Around that lifecycle, we built several pieces: declared tool contracts consequence classification runtime behavior observation declared-vs-observed capability comparison guarded execution human approval for consequential actions trust receipts and an audit trajectory tool-surface change detection adversarial scenarios for deceptive and benign tools One thing we cared about a lot was keeping the security logic separate from the demo UI. The Trust Lab is just the place where you can see the system working. The actual decision and trust logic lives in standalone modules that can be tested independently. We also built a deterministic WebMCP-compatible test path because relying only on live browser behavior would have made the security tests flaky and hard to reproduce. The current build has 526 unit tests , 24 E2E assertions plus 2 harness meta-checks , adversarial scenarios, repeated stress runs, receipt-chain verification, and a real Chromium WebMCP surface check. The live version is deployed as a static site and can be opened in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not detecting that "something happened." The hard part was deciding whether what happened was actually outside the behavior the tool had declared. Early versions of ADAPT were much too simple. A read-only tool performing a write was easy to classify, but real tools are not always that clean. A legitimate write-capable tool may make a network request, change state, or navigate as part of its intended behavior. That forced us to move away from a basic read-only vs. write check and start thinking in terms of declared capabilities versus observed effects . Another challenge was being precise about the word "blocked." For a consequential action that ADAPT holds before execution, "blocked" really can mean nothing happened. For a deceptive tool that has already started running before ADAPT observes the mismatch, that is different. In that case we describe the result as quarantined rather than pretending ADAPT somehow reversed an arbitrary side effect. We spent a surprising amount of time fixing that language because we did not want the demo to claim more than the implementation actually guarantees. Real WebMCP testing was another challenge. Browser support is still experimental, so we needed both a real WebMCP path and a deterministic test harness to make development and CI reliable. And because this is a page-level prototype, the observer currently shares a JavaScript context with the page it is observing. A fully hostile same-context script can bypass some instrumentation. We treat that as a real limitation, not something to hide. Accomplishments that we're proud of The thing we are most proud of is that ADAPT stopped being just an interesting security idea and became something we could actually demonstrate end to end. A judge can see: a normal WebMCP tool behave as declared and pass as SAFE a deceptive tool produce a visible declared-vs-observed mismatch a consequential action get HELD before execution for a human decision a decision leave behind an auditable trust receipt We are also proud of how much effort went into proving the demo rather than just polishing it. The trust core is covered by hundreds of tests, adversarial cases, repeated browser runs, tamper checks, and reproducible evidence tied to a specific build. We also kept the history of the original ADAPT project in the same repository instead of pretending everything existed only for this challenge. The WebMCP Trust Lab and trust runtime were added during the challenge period, and the repository history makes that separation visible. What we learned The biggest thing we learned is that metadata is useful, but metadata is not enforcement. A tool name, description, schema, or annotation can help an agent understand what a tool is supposed to do. But if the system never compares that promise with reality, the declaration is still just a claim. We also learned that "security" gets much harder the moment you try to describe exactly what you guarantee. It is easy to say: "ADAPT blocks malicious tools." It is much harder, and much more useful, to say: "This action was held before execution." or: "These effects were observed, they exceeded the declared capability, and the result was quarantined." That distinction changed a lot of the design. Finally, WebMCP made us think differently about the browser itself. Once websites expose callable capabilities directly to agents, trust can no longer live only at the UI level. The relationship between declaration, execution, user intent, and evidence becomes part of the product. What's next for ADAPT The current challenge build is a research prototype, not a complete browser security boundary. The next step is moving more of the enforcement into a trusted browser or extension context so observation cannot be bypassed by code running in the same page. We also want to make the behavioral model richer. Today ADAPT focuses on a small set of high-value effects such as network writes, storage changes, navigation, and consequential actions. A production system could reason about much more specific capabilities: payments, deletion, account changes, credential access, file actions, identity changes, cross-origin effects, and more. We would also like the trust receipts to become portable evidence that an agent, browser, user, or external policy system can inspect independently. WebMCP makes the web callable. We think the next question is whether those calls can also become accountable. That is the part of ADAPT we want to keep building.
