title: Relocates.io
pitch: Where can all of us live? A map that answers it for a whole household — and negotiates when it can't.
about_excerpt: Where can all of us live? A map that answers it for a whole household — and negotiates when it can't. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration We had one weekend of viewings, in a city none of us had lived in, and a spreadsheet. The question was simple and nothing could answer it: where can all four of us actually live? Property sites filter by price and bedroom count. But nobody is unhappy about a bedroom count. They're unhappy because the school run takes forty minutes, and because that got decided once, in a hurry, from three timezones away, and then paid for every morning for three years. So we guessed. Everybody guesses. It's a constraint satisfaction problem and it deserved a solver, so we wrote one. Every requirement becomes a comparison over a 250-metre grid of the real city: real schools from Google Places with their real ratings, real gyms, real parks, and real terrain, so a hill costs the minutes it actually costs. Where everyone's requirements overlap, a volume lights up over the photorealistic map. Then it goes to zero. Six honest requirements from four people usually don't fit in one city. Every tool we'd used treats that as a dead end. Empty list, try removing a filter. But "nowhere works" is genuinely useful information, as long as you also say which two requirements are fighting and how much one has to give. So the page tests dropping each requirement, then every pair, then sweeps the blocking thresholds to find the smallest concession that reopens the map. It draws both options at once, in the colours of the two people involved. That's the point where WebMCP stopped being a technology choice. The solver can tell you bending one limit reopens more ground than bending the other. It can't tell you that one of those limits is a bad knee and the other is a fourteen-year-old walking to school by herself. It can't know that the cheaper concession is the harder one to live with. Somebody has to say "hers is cheaper, but hers is the medical one" — and a slider is never going to say that. But it doesn't work from a server either. The agent offers two futures, the page draws both over the real city, and the person picks by looking at them. What's being compared is a shape on a map, not a number in a response. The state and the solver have to sit where the person's eyes already are. The loop runs both ways too, which is the part we didn't expect to matter as much as it does. People don't wait their turn. They drag a threshold while the agent is still talking, delete something, accept an option on their own. Those edits are real and they aren't the agent's. So the page logs who changed what and hands the agent everything a human did since its last turn. What it does Relocates.io finds the part of a city where everyone in a household gets what they need at the same time, draws it on a photorealistic 3D map, and when that region doesn't exist, tells you exactly which requirements collide and how far one has to move. You can describe your household to an agent or build it by hand. Both drive the same state. Pick a city. It builds a 250 m grid and loads the terrain. Add people, then their requirements. Not filters — requirements that belong to someone, each carrying their own reason in their own words. "She walks alone, it's her independence." "It's his knee, not a preference." That sentence matters later. Watch where they overlap. The intersection is contoured and extruded over the real buildings. The area in km² is the number on screen. When it hits zero, you get options, not an error. The page finds what's blocking, works out the smallest movement that reopens the map, and draws both candidate futures at once with the area each one buys. You choose. Click one and it resolves. Both numbers were already on screen — what the agent adds is which concession is cheaper, which is easier, and why those aren't the same. Then check a real listing. Paste an address, get pass or fail on every requirement with the margin, plus the nearest spots that would have worked. Or search homes restricted to inside the feasible region, so it can't return somewhere that fails one of your family. The 3D isn't decoration. If you can't fly out for a third viewing, the two things you most need to see are what a street looks like and how steep it is, and a flat map shows neither. Walking times run through Tobler's hiking function over real elevation, so a kilometre uphill costs about 40% more than a flat one. The hill you can see is the hill that makes the school walk eleven minutes instead of seven. Same dataset drives the picture and the arithmetic. How we built it Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Google Maps Platform, WebMCP. About 4,600 lines. No server, no database, no API routes. Browser tab ├── Grid 250 m lattice over the search area ├── Layers one Float32Array per question — walk time, commute, grade ├── Solver masks · marching squares · diagnosis · relaxation sweep ├── Map3D photorealistic tiles + pooled extruded volumes ├── WebMCP 18 tools on document.modelContext └── Cache IndexedDB — a city is learned once Everything runs in the browser through the Maps JS SDK and caches locally. Nothing about the household leaves the page. That started as a constraint and turned out to be the reason the whole thing works: an agent can reach into live state and get an answer in the same tick. Places and Elevation are real. Commute times are modelled from distance and mode rather than routed, and we say so on screen. We skipped the Routes API on purpose. Real routed commutes meant thousands of billed matrix elements per origin and several seconds of latency on every threshold change, which would have killed the thing that makes the sweep feel like an instrument. Two functions carry the project. diagnose.ts answers why there's nowhere to live. With a dozen requirements over a few thousand cells there's no need to be clever, so it tests every leave-one-out combination, then every pair if none of those work. Exhaustive and exact. frontier.ts answers how far a requirement has to bend, sweeping its threshold across the grid for the smallest movement that opens any cell, then the area gained at every step after. It returns a curve, not a point, so the agent can describe what a concession costs. Both measure off the grid. Neither estimates. That's the whole technical claim, so it lives in the code rather than in a paragraph. The map uses Map3DElement with regions as extruded Polygon3DElement volumes and drawsOccludedSegments on, so buildings never hide the answer. Those are DOM nodes, not batched geometry, so they're pooled at startup and mutated in place. Three things about the tools mattered more than the rest. Descriptions say when to call something, not just what it does: "call this whenever the area is 0, before telling the user anything." Every requirement carries a required rationale field. And get_state returns humanChanges , so the agent finds out what a person did while it wasn't looking. Challenges we ran into deck.gl doesn't work over photorealistic tiles. The obvious stack was a dead end. Overlays float above the terrain instead of sitting on it. We dropped deck.gl for native Polygon3DElement , which Google renders against the same terrain as the tiles. Found it with a throwaway HTML file before writing any real code, which saved a day. Google has no ratings for schools. Gyms, parks and supermarkets all return them. Secondary schools returned zero out of eight. Our "4★ or better" filter emptied the pool, so every school requirement became permanently unsatisfiable and the map went permanently blank. Saying "nowhere qualifies" would have been a lie with a straight face, so the filter now drops itself, says so in a banner, and reports the caveat to the agent. Nobody agrees where WebMCP lives. Drafts disagree on navigator.modelContext versus document.modelContext . We built against navigator , and an agent looking at the live page told us exactly what that produces: "exposes WebMCP capability, but currently provides no WebMCP tools." It now checks document first, awaits each registration, and tears down with AbortSignal . Photorealistic tiles take no style array. No saturation: -100 , so the grey-out when there's no answer had to be a CSS filter on the container. It greys the regions too, but during a conflict there are no regions to keep coloured, so that worked out. The numbers sit in an unfiltered layer above. Cutting things. Routes API, air quality, saved sessions, multi-city. All had to go to keep one sequence working reliably: requirements, conflict, two futures, a choice. Accomplishments that we're proud of The empty state is the product. Treating "nowhere works" as the interesting case is the idea everything is built around, and it held up against real data from a real city. Every number is real. Every km² and every minute comes off the grid. The agent is told never to state a figure it didn't get from a tool, and the tools are shaped so it never nee
video_transcript_excerpt: Finding a place for a family usually means juggling dozens of open tabs, trying to guess where everyone's daily life actually intersects. Relocates.io solves this geometrically. We input a family of four relocating to San Francisco. David commuting to Google, Sarah, Leah, and 8-year-old Tom. The agent parses the household and registers the profiles directly into client state. Now we define their daily mobility constraints. David needs transit within 30 minutes. Leah needs a 15-minute walk to high school. Tom needs 10 minutes to primary school, plus a nearby gym and park. The browser intersects these travel boundaries on device, 29.38 square kilometers across five candidate zones. Now the hard constraint. Sarah has an injured knee. Any pedestrian incline over a 6% grade is physically out of the question. That medical requirement is treated as non-negotiable, factoring San Francisco's elevation profiles into the pedestrian routes. >> The viable terrain immediately collapses by more than half down to 13.44 square kilometers. Hills eliminate most of the city. Instead of negotiating back and forth in chat, I open the drawer and adjust the sliders myself, granting Tom 17 minutes and tightening the park to six. Web MCP immediately detects my manual edits and synchronizes the agent state. The polygon updates dynamically to 11.88 square kilometers, highlighting five qualifying neighborhoods, including the Presidio. We drop straight into 3D terrain to verify street inclines before signing a lease. Compromise isn't an argument anymore. It's just geometry.

title: s-m-r-t
pitch: Define a domain once, then give people and browser agents the same safe, structured application.
about_excerpt: Define a domain once, then give people and browser agents the same safe, structured application. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most web applications are built for people to click and for agents to guess. Agents scrape labels and infer controls from fragile DOMs. s-m-r-t asks a different question: what if an application's real domain model, permissions, workflows, and interface also defined a deliberate browser-native tool surface? Job hunting made that problem concrete. Finding opportunities, checking sources, triaging listings, recording notes, and preparing application packets are repetitive and stressful. They benefit from agent help, while final approval and employer submission should remain unmistakably human decisions. What it does s-m-r-t is the entry. It is a TypeScript framework for building operational applications around one typed domain model. Decorated business objects generate aligned persistence, REST, CLI, MCP, WebMCP, browser-data, and AI surfaces. WebMCP is not a separate demo API pasted onto an application: it is a governed browser projection of the same model and application contracts. For the challenge, s-m-r-t gained: canonical WebMCP definitions for deliberately API-exposed models; authenticated execution through the existing REST boundary; explicit exposure policies, effect classification, tool budgets, and namespaces; lifecycle-safe registration through document.modelContext ; mounted form-control and data-surface adapters, giving agents and people the same UI state; staged form edits requiring human review; bounded queries and durable actions with stable identity and confirmation boundaries; declarative view intents and layered playbooks that make the agent surface statically knowable; local, self-hosted, and managed-cloud runtime profiles preserving the same tools and policies. Iolaus is the demonstration application built with s-m-r-t. It is a local-first, single-user employment-search app using SQLite. A browser agent inspects source health, browses and investigates fictional job listings, records a triage decision and note, advances the queue, opens a shortlist, and inspects an application packet. Those actions update the same state the person sees. There is intentionally no WebMCP tool for final approval or employer submission. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, the agent needs brittle DOM automation or a separate privileged integration. With s-m-r-t, each page advertises bounded tools through document.modelContext . Those tools carry effect metadata, use authenticated application routes, respect field and exposure policies, and disappear with the page lifecycle. Mounted view tools change the same state the person sees, while background queries inspect data without disturbing the view. The collaboration is legible: the agent performs structured work, the person sees its results, and sensitive transitions remain behind explicit human review. The implementation is reusable across application domains instead of being tied to one job board or agent harness. How we built it s-m-r-t is a pnpm TypeScript monorepo. Its scanner reads @smrt() declarations and emits manifests, schemas, routes, clients, and canonical tool descriptors. @happyvertical/smrt-web validates and registers generated and bespoke browser tools. @happyvertical/smrt-svelte binds those contracts to mounted forms and data surfaces. Its application runtime composes SQLite/local, PostgreSQL/self-hosted, and managed-cloud profiles without changing domain objects or WebMCP policy. The execution path fails closed. The decorator controls model-operation exposure; authenticated REST remains the authorization boundary; undeclared effects are classified as destructive; sensitive fields are omitted; stale tools refuse execution; and staged edits cannot self-confirm. Integration fixtures exercise generated definitions, authentication failures, registration lifecycle, policy changes, mounted UI tools, and cross-profile parity. Iolaus consumes published s-m-r-t packages and provides an isolated demo profile. pnpm demo:prepare builds and migrates private SQLite state, seeds visibly fictional opportunities and crawl provenance, starts a loopback-only server, and opens a one-time owner handoff. pnpm demo:smoke runs an authenticated browser proof and verifies both the available capabilities and the absence of approval/submission tools. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was preserving one security and lifecycle model across generated model tools, page-mounted controls, custom component tools, and multiple runtime profiles. A capability policy is only useful if every registration path passes through it. We also had to separate discovery from authorization, exclude sensitive candidate fields, and prevent remounts or policy changes from leaving stale tools behind. The local-first install introduced another systems challenge: safe owner bootstrap, idempotent SQLite setup, private on-device state, deterministic fixtures, and recovery commands all had to work without weakening the deployed application model. Accomplishments that we're proud of WebMCP is a first-class generated framework surface, not a hand-built endpoint for one demo. The same declarations drive persistence, APIs, MCP, WebMCP, clients, and knowledge artifacts. Human-visible controls and agent commands converge on shared registries and state. Effect policy and human approval boundaries are explicit and testable. Iolaus installs locally and proves a useful workflow without transmitting an application. Cross-profile fixtures verify that infrastructure choices do not silently change the agent surface. What we learned WebMCP works best as an application architecture concern, not a thin automation layer. Browser tools should derive from the same source of truth as data and authorization. A strong human-agent experience also needs bounded inputs, visible shared state, effect metadata, lifecycle cleanup, deterministic testing, and carefully chosen places where the agent must stop. What's next for s-m-r-t We will continue hardening conformance across generated, mounted, and declared agent surfaces; improve route-aware capability discovery; and make the one-prompt local installation pattern reusable for other s-m-r-t applications. Iolaus will remain a real-world proving ground while preserving private local data and human control of external actions. Source and testing Framework source: https://github.com/happyvertical/smrt Demo application: https://github.com/willgriffin/iolaus Judge instructions: https://github.com/willgriffin/iolaus/blob/main/docs/judge-demo.md Related deployed application: https://willgriffin.dev Both repositories are MIT licensed. The deterministic demo uses Node.js 24.18+, pnpm 11.24.0, and a WebMCP-capable browser. Clone Iolaus, enable Corepack, run pnpm install --frozen-lockfile , then pnpm demo:prepare . Run pnpm demo:test and pnpm demo:smoke for the repeatable proof. The fixture is fictional, local, and never contacts an employer. title: EmailBooster
pitch: A mail client with no AI inside. It teaches your agent, via WebMCP, to reply to your mail in your own voice, saving you everyday time and effort
about_excerpt: A mail client with no AI inside. It teaches your agent, via WebMCP, to reply to your mail in your own voice, saving you everyday time and effort Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every working day starts the same way. Open the inbox. Scroll to find the thread you need. Re-read it to remember where it stood. Think about how to answer. Type it out. Re-read it. Send. Repeat X times. None of those steps is hard. Together they eat an hour or two every single day, and most of it isn't thinking, it's finding and typing . EmailBooster exists to give that hour back. You say one sentence, "reply to Milan and tell him to look for cheaper alternatives", and the finding, the context, and the typing are done for you, in your own words, in your own compose window, waiting for your approval. What it does EmailBooster is a mail client with no AI inside. Instead, it teaches your browser agent, via WebMCP, to do the repetitive part of email for you: Finding the thread : search_emails and resolve_contact turn "Milan's email about S3" into the right conversation in one call. No scrolling, no search box, no guessing the subject line. Reloading the context : read_thread gives the agent the whole conversation so you don't have to re-read it to remember what was said. Writing the reply in your voice : get_writing_style hands the agent a voice profile built from your sent mail. The draft sounds like you, so you edit two words instead of rewriting three paragraphs. Keeping you in control : the draft lands in the compose window, visible and editable. send_email requires your explicit approval in the UI. Every tool call is logged live in the sidebar. The daily flow becomes: read the inbox, say what you want to reply, glance at the draft, approve. Minutes instead of an hour. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Email is the most repeated task of the working day and the worst one for DOM-scraping agents: search, threading and tone all live behind the UI. WebMCP lets the mail client expose exactly the three things an agent needs to save you time, structured search, full thread context, and your writing style, as tools. No API key, no LLM inside the app, no copy-pasting your private mail into a chatbot. Mail never leaves the tab, and the agent you already have does the work. What people and agents can now do together Before, delegating email meant either doing it all yourself or handing your inbox to a bot that writes like a press release. Now the split is clean and the same every day: the human decides what to say and to whom in one sentence; the agent finds the thread, recovers the context, and writes it in the human's voice; the human edits and approves. Multiply that by every reply you send in a day, and it's the difference between an inbox that owns your morning and one you clear before coffee. How I built it Nine tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() (fallback to navigator.modelContext ), each with a JSON inputSchema , a description written for an agent, and an execute handler. Read-only tools ( search_emails , read_thread , get_open_email , resolve_contact , get_writing_style ) carry annotations: { readOnlyHint: true } . Write tools ( draft_reply , archive_email ) update app state and the DOM in one place, so whatever the agent does, you see it happen. Two tools are dynamic : update_draft and send_email are registered when the compose window opens and removed with unregisterTool() when it closes. The agent cannot send mail when there is nothing on screen to send. Static HTML/CSS/JavaScript, no build step, no server. The mailbox is seed data in localStorage . Hosted on GitHub Pages. Static HTML/CSS/JavaScript, no build step, no server. The mailbox is seed data in localStorage . Hosted on GitHub Pages. Challenges The API moved under my feet. The spec migrated from navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext during the build; the app detects whichever exists. Tool descriptions are the product. The agent only saves you time if it picks the right tool first time. Most of the iteration went into the wording of descriptions, not into code. Speed without losing control. Dynamic registration of the write tools plus an on-screen approval step for send_email turned out simpler and safer than any permission system I sketched, and it adds zero friction to the daily flow. What I learned The biggest time saving doesn't come from the agent doing things, it comes from the agent knowing things: where the thread is, what was said, how you write. A get_writing_style tool is worth more than ten CRUD tools, because it's what turns "a draft" into "my draft". What's next Connecting a real mailbox through a standard IMAP bridge, per-recipient tone (you don't write to your boss like you write to your friend), and letting the agent flag threads that have gone quiet so follow-ups don't slip through the cracks. title: HARMONIUM ( AI PLAYS MUSICAL INTRUMENTAL)
pitch: Agents can play music in web using web-mcp . codex played HARMONIUM (Indian piano) .
about_excerpt: Agents can play music in web using web-mcp . codex played HARMONIUM (Indian piano) . Like 2 Comment Story Updates 1 poster GIF agent play GIF human play banner Inspiration codex plays HARMONIUM ( traditional indian musiscal isntrument - similar to a piano ) I was listening to piano music while my team and I were working on Draw Generator , another project for the same hackathon. The music gave me a glimpse of my childhood memories with the harmonium, and that moment gave me this idea. I started wondering: CAN it actually PLAY AN MUSICAL INSTRUMENT with us? and How does AI understand music, and can We tested this idea with Codex using GPT-5.6, and the result was wonderful. That experiment became HARMONIUM . What it does HARMONIUM is a playable 39-key Indian harmonium covering C3 to D6. People can play it using a mouse, touchscreen, or computer keyboard. It supports Western and Sargam notation, lets the user move the Sa reference, loads structured JSON scores, and displays falling notes that remain synchronized with the music. The main idea is simple: people and AI agents can play the same visible instrument together . When an agent plays a note, the human can hear it, see the matching key light up, and continue playing from the same instrument. How we built it We built HARMONIUM with React, TypeScript, Vite, Tone.js, the WebAudio, and WebMCP . The page exposes five WebMCP tools: play_note plays one note. play_score performs a timed melody or chord sequence. set_sa changes the Sargam reference. stop ends the current performance. get_state lets the agent inspect the instrument. Agents and people use the same visible instrument. The tools are registered directly on the page using document.modelContext.registerTool() . A single audio engine owns all note playback. Mouse input, computer-keyboard input, JSON scores, and WebMCP tools all call the same playNote and stopNote logic. This keeps the sound and visible keyboard synchronized instead of maintaining separate implementations for humans and agents. Tone.js schedules the notes using the browser's audio clock. The instrument uses real harmonium samples, while a synthesized reed-like sound acts as a fallback if the samples cannot load. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was understanding how sound works on this instrument. We had never worked with music on the web before. As we started, we got help from a teacher from my childhood, and this gave us a real boost. ChatGPT also did a great job helping us research how the harmonium works, understand browser audio, find useful resources, and build the first working version. Keeping sound and animation synchronized was another challenge. JavaScript timers can drift, especially during longer scores, so we used Tone.js Transport and the Web Audio clock for playback and visual timing. Browsers also block audio until the human interacts with the page. An AI agent cannot unlock the audio by itself, so the user must first press Tap to start . After that, the agent can play notes and complete scores through WebMCP. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that HARMONIUM looks and feels like a complete instrument rather than a WebMCP demonstration attached to a webpage. The project includes real harmonium samples, synchronized visuals, structured tool results, and WebMCP evaluation fixtures for tool selection and multi-step journeys. A person can play manually, hand control to an agent, change the note or Sa reference, and then continue playing. Agent actions remain visible to the human. This synchronizes human mode and agent mode through one shared implementation. That made WebMCP a genuine extension of the product instead of a separate feature added only for the hackathon. We are also proud that every interaction uses the same audio engine. A note sounds and lights up in the same way whether it comes from a mouse, computer keyboard, JSON score, or AI agent. What we learned We learned how music works inside a web browser. Before this project, we had never built a musical instrument for the web. We learned about notes, timing, overlapping sounds, audio samples, the Web Audio clock, Western notation, and Indian Sargam notation. We learned that synchronizing music is different from updating a normal interface. A small delay between the sound and the highlighted key is immediately noticeable. Using Tone.js Transport and the Web Audio clock helped us keep the notes, falling visuals, and keyboard state together. We also learned why one shared implementation matters. Because people and agents use the same audio engine, we do not need separate logic for human mode and agent mode . This made the behavior easier to understand and prevented the two modes from becoming different instruments. WebMCP taught us that an agent should not have to guess where to click on a webpage. Instead, the website can expose clear actions such as play_note , play_score , and set_sa . The agent gets a reliable way to act, while the human can still see and control everything through the normal interface. We learned that tool descriptions, input validation, error messages, and state inspection are important parts of the agent experience. For example, if audio is still locked, the tool must clearly explain that the human needs to press Tap to start . Most importantly, we learned that AI does not have to replace the person using an application. In HARMONIUM, the agent and the human share the same instrument. One can begin a musical idea, and the other can continue it. What's next for HARMONIUM (MUSIC INSTRUMENT - WEBMCP) Next, we will try to turn HARMONIUM into a guided music-practice space for people and agents. other project , agents generate pixel art : https://devpost.com/software/pixel-generator-ibjpfc Built With css react tone.js typescript vite webaudioapi webmcp Try it out github.com web-harmonium.rajmayank-mrb.chatgpt.site Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by frontend and backend Mamini anuradha chakra brainstorming BIKASH Ranjan Baral We built six WebMCP projects that let Codex designs, draws on tldraw- teaches, plays music and creates pixel art. title: NexusOps
pitch: NexusOps lets specialized agents investigate production incidents through real WebMCP tools, resolve disagreements with evidence, and keep humans in control of remediation.

 Inspiration 

 Incident response is often stuck between two extremes: humans doing everything manually, or automation acting without enough context and control. We built NexusOps to explore a safer middle ground where agents investigate operational incidents, compare evidence, and recommend actions while humans remain responsible for approval. 

 What it does 

 WebMCP makes this possible directly inside the website. NexusOps exposes operational tools that compatible agents can discover and call, while the human operator sees the same evidence, reasoning, activity trace, and safety boundaries. 

 How we built it 

 NexusOps is an agent-native operations control plane for investigating production incidents. It exposes 20 WebMCP tools covering observation, investigation, recommendations, human approval, remediation, and verification. 

 For the simulated incident INC-1042, specialized SRE, NOC, Developer, and SOC perspectives inspect different evidence sources. They form independent hypotheses, identify supporting and conflicting evidence, and allow an Incident Commander to arbitrate the disagreement.
The environment is intentionally simulated. Metrics, logs, services, deployments, and remediation state are deterministic demo data. No real production system is monitored or changed. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 I ran into challenge when I was not familiar with WebMCP at all before starting working on project. Also was lacking of AI credits to actually develop the app in 3-4 days. 

 Accomplishments that I am proud of 

 NexusOps exposes 20 genuine WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(), allowing compatible agents to discover and call operational capabilities directly from the website.
I built a complete incident workflow covering observation, investigation, multi-agent analysis, disagreement, Incident Commander arbitration, human approval, controlled remediation, and verification.
The SRE, NOC, Developer, and SOC perspectives use different evidence sources and produce deterministic, explainable conclusions from the same operational data.
I also added a schema-driven Tool Inspector, evidence and causal-chain views, risk and approval metadata, shared execution tracing, and an audit activity feed. 

 What I learnedx 

 First of all, understood concepts of webmcp and its usage.
I learned that WebMCP is most valuable when agents can use the same tools and page state as the human operator instead of interacting through a separate hidden integration.
I learned that agent assistance must be paired with clear safety boundaries, especially when tools can change operational state.
I also learned that specialized agent perspectives are more useful than a single generic assistant because different roles can focus on different evidence and reach different conclusions. 

 What's next for NexusOps 

 The next step is to connect the same WebMCP control-plane pattern to real observability and incident-management systems while preserving human approval for high-risk actions.
Future versions could support additional incident types, organization-specific tools, richer agent arbitration, and persistent audit history.
The current priority is validating the live WebMCP experience in Chrome and compatible agent environments, then using that feedback to improve reliability and real-world integrations.

title: CancelDesk
pitch: CancelDesk makes getting rid of unwanted subscriptions simple. Tell your AI agent what you want to cancel, and WebMCP handles the tedious steps while keeping you in control of the final decision.
about_excerpt: CancelDesk makes getting rid of unwanted subscriptions simple. Tell your AI agent what you want to cancel, and WebMCP handles the tedious steps while keeping you in control of the final decision. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Cancelling a subscription should be easy, but it often isn't. Users have to dig through account settings, find the right membership page, read cancellation policies, decline retention offers, answer surveys, and click through multiple confirmation screens. We built CancelDesk to explore what that experience could look like in a WebMCP-powered web. Instead of making an AI agent navigate a website the same way a human does, CancelDesk exposes structured tools that let agents understand what the site can do and take action directly. What it does CancelDesk is a subscription management dashboard built for both humans and AI agents. A user can simply say: "Cancel everything I haven't used in 60 days that costs more than $15 per month, but keep StreamBox. Show me before actually cancelling anything." Through WebMCP, the agent can discover the user's subscriptions, identify the ones matching those conditions, calculate potential savings, protect StreamBox, check cancellation requirements, and prepare the cancellations. CancelDesk then pauses when a meaningful human decision is required. For example, CloudPro presents a retention offer that the user must accept or decline. Final cancellations also require explicit authorization. In our primary demo, a workflow that would require 24 manual UI steps can be handled with 2 WebMCP calls — 92% fewer interactions. How we built it CancelDesk is a responsive web application with 20 native WebMCP tools exposed through document.modelContext . The WebMCP layer connects directly to the same domain services and application state used by the human interface. There is no hidden browser automation and no simulated DOM clicking behind WebMCP actions. We also built several visual tools to make agent activity transparent: Agent Inspector shows real WebMCP calls, inputs, results, and execution time. Mission Control shows the progress and status of multi-subscription operations. Agent Flow visualizes the manual UI journey being bypassed by WebMCP. Human vs. WebMCP comparisons show the actual number of manual interactions versus semantic tool calls. The production application is agent-agnostic and does not require an OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or other AI API key. The intelligence comes from the agent using the site; CancelDesk provides the capabilities through WebMCP. Challenges we ran into One of the biggest challenges was designing WebMCP actions that were powerful without giving an agent unlimited authority. Cancelling a subscription is consequential, so we separated preparation from authorization. An agent can research policies, calculate savings, prepare cancellations, and surface retention offers, but preparation alone cannot complete a cancellation. We also had to make multi-subscription operations safe against forged confirmation tokens, replayed authorizations, protected subscriptions, unresolved retention decisions, and partial failures. Another challenge was making the benefit of WebMCP visible. Because a successful WebMCP interaction actually removes UI navigation, we created Agent Flow and interaction comparisons so users can see the manual steps that were avoided. Accomplishments that we're proud of We're especially proud that CancelDesk doesn't just demonstrate WebMCP with a single simple action. It supports a complete multi-step, multi-provider workflow while preserving meaningful human control. CancelDesk exposes 20 native WebMCP tools , and our test suite verifies native discovery and execution across all of them. Our primary workflow reduces 24 manual UI steps to 2 WebMCP calls , while still stopping when human judgment or final authorization is required. Most importantly, the WebMCP implementation and human interface share the same underlying application state. When an agent takes action through WebMCP, the user can immediately see what happened in the actual application. What we learned WebMCP changes the relationship between websites and AI agents. The biggest lesson for us was that the goal shouldn't simply be to make agents better at clicking websites. The more interesting opportunity is to let websites expose what they can do in a structured, semantic way. We also learned that reducing interaction doesn't have to mean reducing user control. WebMCP can eliminate unnecessary interaction without eliminating necessary consent. What's next for CancelDesk CancelDesk currently uses simulated subscription providers to demonstrate the complete WebMCP experience safely and deterministically. The next step would be connecting the same architecture to real subscription providers and billing platforms as they expose secure APIs and agent-accessible capabilities. The larger vision is a web where users don't have to learn every company's interface just to accomplish a task. Humans should be able to describe what they want, agents should be able to understand what websites can do, and websites should remain in control of how those actions are safely performed. title: AgentGate
pitch: A WebMCP protocol layer that lets any web page tell agents what it can do, what happened, what's risky, and when to hand the last click to a human.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP protocol layer that lets any web page tell agents what it can do, what happened, what's risky, and when to hand the last click to a human. Like Comment Story Updates AgentGate is a zero-dependency protocol layer on top of WebMCP's document.modelContext.registerTool() . It makes a web page talk to agents: what it can do and what state it's in ( describe_page ), whether a call worked and which field failed (structured receipts), which actions are dangerous ( risk: read | write | irreversible ), how to hand the one irreversible step to a human ( request_human → single-use scoped token), and when async content is actually ready ( ready gating). Three lines to integrate into any site; a real five-step Grant Portal demo shows the same page with and without it. Live demo: https://run58669-maker.github.io/agentgate-webmcp/ (open in Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing or ChatGPT's in-app browser; ?agentgate=off shows the bare-DOM "before" version) Code (MIT): https://github.com/run58669-maker/agentgate-webmcp The problem, from an agent's point of view Every one of these is something an agent actually hits when operating real websites: it dumps every button and guesses which one matters; it clicks Submit, sleeps, and re-reads the page hoping to spot "Thanks"; validation errors come back as one vague sentence with no field name; Submit and Cancel look identical, so nothing marks the irreversible step; "page loaded" says nothing about whether the async content is ready; and a captcha or a payment step either kills the run or gets hard-clicked. WebMCP solves discovery and invocation. AgentGate adds the five things a page needs to say next. Why a site owner would install this (the honest version) We used this exact protocol to ship this submission — and every third-party site we touched today (Devpost, YouTube) had none of it, so we fell back to the old way: dump every button, guess, click an <input> that ignores clicks until you hit its <label> , sleep, re-read the page. That is what agent traffic looks like to a site today: brittle scrapers that break on the next redesign, retry blindly, and sometimes fire the irreversible button. AgentGate is the cheap alternative for the site owner: Three lines, no rewrite. Wrap the handlers you already have. Nothing changes for human visitors. You decide what agents may do. risk: "irreversible" means no agent can submit, pay, or delete without a person on your page clicking Confirm — the site enforces it, not the agent's good manners. Fewer support tickets. Structured receipts and field-level errors mean agents fix their own mistakes instead of retrying, and describe_page means they stop clicking things at random. Ready gating protects your backend. NOT_READY + retry_after_ms replaces the hammering that "sleep and retry" agents do today. It also dogfoods : after building it, the author-agent (Claude) drove the demo site end-to-end purely from receipts — and immediately found a gap (a required field the demo silently accepted), which is now a field-level error in the demo and a step in the video. Why WebMCP is the right fit WebMCP solves discovery and invocation — a page can say "here are my tools" and an agent can call them. But every non-trivial real product built on top of that immediately needs the same five things: a map of what's on the page and what state it's in, a reliable way to know if a call succeeded, a way to mark some actions as more dangerous than others, a way to put a human in the loop before an irreversible action fires, and a way to say "not yet" instead of racing async content. WebMCP itself has an open issue for the human-confirmation problem (#165 "Human in the Loop support" / #50 "Handling multiple elicitation requests", both open) and doesn't specify any of the other four. AgentGate is a direct, minimal-surface-area answer to those five gaps, built entirely on registerTool() / execute() — it doesn't fork or reimplement WebMCP, it wraps it. That's the deepest kind of "WebMCP leverage": we don't just call registerTool() once for a toy button, we use it as the substrate for a full five-step transactional flow with real risk-tiered, human-gated, ready-gated tools. Why the experience is better — for the human and the agent For the agent: instead of dumping the DOM and guessing which of 40 buttons matters, it calls describe_page() once and gets a typed list of tools with risk levels and current state. Instead of sleep(1500) and re-reading innerText hoping for "Thanks!", every call returns {ok, state, errors, next} — including which field failed validation and what to try next. Instead of an agent being able to click "Submit" exactly like a "Cancel" button, irreversible actions are structurally different: they cannot execute without a token that only exists after a human clicked Confirm on a panel that named the exact action and reason. For the human: nothing changes about how they use the page themselves (a human clicking Submit doesn't need a token — see apps/demo/src/render.ts ), but they get visibility and a veto over what an agent does on their behalf, instead of an agent silently automating a UI they never see. What a human + agent can now do together Delegate a genuinely multi-step, stateful, partly-irreversible workflow — filling out a grant application across five pages, including a file upload with real async processing — to an agent, while keeping a hard checkpoint at the one step that can't be undone. Before AgentGate, that checkpoint either didn't exist (the agent submits, period) or existed only as "the agent is supposed to ask the user in chat first," which is a convention the page has no way to enforce. In our demo, submit_application is registered risk:"irreversible" — the browser-mediated tool itself refuses to run without a token minted by a human clicking Confirm in the page. The agent can prepare everything (account, profile, upload) autonomously and fast; the human's involvement is reduced to exactly one deliberate click, on exactly the one step where a mistake can't be undone. How we implemented WebMCP packages/agentgate/ is a ~300-line, zero-runtime-dependency TypeScript library ( AgentGate.init() / gate.tool() / gate.ready() ) that wraps every registered tool's execute with: a readiness check, a risk-tier + single-use-token check for irreversible tools, and a receipt normalizer, then registers the wrapped function with the real document.modelContext.registerTool() (falling back to navigator.modelContext , or to a local-only registry with a console warning if neither exists — see docs/API_NOTES.md for how we verified the actual spec API before writing any of this). request_human() and describe_page() are themselves ordinary auto-registered tools. 25 vitest tests cover all five capabilities against a mocked document.modelContext . apps/demo/ is a Vite + vanilla TypeScript "Grant Portal" with a real five-step flow, an ?agentgate=off bare-DOM comparison mode, and a live "Agent console" panel that drives and logs every tool call for the demo video. title: kontier-ri
pitch: Ask ChatGPT why churn spiked. It reads the page's WebMCP tools, finds the cause, and proposes edits. A different human approves them. Attributed to the agent, undoable in one keystroke.
about_excerpt: Ask ChatGPT why churn spiked. It reads the page's WebMCP tools, finds the cause, and proposes edits. A different human approves them. Attributed to the agent, undoable in one keystroke. Like Comment Story Updates Kontier RI - a shared investigation workspace for humans and agents Inspiration Every agent demo ends the same way. Something impressive happens, and you have no idea whether to trust it. We kept hitting this inside our own product. Kontier is a billing platform, and the question customers ask most is some version of "why did churn spike last month?" An agent can answer that. What it cannot do is convince the person who has to act on the answer - the reasoning scrolls past in a chat window, the edits appear with no author, and no colleague can check the work before it becomes true. So we stopped asking how do we let an agent do more and started asking who reviews it, and how would they even see it. That question has a shape. It looks like code review: a proposal, a diff, a reason per change, a second pair of eyes, and a way back. WebMCP was the missing half - a page can declare what an agent may do, in the same tab a human is already looking at. The report becomes the shared surface instead of the transcript. What it does Several people and their agents work one live report. An agent reads the page's tools through WebMCP, investigates, and proposes. Nothing is applied. A human - often a different human, arriving on nothing but an invite link - reads the staged change set as a diff with a reason on every row, keeps what they agree with, drops what they do not, and approves. The result lands attributed to the agent that proposed it, not the human who clicked, as one entry and one undo step. In our demo, ChatGPT's own browser was asked in plain English why churn spiked in March. It listed the page's tools, read the work context, queried the data, and found the cause: one plan went from €99 to €149 that month, and 40 of the 44 cancellations came from it. Then it wrote two annotations onto the report and stopped, waiting for a human. How we built it A pnpm monorepo, TypeScript throughout, strict everywhere. packages/studio - the collaboration contract and the WebMCP layer. 40 static tools plus small bundles that mount and unmount with the state of the work. Chrome's own guide asks for exactly this: "register tools when they're useful in a certain page state, then unregister when the tool is no longer usable," with static registration as the default. One schema per tool. A zod v4 schema generates the protocol inputSchema via z.toJSONSchema() and re-validates the same shape inside execute, so the contract cannot drift from the implementation. packages/datasource - DuckDB-WASM. SQL runs in the tab, and registerRemoteParquet range-reads remote Parquet over HTTP, so 100 million rows are queryable without downloading them. packages/workspace - one WorkspaceStore interface, local and HTTP implementations, and a 23-test conformance suite run against both. apps/web - Next.js. Guest workspaces where the invite link is the credential, real OIDC through the platform's existing Keycloak, an ordered command log with server-assigned seq, presence, and cross-user approval. Deployed as a Node container at ri.kontier.eu, on the same infrastructure as the rest of the platform. What we learned WebMCP rewards being specific. Chrome publishes character budgets - 500 per description, 150 per parameter, 30 per name. Ours had one tool at 888 characters, repeating a grammar its own inputSchema already expressed. Nothing enforces those budgets, which is exactly why we wrote a test that does. Declaring nothing is worse than declaring false. Silence on a mutating tool is a missing signal, not a neutral one. All 46 tools now declare readOnlyHint explicitly - 13 reads true and untrusted-hinted, 33 writes false - pinned by a test that fails on any future tool that says nothing. Rejected calls are the ones you cannot see. A call the host rejects on schema validation leaves no trace anywhere — no document change, no activity entry. We had excluded those from our ledger, reasoning nothing ran. Wrong: an agent sending the wrong shape is one of Chrome's named failure modes, and the ledger is the only place it can surface. Chrome 152 wants a JSON string. executeTool(tool, {}) fails with "Failed to parse input arguments." It needs executeTool(tool, JSON.stringify(args)). We only found that by driving the real runtime. Challenges we ran into Two workers, one contract, five silent failures. We built the client store and server API in parallel against a written contract. Every piece passed its own tests. Then they met: /identity was never implemented, so nothing ever connected. The client PUT a shape the server rejected - and the conformance mock read the id from the body, so 79 tests passed against a server that did not exist. loadDashboard read a bare record where the server enveloped it, so documents arrived undefined and the report opened empty with no error. The workspace package re-exported its test suite, dragging vitest into the browser bundle. And peers tracked each other through the command stream alone, so a change producing no activity entry left a peer stale forever. The bug only production had. A reviewer opening an invite link erased the proposal they came to review - a freshly joined tab publishes an empty presence before its first read. It reproduced every time against the live site and never locally, because it is a race the fast path wins. The fix is one rule: read before write. We found it while recording the demo. Local edits that undid themselves. A poll could list dashboards before a save landed and finish after it, applying a stale document over edits made in between. A change that quietly reverts a second later is the worst thing an editor can do. Config describing a server nobody ran. Keycloak honours wildcards in the path, not the host - https:// .kontier.eu/ had always been a no-op that merely looked correct. And the realm file declared an organization scope the live server lacked, which fails the whole authorization request rather than being ignored. We put sign-in behind a wall to keep tests passing. It broke 41 of 42 end-to-end tests in one run - exactly what a first-time visitor would have experienced. The tests were right and we were wrong. What's next Entitlement-scoped tools. Our API keys already carry explicit permission scopes, so the toolbelt an agent sees can be derived from what the credential allows - an agent could not even see a tool it is not authorized to call, and the server would refuse it anyway. The machinery exists; it is scoped by workflow phase today and by permission tomorrow. title: GridTwin
pitch: A WebMCP civic microgrid sandbox where AI explores deterministic energy scenarios while humans retain final authority.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP civic microgrid sandbox where AI explores deterministic energy scenarios while humans retain final authority. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Planning context — synthetic baseline, approved criteria, and seven WebMCP tools ready. Visible exploration — genuine tool calls create and compare three deterministic scenarios. Outage proof — grid at 0 kW while the battery serves all eight critical hours. Human authority — the agent shortlists; only the planner approves. Decision brief — the approved plan becomes a transparent, print-ready recommendation. GridTwin One-line Summary GridTwin is a WebMCP civic microgrid sandbox where an AI agent visibly explores deterministic energy scenarios while the human retains authority over constraints, final plan selection, and export. Problem Climate and resilience officers at small councils and housing associations often need to choose one indicative solar-and-battery configuration before they can pursue a grant or commission a professional feasibility study. The decision spans budget, emissions, and outage resilience, but existing energy tools are usually designed for specialists and generic AI interfaces can hide what an agent changed or why it recommended an option. That is a poor fit for a consequential early-stage decision. A useful agent must make the decision space easier to navigate without obscuring assumptions, silently relaxing constraints, or taking final authority from the person accountable for the outcome. Solution GridTwin turns the fictional Riverside Estate into a shared, visible planning workspace. The human approves a £400,000 capital budget, a 40% emissions-reduction target, eight hours of critical-load coverage, and a resilience-first priority order. A real browser agent then uses seven page-defined WebMCP tools to read the baseline, run bounded solar-and-battery scenarios, compare transparent metrics, diagnose infeasibility, and shortlist a feasible candidate. Every scenario uses the same deterministic hourly dispatch model. Every tool action appears in the activity rail and visibly changes scenario cards, comparisons, or report state. Infeasible candidates show every violation in natural units. Agent advice remains reversible. Only the human can approve criteria, select the final plan, or open the browser print flow. The signature result is the fixed 18:00–02:00 outage: grid contribution falls to zero, the balanced 275 kWp solar / 500 kWh battery plan supplies critical load for all eight hours, and the final action belongs to the human approving the plan. Why This Matters GridTwin demonstrates a WebMCP pattern for consequential human-agent work—not just an energy calculator. Before WebMCP, a generic assistant could describe possible configurations, but it could not reliably operate the same visible, structured planning state as the human or leave an auditable trail of each action. With WebMCP, the agent can navigate a non-trivial decision space through narrow tools while the application remains the source of truth for calculations, feasibility, lifecycle state, and authority. The result is a better user experience because the human sees the work happen, can inspect assumptions and violations at the point of use, and retains explicit control over every consequential transition. The civic-energy example makes that collaboration concrete: abstract capacities become continued critical services during an outage. GridTwin does not claim to produce an engineering design. It helps a real target user make a transparent decision about what deserves professional evaluation next. How We Used AI GridTwin contains no embedded chatbot and calls no model API. AI enters through an external agent in ChatGPT's in-app browser, which discovers and invokes the page-defined WebMCP tools. The agent can: read the synthetic Riverside Estate baseline and fixed assumptions; stage constraint suggestions for human review without applying them; choose bounded solar and battery inputs and run real deterministic scenarios; compare two or three current scenarios without an opaque score; diagnose the nearest candidate when every option is infeasible; create a reversible shortlist for a feasible plan; and prepare an immutable decision-brief preview after human approval. The agent cannot approve constraints, approve or reconsider a plan, reset the comparison, print, download, or publish. Those actions have no WebMCP schema. After human approval, advisory mutations are frozen until the human explicitly reconsiders the decision. All authoritative metrics come from GridTwin's pure client-side model, not from model-generated arithmetic. WebMCP makes the agent's structured actions visible, testable, and subordinate to the application's lifecycle rules. How We Used Codex Codex was the primary development agent across the 30-hour solo build. It helped turn the initial idea into the scope, PRD, technical specification, and sequenced checklist; implemented the deterministic dispatch engine, reserve policy, lifecycle reducer, persistence, WebMCP adapter, civic interface, outage visual, and A4 report; added regression and browser tests; diagnosed integration failures; rehearsed the real in-app-browser workflow; deployed to Vercel; and prepared the handoff documentation. The builder actively directed the work rather than accepting a generated solution wholesale. Three mandatory review pauses produced concrete corrections, including refresh-safe activity identity, stricter restored-state validation, full post-approval agent freeze, HTTPS in-app-browser verification, and a settled chart capture. The builder also rejected an embedded-chat fallback, an opaque composite score, hidden constraint relaxation, and dramatic but dishonest tariff assumptions. That collaboration mirrors GridTwin itself: Codex explored and implemented within an explicit plan, while the human reviewed the consequential product, authority, credibility, and scope decisions. Key Features Exactly seven direct WebMCP tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() . One shared deterministic engine for every bounded solar/battery combination—no optimizer, randomness, precomputed scenario cards, or special-case balanced branch. Visible tool activity, a fixed 600 ms abortable pending interval, atomic scenario commits, and safe interruption handling. Versioned human-approved constraints with current/stale scenario lineage. Direct cost, emissions, reserve, resilience, feasibility, and natural-unit violation metrics with no composite score. Transparent all-infeasible diagnosis and staged—but never automatic—constraint suggestions. Distinct reversible agent shortlist and direct human-approved selection. Signature 18:00–02:00 outage view with grid at 0 kW and eight uninterrupted critical hours for the balanced plan. Immutable A4 decision-brief snapshot and human-controlled Print → Save as PDF flow. Session refresh recovery that restores committed work but never converts partial operations into completed results. Persistent synthetic-data, model-version, constraint-version, and indicative-planning caveats. Architecture GridTwin is a static React 19, TypeScript, and Vite application deployed on Vercel. Human UI or WebMCP callback ↓ shared validated command boundary ↓ pure deterministic domain calculation ↓ complete atomic reducer transition ↓ session snapshot and visible workspace/report src/domain/ : fixed synthetic inputs, validation, hourly dispatch, convergence, annualization, outage stress test, feasibility, and non-composite nearest ordering. It imports no React or browser code. src/state/ : context/reducer, versioned lifecycle, authority gates, interruption recovery, and sessionStorage compatibility. src/webmcp/ : seven JSON schemas, direct imperative registration, all-or-nothing discovery, cleanup, cancellation, readiness, and stable result envelopes. src/components/ : purpose-built civic planning interface, Recharts analysis, and a small fixed-node energy-flow SVG. Report path: an immutable snapshot of matching approved state; no recalculation, automatic download, or publication. The annual operating estimate and outage stress test share one dispatch function but remain separate calculation paths. Battery state converges across repeated representative days, a noon-to-outage reserve policy applies consistently, and the outage test clones the actual prepared 18:00 state. Testing Instructions No credentials are required. Judge-facing live path Open https://gridtwin.vercel.app in ChatGPT's WebMCP-enabled in-app browser or Google Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Confirm the header reads WebMCP ready · 7 agent tools available . Approve the default £400,000 / 40% / 8-hour criteria through the direct human button. Ask the browser agent: Inspect Riverside Estate and respect the approved budget, emissions, and eight-hour resilience criteria. Explore distinct solar-heavy, battery-heavy, and balanced configurations within the allowed increments. Run each s

title: AI API Prices
pitch: Compare AI inference prices across providers manually or with AI agents. WebMCP lets agents search models, compare providers, estimate workload costs, and return results to the page
about_excerpt: Compare AI inference prices across providers manually or with AI agents. WebMCP lets agents search models, compare providers, estimate workload costs, and return results to the page Like Comment Story Updates 01 Workload calculation 02 Human-agent-handoff 03 WebMCP site tools 04 Model comparision Inspiration AI API pricing is fragmented. One model can appear across several providers at very different prices. If you want to compare them, you may need to open several sites, understand different pricing formats, and calculate the cost of your workload. I had built AI API Prices as a website for comparing published inference prices before this challenge. The WebMCP Challenge gave me a reason to test whether an agent could use the same product without pretending to be a person clicking through it. I chose price comparison because the task needs little explanation. You ask for a model or a workload, and you can see the value of WebMCP in one short interaction. What it does You can search for a model on AI API Prices and compare provider prices in the browser. With WebMCP enabled, your agent gets five tools built on the same pricing data: find models and prices compare providers for one model calculate a workload cost from input and output token counts compare models for the same workload open the matching model or provider view on the page Before I added these tools, an agent had to infer meaning from the page and interact with the interface like a person, or the user had to carry information between the chat and the site. The WebMCP tools give the agent explicit actions and structured results. You can ask for the research or calculation in chat, then continue on the website with the relevant view open. How I built it I built the site with Next.js, React, TypeScript and Node.js. I connected the five WebMCP tools to the same normalized catalogue, provider comparison rules and workload calculations used by the browser interface. I kept one pricing system for both humans and agents. At submission time, users can compare published prices from 12 AI inference providers. I started the project before the challenge and added the WebMCP integration during the submission period. You can verify both stages in the dated commit history of the public repository. Challenges I ran into A live ChatGPT test exposed the most useful bug I found during the challenge. ChatGPT found the cheapest providers for a model, then handed the model name to the provider directory. The answer was right, but the page showed no matching provider because the two views expect different kinds of queries. I changed the handoff contract so a resolved model opens the model comparison view. I kept provider-name searches in the provider directory and added regression tests for both paths. I then repeated the same test in ChatGPT's in-app browser and confirmed that the agent's answer and the page state matched. Accomplishments I'm proud of I am most proud of the handoff between the agent and the regular website. You can ask an agent to compare prices or calculate a workload cost, get the answer in chat, and continue on the site with the relevant model open. I also kept the WebMCP tools tied to the product's existing pricing logic. I did not create separate data or calculations for the challenge demo. What I learned I had heard of WebMCP before this challenge, but I had not used it. Working on AI API Prices gave me a practical model for agent support on websites: give the agent explicit actions over product logic you already use, then return the user to a page state where they can continue the task. That approach let me keep the existing human interface while giving agents access to the same pricing work. What's next for AI API Prices I plan to expand price coverage and improve data quality after the challenge. I also want to keep testing handoffs where an agent handles the research or calculation and the user continues the task in the browser. title: Recall — User-Controlled AI Memory
pitch: Instead of giving an agent access to your memory, Recall gives your memory a controlled interface the agent must use.
about_excerpt: Instead of giving an agent access to your memory, Recall gives your memory a controlled interface the agent must use. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Homepage Tool surface Memory Insights dashboard Memory Canvas Agent tool-call simulator Permissions Audit export WebMCP Diagnostics page Inspiration I was sitting in a coffee shop in Lagos, half-watching a friend talk to ChatGPT on his phone. He asked it, "What do you remember about me?" ChatGPT rattled off his job, his preferences, and a trip he'd mentioned weeks earlier. He laughed, then paused: "But I never told it to remember any of that." That moment exposed a problem that only gets more important as AI agents become more capable: your AI can remember things about you, but you have almost no control over the memory itself. You can't inspect individual facts, edit them precisely, audit when a memory was used, selectively revoke access, or independently verify what actually happened. When I read the WebMCP specification, I saw a fundamentally different way to approach this. Most agent architectures put the agent at the center — the agent calls out to servers, and the server owns the capability surface. WebMCP inverts that relationship: it lets a website publish its own state as a tool surface that an external agent can access through the browser. So I inverted the architecture around that idea. Instead of giving an agent access to your memory, give your memory a controlled interface the agent must use. That became Recall: the website is the memory, the agent is the consumer, the browser is the trust boundary, and the user controls the capabilities. What It Does WebMCP changes the boundary. Traditional agent memory is an API the agent consumes. Recall makes the website itself the memory boundary and publishes only the capabilities the user has enabled. Recall is a user-controlled memory layer for AI agents, implemented as a WebMCP website. Your AI's memory of you lives in a website you can inspect, edit, control, and audit, instead of disappearing into an opaque agent platform. The clearest demonstration of that is this sequence: ChatGPT ↓ discovers Recall's WebMCP tools ↓ addFact("I prefer TypeScript") ↓ Recall updates the memory ↓ signed audit event appears ↓ user disables addFact in Settings ↓ agent attempts a write ↓ ❌ blocked by Recall ↓ user re-enables addFact ↓ ✅ access restored Disable the addFact tool in Settings, and the capability token's scope narrows immediately. Ask the agent to remember that you prefer Rust, and it can no longer perform the write — the call simply fails. Re-enable addFact , and access returns just as quickly. In one sequence, this demonstrates WebMCP capability exposure, user governance, authorization enforcement, and agent behavior in a directly observable way. The website isn't only exposing capabilities to an agent; it is actively enforcing the user's decision at the capability boundary in real time. Under the hood, when a signed-in user opens Recall in a WebMCP-capable browser, it registers six tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : Tool Purpose query Retrieve matching memories using content and tag search addFact Add a memory updateFact Update a memory forgetFact Soft-delete a memory summarize Produce a deterministic summary timeline Retrieve recent agent activity These tools carry WebMCP annotations such as readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint , and Recall also demonstrates origin-scoped access, declarative tool exposure, browser-mediated authentication, and capability-token authorization. Every action in the sequence above also leaves a receipt. Each tool call is signed with ECDSA P-256 and appended to a tamper-evident audit record, then made available as an exportable JWS bundle. Anyone can independently verify, using the included public key, that a given audit event was signed by Recall and has not been altered since. Recall is designed for people who increasingly rely on AI across multiple agents and need their memory to remain under their control rather than becoming locked inside a single agent provider. As context, preferences, and history become distributed across ChatGPT, Claude, and future agents, the question becomes not only how AI personalizes itself, but who owns and governs the persistent context behind that personalization. Recall's answer is portable, governed, auditable personal memory for the agentic web: memory that can outlive any one agent relationship because the user, not the platform, holds the capability boundary. The distinctive part of Recall is not simply "user-controlled AI memory" as a category. It is that the memory itself is exposed as an agent-facing WebMCP capability boundary, with real-time capability revocation and independently verifiable action receipts. Beyond the core protocol, Recall is implemented as a complete product: a memory canvas with full CRUD operations, tag-aware search with a graceful fallback when nothing matches, a Memory Insights dashboard, a real-time activity feed, per-tool permissions, short-lived capability tokens, a signed audit export, an interactive WebMCP playground, a diagnostics page, and an in-app tool-call simulator. The goal was never to maximize the number of AI components; it was to build the smallest system that makes user-controlled agent memory real and demonstrable. How We Built It The architecture follows the inversion deliberately: Traditional Agent Architecture Recall Subject Agent Website Client Server ChatGPT Tool surface Server TLS origin Trust boundary Network Browser Memory owner Agent platform User Recall is built with Next.js 16 and the App Router, TypeScript, WebMCP's document.modelContext , Turso/libSQL for edge-replicated SQLite, WebCrypto for signing, socket.io for real-time updates, TanStack Query on the client, and Vercel for deployment. We use GitHub OAuth for browser-mediated authentication. The /playground page offers a no-sign-in interactive tour of the tool surface (using a simulated vault), while /app provides the full WebMCP experience with real tool registration, the signed audit log, and per-tool permission controls. The stack is intentionally restrained: there is no blockchain, multi-agent orchestration, or RAG pipeline in the MVP because none of these would strengthen the core product. We deliberately optimized the system for verifiability and user control rather than making its architecture dependent on opaque retrieval behavior. The security model treats WebMCP's browser topology as the foundation rather than a layer bolted on afterward. TLS-origin tool publication, browser-mediated execution, fromOrigins restrictions, per-tool permissions, short-lived capability tokens, audience and scope restrictions, ECDSA signatures, and tamper-evident audit records all work together. The user can disable any of the six capabilities; the WebMCP bridge only exposes the enabled set, and each capability token is scoped to the current permission state. Revocation is therefore part of the actual execution path, not simply a UI preference. Without WebMCP, an agent would need a separate integration layer just to reach a memory service. Recall instead makes the memory itself a web capability surface: the agent discovers tools from the website, the tools operate against the website's state, the browser mediates each call, and the user decides which capabilities exist at all. That is a relationship that is difficult to reproduce cleanly with a conventional hidden memory API. Challenges We Ran Into Tool lifecycle management was one of the harder WebMCP problems. registerTool() throws a duplicate-name error if a tool is registered twice, which matters as soon as a user toggles a permission and the tool surface needs to be rebuilt. We solved this with an AbortController per registered tool and explicit cleanup before re-registration, so permission changes never collide with the existing surface. Data layer constraints: Prisma's Rust query engine rejects libsql:// URLs outright, since its SQLite provider only accepts file: URLs. We worked around this by calling @libsql/client directly — the same client the Prisma adapter wraps internally — while keeping the Prisma schema as the source of truth for the data model and DDL generation. Real-time updates in serverless: We use a small socket.io service for near-instant activity events, with a polling fallback if the WebSocket connection does not establish within a few seconds. That keeps the activity feed working even in environments such as Vercel's serverless functions, where a persistent socket service cannot run directly. Accomplishments That We're Proud Of The architectural inversion isn't just a pitch — it's a deployed, working product. The website is the memory, the agent is the consumer, the browser is the trust boundary, the capability token is the credential, and the audit log is the receipt, end to end, in production. We're especially proud that user governance over agent capability actually works: d

title: FigureFoundry
pitch: Publication-ready figures, graphs, and charts in less than a minute. Powered by Webmcp for safe and efficient collaboration with AI-agents.
about_excerpt: Publication-ready figures, graphs, and charts in less than a minute. Powered by Webmcp for safe and efficient collaboration with AI-agents. Like Comment Story Updates Showcase Why FigureFoundry Is a Strong Fit for WebMCP Scientific figure editors are exactly the kind of dense, form-heavy applications where agents currently struggle. Agents are often forced to navigate these interfaces by clicking through an unfamiliar DOM, while researchers spend excessive amounts of time manually performing tasks that an agent could draft in seconds. FigureFoundry addresses this directly. It registers seven document.modelContext tools: inspect_dataset_catalog inspect_dataset_fields inspect_figure_workspace analyze_dataset analyze_group_comparison propose_figure_revision apply_figure_revision This allows an agent to inspect the actual dataset schema and current figure state rather than guessing at the interface structure. The agent can then propose a structured revision that FigureFoundry itself validates. How It Creates a Better User Experience A researcher can request something as simple as: "Compare body mass by species, colored by island." Instead of blindly interacting with the editor, the agent inspects the bound dataset's actual fields, runs a deterministic analysis, and stages a typed Figure Spec diff against the relevant panel. Nothing immediately changes on the canvas. Every proposal is presented as a preview, and applying it requires explicit user confirmation showing both the target panel and the revision being applied. The result is an agent that assists with the tedious work without taking scientific control away from the researcher. What's Newly Possible Previously, turning a request such as "compare these groups" into a correct, publication-ready panel required manual field mapping, chart-type selection, and statistical setup. With WebMCP, the agent can perform the data inspection and analysis steps first. The researcher remains responsible for the scientific judgment: approving, discarding, or editing the proposed revision. Every applied change is also recorded in an append-only provenance ledger, including the revision it was based on. This keeps the figure's history reproducible even when an agent contributes to its construction. How We Implemented It The tools are schema-bound to the active dataset, meaning an agent cannot propose a field that does not actually exist. apply_figure_revision uses optimistic concurrency control through basedOnRevision and rejects proposals that are stale, unapproved, or target an invalid panel. This makes the agent integration operational rather than cosmetic: the model is given structured access to the application's actual state, while the application remains responsible for validation and state changes. Why FigureFoundry There is no doubt that FigureFoundry is a straightforward concept. That is precisely why I chose to build it. Its value is not in being a flashy novelty application. The efficiency implications are the point. Scientific figure editing contains exactly the kind of repetitive, structured interaction where WebMCP can have a meaningful impact: the agent can understand the data and application state, prepare the work, and explain what it intends to change, while the researcher retains control over the final scientific decision. That is where I believe WebMCP has the greatest potential: not replacing the user, but removing the friction between what the user wants to accomplish and the interface they currently have to operate manually.
