 Haven: Devpost Submission Story 

 Copy and paste the markdown below directly into the "Story" section of your Devpost project page. 

 

 💡 Inspiration 

 When it comes to personal finance apps, users face a massive compromise. You either manually enter every transaction by hand, or you hand over your secure banking credentials to a third-party server via aggregators like Plaid. We believe AI can solve this friction, but sending sensitive bank statements to an external AI backend is a massive privacy risk. Most people simply refuse to do it. 

 We built Haven to solve this using a zero-backend architecture powered by the WebMCP protocol. We were inspired by the idea that the frontend browser itself is powerful enough to be the entire application. 

 ⚙️ What it does 

 Haven is a completely client-side, React-based financial dashboard. There is no database. All state is securely persisted right in the browser's local storage. By opening Haven inside a WebMCP-enabled environment (like the ChatGPT desktop app), the frontend instantly registers custom WebMCP tools ( add_transaction , set_net_worth ) directly to window.modelContext . 

 Users simply paste their raw, messy bank statements into the chat. The AI extracts the entities and executes our client-side WebMCP tools, instantly updating the React context state. Transactions appear, monthly spend calculates, and net worth dynamically updates—all without a single byte of financial data ever hitting a backend server. 

 🛠️ How we built it 

 We built Haven using a modern stack focused entirely on the client side: 

 
 Frontend: React (Vite) + TypeScript for type-safe components. 
 Styling: TailwindCSS and Lucide Icons for a senior-grade, premium aesthetic that avoids the generic "AI dashboard" cliches. 
 State Management: React Context API paired with custom useLocalStorage hooks to ensure data persistence across sessions. 
 WebMCP Integration: We built a custom useWebMCP hook that intelligently polls for window.modelContext and registers strict, JSON-schema-typed tools ( add_transaction , set_net_worth ). When the agent triggers these tools, they directly manipulate the React Context state, bypassing the need for any API routes. 
 Deployment: Vercel (configured with vercel.json for SPA routing, ensuring deep links work perfectly inside the ChatGPT in-app browser). 
 

 ⚠️ Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was bridging the gap between an external AI environment and our React application state. 
Initially, we explored building a Chrome Extension to inject the tools, but modern browser security policies (and a desire for a frictionless user experience) pushed us to rely on native WebMCP support. 

 We also had to solve a race condition where the React app would load faster than the host environment could inject window.modelContext . We solved this by writing a resilient polling mechanism that waits for the context to become available before registering the schemas. Lastly, configuring Vercel to correctly route SPA traffic inside the ChatGPT embedded browser required some deep-dive debugging into routing rules. 

 🏆 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 True Zero-Backend Architecture: We proved that you do not need a heavy server-side MCP protocol to build highly ambitious, agent-native applications. 
 Absolute Privacy: We created a powerful AI financial advisor with zero privacy risk. 
 Execution & Polish: We strictly adhered to the hackathon judging criteria, delivering a premium UX that feels like a production-ready product. 
 

 📚 What we learned 

 We learned the immense power of Client-Side MCP . Before this project, we assumed LLM integration required API keys, cloud functions, and backend tool execution. WebMCP flipped our mental model upside down. Learning to trust the client environment and exposing typed JSON schemas directly to the browser DOM opened our eyes to a whole new paradigm of privacy-first AI apps. 

 🚀 What's next for Haven 

 Our next steps are to expand the WebMCP tool registry to include: 

 
 analyze_spending_trends : Allowing the AI to read the local historical data arrays and output insights. 
 CSV Parsing Tools: Enabling the agent to natively ingest full CSV exports from major banks entirely client-side. 
 Cross-Device Sync: Exploring encrypted peer-to-peer sync (like WebRTC) so users can share their local dashboard across devices without a central database.

The page can expose real design actions — add a shape, set a fill, align a selection, export — as tools on the live canvas you’re already looking at. title: ShieldOn
pitch: WebMCP gives AI agents access to investigate evidence, while ShieldOn keeps the final decision under human control.
about_excerpt:
WebMCP gives AI agents access to investigate evidence, while ShieldOn keeps the final decision under human control.

 Inspiration 

 I learned that AI agents are getting really good at reading information, connecting evidence and proposing conclusions. There's one question that pushed me to build shieldOn WebMCP prototype: "Should it also have the authority to make the final decision because it can access the evidence?"
ShieldOn is a revenue engineering system built around evidence, verification, contradictions, missing information and governed findings. For this challenge, I wanted to test one simple principle:
"WebMCP can give an AI agent access to investigate, without giving it authority to govern the conclusion." 

 What it does 

 The demo uses a synthetic revenue investigation for a dental business. Through WebMCP, the agent gets six read-only ShieldOn tools. It can inspect the investigation, evidence, missing evidence, contradictions, candidate findings and governed findings. The agent can analyze the case and explain what may be going wrong. But it cannot approve or reject the finding. There are 6 read-only tools, 0 approval tools and 1 protected human decision. 

 The workflow is: 

 AI investigates → human reviews → human decides → AI rereads the governed result 

 Before human review, the finding remains a candidate. If the agent is directly asked to approve it, it cannot. No approval tool is exposed through WebMCP. The human reviewer must make that decision inside ShieldOn. Once approved, the finding becomes governed, the human reviewer is recorded and the agent can then reread the result. Importantly, unresolved evidence gaps and contradictions remain visible. 

 How we built it 

 I made a conscious decision not to build too much for this challenge. Rather than trying to build the entire ShieldOn product, I built one complete human-governance loop. The investigation contains directly verified evidence, operator-confirmed information, unverified claims, missing evidence, contradictions and a candidate finding. One part of the case shows qualified leads increasing while consultation conversion declines. The evidence also shows slower response times, incomplete follow-up and CRM records that don't always match the communication history. This gives the agent something meaningful to investigate rather than a perfectly clean dataset. The most important design decision was separating analysis authority from decision authority. Approval and rejection exist only inside the human review interface. They aren't exposed as WebMCP tools. The agent can read the governed result afterward and it can't create that governed state itself. 

 ShieldOn existed before this challenge as a governed revenue investigation system. What I built during the WebMCP Challenge is the agent-facing WebMCP layer: six read-only browser tools, the synthetic investigation demo, the protected human-review loop, and the ability for the agent to reread a governed finding after human approval. The underlying ShieldOn product predates the challenge. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One thing I had to keep reminding myself was not to make the agent autonomous just because technically I could. It would have been easy to expose an approval tool and let the agent complete the entire workflow. For me, that would have missed the whole point of what I wanted to prove. So I tested the opposite. I intentionally asked the agent to approve the candidate and mark it as ShieldOn's official conclusion. And it couldn't. That became one of the strongest parts of the demo because the governance boundary is demonstrated. Another challenge was keeping uncertainty after approval. A human decision shouldn't magically erase missing evidence or contradictions, so those stay visible even after the finding becomes governed. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I am proud that the demo proves a complete collaboration loop rather than only showing an AI calling tools. The agent can investigate real structured evidence, identify missing information and contradictions and prepare a candidate conclusion. A human then makes the protected decision. After that decision, the agent can see and understand the newly governed result without gaining the authority to create it. The negative test is especially important to me: 

 
 the system successfully demonstrates what the AI can't do. 
 that boundary is a core part of the product and not a limitation. 
 

 What we learned 

 What became very clear to me while building this is that giving an AI more capability shouldn't by default mean giving it more authority. WebMCP can give an AI agent powerful access to application context while the application still decides which actions remain protected. I also learned that good human-agent systems shouldn't only expose useful capabilities. They should make boundaries explicit. In this case, one of the most important decisions was actually the tool I chose not to expose. 

 What's next for ShieldOn 

 This challenge prototype focuses on one narrow governance loop. The larger ShieldOn direction is to apply the same model to deeper revenue investigations with more evidence sources, more complex contradictions, stronger traceability and eventually governed interventions. As ShieldOn grows, I want the agent to be able to investigate much more of the business but without silently gaining authority it was never supposed to have. 

 The principle will remain the same:
AI investigates. Humans govern the conclusion. WebMCP gives the agent access. ShieldOn keeps the decision governed.

title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about. pitch: AI-powered business data agent using WebMCP to inspect datasets, find issues, compare records, detect anomalies, create action plans, and safely export cleaned data with human approval.
about_excerpt:
AI-powered business data agent using WebMCP to inspect datasets, find issues, compare records, detect anomalies, create action plans, and safely export cleaned data with human approval.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story

 Inspiration i built data bridge from watching bloomberg tv on a segment where they spoke about fragmented data being held in all these companies. That was my inspiration for this project 

 Businesses often rely on data spread across CSV files, supplier records, inventory systems, purchase histories, and other disconnected sources. The idea behind DataBridge Agent was to create a practical AI workflow that can inspect that fragmented data, identify problems, and turn the findings into clear business actions without allowing the agent to make consequential changes without human approval. 

 What it does 

 DataBridge Agent is a WebMCP-enabled business data assistant. 

 It exposes eight structured tools: 

 
 inspect_dataset 
 find_duplicates 
 detect_missing_fields 
 compare_datasets 
 detect_anomalies 
 analyze_price_changes 
 create_action_plan 
 export_clean_data 
 

 The agent can inspect loaded business data, detect duplicate records and missing fields, compare related datasets, identify unusual numeric values, analyze price movements, and generate a prioritized action plan. 

 Export is intentionally protected by a human-approval gate. The source data remains unchanged, and a cleaned copy is only created after explicit approval. 

 How I built it 

 I built DataBridge Agent as a React and TypeScript application hosted on Replit. 

 The WebMCP tool layer is registered through the browser model context so compatible agents can discover and call structured tools instead of relying on page scraping or fragile UI automation. 

 The application also includes an embedded AI Agent Demo that runs the same DataBridge business logic locally when native WebMCP is unavailable. The interface clearly distinguishes native WebMCP activity from local demo-agent activity. 

 The core data-analysis functions are shared between the WebMCP tool wrappers and the embedded demo workflow so the results come from the loaded data rather than hardcoded demo values. 

 Challenges I faced 

 One major challenge was testing an experimental browser capability across different environments. In a normal browser, the WebMCP API was not exposed, so I added clear capability detection rather than falsely presenting local execution as native WebMCP. 

 After enabling WebMCP testing in a compatible Chrome environment, the live application successfully detected native WebMCP support. 

 Another challenge was designing safe agent behavior. Data analysis can run automatically, but export is treated as a consequential action and requires explicit human approval. 

 I also focused on making the execution transparent by showing the tool sequence, results, data source, and approval status directly in the interface. 

 What I learned 

 This project showed me how WebMCP can make web applications much more useful to AI agents by exposing structured capabilities instead of forcing agents to interpret interfaces visually. 

 I also learned that agent capability should be paired with transparency and human control. A useful business agent should not only produce an answer; it should make its actions auditable and clearly separate analysis from actions that can affect data. 

 What's next 

 The next step is to expand DataBridge Agent beyond CSV-based workflows into more live business systems, including databases, procurement platforms, inventory systems, and other operational data sources. 

 I would also like to add more configurable tool schemas, stronger cross-dataset matching, and reusable approval policies for different business actions.

about_excerpt: 333k+ SVG icons available to create a logo for your project. Best when you are converting any PNG logo to SVG logo. Logo quality highly dependent on instructions. Like 1 Comment Story Updates state with final logo created, from png to svg default starting point Inspiration Every "make me a logo" tool on the web makes the same bet: a human sits at a canvas, drags shapes, and tweaks colors by eye. That bet breaks the moment an agent is the one trying to help. ChatGPT can describe a great logo in a sentence, but it had no way to actually place it, resize it, or apply a brand's real colors on a live canvas. WebMCP closes that gap: it lets an agent drive the same tool a person uses, through the same page, with no separate API to build or maintain. What it does Logo Maker ( https://logo.allsvgicons.com/ ) is a free, no-signup SVG logo editor. Six WebMCP tools are registered on the page via document.modelContext.registerTool : get_logo_maker_state : reads canvas size, background, every layer (with IDs and index), the current selection, safe-zone settings, and a shareable code/URL, optionally with the rendered SVG. update_logo_maker_state : partial, smart edits: apply an authentic brand preset (Instagram, Spotify, Stripe, Linear, Supabase, and more), toggle the safe-zone keyline, add/update/remove/clear layers by ID or index, or change selection, all without resending the full state. set_logo_maker_state : full-state replacement for bulk rebuilds. search_logo_icons : finds icons from the site's SVG library to drop onto the canvas. load_logo_maker_share : restores a saved design from its share code. get_brand_presets : lists the brand color/style presets an agent can apply by name. A person can open the same editor, drag layers, and see exactly what the agent changed, live, on the same canvas. What agents and people can now do together Ask ChatGPT (or any WebMCP-aware agent) for "an Instagram-style logo with a mountain icon, rotated 15 degrees" and it composes the layers itself, then hands back a working canvas a human can immediately refine by hand: nudge a layer, swap a color, export. Neither side has to fully finish the job alone; the agent handles the tedious part (search, place, apply preset, iterate on args) and the person keeps final visual judgment. How we built it Built with React inside an Astro site (allsvgicons.com), using document.modelContext.registerTool for each tool with Zod-derived JSON schemas for inputs. Layer state lives in a single React ref so both the UI and the WebMCP tool handlers read/write the same source of truth, no separate agent-facing state to keep in sync. Designs are shareable via a compact encoded string decoded by load_logo_maker_share , so an agent's output is a URL a person can open directly. Challenges we ran into Getting execute_tool semantics right from the agent side: getTools() returns a Promise and hands back tool handles, not names, so calling a tool means holding the handle rather than looking it up by string each time; args also need to go over as JSON-stringified payloads. On our end, the trickiest part was making update_logo_maker_state genuinely incremental (index-or-ID addressing into an array of layers) without forcing every agent call to resend a full canvas state. title: VibeStudio
pitch: A shared creative workspace where creators and Codex turn inspiration and editable memory into consistent content through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A shared creative workspace where creators and Codex turn inspiration and editable memory into consistent content through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Problem General-purpose AI can generate copy and images, but creators repeatedly have to explain who they are, what their brand sounds like, what they like, and how each format should be produced. The context becomes scattered across chats, the agent cannot reliably act inside the creative workspace, and creators lose control over what the system remembers. Solution VibeStudio gives the creator and Codex one visible, shared workspace. The creator curates multimodal inspiration, records explicit taste signals, edits a persistent Template of brand and production rules, and works in Sessions that retain their source, context receipt, version history, and status. Through page-contextual WebMCP tools, Codex can read only the context needed for the current task, create or revise a carousel inside the workspace, and leave every material change visible and reversible. The challenge proof is one complete path: select an inspiration, state what is worth borrowing, retrieve a bounded creator context receipt, create an original seven-slide carousel, revise one slide, undo it, mark the piece Ready, and inspect the traceable learning that can shape the next piece. Why This Matters Content creation is not a single generation step. It is an ongoing collaboration among taste, brand memory, source material, format rules, iteration, and publishing state. VibeStudio makes that system durable and inspectable while letting creators keep the conversational agent they already trust. WebMCP is central to this experience because the agent and human work on the same live artifact. The agent does not have to infer the whole interface from pixels or receive an unrestricted export of the creator's memory. The page exposes a small typed tool set for the current view, while the creator sees the resulting session, version, status, and undo trail immediately. How We Used AI Codex transforms selected inspiration and a bounded creator-context receipt into an original seven-slide story. OpenAI image generation creates up to three text-free visual layers; VibeStudio's deterministic renderer owns typography, layout, and the final 1080 x 1350 slides. AI can propose focused revisions to a selected slide or Template slot without replacing the whole artifact. Accepted creator feedback can become source-linked learning, but one-off instructions do not silently become permanent rules. Existing optional Claude-backed routes remain in the broader local Studio, but the challenge's WebMCP collaboration path was tested with Codex. How We Used Codex Codex Desktop was the primary design, implementation, debugging, and testing partner. It helped research current WebMCP interaction patterns, turn the product thesis into a scoped PRD and technical specification, implement typed contextual tools, iterate on the UI with the creator, and run the end-to-end acceptance journey. For the product demo, Codex is also the user's agent. In ChatGPT's in-app browser it discovers VibeStudio's current page tools, reads the selected inspiration and bounded Template context, connects to the current Session, and creates or revises the artifact. This is not a simulated chat panel inside VibeStudio; it is the creator's existing agent operating the real workspace through WebMCP. Key Features Multimodal Inspire feed organized by YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, Facebook, news, and websites. One-field source intake that accepts a link, free text, or both. Explicit likes, dislikes, notes, saves, and source following that curate the creator's taste. Editable Template containing identity, audience, voice, visual taste, goals, examples, and production rules. Session-based work with Draft, Ready, Scheduled, and Live states. Page-contextual WebMCP tools rather than one large global tool catalog. Shared Attention: the creator can point, draw, and place multiple UI targets in a visible Talking about tray for the agent. Versioned agent changes, attribution, review state, and undo. Reusable carousel skill with exactly seven validated slides and deterministic final rendering. Bounded context receipts that show which creator memories and rules shaped an artifact. Safety boundary: no publishing, scheduling, permanent deletion, arbitrary URL fetch, filesystem path, shell, or unrestricted creator-memory tool is exposed through WebMCP. Architecture VibeStudio is a Next.js 16, React 18, and TypeScript application. Its WebMCP adapter detects document.modelContext , registers typed tools for the current page, and unregisters stale tools when the view changes. The current challenge tool surface includes Session, Inspire, Template-context, carousel, status, review, and undo operations. Local records use append-friendly JSONL files for creators, inspiration, Template memory, context receipts, Sessions, and activity. Mutations use version checks and idempotency keys. External inspiration is marked as untrusted content, reads are annotated as read-only, responses are bounded, and the final carousel renderer deterministically composes text and generated image layers. The public judge build runs in a sanitized demo mode with generic seed data and an isolated writable root. It does not read the creator's adjacent private project data, reports local integrations as disconnected, and blocks server-side fetch, scraping, upload, publishing, metrics-sync, and embedded-assistant routes. title: Blink Borrow
pitch: Let AI borrow a capability. Take it back when you're done.
about_excerpt: Let AI borrow a capability. Take it back when you're done. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI integrations are based on persistent access: connect an account, grant permissions, and leave those permissions available until somebody revokes them. I wanted to explore a different model: What if an AI could borrow a capability instead of permanently owning it? Blink Borrow treats access as temporary authority. A person makes a capability available only when they choose. The AI can discover that the capability exists, but it cannot see the private payload. When the AI requests it, the capability holder sees what is being requested and why, then chooses whether to Approve once or Deny. The core lifecycle is: Discover → Request → Approve → Borrow → Revoke What it does Blink Borrow connects two browsers: an Agent browser exposing tools through WebMCP a Capability Holder browser containing temporary capabilities and the human approval gate The current build demonstrates: Private Note — one-time private text Text / JSON — structured or larger text payloads Small Text File — TXT, JSON, CSV or Markdown, with metadata inspection separated from content access Page Context — sanitized title, URL and visible page text The AI first sees only a manifest describing what capabilities are available. It does not receive the private payload during discovery. When the AI requests a capability, the remote holder receives a live permission request showing the capability and the AI's stated reason. The holder then chooses: Deny — nothing is released. Approve once — the payload crosses the direct browser-to-browser connection and the one-time capability is immediately consumed. Blink Borrow also includes END & FORGET, which closes the temporary session and removes access to the borrowed capabilities. How we built it Blink Borrow uses: WebMCP / document.modelContext.registerTool() for the AI-facing tool interface WebRTC DataChannel for direct browser-to-browser capability transfer Netlify Functions and Netlify Blobs for temporary connection rendezvous/signaling JavaScript, HTML and CSS Browser memory for armed capability payloads until approval Netlify helps the two browsers establish the connection, but the private capability payload is designed to travel over the direct peer-to-peer WebRTC DataChannel. The Agent side registers six WebMCP tools for capability discovery, requests, private notes, file metadata, file contents and session status. For Small Text Files, metadata inspection is deliberately separated from actual content access. The AI can inspect what has been offered without automatically receiving the contents. Privacy and human control Blink Borrow is designed around temporary authority: private payloads remain local until approval discovery exposes metadata instead of private contents the AI can provide a reason for each request the human can deny any request one-time capabilities are consumed immediately after successful delivery refreshing the holder destroys armed in-memory capabilities END & FORGET terminates the temporary session Page Context adds another privacy layer. Before it can be shared, Blink Borrow sanitizes the context locally by removing control-plane UI, stripping URL query strings and fragments, and redacting the active session code. Challenges we ran into One major challenge involved file access. A generic file capability approach was blocked by the browser security layer before the request reached the human approval stage. Instead of attempting to bypass that protection, I redesigned the capability flow: expose a dedicated metadata-only inspection tool use a separate explicit tool for requesting file contents limit access to the file already selected by the holder require human approval before the contents cross the P2P connection Another challenge involved Page Context privacy. An early version could include visible session information, so I added local sanitization before the capability is armed. Accomplishments that we're proud of The working build demonstrates the complete WebMCP capability lifecycle with a real agent environment: ChatGPT discovers remote capabilities through WebMCP private payloads stay hidden during discovery the AI requests a capability with a stated reason another browser receives the live approval request the human can approve once or deny approved data crosses the direct P2P connection one-time capabilities disappear after use file metadata can be inspected without reading file contents file contents require a separate explicit request Page Context is sanitized before sharing the session can be terminated with END & FORGET The most important part is that the human approval screen is not decorative. It is genuinely in the data path. What we learned WebMCP gives websites a powerful way to expose structured tools to AI agents, but tool access also needs a permission model that humans can easily understand. Blink Borrow showed me that agent access does not always have to mean permanent authorization. Temporary capability leases can make the request, reason, scope, approval and revocation visible to the person who controls the data. What's next for Blink Borrow Blink Borrow could evolve into a reusable temporary capability layer for AI agents. Future directions include: capability receipts without logging private payloads explicit expiration timers richer capability manifests optional TURN support additional browser and device capabilities standardized temporary-capability semantics across different agents and applications The larger idea is simple: Let AI borrow narrowly scoped powers when needed, instead of giving it broad permanent access. title: Entorno Camaleón
pitch: Camaleón is a WebMCP-powered neuroinclusive learning experience that adapts educational interfaces to the way each student learns. The learning goal stays the same, the experience finally adapts.
about_excerpt: Camaleón is a WebMCP-powered neuroinclusive learning experience that adapts educational interfaces to the way each student learns. The learning goal stays the same, the experience finally adapts. Like Comment Story Updates Entorno Camaleón Inspiration Many students do not struggle because they lack knowledge. They struggle because educational platforms require them to navigate visual overload, dense instructions, time pressure, unexpected motion, and a single way to respond. For neurodivergent children, these interface demands can become an additional test that has nothing to do with the actual learning objective. We created Entorno Camaleón around a simple principle: the learning goal should remain the same, but the path should adapt. Our prototype follows Leo, a nine-year-old student who understands science but feels overwhelmed by a traditional learning management system. Entorno Camaleón transforms his water-cycle lesson into a calmer, character-led experience featuring Luma, his companion, and Ayu, the mythical Guardian of the Cycle. What it does Entorno Camaleón is a WebMCP-powered neuroinclusive learning experience that allows a browser agent to adapt an educational interface in real time. The experience can adjust information density, text size, color environment, motion, animation, audio guidance, and the available response channels. Students can participate through voice, text, or visual interaction. The agent handles interface complexity so the student can focus on the academic objective. WebMCP also provides an important safety boundary. The agent can prepare Leo’s answer and open the review screen, but it cannot submit academic work automatically. Leo or an authorized adult must explicitly confirm the final action. How we built it We built the proof of concept as a client-side HTML, CSS, and JavaScript experience and deployed it on Vercel. The application registers five imperative WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(): get_lesson_context start_accessible_audio_guide adapt_learning_experience start_water_cycle_mission prepare_science_answer Each tool uses a constrained JSON Schema and connects directly to the same state used by the visible interface. These tools allow an agent to understand the current lesson without scraping the page, start an accessible Spanish audio guide, apply reversible interface adaptations, open the correct learning activity, and prepare a spoken or typed answer for human review. The prototype also uses the browser’s Speech Recognition API for real microphone input and the Speech Synthesis API for audio guidance. A typed response remains available whenever voice recognition is unsupported or microphone permission is denied. The visual system combines Atkinson Hyperlegible for reading with Geist for interface hierarchy. The experience includes responsive layouts, keyboard navigation, reduced-motion support, high-contrast focus indicators, accessible dialogs, and multiple ways to complete every important interaction. Challenges we faced One of our biggest challenges was determining the correct boundary between agent assistance and student agency. An agent should be able to remove interface friction, but it should not make academic decisions or submit work without meaningful consent. We therefore separated answer preparation from final submission. The WebMCP tool reports submitted: false and opens a visible confirmation dialog. Another challenge was balancing sensory calm with engagement. We wanted to avoid overstimulation without producing a cold or purely functional interface. The narrative involving Leo, Luma, and Ayu gives the lesson continuity, emotional context, and a clear sense of progress. Voice interaction also required careful attention. We designed microphone controls for press-and-hold interaction, keyboard activation, permission errors, and typed fallback. Audio guidance and microphone recording are mutually exclusive so the guide cannot accidentally be transcribed as Leo’s answer. What we learned We learned that WebMCP is more powerful when it represents meaningful product capabilities instead of reproducing individual button clicks. Rather than giving the agent unrestricted control over the page, Entorno Camaleón exposes a small set of understandable and governed actions. This makes agent behavior more reliable, visible, and safer for students. We also learned that accessibility should not be treated as a final compliance step. In this project, accessibility became part of the product concept itself. Multiple response channels, adjustable presentation, predictable navigation, audio guidance, and explicit confirmation improve the experience for a much broader group of learners. What we are proud of We are proud that Entorno Camaleón is both a functional WebMCP demonstration and a complete product story. The deployed prototype includes five working WebMCP tools, real voice input with a typed fallback, accessible audio guidance, a responsive five-chapter learning journey, student-controlled presentation preferences, keyboard and reduced-motion support, an explicit human-confirmation boundary, and a complete manual fallback when WebMCP is unavailable. What is next The next step is to replace the simulated school receipt with an authenticated LMS sandbox and add durable consent and audit records. We would also co-design future versions with neurodivergent students, families, teachers, accessibility specialists, and school administrators. Entorno Camaleón is currently a proof of concept, not a clinical intervention or production LMS integration. Its purpose is to demonstrate how agentic technology can make educational interfaces more flexible without taking control away from the learner. Entorno Camaleón: The learning goal stays the same. The experience finally adapts. title: Verdiqt
pitch: Verdiqt is an agent-native web app that runs a SaaS idea through a real evidence trial: it gathers live signals, scores the idea across six judges, and returns a Build, Pivot, or Kill verdict.
about_excerpt: Verdiqt is an agent-native web app that runs a SaaS idea through a real evidence trial: it gathers live signals, scores the idea across six judges, and returns a Build, Pivot, or Kill verdict. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI made building software cheap. It did not make building the right software cheap. People now ship a SaaS product in a weekend, and find out at launch that nobody wanted it. Verdiqt moves that painful discovery to before you write the first line of code. You put your idea on trial, and a court decides whether it deserves to live. What it does You file a case: your SaaS idea in a sentence, or a link to a public GitHub repo you already built. Then the courtroom goes to work, and you watch every step happen live: The case file. The court reads your idea and writes it up: who it's for, what problem it solves, what to search for. The investigation. Real research across five real communities : Hacker News, Reddit, GitHub, Stack Overflow, and Product Hunt. Every finding appears on screen with a link to its source, and every source reports honestly: gathered, failed, or empty. If the first search comes back thin, the court automatically widens its search. The deliberation. Six AI judges each take one question: "Is the pain real? Is anyone actively looking for this? Who already exists? Who would pay? Can you reach these people? Can you build it fast enough?" Each judge delivers their score the moment they finish, you literally watch the bench board fill in, one verdict at a time. The ruling. A presiding judge reads the entire case file and rules: BUILD, PIVOT, or KILL —> with a score out of 100, the reasoning behind every number, and exactly one recommended next step (a real, cheap test you can run this week). A full trial takes about a minute. And if you refine your idea and try again, the court remembers: the evidence you marked as important and the previous ruling follow your case, so every iteration builds on the last. How we built it Zero cash out of pocket. The whole product runs on free tiers and hackathon credits: one small server runs the website and the research pipeline, the AI judges run on free model APIs, and when one provider's daily quota runs dry, the court automatically switches to a backup provider mid-trial and keeps ruling. Constraints became design: the court paces itself under rate limits, shows its deliberation while it works, and never wastes a token. The model argues; the code rules. Anti-hallucination isn't a prompt, it's enforced in code. Judges may only cite evidence the court actually gathered: invented citations are stripped automatically, and a high score that loses its citations gets capped. When public evidence is thin, the judge is allowed to use domain judgment but the ruling must say so, out loud, in the rationale. Uncertainty is never dressed up as certainty. Privacy without accounts. No sign-up. Your browser gets an unguessable key; only its fingerprint is stored. Your cases are yours, anyone else asking for them gets an identical "not found.", don't worry. Challenges we ran into Running a multi-stage AI pipeline on free tiers meant treating every token and every request as scarce... the wait-and-retry pacing, the provider failover, and the one-at-a-time trial queue all exist because of it. And WebMCP is new enough that the tool contract itself was a design problem: we learned that the workflow belongs inside the tool descriptions, so agents teach themselves the journey. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete, evidence-cited validation trial in about a minute. A deliberation you can actually watch. A surface that serves two audiences at once... humans get a courtroom, agents get a toolbox, and each can see the other working. What we learned Never think you have enough time to build something. What's next for Verdiqt GitHub sign-in to put your whole repo graveyard on trial at once, re-trials over time to watch a verdict change as markets move, and Reddit's expanded API access for even deeper community evidence. title: BusTravelAssistant
pitch: Reimagining bus travel for the agentic web. BusTravelAssistant uses WebMCP to let AI discover, compare, select, and book buses through the web—not just navigate it.
about_excerpt:
Reimagining bus travel for the agentic web. BusTravelAssistant uses WebMCP to let AI discover, compare, select, and book buses through the web—not just navigate it.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Project homepage 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Project homepage 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Project homepage 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 The web has traditionally been built for humans: users navigate pages, understand UI elements, apply filters, select options, and complete forms. With the rise of AI agents, we believe the web needs to become equally usable by agents. 

 Bus booking is a great example of this problem. A user may simply say, "Find me the best bus from Bangalore to Chennai tomorrow evening with good reviews and a window seat." Today, an AI assistant can help explain options, but the actual interaction still requires navigating the booking website. 

 We wanted to explore what happens when the website itself becomes agent-ready. 

 With WebMCP, we can expose meaningful capabilities of the bus booking experience as tools that an AI agent can understand and invoke directly. This led us to build BusTravelAssistant — an experiment in making a real-world travel booking journey native to the agentic web. 

 What it does 

 BusTravelAssistant enables an AI agent such as ChatGPT to interact with the bus booking experience through WebMCP. 

 Instead of asking an agent to simply navigate and click through a website, the website exposes high-level capabilities such as: 

 
 Searching for buses between two locations 
 Exploring available travel options 
 Applying relevant filters 
 Comparing available buses 
 Selecting a bus and travel option 
 Viewing and selecting available seats 
 Progressing through the booking journey 
 

 The key idea is that the website provides the capabilities and context , while the AI agent determines how those capabilities should be used to accomplish the user's goal. 

 This creates a much more natural interaction model: 

 
 User → AI Agent → WebMCP Tools → Website → Booking Journey 
 

 The user can express an intent in natural language, while the agent can use the website's structured capabilities to execute that intent. 

 How we built it 

 We built BusTravelAssistant by exposing key capabilities of the bus booking funnel as WebMCP tools. 

 The tools are designed around meaningful user actions rather than low-level UI interactions. For example, instead of asking an agent to identify a button and click it, we expose capabilities such as searching for buses, applying filters, and selecting seats. 

 The architecture broadly consists of: 

 
 Web application — the existing bus booking experience. 
 WebMCP tool layer — exposes booking capabilities to compatible AI agents. 
 AI agent — understands the user's intent and decides which tools to invoke. 
 Booking funnel — executes the requested actions and maintains the user's journey. 
 

 A key design principle was to keep the tools task-oriented and composable . The agent should not need to understand the internal implementation of the website. It should only need to understand what each capability does, what inputs it accepts, and what information it returns. 

 This allows the same web experience to serve both human users and AI agents. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the biggest challenges was deciding the right abstraction level for WebMCP tools. 

 If tools are too granular, the agent has to orchestrate dozens of low-level actions. If they are too broad, the tools become difficult to compose and less reusable. 

 We therefore focused on exposing capabilities that map closely to real user intent while still giving the agent enough flexibility to make decisions. 

 Another challenge was maintaining the state of a multi-step booking journey. Searching for a bus, applying filters, selecting a specific service, and choosing a seat are all connected actions. The tools need to work together while preserving the context of the user's journey. 

 We also had to think carefully about validation and safety. An AI agent should be able to explore and narrow down options autonomously, while actions that have real-world consequences should remain appropriately controlled. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are particularly proud of demonstrating that a complex, multi-step travel workflow can be exposed to an AI agent through WebMCP without turning the website into a collection of UI automation scripts. 

 The project demonstrates a different mental model for building websites: 

 Don't just build pages for agents to navigate. Build capabilities for agents to use. 

 We also built the tools around an actual booking funnel rather than a simplified demo, which helped us understand the practical challenges of making a production-scale web experience agent-ready. 

 Most importantly, BusTravelAssistant gave us an opportunity to explore what an agent-native version of a real-world web application could look like. 

 What we learned 

 The biggest learning was that WebMCP changes how we think about the boundary between an AI agent and a website. 

 Traditional browser automation makes the agent responsible for understanding the UI. WebMCP allows the website to communicate its capabilities explicitly. 

 This creates a much cleaner separation: 

 
 The website owns the capabilities and business context. 
 The agent owns reasoning and orchestration. 
 The user owns the intent and final decisions. 
 

 We also learned that designing good tools is as important as exposing tools. Tool names, descriptions, inputs, outputs, validation, and state management all significantly influence how effectively an agent can use a web application. 

 What's next for BusTravelAssistant 

 We see this project as the beginning of an agent-native travel experience rather than simply a WebMCP integration. 

 The next step is to expand the capabilities exposed through WebMCP across the complete travel lifecycle — from discovery and booking to managing trips and finding relevant services around a journey. 

 We also want to explore richer agent interactions where the user can express a high-level goal and the agent can intelligently combine multiple web capabilities to accomplish it. 

 Ultimately, our vision is simple: 

 The future web should not only be human-readable. It should be agent-readable, agent-understandable, and agent-actionable — while keeping humans in control. 

 BusTravelAssistant is our experiment toward that future.

 Inspiration 

 Cerveza Tools started several years ago as a small open-source project: a collection of React components and TypeScript functions for common homebrewing calculations. Over time, it became one of those side projects that mostly sat untouched. 

 While exploring ideas for the WebMCP Challenge, I realized it was a good project to bring back to life. The calculators already represented useful, deterministic domain capabilities that could be exposed to agents without asking a language model to perform the calculations itself. 

 That idea became Cerveza Tools Lab. 

 What it does 

 Cerveza Tools Lab is a shared brewing workspace where a brewer and an AI agent can work on the same batch. 

 Through WebMCP, the agent can read the current brew, use tools for hydrometer correction, alcohol, dilution, IBU and carbonation, and update the brew when requested. Changes made manually in the UI are also immediately available to the agent. 

 For example, if the measured gravity is higher than the target, the agent can read the values directly from the brew, calculate the required dilution and, after user approval, apply the adjustment. 

 How I built it 

 Cerveza Tools is my existing React and TypeScript library. During the challenge, I added optional WebMCP bindings to expose its calculation functions as agent-accessible tools. 

 Cerveza Tools Lab is the new application built for the challenge. It adds shared Current Brew state and contextual WebMCP tools, allowing the UI and the agent to work with the same data and underlying brewing logic. 

 Challenges and learnings 

 The main challenge was deciding where agent capabilities should live and keeping human and agent state synchronized. 

 Separating deterministic calculations from application context resulted in a simple architecture: Cerveza Tools knows how to calculate, while the Lab knows what the user is currently brewing. 

 My primary takeaway was that WebMCP becomes particularly beneficial when an application reveals both its existing functionalities and its current context. Instead of merely adding a chatbot on top, it facilitates the seamless collaboration between humans and agents within the same application.

title: BranchLine
pitch: BRANCHLINE lets humans and browser agents share the same live supply-chain reality—fork recovery futures, simulate their consequences, and commit only the plan a human explicitly approves.
about_excerpt: BRANCHLINE lets humans and browser agents share the same live supply-chain reality—fork recovery futures, simulate their consequences, and commit only the plan a human explicitly approves. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Supply-chain disruptions are rarely isolated events. A supplier outage can cascade through component availability, transport lanes, factory capacity, production schedules, customer commitments, revenue, and cost. Operations teams often have to reconstruct this chain manually across ERP systems, spreadsheets, supplier messages, logistics tools, and planning software before they can even decide what to do. At the same time, browser agents are becoming capable of operating websites, but most applications still expose their operational meaning only through buttons, forms, and DOM elements. We built BRANCHLINE around a different idea: What if a human and a browser agent could operate inside the same live operational reality? BRANCHLINE — Fork reality. Simulate the consequences. Commit the future. It is an agent-native operational recovery control plane where humans steer intent, agents traverse consequences, and both operate on one shared supply-chain digital twin. What it does BRANCHLINE models a synthetic commercial EV supply chain for Asterion Mobility , including suppliers, components, factories, transport lanes, inventory, products, customers, and 24 customer orders. The featured scenario begins with a healthy network. A human triggers a 12-day production outage at the battery supplier NoriCell . Instead of simply displaying an alert, BRANCHLINE calculates and visualizes the complete causal cascade: supplier → component availability → factories → products → customer orders → exposed revenue The browser agent can then use semantic WebMCP tools to: inspect the operational state; trace downstream consequences; inspect suppliers, factories, products, customers, and orders; find compatible substitute suppliers; create multiple recovery branches; simulate each future across a 30-day horizon; compare service, cost, risk, emissions, and delays; explain tradeoffs using causal evidence; stage a recovery plan for human approval; apply only an explicitly approved plan; verify the committed result; restore the previous operational checkpoint. The central experience is Branchspace . Instead of presenting three AI recommendations as ordinary cards, BRANCHLINE renders different recovery strategies as parallel futures emerging from the same present. For example: Service First prioritizes customer service and on-time revenue. Cost Guard prioritizes lower incremental cost. Balanced Recovery trades off service, cost, resilience, and logistics. Resilience reduces supplier concentration and future single points of failure. The simulation is deterministic and calculated from the underlying supply, compatibility, capacity, logistics, inventory, and customer-order data. How we built it BRANCHLINE is a static TypeScript web application built around one architectural principle: Human UI ─┐ ├─ shared command bus → domain engine → one live state WebMCP ───┘ The visual interface and WebMCP tools do not maintain separate copies of reality. Every meaningful operation passes through the same domain engine and shared state. The application includes: a deterministic synthetic supply-chain digital twin; causal impact tracing; a bounded recovery-planning engine; a day-by-day simulation from T+0 through T+30; supplier and product compatibility enforcement; inventory and factory-capacity constraints; customer-tier and human-authored priority constraints; transactional execution; verification; checkpoints and exact rollback; an append-only causal audit trail. The WebMCP integration uses the native imperative API directly with: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) BRANCHLINE exposes 14 semantic tools: get_ops_snapshot inspect_entity trace_impact list_constraints find_substitutes read_external_alerts create_branch simulate_branch compare_branches explain_tradeoff stage_plan apply_plan verify_plan rollback_plan The capability surface is dynamic. For example, apply_plan is not registered at all while a recovery plan is waiting for human approval. When the human approves the exact staged plan in the BRANCHLINE interface, apply_plan becomes available to the browser agent. If the operational context changes, the approval becomes stale and the capability is revoked again. Challenges we ran into Keeping the human and agent in one reality The most important technical challenge was preventing the application from becoming a dashboard with a separate agent workflow. Human interactions and WebMCP calls therefore use the same command bus and domain functions. If a human changes something visually, the next agent call immediately encounters the changed state. Making stale reasoning visible and enforceable A recovery simulation can become invalid the moment a constraint changes. BRANCHLINE maintains separate stateVersion and contextVersion values. Every simulation records the context on which it was produced. When the human changes operational intent: the context version increments; existing simulations become visibly stale; staged plans are invalidated; previous approval is revoked; execution capabilities disappear; the agent must re-simulate. Human authority over consequential actions We deliberately did not create an approve_plan WebMCP tool. Approval must happen in the visual interface. Only after that approval does the consequential apply_plan capability become registered. Modeling real compatibility constraints Substitution cannot simply mean choosing the cheapest available supplier. For example, Voltra V-2170 battery cells are incompatible with ORION-X. That restriction is enforced inside the domain engine and simulation rather than merely displayed as UI text. Building meaningful simulation rather than prewritten outcomes Recovery metrics are derived from the underlying operational state. The planner evaluates supplier allocation, logistics, inventory movement, production scheduling, compatible substitutions, and eligible order delays before choosing a deterministic result for each strategy. Accomplishments that we're proud of The interaction we are most proud of involves order_1082 for Apex Health Logistics . Before human intervention, an otherwise attractive recovery future can delay this order. The human opens the order directly in the visual application and presses: Protect this order A gold human-intent pin appears on the order and propagates upstream through its dependencies. That single human action: changes the shared operational context; invalidates every simulation based on the previous reality; removes stale execution capabilities; becomes immediately visible to the browser agent. The agent then re-simulates the recovery using the new constraint. Scarce compatible supply is reallocated to protect Apex Health, while a lower-priority order takes the delay instead. This is not a hardcoded visual effect. It emerges from the planner and shared constraints. In our verified featured recovery, BRANCHLINE produces approximately: $26.56M revenue protected 93.4% of exposed revenue recovered $258,849 incremental cost 23 of 24 orders on time 1 lower-priority delayed order 0 hard compatibility violations 1 explicit human approval 1 rollback checkpoint We are also proud that every WebMCP action has a corresponding visual response. Agents do not disappear into an invisible automation layer—their semantic investigation is visible in the operational world. What we learned WebMCP becomes much more interesting when tools are treated as part of application state rather than as a static API catalog. BRANCHLINE demonstrates that the application can expose only the actions that make sense right now . The project also reinforced an important principle for human-agent systems: Human intent should not have to travel through chat to matter. A planner can simply change something in the interface. The application can make that change part of the same structured context the agent uses on its next call. We also learned that simulation results become significantly easier to trust when their causal evidence, assumptions, actions, and counterfactuals remain inspectable after the recommendation is produced. That led to Causal Proof , which explains decisions from simulation evidence rather than from an embedded LLM. title: RoutineForge
pitch: Teach a website new agent tools by demonstrating once.
about_excerpt: Teach a website new agent tools by demonstrating once. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Web agents are often forced into two extremes: fragile visual automation that guesses where to click, or fixed APIs that only expose workflows developers anticipated in advance. We asked a different question: what if a website could learn a new agent tool from a human demonstration? People already teach coworkers by showing a task once. RoutineForge brings that interaction to the web: the human demonstrates intent inside the real product, the application records the underlying business actions, and WebMCP turns the reviewed routine into a reliable tool an agent can discover and invoke. What it does RoutineForge is a WebMCP-native commerce operations workspace with Home, Orders, Products, Customers, Analytics, and Marketing. Its central feature is Routine Studio: A merchant selects Record workflow . They set a date range and market, select metrics, generate a report, and save it. RoutineForge captures five typed, verified semantic actions—not clicks or selectors. The merchant reviews the trace and chooses which values the agent may supply. They publish the routine as generate_weekly_report . An agent discovers and calls the new WebMCP tool with different inputs. The live page follows the execution and returns a report ID, URL, summary, and five verification receipts. The app also exposes ten atomic WebMCP tools for dashboard state, orders, inventory, customers, campaigns, analytics filters, and reports. The demonstrated routine becomes the eleventh tool. Why WebMCP A reporting API could return numbers, but it would miss the shared, visible teaching surface between a person, an agent, and the application. With WebMCP, the human UI and agent tools use the same business actions, validation rules, state, and feedback. The agent does not reverse-engineer the DOM, and the developer does not maintain a second integration that can drift away from the product. RoutineForge also uses WebMCP dynamically. The site begins with ten developer-defined tools. After a person demonstrates and approves a routine, the page registers a new composite tool at runtime. This explores a future where a website's agent interface is shaped safely through use, not limited to a static tool catalog. How we built it RoutineForge is a client-only React and TypeScript app with no login, backend, API key, or third-party dataset. At its core is an Action Registry of versioned definitions. Each definition includes a JSON Schema, effects, input validation, execution logic, and post-execution verification. A shared Action Bus runs the same definitions for human UI events and WebMCP calls. The recorder stores action IDs, versions, typed inputs, structured outputs, sources, timestamps, and verification evidence. It never records coordinates, screenshots, CSS selectors, or generated JavaScript. The Routine Compiler accepts only registered actions. Every binding must be a demonstrated literal, a reviewed routine input, or a prior step output. The Routine Runner resolves bindings, validates each step, stops safely on failure, and returns structured receipts. The app feature-detects document.modelContext.registerTool() and registers ten atomic site tools. Publishing a taught routine registers generate_weekly_report with its own JSON Schema and verified execution handler. Published routines persist in IndexedDB and re-register after refresh; Reset demo restores deterministic seed data. Challenges The hardest problem was choosing the right abstraction boundary. Raw click recording looks general but is fragile and difficult to verify. A semantic action layer requires deliberate product architecture, but it survives UI changes and produces meaningful evidence. Dynamic publication also had to remain safe: recorded data or agent input can never become executable code. We solved that with a deliberately small binding language and a compiler that references only registered, versioned actions. Finally, agent activity needed to remain legible to a human. RoutineForge synchronizes the visible workspace with each execution and shows step-level receipts in the same interface. Accomplishments Ten atomic WebMCP tools plus a human-taught composite tool registered at runtime. One semantic execution layer shared by human interactions and agent calls. Typed validation and verification at every action boundary. No selectors, coordinates, screenshots, or generated code in recorded routines. Visible synchronization between agent execution and the human dashboard. A public, deterministic deployment with automated tests and no credentials required. What we learned Agent-native design is not simply adding tools beside an interface. The strongest experience comes from making the human UI and agent interface two views over the same semantic application model. Demonstration alone is not authorization; the human review step transforms a trace into a contract. Verification belongs inside each action definition, so composite routines can remain trustworthy. What's next Next we would generalize the compiler across all registered actions, add a visual routine editor, controlled branches and approval checkpoints, versioning and rollback, dry runs, audit logs, and a developer SDK. Our long-term vision is a web where developers provide safe semantic building blocks, people teach the workflows that matter to them, and agents execute those workflows transparently in the applications where work already lives. Try it Open the live app , select Reset demo , and follow the Routine Studio flow. Source and technical instructions are available in the public MIT-licensed repository . title: PriceMCP
pitch: Browser-native WebMCP tools that give agents current, comparable price evidence—including landed cost, freshness, and why misleading deals were excluded.
about_excerpt:
Browser-native WebMCP tools that give agents current, comparable price evidence—including landed cost, freshness, and why misleading deals were excluded.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 PriceMCP’s live search interface with the WebMCP-ready status visible. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 PriceMCP’s live search interface with the WebMCP-ready status visible.

 1 2 



 
 PriceMCP — WebMCP Challenge 

 
 Live application: https://pricemcp.vercel.app 
 Public 1:30 YouTube demo: https://youtu.be/8UA3jLzF6_s 
 Reproducible video backup: https://github.com/tobias-minibot/pricemcp/releases/download/webmcp-challenge-v2/pricemcp-webmcp-demo.mp4 
 Implementation pull requests: #30 , #31 
 

 What people and agents do together 

 A person opens PriceMCP and asks their browser agent to find an exact product
variant. The agent calls find_best_price instead of guessing through page
controls or scraping rendered text. PriceMCP resolves the canonical product,
excludes stale, unavailable, conditional, or untrusted offers from the winner,
and returns compact evidence with timestamps, conditions, and source URLs. 

 The result is also rendered into the open page. Person and agent can inspect the
same winning offer and ranking explanation, then use
 inspect_price_evidence to audit the underlying seller records. This shared
page state is the collaboration boundary: the agent researches; the person sees
and judges the evidence. The WebMCP tools are read-only and never purchase,
reserve, subscribe, message a seller, or write a procurement decision. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Ordinary browser automation would have to infer PriceMCP's meaning from forms,
cards, and text. The existing backend MCP endpoint is structured but is not
automatically available to a browser agent. WebMCP bridges the actual web app:
the page advertises purpose-built tools, validates structured arguments, calls
the same read-only price pipeline as the human interface, and visibly shares the
result back into the page. 

 Implementation 

 src/webmcp.ts registers three imperative WebMCP tools with
 document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : 

 
 find_best_price({ query }) calls PriceMCP's read-only MCP diagnostic bridge
at /v1/mcp/search . It returns the canonical subject, best qualifying offer,
two alternatives, ranking reasons, observation time, and provenance. 
 inspect_price_evidence({ product_id, max_age_hours }) calls the canonical
product offer endpoint and returns up to three seller observations with their
trust, availability, membership, freshness, and source fields. 
 run_flight_price_demo({}) runs a permanent, explicitly synthetic and
non-bookable WAS–BER fixture through the existing read-only MCP diagnostic
bridge. It lets judges verify discovery, execution, shared page state, and
normalized conditions even after the deployed product snapshot has aged. 
 

 Tool descriptions and outputs follow Chrome's recommended character budgets.
Both tools set readOnlyHint: true and untrustedContentHint: true . Fetches
receive the WebMCP execution AbortSignal . Returned data is capped before the
1,500-character recommendation, and DOM updates use textContent rather than
injecting retailer content as HTML. 

 The original PriceMCP repository was created on August 29, 2026, inside the
challenge period that began August 25. Browser WebMCP support was added on
September 3; its commits and pull request distinguish this challenge-specific
implementation from the prior backend MCP work. 

 Reproduce 

 
 Open https://pricemcp.vercel.app in ChatGPT's in-app browser, or Chrome
149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled. 
 Ask the agent: Find the best trustworthy price for AirPods Pro 3 and explain
why it wins. 
 Confirm that it discovers and calls find_best_price . The page should display
a Shared agent result containing the same winner and explanation returned
to the agent. 
 Ask: Inspect the source evidence for the canonical product you found. 
 Confirm that it calls inspect_price_evidence and reports seller trust,
availability, membership dependency, freshness, timestamp, and source URL. 
 For a permanent reproduction path, ask: Run PriceMCP's disclosed WebMCP
flight demo. Confirm that the response and page both label it synthetic and
non-bookable. 
 

 In a browser without WebMCP, the fixed status pill explains how to enable it.
All production tools remain read-only. Product data is a deployed timestamped
snapshot; location-dependent tax is excluded and unknown shipping is disclosed
rather than estimated. 

 Verified evidence 

 On September 3, 2026 UTC, Chrome 152 with WebMCPTesting enabled discovered all
three tools through document.modelContext.getTools() and executed
 run_flight_price_demo through document.modelContext.executeTool() . The live
result reported dataset: pricemcp-demo-v1 , synthetic: true , and the boundary
 Synthetic demonstration; not live, purchasable, or bookable. The same
execution rendered the shared WAS–BER result into the page. 

 The YouTube upload is 1:30, public, contains OpenAI Cedar narration, and passed YouTube's checks
with no issues found. Its exact release backup has SHA-256 digest
 c215d98c83b331ea1cfad8cce71e4de61fa03ef84232f6826a1e75d55bbe5ee0 .
