title: Glassbook
pitch: Your money. Your browser. Your agent. The ledger never leaves this tab. The agent comes to it. You see every call. You can rewind every write.
about_excerpt: Your money. Your browser. Your agent. The ledger never leaves this tab. The agent comes to it. You see every call. You can rewind every write. Like Comment Story Updates Dashboard. Spend, income, and net for the month. Transactions. Search, filter, and categorize. Activity log. Every agent call, and undo on writes. Budgets. Monthly limits and how much you spent. Import. CSV, Excel, OFX, or a text PDF. Rules. Save a merchant match and apply it. Inspiration Every budgeting app I have tried wants the statement first. Connect Plaid, upload a CSV, or paste it into a chat so a model can read it. You hand over a year of swipes, then get told you spend too much on dining. I started with a simpler question: can the ledger stay on your machine, and can you still get help? WebMCP is how I tried that. What it does Glassbook is a budgeting app that never leaves the tab. You import a statement, sort your spending, set budgets, and teach it a few rules about merchants you recognize. There is no account and no server. The ledger sits in localStorage . Connect an agent and it gets 18 WebMCP tools pointed at that same ledger. It can categorize a few hundred rows in one call, save a rule when you correct it, find a subscription you forgot about, work out why June cost so much, and set a budget. Every call lands in an activity log. If a write goes wrong, you can undo the last one, or walk back everything the agent touched. Doing this by hand is an hour of clicking category chips. A chat-only agent wants the statement uploaded first. Load the demo and you get about 320 uncategorized rows across four months. Ask the agent to categorize everything and the chips update on screen while it works. Once you connect an agent, tool results do enter its context. The tools send summaries and cleaned merchant names rather than your raw statement, unless you ask for more of them. Every call sits in the log. How I built it There is no MCP server sitting somewhere with a copy of your ledger. The tools run in the page, against the same Zustand store the UI is reading from. The site decides the schema, how little a read hands back, and what undo means. Each tool is defined once and registered on document.modelContext after the store loads, with fallbacks to navigator.modelContext and window.modelContext . Hosts do not agree on where to put it yet. ChatGPT injects it after first paint, and registration retries if it is not there. Then there is one wrapper around every call. It writes the activity row, and on a write it snapshots the whole ledger first, up to fifty deep. undoLast pops one. undoAll walks back a consecutive run of agent writes, including a streak where one call was wrong. Some tools only return text. The ones that make it feel shared also move the screen: highlight_transactions rings a row and scrolls it into view, set_view_filters puts you both on Dining for August, pin_insight leaves a card on the dashboard. Those do not work if the tools live on a server. Import follows the same rule as the ledger. CSV and TSV go through PapaParse, OFX and QFX through a local parser, Excel and text PDFs through AnyDoc WASM in a worker. Nothing is uploaded. await document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "get_overview", description: "Call this first to understand the user's ledger.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: {}, additionalProperties: false }, annotations: { readOnlyHint: true }, execute: async (input) => { const text = await executeRegisteredTool("get_overview", input); return { content: [{ type: "text", text }] }; }, }); Challenges I ran into The first real problem was that I could not get site tools to appear at all. I had ChatGPT desktop from the Microsoft Store, and document.modelContext was simply undefined. The permission settings had no site tools entry in them either. I updated the app, restarted it, tried again, got nowhere, and eventually decided the Windows build did not support WebMCP, wrote that into the README, and pushed it. What actually fixed it was uninstalling the Store version and installing the same app from the ChatGPT website. Different build, same machine. I could not find that documented anywhere. Undo was harder than it looked. Logging what the agent did is easy. I still needed a way to take a write back. The store ended up snapshotting the full ledger on every agent write. That felt heavy until I watched an agent categorize three hundred rows, save a rule, and set a budget in one streak, then rewound all of it with one click. Bank files are not one format: OFX, .xls files that turn out to be HTML tables, European statements where 1.850,00 means one thousand eight hundred and fifty and imports as one euro eighty-five if you are not looking for it. Scanned PDFs still do not work. The fix is OCR, and I am not adding a cloud one. What I'm proud of The demo works end to end. Load 320 rows, connect an agent, categorize the lot, correct a chip, save a rule so the correction sticks, find Scribd at $11.99, ask why June was expensive and watch it ring the Delta and Airbnb rows from the 18th, set a dining budget, then rewind all of it from the activity log. Data minimization is in the tools on purpose. get_spending_summary returns grouped totals instead of three hundred rows. list_transactions sends cleaned merchant names, fifty at a time, and never the raw description. There are no account numbers in the model. What I learned The useful part of WebMCP is that the page owns the contract. The site decides what is readable, how much comes back, and whether it can be undone. Someone who would never paste a bank statement into a chat might still let an agent help. The activity log and the ring around the Delta row mattered more than another read endpoint. If you cannot see the tool call, it is hard to trust it. What's next for Glassbook Rules need to get smarter. Right now it is substring matching on the merchant, and it should handle amounts and date ranges too. The date-order override in the importer works but it is easy to miss, and sooner or later someone will import a European statement and get the days and months flipped. localStorage is also not where a multi-year ledger belongs. IndexedDB at some point. Scanned PDFs stay broken until on-device OCR is good enough. title: BridgeAble - Bridging The Gap
pitch: BridgeAble turns any confusing website into an accessible one — an AI agent fills forms and navigates for people with disabilities, while they see and approve every step.
about_excerpt:
BridgeAble turns any confusing website into an accessible one — an AI agent fills forms and navigates for people with disabilities, while they see and approve every step. 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Why This Use Case Is a Strong Fit for WebMCP 

 Assistive form-filling is one of the few agentic use cases where "just scrape the DOM and click around" is actively dangerous: 

 
 The cost of a wrong guess is serious. A shopping-assistant agent that misclicks can be retried. An agent that misreads an unlabeled housing-benefits field and submits a wrong income figure or the wrong document can cost someone real benefits, or force them to redo a multi-step application alone. WebMCP's structured, explicit tool schemas ( fill_field(field_id, value) , not "click the third gray box") remove the guessing entirely — the page tells the agent exactly what's fillable, what it's called, and what values are valid (e.g. the housing_status enum), instead of the agent inferring it from pixels and placeholder text. 
 Screen scraping and vision models are exactly what disabled users can't rely on. A blind user's agent can't "look" at a tiny unlabeled button any better than a screen reader can — both need the page to declare its own semantics. WebMCP's document.modelContext.registerTool is that declaration, machine-readable and unambiguous, which is precisely the gap screen readers have never been able to close on their own. 
 Retrofit, not redesign, is the only realistic path for legacy government/benefits sites. These are exactly the sites least likely to ever get an accessibility redesign. WebMCP lets a site owner bolt on a config object and one <script> tag and get agent-legible tools immediately — no rebuild, no waiting on a procurement cycle. 
 The same tool surface serves both a real browser-native agent and our own bundled LLM loop , so the use case naturally showcases WebMCP as a genuine web platform primitive (via document.modelContext ) rather than something that only works inside one vendor's chat widget. 
 

 

 How It Creates a Better User Experience 

 
 From "hand over your laptop" to "stay in control." Before WebMCP-style structured tools, the only real options for someone who can't operate a confusing form were to struggle through it alone or hand full control to a caregiver/bot. BridgeAble's tool-gated actions mean the person can direct an agent conversationally while remaining the one who approves every change — no full hand-off of control required. 
 Every action is visible, not a black box. Because each tool call acts on the real DOM element (via the BridgeableConfig selector), the actual page visibly highlights and updates as the agent works — the person watching (whether low-vision, using a screen reader, or a family member helping) sees the same ground truth the agent is acting on, in real time. 
 Plain language replaces jargon. explain_field and read_field_aloud turn a confusing government-form label into a spoken, plain-language explanation on demand — something a static form or a generic screen reader narration cannot do, because the form itself doesn't know what its own fields mean. 
 Mistakes are cheap to fix. undo_last_change and simply re-calling fill_field mean a correction is a single spoken sentence ("actually my income is $2,600"), not a re-navigation of a multi-step wizard with tiny, hard-to-hit controls. 
 Consent is structural, not just polite. request_submit can only ever open a large-text, high-contrast confirmation card — it can never submit. The person (or their caregiver) always makes the final, deliberate tap. That single design choice is what turns "an agent that could act for me" into "an agent I can actually trust to act for me." 
 

 

 What People and Agents Can Now Do Together That Was Difficult or Impossible Before 

 
 Reliable multi-step form completion by voice or plain chat, with zero blind trust. Before, a person with a motor or visual disability could either painstakingly tab/zoom/scroll through a 4-step, unlabeled form themselves, or dictate instructions to a human/bot that had no structured way to confirm it acted correctly. With WebMCP tools exposed, a person can say one natural sentence and watch, in real time, exactly which fields were set to what — then correct or undo any single one without redoing the rest. 
 Mid-conversation correction without losing progress. Because each field is an addressable tool call (not a scripted macro), a person can course-correct ("actually, two dependents, not one") at any point, and the agent calls fill_field again on just that field — something a recorded macro, a scripted RPA bot, or a caregiver relaying instructions secondhand can't do cleanly. 
 A meaningful, plain-language "explain this to me" conversation embedded in the task itself. explain_field lets someone ask "what does housing status mean?" in the middle of filling out the form and get an answer that maps to that exact field, then keep going in the same flow — rather than leaving the page to search a FAQ or call a helpline. 
 Human-gated agentic submission that's provably safe, not just prompted to be careful. Previously, "the agent will ask for confirmation" was a matter of trusting a prompt. Here, the agent literally has no callable tool that finalizes anything — request_submit only opens a UI, and the real submit path is wired exclusively to a human click handler. That means a person can delegate the tedious, error-prone filling work to an agent while keeping the consequential, irreversible submitting action entirely their own — a split of labor between human and agent that wasn't safely possible when agents only had "click here" style access to a page. 
 The exact same tool surface working for a real WebMCP-aware browser/extension and our own accessible chat panel. A person isn't locked into one vendor's assistant; any WebMCP-compliant agent (verified here with the Model Context Tool Inspector extension) can discover and drive the same accessible form-filling flow. 
 

 

 How We Implemented WebMCP (Briefly) 

 
 Each host page (e.g. portal.php ) declares a small window.BridgeableConfig object mapping semantic field/document/step keys to real CSS selectors, human-readable labels, and types — the only integration work a site owner does. 
 assets/bridgeable-widget.js defines one canonical TOOLS array (name, description, JSON Schema, handler) for get_application_state , fill_field , go_to_step , upload_document , explain_field , read_field_aloud , review_summary , request_submit , and undo_last_change . 
 Every tool in that array is registered with the browser via document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) , per the WebMCP Imperative API , so any WebMCP-aware agent or extension can discover and call it directly against the live page. 
 The same TOOLS array is mirrored into a local registry that powers BridgeAble's own bundled chat/voice panel and agent loop ( agent_api.php / llm.php ), so the identical tool implementations run whether they're invoked by a real WebMCP client or by our fallback LLM loop — no duplicated logic, and the demo works even where document.modelContext isn't available yet. 
 The one deliberately un -registered function, finalizeSubmission() , is wired only to a human click event on the confirmation card — enforcing human-in-the-loop consent at the architecture level rather than via a system prompt. 
 

 See How We Built It below for the full architecture breakdown. 

 

 Inspiration 

 Every day, millions of people with disabilities hit a wall online — not because they can't use a computer, but because the web was never built for them. A 12-step government benefits form with no screen-reader labels. A healthcare portal with tiny, unlabeled buttons scattered across five tabs. A visually impaired parent trying to book a school appointment through a form that assumes perfect vision and fine motor control. 

 Existing "solutions" force a bad trade-off: either the person struggles through alone, or they hand over their laptop entirely to a caregiver or an autonomous bot that clicks blindly and makes mistakes on their behalf — with zero visibility or consent along the way. 

 We kept coming back to one moment in the WebMCP spec: the idea that a website can expose structured, trustworthy tools that an agent calls directly — no guessing, no fragile scraping, no misclicks. That's not just a technical convenience. For someone with a disability, it's the difference between an agent that might get it

title: LingoMargin
pitch: LingoMargin turns any text into a personalized language lesson where learners and agents collaborate through contextual annotations, grammar missions, and review practice powered by WebMCP.
about_excerpt: LingoMargin turns any text into a personalized language lesson where learners and agents collaborate through contextual annotations, grammar missions, and review practice powered by WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Language learners increasingly use AI to understand given texts, but the usual workflow is fragmented: read in one place, copy a confusing sentence into chat, receive an explanation elsewhere, and manually save useful vocabulary. I wanted to explore a more natural model where the learner and agent share the same reading workspace. The learner stays focused on the text while the agent understands the current passage, proficiency level, annotations, exercises, and learning progress. What LingoMargin does LingoMargin turns any passage into an interactive, level-appropriate language lesson. Learners can paste their own text or request a new passage by specifying a language, level, length, and topic. They can select unfamiliar phrases, save vocabulary, inspect contextual explanations, complete Grammar Detective missions, review mistakes, and export learning material. The agent can directly update the workspace by: Adding selective vocabulary, grammar, and cultural annotations Creating hidden-answer Grammar Detective missions Generating contextual review activities Leaving feedback in the margin Producing new level-appropriate passages Every agent action creates a visible change in the interface. The learner decides what to study and can undo passage replacements when needed. How I built it LingoMargin is built with React, TypeScript, Vinext, and WebMCP, and is deployed using ChatGPT Sites. The application registers six tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : get_learning_context annotate_text create_grammar_mission create_activity add_feedback create_generated_passage These tools give the agent structured access to the current lesson and allow it to make precise, verifiable updates. Mutating tools return confirmation describing what changed, while the learner immediately sees the result in the passage or margin. The workspace is stored locally in the browser. Passage content and learning state are shared with an agent only when the learner asks for help through a WebMCP tool. Challenges The main challenge was designing genuine human-agent collaboration instead of attaching a chatbot to a reading app. Annotations had to remain anchored to exact character ranges while preventing duplicates and overlaps. Grammar missions needed to accept the complete intended phrase without incorrectly accepting tiny fragments. Agent-generated activities also required validation so malformed exercises could not enter the interface. Another challenge was preserving learner control. Replacing a passage clears lesson-specific state, so I added confirmation, recovery, and one-step undo. I also had to make the relationship between the page and adjacent agent chat understandable without filling the interface with technical WebMCP terminology. Finally, the workspace needed to remain usable on mobile, where the mission must appear before a potentially long passage. What I learned WebMCP changes interface design, not just integration code. A useful agent-native application needs carefully scoped tools, observable outcomes, reliable validation, and clear boundaries between human and agent responsibilities. The best result came from giving each participant a distinct role: the agent analyzes and adapts the lesson, while the learner notices, selects, answers, and decides what becomes knowledge. pitch: Show Echo any workflow once it saves a portable SKILL.md. Your in-browser agent can then call that skill via WebMCP, anytime, with whatever inputs it wants.
about_excerpt: Show Echo any workflow once it saves a portable SKILL.md. Your in-browser agent can then call that skill via WebMCP, anytime, with whatever inputs it wants. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every team has the same five workflows they run by hand every week. Sort the inbox, post the metrics to Slack, follow up on the new leads, fill the report, archive the receipts. The thing nobody admits out loud is that a human in the loop is the most expensive part of automation , not the script. We'd been following Microsoft's Skill Recorder and loved its shape, but it was an Electron app, it required the Copilot CLI, and it didn't have a path for an AI agent to actually call the workflows. WebMCP — a standard for letting web pages expose structured tools to in-browser AI agents — changed that. It said: a website can register its buttons as tools, an agent can see them, and the user can ask the agent to do the thing. We wanted to build that, end to end, on top of Echo. What it does Echo is a multi-composer agent-skill platform. Two halves: The Recorder records a screen via navigator.mediaDevices.getDisplayMedia , ships the frames + a browser-level event timeline to a Describer LLM, and produces a structured SkillPlan (an ordered list of steps, each mapped to a tool from Echo's catalogue, with {{token}} placeholders for anything dynamic). The result is a portable SKILL.md file. The Composer is a 2×2 grid of parallel agents. Each slot owns its own goal, plan, dispatched run, and live progress. Dispatch all four and they run in parallel against a real headless Chromium. The WebMCP integration exposes the whole dashboard to an in-browser agent. Open /compose in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, install the Model Context Tool Inspector extension, and you see 29 tools registered on the page: 5 global tools (available on every Echo page): navigate_echo , get_echo_status , show_toast , wait , echo_ping . 6 composer tools: preview_echo_plan , compose_echo_agent , set_composer_goal , start_planning , dispatch_current_plan , get_composer_state . 7 skills tools: list_skills , get_skill , find_skills_by_name , get_skill_md (returns the portable markdown), create_skill_from_text , dispatch_saved_skill , delete_skill . 5 runs tools: list_runs , get_run , get_run_stats , find_runs_by_goal , cancel_run . 6 agents tools: list_agents , get_agent , dispatch_saved_agent , archive_agent , delete_agent , get_agents_overview . The headline tools: tell the agent dispatch_saved_skill with a skill id and a goal, and a real headless-browser run starts. Tell it get_skill_md with any skill id, and it gets back the full portable markdown it could paste into any other runtime. Tell it compose_echo_agent with a plain-English goal, and it gets back a structured plan, then a runId, then a real stream of progress events. The live site is at echo-one-liard.vercel.app . Sign in, navigate to /compose , and the topbar shows a WebMCP · 29 tools pill. Click it for the live tool list and a link to the Inspector extension. How we built it The architecture is a single Next.js 16 + React 19 app, deployed on Vercel. The WebMCP layer is a thin src/lib/webmcp/ folder: types.ts — TypeScript declarations for the WebMCP API surface ( document.modelContext.registerTool , the content envelope, the result shape, the annotations). No new dependencies — the API is browser-native. use-webmcp.ts — a React hook that feature-detects document.modelContext , registers a list of tools on mount, and unregisters them atomically on unmount via one AbortController . The tool body is looked up from a ref-map on every invocation so a body-only update never forces a re-register. One file per page: global-tools.ts , composer-tools.ts , skills-tools.ts , runs-tools.ts , agents-tools.ts . Each file exports a buildXxxTools() function that returns the page's tool set. webmcp-badge.tsx — a topbar pill that polls document.modelContext.getTools() every two seconds and shows the live count. Click it for the full list + Inspector link. webmcp-toast-host.tsx — listens for the show_toast tool's echo:webmcp:toast window event and renders a transient notification. Every tool declares its inputs as a JSON Schema ( type: "object" , properties , required , enum ) so the agent can validate before calling. Read-only tools set annotations.readOnlyHint: true ; mutating tools leave it false . The execute function returns a plain JSON-serializable value; the hook wraps it in { content: [{ type: "text", text: JSON.stringify(result) }] } and catches thrown errors as { content: [...], isError: true } . /compose is the headline page — it mounts all five tool sets so the full 29-tool surface is live. The other pages ( /skills , /agents , /runs , /record ) mount their page-local set plus the global five. The agent does the full "library-inspect → compose-plan → dispatch-run" flow from a single page. Everything else in the project is unchanged: the existing Next.js API routes ( /api/agents/compose , /api/agents/run-autonomous , /api/skills/save ) are what the buttons hit and what the WebMCP tools hit. The WebMCP integration is a pure progressive enhancement — pages work exactly as before if the browser doesn't expose document.modelContext . Challenges we ran into The stale-closure trap. My first pass captured the tool body at registration time. When the page state changed (goal text, plan, runId), the registered tool was still pointing at the old closure. Fixed with the ref-map pattern: the registration wraps the body in a function that looks up the latest body from bodiesRef.current on every invocation. Now a body-only update doesn't force a re-register. Duplicate name collisions across pages. Several tools exist with the same purpose in different files ( list_skills vs list_agents vs list_runs ). Names are unique across the codebase so we never collide, but I added explicit console.warn per failed registration to surface any future collision immediately. Progressive enhancement without breaking the page. A WebMCP integration that crashes when document.modelContext is undefined is worse than no integration. The hook is a no-op in that case; the badge doesn't render; the toast host listens but never gets events. The page is identical to the pre-WebMCP version. The 29-tool discoverability problem. An agent landing on /compose for the first time sees 29 tools in a flat list. The tool descriptions had to be clear and self-contained — no "see also", no implicit context. I rewrote every description to be standalone-readable, with explicit inputSchema enums where the value space is bounded (route names, run statuses, agent statuses). What "fully functional" means. The easy win is registering 29 tools. The hard win is making sure the output of every tool is something the agent can act on. get_skill_md returns the portable markdown; dispatch_saved_skill returns a runId and a server message; find_skills_by_name returns summaries with id fields the agent can feed straight into dispatch_saved_skill . Every tool's output is designed to be a useful input to another tool call. Accomplishments that we're proud of 29 WebMCP tools, all live on production. Every tool uses the spec-correct document.modelContext.registerTool() API. Every input is a JSON Schema. Every read-only tool sets readOnlyHint: true . The 29-tool count is verifiable: open the badge in the topbar on /compose , click it, count. One page mounts the full surface. /compose registers all five tool sets — composer, skills, runs, agents, plus the global five — so an agent can do the entire library-inspect → compose-plan → dispatch-run loop from a single URL. The portable markdown is the artifact, not an afterthought. The Recorder produces a SKILL.md file with YAML frontmatter, parameterized body, rules, and error codes. The get_skill_md tool returns that exact markdown. An agent that wants to use a skill elsewhere can take the markdown and run with it. Real headless, not a mock. When a tool dispatches a run, the agent runs in Vercel-hosted Chromium ( @sparticuz/chromium + puppeteer-core ) with real screenshots and a real 📸 1 real headless badge on the runs page. Not a simulator. Eval harness on the recorder side. pnpm run eval:recorder runs 6 fixture recordings through the real Describer + Builder and scores each on tokens, no-forbidden-phrases, tool picks, step count, generalization, and browser-kind. 60% gate, currently 64% — the eval caught a real tokenization regression that I fixed by tightening the Builder prompt. What we learned WebMCP is the right shape. The 4-phase pipeline (Record → Describer → Builder → SKILL.md) and the WebMCP tool surface are the same idea: structured schemas, human-in-the-loop gates, and a portable artifact at the end. The standard is genuinely enabling, not just a spec to comply with. The hard part isn't registering the tools — it's the tool descriptions. An agent picks which tool to call by reading the description. "List Echo skills from local storage" i

title: INTENT
pitch: INTENT is a workspace where humans and AI agents can figure out what matters and turn it into a clear direction. With WebMCP, agents can directly inspect with the intent instead of just chatting.\n
about_excerpt:
INTENT is a workspace where humans and AI agents can figure out what matters and turn it into a clear direction. With WebMCP, agents can directly inspect with the intent instead of just chatting.

 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Why I Built INTENT 

 I kept coming back to a simple problem: when we use AI, we usually start with a prompt and immediately ask it to do something. But sometimes the hardest part is figuring out what we actually want to do in the first place. 

 That became the idea behind INTENT — a workspace where the human and the AI can work on the intent itself before jumping into execution. 

 How I Built It 

 I built INTENT as a Next.js web app with a structured workspace for an evolving intent. Instead of keeping everything inside a chat, the application keeps track of things like intent nodes, decisions, actions, and open questions. 

 The interesting part for this challenge was connecting that workspace to AI agents through WebMCP. 

 I exposed six tools that let an agent work with the actual application state: 

 
 "inspect_intent" 
 "add_intent_node" 
 "focus_attention" 
 "surface_contradiction" 
 "propose_intent_evolution" 
 "fork_intent" 
 

 These aren't just functions that return text. They are connected to the workspace, so when an agent uses them, the changes can be reflected in the UI. 

 What I Learned 

 The biggest thing I learned was that agent interaction feels different when the agent can actually interact with the application instead of only generating a response. 

 Designing the tools also made me think carefully about what an agent should be allowed to do. I wanted the human to remain in control while still giving the agent enough access to be genuinely useful. 

 I also learned a lot about the practical side of WebMCP — especially tool registration, connecting tools to application state, and testing the experience in the browser. 

 Challenges 

 The main challenge was getting the WebMCP integration working with the current API. My initial implementation used an older registration pattern, which caused the tools to fail during registration. 

 I had to update the implementation to the current "ModelContext" API and make sure the tools were registered correctly without causing repeated registrations during React development and refreshes. 

 Another challenge was making the tools useful enough to represent real actions in the workspace rather than just creating a collection of demo functions. 

 What's Next 

 INTENT is still an early version, but the direction I find interesting is giving agents more meaningful ways to participate in applications while keeping the human in control. 

 For me, WebMCP makes that interaction feel much more direct: the agent doesn't just talk about the workspace — it can actually work with it.

title: Enclave
pitch: The data stays in your browser. The agent gets tools, not rows — and anything it wants to change waits for you to approve it.
about_excerpt: The data stays in your browser. The agent gets tools, not rows — and anything it wants to change waits for you to approve it. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Enclave keeps the store's data in the browser and hands the agent tools instead of rows. Anything it changes waits for a human. The landing page. The demo store is already loaded — no account, no upload, nothing to install. A write tool does not act. It proposes, shows its reasoning, and blocks until the operator approves or declines. Every tool call, with its cost in bytes. A full investigation of 59,615 rows: 6,851 bytes out, zero rows uploaded. Approved: four restock orders raised by the agent, and products below reorder level drop from seven to three. Asked why EMEA fell in March, the agent builds the board as it works: a chart, a table, a KPI, and a written finding. Inspiration Two things stop an AI agent being useful inside a real business, and they pull in opposite directions. It cannot see your data. Revenue, customers, orders — none of it can be pasted into a chat window, so the analysis that would actually help never happens. And it should not be clicking around your admin panel. An agent guessing its way through a UI is slow, brittle, and occasionally catastrophic. Nobody wants to find out it changed the wrong price because it inferred which button said "Save". WebMCP resolves both at once. The page declares exactly what an agent may do, so it never has to guess. And because the tools run inside the page, the data can stay in the browser: the agent asks questions of it without ever receiving it. What it does Enclave is the back-office of Northwind Trading Co., a fictional store. Its orders and catalogue load into the browser tab and stop there. Overview, Orders, Products and Analytics are all real views over that data — there is no server. An agent — ChatGPT over WebMCP, or a built-in panel using your own OpenAI key — operates the store through 22 registered tools . It investigates freely. When it wants to change something, it proposes and waits for you. The story the demo store carries The data has one real problem seeded in it, and the whole route to the fix is discoverable without the agent ever seeing a row. Asked "EMEA fell in March. Find the cause and fix it," GPT-5 walks it end to end: It notices. Revenue by region, month by month — EMEA falls 52% in March 2025 and no other region moves. It finds the cause. Broken down by supplier, one name is missing from March entirely: Aurora Supply sold nothing in EMEA that month. It checks the shelf. All four Aurora products are still at zero stock, below their reorder level. The revenue hole and the empty shelf are the same fact. You decide. It proposes restock orders with its reasoning, and stops. Sixteen tool rounds. No failed calls. About 7 KB left the browser. Zero rows uploaded. Nothing changes without you Reading is free. Anything that touches the business — a restock order, a price — is proposed : tool.execute() ├─ validate the product and the quantity ├─ await requestApproval({...}) ←── the call blocks here │ │ an approval card appears carrying the agent's own reason. │ "The agent is waiting. Nothing has changed yet." │ │ … the operator approves … │ ├─ raise the restock order └─ "Approved. RS-1042 raised for 900 × Nimbus Charging Dock." Decline it, or take too long, and the tool reports back honestly that nothing happened. That pause is the product. "The agent is supervised" is a policy; a tool call still blocked while a card says nothing has changed yet is a mechanism. How it works ┌─────────────── Enclave (browser tab) ───────────────┐ │ │ ChatGPT ───┼──→ document.modelContext ──┐ │ │ ├──→ TOOL REGISTRY │ Built-in ──┼──→ OpenAI Responses API ───┘ (22 tools, one │ panel │ (your own key) definition site) │ │ │ │ │ ┌──────────────┴───────────┐ │ │ ▼ ▼ │ │ approval gate DuckDB-WASM │ │ (writes only) store data │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ no server · data never leaves the tab One registry, two runtimes. Tools are defined once. One adapter registers them with document.modelContext ; another exposes the same list to the OpenAI Responses API. Identical capabilities and identical approval gates either way. The tool surface reads as well as it writes. Most only let an agent act. Enclave's lets it read the current state of the data, the analysis board and the catalogue — which is what lets it revise work it did not do itself. The global filter is a view swap. Analytics cards read from a view, not a table. set_global_filter runs one CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW and every card on the board re-renders against the filtered data. Every result is budgeted. Tool output passes through a single cap — 50 rows and 4 KB, adjustable in settings — before it can reach an agent. Raw row dumps are refused with a message steering the agent toward aggregation. The Activity Log counts the bytes on screen the whole time, so the privacy claim is metered rather than promised. How we built it Vite, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, Zustand, DuckDB-WASM and ECharts. No backend — the only server-side artefact in the repository is a vercel.json that sets one header. 142 tests cover the data layer, the store, all 22 tools, the approval gate and both runtime adapters. Two scripts in the repo are receipts a judge can run: verify-native-webmcp.mjs proves a real WebMCP browser discovers and executes the tools on the deployed URL, and live-agent-check.mjs measures a full agent run against the real API. Challenges we ran into DuckDB-WASM versus WebMCP's headers. DuckDB's threaded coi bundle needs cross-origin isolation, which conflicted with how the page had to be served. It turned out selectBundle() only picks coi when the page is already cross-origin isolated — so by deliberately not setting COOP/COEP we get the eh bundle, which needs neither, alongside the Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 that WebMCP does require. Arrow's numbers are not numbers. DuckDB returns sum() over integers as DECIMAL(38,0) , which Arrow hands back as an object, and count() as a BigInt. Both had to be flattened before anything downstream could read them. An agent will happily spend its entire budget exploring. The first live run against GPT-5 used all ten tool rounds profiling columns and reached no conclusion. Raising the ceiling to thirty just moved the wall — it then made nine get_product calls, one product at a time, and still never proposed a fix. The fix was direction, not budget: tell the agent to group several dimensions in one query, to use list_low_stock instead of get_product per item, and to propose the fix as soon as the cause is established. The same investigation now finishes in 16 rounds with no failed calls. A race we only found in a screenshot. React StrictMode runs effects twice, and two concurrent bootstraps collided on the same DROP / CREATE . Bootstrap is now single-flight per engine, with a test that calls it three times at once. The native API is string-based. executeTool takes its arguments as a JSON string and returns the result envelope as one; passing a plain object fails with "Failed to parse input arguments" . inputSchema comes back as a string too. What we learned A good tool surface is mostly good error messages. Name a column that does not exist and the tool lists the ones that do. Give an ambiguous product name and it returns the candidates and asks for a product_id . Ask for a chart whose y column is missing from the query result and it names the columns the query actually returns. That did more for reliability than any prompt change — the agent recovers by itself instead of stalling. Context hygiene and privacy turned out to be the same mechanism. The 50-row / 4 KB cap started as a way to keep the agent's context small. It ended up being the thing that makes the privacy guarantee auditable. Accomplishments that we're proud of The approval gate, because it is a mechanism rather than a claim. And the byte counter, for the same reason: a figure a sceptical person can watch tick upward and check. What's next Multi-store tenancy; approval policies that let an operator pre-authorise low-risk actions while holding the rest; sharing a saved board as a link so another operator's copy re-runs it against their own data — the analysis travels, the data never does. title: Toban
pitch: Turn one plain-language request into a structured, editable duty roster.
about_excerpt: Turn one plain-language request into a structured, editable duty roster. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Toban is a WebMCP app that turns a single natural-language request into an editable duty roster, reducing the effort and errors in schedule creation. Inspiration Duty rosters look simple, but the request behind one is usually scattered across names, duties, dates, rotation intervals, exceptions, presentation choices, and sharing rules. Toban already gave people a visual way to create and manage these rosters. The WebMCP Challenge made it possible to add a faster path: describe the whole intent once, let an agent translate it into typed product actions, and keep Toban responsible for validation and rotation math. What it does With a WebMCP-capable client connected to Toban, a person can ask for a complete roster in ordinary language. The request can include members, separate duties, a start date, an automatic or manual rotation, weekends and Japanese holidays to skip, a Table, Calendar, or Wheel view, and a visual style suited to the setting. The agent calls Toban's page-defined tools. Toban validates the structured input, calculates the roster, saves it, and displays the result as a normal editable schedule. Follow-up requests can change one duty, adjust appearance, restrict task eligibility, query a future assignment without changing state, advance a manual rotation, or rename a member while preserving unrelated settings. Public sharing stays under human control. The agent can prepare the share step, but Toban opens its own confirmation dialog and waits for a person to decide whether to publish. How it was built Toban is a React and TypeScript application served through Cloudflare Workers. For the challenge, I extended its WebMCP interface to 18 typed page tools around the existing roster domain: create, read, target, refine, present, calculate, print, and prepare sharing. Tool schemas use stable roster identifiers and structured results so an agent can operate on product concepts instead of guessing through DOM clicks. The roster engine remains the source of truth for validation, eligible-date calculation, Japanese public-holiday handling, rotation state, and persistence. The agent interprets intent; Toban performs deterministic application logic. The demo was captured in the ChatGPT desktop app's in-app browser, which the official Challenge rules list as a WebMCP testing method. During the capture, the agent calls those real tools on the live page. Challenges The hardest part was making follow-up language safe. A request such as “replace Plant Care with Supply Check” should update one duty without silently changing members, dates, rotation rules, view, or appearance. The implementation adds stable target resolution, typed partial updates, explicit errors, idempotent mutation behavior, structured read-back, and verification after meaningful writes. Another challenge was drawing the right publication boundary. Sharing has an external effect, so the WebMCP tool prepares a reviewable confirmation but does not publish. That keeps the final decision visible and human-controlled. Accomplishments One natural-language request creates a complete, styled roster. The same typed roster model supports Table, Calendar, and Wheel views. Calendar assignments account for weekends and Japanese public holidays. Narrow follow-ups preserve fields the person did not ask to change. Read-only tools answer assignment questions without mutating the roster. The agent stops at Toban's sharing confirmation; publication requires an explicit click in Toban. The public repository includes the full challenge-period commit history and an MIT license. What I learned WebMCP works best when the page exposes domain actions rather than a catalog of UI gestures. The agent is useful at interpreting a flexible request, while the application is better at enforcing invariants, calculating dates, storing state, and presenting the result for human review. What's next Next steps include more locale-aware holiday calendars, richer rule explanations, and additional verification views for complex eligibility constraints, while preserving the same typed-tool and human-confirmation boundaries. title: Keepsake
pitch: A living family timeline written by an elder, her family, and their agent. Grandma tells a story; it becomes a card; the family asks the next question.
about_excerpt: A living family timeline written by an elder, her family, and their agent. Grandma tells a story; it becomes a card; the family asks the next question. Like Comment Story Updates What it is Rose is 84. She tells stories the way people do: out of order, with the best details buried in the middle. Keepsake listens. Her agent turns each story into a memory card on a shared timeline, links the people in it, picks a picture, and queues the question the family should ask her next time. Her granddaughter Maya reads the timeline, fixes a title by hand, asks "what was Grandpa like when they first met?", and the agent answers from Rose's own words and scrolls to the card. Live: https://keepsake-timeline.vercel.app · Code: https://github.com/chinesepowered/keepsake-timeline Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP A memory book only works if the agent can write into the same book the family reads. Keepsake exposes the timeline as eleven structured tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool : get_timeline , search_memories , add_memory , update_memory , remove_memory , add_person , link_people , add_question , mark_question_answered , focus_memory , export_book Any WebMCP-capable agent, whether ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with WebMCP enabled, or the built-in listener, edits exactly what is on screen. The tool descriptions carry the editorial rules: keep the teller's words, first person if Rose told it, never invent facts, split a story that spans two events into two cards, queue a question when a thread is left hanging. How it creates a better experience For the elder: just talk. Voice or text, no forms, no dates to look up. The agent asks at most one gentle follow-up. For the family: a timeline you can read in a minute and edit in a second (double-click a title, remove a card), with a running list of "ask Rose next time" prompts that the agent keeps topped up. Shared attention: focus_memory scrolls to and lights up the card the agent is quoting, so a question about the past ends with both of you looking at the same memory. Portable: export_book returns the timeline as a Markdown book by decade. What people and agents can do together that was hard before Before: a recording nobody transcribes, or a family member typing while Grandma waits, or a chatbot that produces a paragraph and forgets it. Now: the story goes straight into a structured, shared, editable timeline, in her words, with the loose threads turned into questions. The elder supplies the memories, the agent supplies the structure, the family supplies the judgment. Nothing is lost between visits. How WebMCP is implemented lib/webmcp.ts : tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool(..., { signal }) and unregistered via AbortController on unmount. Native browser-agent calls and in-page agent calls share one execute path and one activity log. lib/tools.ts : the eleven tools with JSON Schema inputs, descriptions, and read-only / destructive annotations. lib/memories.ts : the shared store (memories, people, questions, focus). The UI's inline edits and the tools mutate the same state. components/AgentPanel.tsx + app/api/agent/route.ts : a Gemini function-calling loop that discovers the registered tools and dispatches through WebMCP, with Web Speech API for voice and a model fallback chain for free-tier limits. Tested in Chrome 153 with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing (DevTools → Application → WebMCP lists all eleven tools) and with the in-page Gemini agent. title: MapForge
pitch: AI-powered indoor mapping that lets organizations build and navigate custom maps relying on ai agents intervention through WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
AI-powered indoor mapping that lets organizations build and navigate custom maps relying on ai agents intervention through WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 MapForge logo 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 MapForge logo 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 MapForge logo 
 
 1 2 



 
 \section*{Inspiration} 

 I got the though for the first time when I arrived at the "Mediterranean Village" in Oran, which to my surprise didn't have a proper map that indicates the places of the buildings. I ended up spending about 30 walking around searching for the building where my room is located. 

 After watching a certain video on Youtube explaining how google maps calculates the different routes and its relation with dijkstra's algorithm, I figured out a way to solve a problem, which is by building my own google maps, but rather than mapping the entire earth, a single organization is mapped, and the map is created by the organization itself to provide to the users a way to walk around. 

 \section*{What it does} 

 MapForge is a platform where organizations can build structured indoor maps for their facilities so that users can use them for navigation, I believe everyone has had at least one experience of getting lost inside a building, whether it was the first time to go to university, the first time to visit a certain amusement park or maybe even staying in a big hotel. MapForge is a tool that ensures doesn't happen, an editor can import a blue print to create the map he wants, trace the different building of the organization, add floors to them and create rooms, entrances and other different types of instances inside the buildings. A normal user on the other hand inspects the maps created by the editors and uses them for navigation 

 \section*{How we built it} 

 The tech stack i relied on consists of symfony-php for the backend and a create-react-app setup for the frontend. 

 The backend is responsible for the application logic, persistence, map structure, validation, and routing, while the React frontend provides the visual map editor and navigation interface. The platform uses a graph-based representation of maps, with nodes representing locations such as rooms, entrances, and stairs, and edges representing the connections between them. 

 For the hackathon, I also integrated WebMCP into the frontend, exposing MapForge's core capabilities as tools that AI agents can use to inspect and modify the actual map state. Routing is handled by a deterministic Dijkstra-based shortest-path system, allowing both users and agents to find routes through the map. 

 \section*{Challenges we ran into} 

 Given that I have participated as a solo developer, the main challenge that I ran into was time, I had to brainstorm ideas for the project, determine the core functionalities, what to implement and what to sacrifice, come up with the business logic and of course implement everything by coding the backend, the frontend, the webMCP integration, testing, fixing the different errors and bugs and finally deploying the application. So if anything, I believe that my greatest adversary throughout this challenge was time. 

 \section*{Accomplishments that we're proud of} 

 There is nothing that I am particularly proud of, because I am proud of everything, this challenge was by far the greatest experience that I had in my entire life, it helped me learn a lot of new things and concepts including webMCP itself as i wasn't aware of its existence before. 

 \section*{What we learned} 

 I learned a lot of things throughout the course of this challenge, but I must admit that the greatest concept was webMCP itself, the main idea of this challenge considering the fact the i didn't know it even existed before this experience. 

 \section*{What's next for MapForge} 

 The current version of MapForge can be considered as a draft or a proof of concept if I may say, the perfect version of the project that is in my head would go much further. It would integrate indoor localization, similar in principle to GPS, so that the user could be located inside a building and receive directions from their actual position. Navigation would become much more sophisticated, with support for accessibility-aware routes, multiple route options, complex floor and building transitions, and potentially real-time navigation. The platform would also have a much more robust authentication and authorization system, where organizations control their own maps, administrators only access the maps they are responsible for, and different users can have different permissions. QR codes could also be placed at entrances, rooms, or specific locations, allowing visitors to instantly open the corresponding location in MapForge and start navigating. Other future improvements could include better floor-plan importing and tracing, more detailed building geometry, richer location information, mobile support, and more advanced tools for organizations to maintain and update their maps over time. The WebMCP integration could also become much more powerful, allowing agents to perform more complex maintenance, validation, and navigation tasks while still keeping humans in control.

title: Zingposts
pitch: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust.
about_excerpt: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browsing old cars, boats, campers, motorcycles, and machinery is fun. Managing the hunt is not. Good finds get lost across tabs, marketplace search misses obvious matches, alerts are rigid, research lives in scattered notes, and negotiations have no shared memory. A three-way trade is almost impossible to reason about cleanly. Zingposts starts from a different premise: the marketplace should be equally legible to people and their agents without embedding a model in the product. The site owns its native listings and structured deal workflow, while outside listings can be tracked as clearly labeled snapshots. What it does Zingposts is a complete peer-to-peer marketplace and durable workspace for interesting things. People can browse realistic native inventory, create and publish listings, upload photos, save finds, build boards, set alerts, keep research notebooks, message sellers, prepare offers, and create structured multi-party trade rooms. Outside finds can be tracked without confusing them with Zingposts-owned inventory. A connected outside agent receives a compact persistent core plus one focused pack drawn from 121 structured WebMCP tools. It can search with compound criteria, compare candidates, organize boards, tag and rank finds, record cited research and inspection risks, monitor price changes, draft communications and offers, calculate acquisition cost, propose trade scenarios, and coordinate the shared gallery, focus, or thumbnail canvas. The human uses the same structure through a canvas-first interface. Zingposts itself contains no LLM. The centerpiece is the shared canvas: an outside agent opens a durable session, places a shortlist, recommendation, or focused question beside the marketplace objects, and pauses only when human judgment matters. The person can inspect the exact listings and rationale, choose an option or add context, and return structured guidance. The agent reads that durable response on its next tool call and continues. This is turn-taking over shared marketplace objects, not a chatbot transcript. The loop now extends across visits. get_workspace_resume returns the last acknowledged checkpoint, everything that changed since, structured blockers, human responses, proposal status, and safe next actions. An agent can acknowledge the checkpoint only after processing it, so “come back later” is an explicit protocol rather than a hope that conversation context survived. For broad edits, the agent can prepare a sourced, versioned change set instead of making a trail of one-off mutations. Zingposts previews each proposed change in plain language, checks the expected object versions, and lets the person selectively accept only the changes they want. Agents cannot approve their own change sets. Completed deals can be recorded as private outcomes, and transparent aggregate patterns report counts, prices, and reasons without inventing a model-generated score. Either side can arrive first. A person can explore immediately in a prototype workspace, then replace a test email and verify the real address through Supabase only when work reaches the marketplace boundary. One Bring my agent click copies the canonical guide URL. Or an unauthenticated agent can inspect five setup-only tools and open a prototype handoff for the person. Once the person signs in, safe private tools appear automatically to an outside agent operating that browser document. Independent 12-hour revocable sessions remain available through one-use invites or codes for separate-browser or unattended work. The human remains in control. Publishing, enabling notifications, sending a message, submitting or responding to an offer, and inviting a trade participant stop at a visible confirmation gate. Every human and agent action is attributed, and reversible work can be undone. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer intent from buttons and screen position. That is brittle for a marketplace with dozens of interdependent objects: listings, boards, research, alerts, conversations, offers, people, assets, and constraints. WebMCP gives Zingposts a stable collaboration language. “Find pre-1980 boats under $15,000, put the best four on a board, record the title risks, and draft a message to the strongest seller” becomes a sequence of typed, attributable actions. The human can watch the same state change, refine it directly, and approve the parts that cross a consequential boundary. That makes the product meaningfully better with an agent—not merely automatable. How we built it Zingposts uses React 19 and Next.js on Netlify. Supabase Auth provides verified human sessions, Supabase Postgres holds marketplace, identity, agent-session, and workflow state, and Supabase Storage holds listing photos. Versioned SQL migrations keep direct browser access locked behind row-level security. The browser client exposes 121 declarative tools through the WebMCP modelContext surface, but only five setup tools while signed out. After the person signs in, AbortSignal-managed registration keeps a compact persistent core plus one replaceable focused capability pack, so navigation never accumulates an oversized registry or silently unlocks business actions. get_agent_bootstrap returns setup guidance while signed out, then canonical browser-delegated identity, workspace, attention, active collaboration, capability index, and guide version after sign-in. activate_capability switches the focused pack without moving the person; open_for_human_review is optional. The action layer derives canonical human and agent identity on the server, prevents duplicate profiles, enforces ownership and state-transition enums, creates reviewable drafts, writes attributed activity, stores inverse operations for undo, supports idempotency keys and optimistic versions, returns stable deep links and WebMCP-native structured errors, and converts consequential operations into pending confirmations. Isolated QA runs register only their own artifacts, provide an exact cleanup preview, and require human approval before deletion. The marketplace is seeded with original project-owned imagery and realistic records so the full human-agent workflow is understandable immediately. WebMCP registration is document-scoped, while Zingposts durably stores connection profiles, scopes, alerts, boards, research, drafts, versions, and audit history. The public /for-agents guide and /api/agent-guide contract show agents how to reconnect safely without storing an invite, code, or stale catalog. Challenges The main design challenge was not adding more agent power; it was deciding where that power should stop. We separated preparation from commitment. Research, organization, comparison, and drafting can proceed quickly. Communication, publication, notifications, invitations, and financial commitments pause for the human. We also designed external-listing tracking so provenance stays honest. Zingposts can organize an outside find, but it never claims that its cached price, availability, or seller statements are authoritative. Accomplishments A coherent marketplace, not a WebMCP proof of concept 121 tools spanning authentication, onboarding, resumable work sessions, versioned proposals, outcomes, canvas views, discovery, organization, negotiation, and multi-party trade Agent-first and person-first onboarding with a five-tool setup surface before human sign-in Durable agent-to-human-to-agent turn-taking with a unified attention queue Explicit resume checkpoints and structured blockers for work that continues across agent runs Sourced, versioned change sets with semantic previews and selective human acceptance Private outcome recording with transparent, non-AI aggregate patterns Live agent activity, exact-payload approval, idempotency, dry runs, structured errors, and stable deep links No built-in AI or model dependency Supabase human authentication plus opaque invite URLs, code fallback, and single-use, expiring, revocable agent sessions—without password or session sharing Persistent bootstrap plus navigation-independent focused capability activation Structured errors, strict workflow transitions, optimistic concurrency, and namespaced QA cleanup Durable attribution, confirmations, and undo Native seller photo upload and publishing workflow Clear separation between owned listings and outside tracked snapshots Production build, automated API smoke tests, desktop browser testing, and mobile verification What we learned Human-agent collaboration works best when both sides operate on the same durable objects. A board is better than a chat-only list. A research notebook is better than an ephemeral summary. A pending confirmation is better than asking the model to remember which action is sensitive. We also learned to separate document-scoped WebMCP
video_title: Zingposts — Human + Agent Commerce on One WebMCP Canvas
video_transcript_excerpt: What if a marketplace did not contain its own AI? What if it simply gave people and any outside agent a beautiful shared place to work? This is Zing Posts, peer-to-peer commerce designed for Web MCP. The first visit is deliberately small. While signed out, the browser exposes only five setup tools. An agent can inspect the bootstrap guide, prepare a handoff for the person, or accept a one-use credential. After sign-in, it re-discovers the real workspace. Now, human and agent share the same durable canvas. The person can browse visually, flip through finds, drag items onto colored boards, and set preferences. The agent can search the same listings, compare candidates, rank a board, tag discoveries, and leave its reasoning beside the work. Web MCP is not hidden behind one giant prompt. Zing Posts keeps a persistent core, then activates the focus capability for the page. Here, the marketplace pack includes search, view control, comparison, board organization, and the option to open exactly the item a person should review. On a listing, the collaboration gets deeper. An outside agent can build a cited research notebook, record comparable sales, calculate a price range, and draft an offer plan with repair, transport, tax, contingency, and budget assumptions. The evidence stays visible. The private target stays private. The workbench is the shared memory: agent findings, human notes, decisions, undo history, alerts, conversations, offers, and even multi-party trade rooms persist as structured marketplace state. The agent does not own the experience. It helps move evidence toward a decision, while the person stays in control. That control becomes explicit at the verification boundary. Browsing, organizing, research, and drafting stay fluid. Publishing a listing, enabling an alert, contacting a seller, sending an offer, or advancing a trade creates a pending approval. Only the human can cross that line, and every outcome is recorded. The result is a web MCP native marketplace with no built-in model and no agent lock-in. Five tools for setup, 34 focused tools on this marketplace canvas, and 121 across the complete signed-in catalog. zingpost.com Bring your agent and find something worth saving.

title: Cortex
pitch: Cortex is a private research library that a browser agent can operate. All tools are registered with WebMCP, and agent works your papers on the same page you're looking at.
about_excerpt: Cortex is a private research library that a browser agent can operate. All tools are registered with WebMCP, and agent works your papers on the same page you're looking at. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I read papers for a living. Over one week my reading loop touched five tools: a PDF viewer, a notes app, a folder of downloads, a project tracker, and a chat window where an agent could see none of them. Every "which paper said X" or "file this one" was me copying text between windows. WebMCP's proposal, that a page should hand an agent real actions instead of pixels, described the fix exactly. So the question for the weekend was: what if my own library was a page whose buttons were also the agent's tools? What it does Cortex is a private research library with three panes: papers on the left, the open PDF in the middle, chat on the right. Projects are spaces, a named group of papers with a one-line verdict and a next action. Everything is a file in a folder: markdown notes with LaTeX, a PDF per paper with extracted text, a small metadata file next to it. The page registers ten tools with document.modelContext, the same actions a person does by clicking: read: search_brain, read_note, read_paper, list_projects show: open_item write: write_note, append_today, file_paper, set_paper, update_project A browser agent (ChatGPT's browser, or Chrome 149+ with the WebMCP flag) can ask "which papers here are about deception", open the strongest one in the center pane, mark it reading with a takeaway, download and file a new arXiv paper, and leave a line on today's page. An agent ledger shows every call with its arguments and outcome, and each write lands in the UI as it happens. How I built it The server is FastAPI over plain files, with SQLite FTS5 for search across notes, projects, and the text pulled out of every PDF. The front end is Vite, React, and TypeScript, with CodeMirror 6 for notes and KaTeX for math, so a note can hold 𝑝 ( deceptive ) 1 𝐿 ∑ ℓ 𝜎 ( 𝑤 ℓ ⊤ ℎ ℓ + 𝑏 ℓ ) p(deceptive)= L 1 ​ ℓ ∑ ​ σ(w ℓ ⊤ ​ h ℓ ​ +b ℓ ​ ) and render it live. The PDF viewer is the browser's own, inverted in dark theme so figures keep their hue. The WebMCP layer is one file. Each tool wraps the same API call the matching button makes, coerces and bounds every argument, and returns an MCP content block. Read tools carry readOnlyHint. Errors come back as {error} text so the agent gets a correction instead of a dead page. The built-in chat runs on OpenCode Go (any OpenAI-compatible model works) with the same ten tools on the server side, and it knows which paper is open and which space is active. Getting papers in is one gesture: drop a PDF on the window, paste an arXiv link, or leave a file in ~/Cortex/inbox and a watcher files it within seconds. Challenges The spec moved. Early WebMCP writing puts the entry point on navigator.modelContext; the current explainer and ChatGPT's browser use document.modelContext. My first build registered on the wrong object, and the agent in ChatGPT's browser fell back to clicking around the UI. Registering on whichever the browser exposes fixed it. Chrome's PDF viewer swallows keystrokes once you click into it, so Cmd+K went dead on the most used screen. The frame is same origin, so the app now forwards the shortcut chords out of it. The first version had too many fields. A metadata strip with nine inputs felt like a form, not a reader. The rebuild kept the five things I edit weekly (status, rating, takeaway, verdict, next action) and moved everything else behind Cmd+K. Hosting: the domain I own runs on ChatGPT Sites, which can't run a Python server, so the demo lives on Render under a subdomain, and Render's build cache once served a stale bundle after a deploy said "live". What I learned An agent that can call open_item is a different collaborator from one that can only describe. Watching the paper appear in the pane while the ledger prints search_brain, open_item, set_paper made the WebMCP argument for me better than any spec. Also: fewer controls is a feature, and everything an agent can write should be a file you can see and revert. What's next Reading notes that the agent drafts and you edit, a nightly agent that clears the inbox and updates verdicts, and the Worker port so Cortex can live inside the ChatGPT Site. pitch: An audio editor your AI agent can hear. Via 43 WebMCP tools it detects silences, reads the transcript, and proposes surgical edits on the timeline — you approve.
about_excerpt: An audio editor your AI agent can hear. Via 43 WebMCP tools it detects silences, reads the transcript, and proposes surgical edits on the timeline — you approve. Like Comment Story Updates Audio editing with webmcp Inspiration A while back I really wanted to be a YouTuber. The part that always killed it for me was editing — cutting out the ums, the long pauses, and the takes where I fumbled. It was slow and boring, and I'd give up. Now I know there are agentic tools for video editing but I did not find anything for just audio editing. title: Archipelago
pitch: Map your Notion workspace as a shared visual interface for humans and AI agents, powered by WebMCP and running entirely in the browser.
about_excerpt: Map your Notion workspace as a shared visual interface for humans and AI agents, powered by WebMCP and running entirely in the browser. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Ask your AI to map your Notion. That single sentence is all it takes: Archipelago draws the chart on the right. Each database is an island sized by its rows; used relations become routes. The lighthouse marks the hub, a black flag an isolated base. The four WebMCP tools: draw a map, read it as structured data, highlight a computed set, annotate islands. Human and agent share one screen. One call to archipelago_draw_map: database names, row counts and relation metadata in, a live chart out. Rendered locally in the browser. Why I built it I'm a certified Notion consultant. A lot of my work is helping companies turn collections of databases, documents and workflows into actual operational systems. The problem is that systems are hard to explain. Most people are not technical, and looking at a workspace page by page makes it difficult to understand the whole thing. Is everything connected? Where does the structure actually live? Which databases are sitting alone? So I wanted a very simple visual language. In Archipelago, databases become islands, relations become routes, and linked data becomes convoys on those routes. You can look at the map for a few seconds and start asking better questions. That was the original idea: make a complex workspace easier to see and discuss. What it does Drop a Notion .zip export into Archipelago and it builds the map directly in your browser. Nothing is uploaded and Archipelago never connects to your Notion account. The result is deliberately playful rather than overly analytical. No score, no grade. The map gives you the structure and a one-line reading of it; what it means stays your call. It also makes a useful teaching tool when discussing a workspace with people who would never want to look at a database schema. Then came WebMCP The WebMCP part felt obvious to me quite quickly. If a human can use the map to understand a system, an AI agent should be able to use the same map rather than living in a separate chat window. So during the Challenge I added four WebMCP tools that let an agent: build a map from structured workspace data; read the map currently on screen; highlight databases; add its interpretation directly to the map. A user can now ask something like: "Show me everything connected to Clients." and the answer appears on the map they are already looking at. The actual challenge I'm not a developer by background, so part of the challenge was simply understanding a very new standard well enough to implement it properly. But the harder problem is still the one I'm working on: How do you make an agent visiting a website immediately understand that it can act there? I don't want the user to have to explain: "This site supports WebMCP. Go read the documentation, find the tools, then use them." The ideal experience is that the agent arrives, understands the capabilities exposed by the page, chooses the right tool and acts. Because WebMCP is still experimental, getting that discovery and tool-routing behavior to feel reliable across agents and browsers has been the most interesting part of the project. I have tried to follow the emerging best practices closely: explicit tool names, precise descriptions, structured schemas, state-aware error responses , and additional agent-oriented documentation. There is still a lot to learn. How I built it Archipelago is intentionally small: vanilla JavaScript, static files, no application backend and no build step. I built it with extensive AI assistance: ChatGPT as a strategic and tactical sparring partner, and Claude Code as the primary implementation agent. That workflow is also part of what made this project interesting to me. I don't come from a traditional software engineering background, but I could still spend most of my time on the parts I care about: the concept, the interaction model, the visual language and what the tool should actually do. What's next Notion is the first use case because it is the environment I know best, and because it already has a large community of people building increasingly complex systems with it. But I think the underlying idea can go further than mapping. Once a human and an agent can share the same visual representation of a system, the next step is to design and evolve that system together . The map could become a working surface for proposing a new structure, comparing it with the current one, highlighting dependencies, testing changes and progressively co-constructing an operational system. Archipelago starts with visibility. What interests me next is what happens when that shared visual interface becomes a place where humans and agents can actually build together.
