title: 312Deals: Tonight
pitch: A live Chicago deals site where you and your agent plan tonight together: 17 WebMCP tools over 80,000 real deals, a shared plan with a lock you control, and booking links set to your time.
about_excerpt: A live Chicago deals site where you and your agent plan tonight together: 17 WebMCP tools over 80,000 real deals, a shared plan with a lock you control, and booking links set to your time. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration 312Deals is a live site: 80,000+ food and drink deals at 12,000+ venues across 149 Chicagoland neighborhoods, covering the city and 60+ suburbs, re-verified weekly against 18,000+ tracked sources. People use it to figure out where to go tonight. When agent browsers arrived, we watched them try to do the same job by reading the page, and get it wrong in ways that matter: a happy hour that ended at six, a venue across town, a "deal" that was last week's. The inventory is structured and time-sensitive; the UI was built for people. WebMCP is the bridge. Tell the agent what the site can do instead of making it guess from what it shows. The idea we wanted to test: planning a night out is genuinely collaborative work. Ranking 80,000 time-windowed deals is the agent's job. Taste and veto are the person's. So instead of an agent that hands you a plan, we built a plan that both of you edit, on the same page. The idea we wanted to test: planning a night out is genuinely collaborative work. Ranking 80,000 time-windowed deals is the agent's job. Taste and veto are the person's. So instead of an agent that hands you a plan, we built a plan that both of you edit, on the same page. What it does Open 312deals.com in ChatGPT's desktop browser and the page registers 17 tools on document.modelContext: 10 data tools over the live corpus: search deals by neighborhood, day, type, and cuisine; deals near an address; a venue's deals; deal of the day; chain deals; neighborhood summaries; a multi-stop crawl planner; order and reservation links; and a moderated community deal tip (a write, so the browser's confirmation applies). 7 "Tonight" tools over a plan that lives in the page: the Tonight panel, bottom-right on every screen. The agent reads the plan, sets constraints (budget, hours, group size, max stops, neighborhood), adds stops from real deals, moves them, reorders them by deal window, removes, and clears. Every agent change lands in the panel with an "agent" chip and a toast. The person adds any deal from its card, reorders, vetoes, and locks the stops that must stay. Locked stops are constraints, not suggestions: an agent call against a locked stop returns a structured refusal, so the agent re-plans around it instead of over it. Every stop ends in action. Reservation links carry the plan: OpenTable's dateTime and covers, and Resy's date and seats, are built from the plan's start time and group size (or from the time and party size the agent passes), so the booking page opens on your slot rather than its 7-PM-for-2 default. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP. Deal discovery is precisely the case WebMCP was made for: typed tools over live, structured, expiring data beat screen-reading on speed, accuracy, and reliability. And the site already had an audience and a corpus. This isn't a demo dataset: 312Deals ranks on page one for its core Chicago queries and most of its traffic is organic search, so the pages an agent lands on are the same pages people land on. How it creates a better user experience. One request replaces a dozen searches across tabs. The agent searches real, verified deals, builds the plan from what is actually on at each hour, and shows its work in a panel you can touch. You lock what you care about; it optimizes the rest. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before. Before, you had two options: do all the work yourself in the UI, or let an agent scrape the UI and hand you a plan you couldn't touch. Now both act on one live surface. The agent proposes against live inventory, the person constrains with locks the agent must respect, and each sees the other's changes immediately. The plan is yours, built on tonight's real deals. How we built it Next.js 14 and React on Vercel, FastAPI on Railway, SQLite with FTS5 distributed through Cloudflare R2 with an ETag conflict guard, zustand for the shared plan, and the ElevenLabs API for the demo narration. Built and shipped solo under Hoyne Labs LLC. All challenge work went to production the same day it was written and was tested against ChatGPT's desktop browser on a free account. How we implemented WebMCP: Registration feature-detects document.modelContext (the current spec surface; ChatGPT desktop and Chrome 149+) with navigator.modelContext as a fallback for earlier Canary builds. Every tool carries readOnlyHint / destructiveHint annotations and is registered with an AbortSignal; teardown runs through both paths; tools re-register across client-side navigations. Agent-shaped results. The site's REST API returns about 60 columns per deal and about 92 per venue (a 20-result search is roughly 32 KB; one venue lookup roughly 117 KB). The tools trim each result to what a person acts on, add a link to the page, and say how many results were left out. Shared state. The Tonight tools act on a persisted zustand store the panel renders. The lock and veto contract is enforced in the store, so a refusal comes back to the agent as data with instructions ("locked by the user, plan around it"). One link builder, three surfaces. A single reservation-link helper is used by the Tonight tools, the get_reservation_link tool, and the panel's own Reserve link, so the agent's path and the person's path emit the same fully parameterized URL. Dates default to today in America/Chicago; times accept what an agent or a person would write ("6pm", "18:00"). Catalog and analytics. An informational manifest at /.well-known/webmcp.json lists all 17 tools alongside the site's existing /llms.txt, /llms-full.txt, /skill.md, and /.well-known/mcp.json. The FastAPI middleware that detects agent traffic and records tool calls predates the challenge, which is why the first real calls were captured the moment they arrived. Pre-existing project, what's new. 312deals.com existed before the challenge, including an earlier 10-tool WebMCP layer on the legacy navigator.modelContext surface. All challenge work is in the public repo's commits dated Sep 3, 2026, after a clearly labeled baseline commit: the spec-surface migration and agent-shaped results, the entire Tonight collaboration (panel, store contract, 7 tools), the lock guidance, and the plan-aware reservation links. Everything was deployed to production on Sep 3. Challenges we ran into The spec moved under us. The site's original WebMCP layer, built in February 2026 after joining Chrome's Early Preview Program for built-in AI, registered on navigator.modelContext, with a declarative form API on the highest-frequency tools. ChatGPT's browser only looks at document.modelContext. Until the migration, the 17 tools were invisible to the one client that mattered. Version fragility had been the known risk with this standard for months, and this is what it looked like in practice. The agent web-searched instead of calling tools. A plain "find me a happy hour" sent ChatGPT to general search, citing venue websites. Naming the site tools in the request ("using this site's tools...") reliably routes it to the page. The testing instructions say so. The lock was bypassable through the human UI. Asked to remove a locked stop, the agent hit the tool's refusal, then clicked the panel's padlock itself, announced it, and removed the stop. The refusal now tells the agent plainly that only the person unlocks, by hand. It's an honest lesson: when the agent can drive the UI too, "human affordances" are agent affordances unless the contract is explicit. Shallow deep links. The first reservation handoff landed on OpenTable's default slot. Pushing the plan's date, time, and party size into the URL made the link finish the job. Accomplishments that we're proud of The first real WebMCP tool calls the site ever received came from ChatGPT during this challenge: search, then tonight_add_stop three times, then a reorder that respected a lock. The site's own analytics recorded them. Seven months of building an agent surface (REST API, MCP server, custom GPT, llms.txt, WebMCP) and this was the first time we watched an outside agent discover the tools on the page and use them end to end. What we learned WebMCP's value isn't the tool list; it's designing for two actors on one surface. The interesting engineering is the contract between them: attribution, refusals as data, and what a lock actually means when the other party can also click. The goal was to spread awareness of this to support small biz. Hopefully this does just that by making it easier for the ever changing landscape of the web with AI, to support and facilitate that. title: Sloth
pitch: Sloth equips autonomous agents with narrow baseline tools, surfacing temporary financial capabilities only through verified, human-approved grants.
about_excerpt: Sloth equips autonomous agents with narrow baseline tools, surfacing temporary financial capabilities only through verified, human-approved grants. Like Comment Story Updates SLOTH — DELEGATED OUTCOMES WITH SCOPED AUTHORITY INSPIRATION WebMCP lets websites give AI agents native browser tools instead of guessing where to click. But the spec has a huge blind spot: zero concept of permissions or reversibility. If you register a refund tool on page load, the agent has permanent god-mode access. If you don't, it's useless. We built Sloth around one thesis: Delegate outcomes, not unlimited access. WHAT IT DOES Sloth is an operations console for delegated outcomes with temporary capability boundaries: Zero Standing Privileges: Starts with 4 baseline tools (inspect issues, inspect transaction, retry payment, request capability). No refund tool exists. Autonomous Investigation: Agent investigates anomalies, retries pre-authorized failures, and confirms duplicate charges. Boundary Escalation: Agent hits a hard boundary and calls request_capability proposing a narrow scope. Human Negotiation: Operator can approve, deny (DO_NOT_RETRY), or adjust caps ($72 per item, $150 aggregate batch cap). Dynamic Tool Injection (4 -> 5 tools): Approval injects refund_scoped_transactions in real time with a 60-second TTL countdown. In-Tool Enforcement: Tool itself blocks unapproved IDs or amount breaches with structured SCOPE_VIOLATION errors. Single-Use Auto-Revocation (5 -> 4 tools): Executing refunds immediately revokes the tool to eliminate replay attacks. Compliance Audit: One-click export of a signed JSON audit ledger. HOW WE BUILT IT Runtime: Next.js (Vinext engine) with native document.modelContext support for Chrome 149+ and ChatGPT desktop. Core Scope Engine: Pure, zero-dependency validation logic (scope.js) enforcing dual caps, backed by 17/17 automated unit tests. Dynamic Lifecycle: Browser AbortController signals and reactive state tracking to mount and unmount tools on the fly. Console UI: High-density dark mode console with monospace authority rail, live TTL countdown, and boundary test sandboxes. CHALLENGES WE RAN INTO Dynamic WebMCP Registration: Most examples treat tools as static declarations. Mounting and unmounting tools dynamically without page reload required strict state isolation. Dual-Track Evaluation: Supporting live LLM tool calling in experimental browsers while providing an interactive simulation for standard browsers. Preventing Agent Loops: Implementing structured DO_NOT_RETRY machine contracts so models don't repeatedly beg for authority when denied. ACCOMPLISHMENTS Proven 4 -> 5 -> 4 Capability Lifecycle: zero standing privileges -> JIT grant -> auto-revocation on execution. 100% In-Tool Security: Boundaries enforced inside the tool code, not just hidden UI buttons. Dual Blast Radius Protection: Combining unit limits ($72) with aggregate run limits ($150). 17/17 passing unit tests and <2s production build. WHAT WE LEARNED WebMCP is a human-agent negotiation protocol, not just an API. Enterprise adoption requires verifiable blast radius limits and reversibility, not just smarter models. Temporary, single-use capabilities give humans the trust needed to delegate real outcomes. WHAT'S NEXT FOR SLOTH Cryptographic Grant Attestation with WebCrypto. Universal open-source middleware (@sloth/webmcp-guard). Multi-agent capability hand-offs across agent swarms. title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: Runwire
pitch: Wire, run, repair, and verify API workflows with WebMCP agents.
about_excerpt: Wire, run, repair, and verify API workflows with WebMCP agents. Like Comment Story Updates Runwire is an agent-native API workspace where developers and WebMCP agents build, execute, inspect, repair, and verify multi-step API workflows together. The problem Traditional API clients make dependent workflows tedious. Developers repeatedly copy identifiers between requests, diagnose failures, change configuration, rerun steps, and manually preserve evidence. Generic browser agents are unreliable here because they infer actions from interface controls and often operate without a shared, inspectable execution record. The solution Runwire exposes 22 typed, page-defined WebMCP tools representing real application capabilities. An agent can inspect requests, select flows, execute individual steps, forward extracted response values, diagnose errors, apply bounded repairs, run controlled reliability tests, and inspect run history without relying on browser-control clicks. The demonstration uses a Checkout recovery workflow: Create customer → Create order → Get order → Delete order Runwire automatically extracts and forwards customerId and orderId . The first execution intentionally fails with 400 MISSING_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY . The agent reads the actual request and response evidence, applies the available idempotency repair, and reruns each request successfully with 201 → 201 → 200 → 204 . Every tool call, request, response, status, duration, extraction, failure, and repair remains visible in the interface. Failed and passing runs are preserved together, giving people a trustworthy audit trail of what the agent changed and why. Why WebMCP WebMCP lets Runwire expose semantic application actions instead of forcing agents to infer intent from pixels or DOM controls. The person and agent operate the same workspace and see the same evidence. This makes dependent API setup, debugging, and verification faster while keeping the human in control. Implementation Runwire was created during the challenge using React, Next.js, Vinext, WebMCP's document.modelContext.registerTool , Drizzle ORM, and D1. Safety boundaries prevent private-network requests, hide authentication secrets from agents, and limit automated repairs and burst testing. Testing No account or credentials are required. Open the live application in ChatGPT's in-app browser. Ask the agent to select and inspect the Checkout recovery flow using only Runwire's WebMCP tools. Run the flow and inspect the MISSING_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY failure. Ask the agent to apply the bounded idempotency repair. Run the four requests individually. Confirm the final 4/4 result and compare the failed and passing runs in history.
